title: Minimum Experimental Information for Certifying Bell Nonlocality of Gravity
summary: A Bell violation by material probes certifies nonlocal behavior, but it does not identify which internal subsystem carried or was measured to produce that behavior. We determine the additional information required to attribute such a violation to a gravitational field. For any setting-independent field-to-probe channel completed before the Bell settings are chosen, an entanglement-breaking channel makes all induced field measurements jointly measurable. A static Newtonian phase pickup belongs to this class, even with arbitrary adaptive probe control. Applied to a recent four-mass proposal, the claimed field-only measurements obey the stronger CHSH bound \(\sqrt2\), whereas the Bell-active operation is the source-to-probe instrument that includes the coherent source herald. At the published parameters, the observed flagged behavior is at least \(0.1630\) from the claimed field-detector family, exceeding its \(0.0898\) distance from Bell locality. We then incorporate a common field slice, gravitational constraints, dressing, detector backreaction, and coherent references into a robust certification theorem. The result isolates the minimum missing information: field-only factorization and a local measurement- incompatibility witness on each wing. More precise phase data cannot replace either requirement.

AI.tldr: A gravitational Bell violation cannot be attributed to the field until two additional pieces of information are supplied: field-only factorization and a local measurement-incompatibility witness per wing; no improvement in phase precision can substitute for them.
AI.motivation: A Bell violation by material probes certifies nonlocal behavior but does not reveal which internal subsystem carried or was measured to produce it. The paper asks what extra information is needed to legitimately attribute such a violation to a gravitational field.
AI.method: For any setting-independent field-to-probe channel completed before the Bell settings are chosen, showing that an entanglement-breaking channel renders all induced field measurements jointly measurable. Identifying the static Newtonian phase pickup as belonging to this class even under arbitrary adaptive probe control. Re-examining a recent four-mass proposal to separate the field-only measurements from the Bell-active source-to-probe instrument containing the coherent source herald. Extending the analysis with a common field slice, gravitational constraints, dressing, detector backreaction, and coherent references into a robust certification theorem.
AI.result: The claimed field-only measurements obey the stronger CHSH bound of sqrt(2), while the Bell-active operation is the source-to-probe instrument including the coherent source herald. At published parameters the observed flagged behavior lies at least 0.1630 from the claimed field-detector family, exceeding its 0.0898 distance from Bell locality.
AI.conclusion: The minimum missing information is isolated as field-only factorization plus a local measurement-incompatibility witness on each wing. More precise phase data cannot replace either requirement.

title: The Quantum Sphere: A Physically Realizable Optimization Benchmark with Provable Linear Convergence in White- and Black-Box Settings
summary: We revisit an established Quantum Control objective, characterize its exact local metric geometry, and reposition it as a rigorous benchmark for Search and Optimization. The trap-free topology of the landscape, established two decades ago, guarantees unhindered optimal pathways, but global topology alone does not govern convergence speed. Although the so-called Quantum Sphere is defined by the fourth power of the control field, we show that its yield gap admits an exact representation as a nonnegative linear combination of $\sin^2$ terms. From this single identity, we derive a two-sided quadratic sandwich with ratio $4/π^2$ on a certified, worst-case quarter-wave region, proving the optimal peak nondegenerate modulo its affine gauge and well-conditioned. For white-box optimization, on a halved (eighth-wave) region, the objective satisfies a Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality with an explicit constant, granting Gradient Descent a linear rate of $1 - 16/(π^4κ_r)$, where $κ_r$ is the condition number of the relevant Hessian block. For black-box optimization, we prove that the elitist single-parent Evolution Strategy converges linearly, almost surely and in expected hitting time, from a certified sublevel set, despite the landscape's continuous gauge symmetry and its lattice of periodic optima; the certified level is explicit whenever the landscape is trap-free, and near the optimum the strategy provably sees only the quadratic tangent of the peak. Systematic numerical simulations corroborate the theory. Finally, we show that additive input (actuator) noise reweights each term of the representation by a Debye-Waller factor without disrupting the landscape's structure, and outline open challenges: output (signal) noise, far-field plateau escape, angular-synchronization certificates, and another physically scalable benchmark (SHG with Glass).

AI.tldr: This paper reinterprets a Quantum Control objective (the "Quantum Sphere") as a rigorous benchmark for search and optimization, deriving exact local metric geometry: a sin²-based decomposition of the yield gap, a two-sided quadratic sandwich with ratio 4/π², PL-inequality guarantees for gradient descent, and linear convergence of an elitist single-parent Evolution Strategy.
AI.motivation: The trap-free topology of this landscape has been known for two decades, but global topology alone does not determine convergence speed. The authors aim to characterize the exact local metric geometry and reposition the problem as a rigorous, physically grounded benchmark for search and optimization.
AI.method: The yield gap is shown to admit an exact representation as a nonnegative linear combination of sin² terms. From this identity the authors derive a two-sided quadratic sandwich with ratio 4/π² on a certified worst-case quarter-wave region, proving the optimal peak nondegenerate modulo affine gauge and well-conditioned. For white-box optimization they establish a Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality with explicit constant on a halved (eighth-wave) region; for black-box optimization they analyze an elitist single-parent Evolution Strategy. Additive actuator noise is modeled as reweighting each representation term by a Debye-Waller factor. Numerical simulations accompany the theory.
AI.result: The objective is proven well-conditioned with an optimal peak nondegenerate modulo its affine gauge. Gradient Descent achieves a linear rate of 1 − 16/(π⁴κ_r), where κ_r is the condition number of the relevant Hessian block. The elitist single-parent Evolution Strategy converges linearly, almost surely and in expected hitting time, from a certified sublevel set, despite continuous gauge symmetry and a lattice of periodic optima; near the optimum it provably sees only the quadratic tangent of the peak. Additive input noise reweights terms by a Debye-Waller factor without disrupting the landscape structure. Simulations corroborate the theory.
AI.conclusion: The Quantum Sphere is established as a rigorous benchmark for search and optimization with exact local geometry and provable convergence guarantees for both white-box and black-box methods. Open challenges include output (signal) noise, far-field plateau escape, angular-synchronization certificates, and a further physically scalable benchmark (SHG with Glass).

title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions for Formal Verification of Quantum Error-Detection and Entanglement Circuits over {H,X,C-NOT}: CSS Constructions, Soundness, and Mutation-Based Validation
comment: Accepted for publication in SN Computer Science, final version will be available through journal once published. Abstract is modified to account for arXiv character count
summary: Formal verification of quantum circuits becomes difficult as circuit size grows because exhaustive reasoning over the Hilbert space is computationally expensive. In previous work [1], we introduced a bit-vector abstraction that separates superposition tracking from basis-state behavior, enabling SMT-based verification of fixed-size error-detection and entanglement circuits built from H, X, and C-NOT gates. This paper extends the framework in five directions. First, we generalise correctness properties to parametrised repetition and concatenated phase-flip codes with up to 101 logical elements. Second, we verify syndrome extraction for CSS codes specified by arbitrary parity-check matrices, including the Steane, [[15,7,3]] Hamming, [[15,1,3]] Reed-Muller, and rotated surface codes with distances up to 101. We consider arbitrary error patterns, detection up to a specified weight, and recovery using a classical decoder, with counterexamples beyond each code's correction or detection capability. Third, we characterize the {H,X,C-NOT} fragment for which the abstraction faithfully represents Hilbert-space semantics. We prove soundness, demonstrate necessity with counterexamples, validate the characterisation against state-vector simulation, and prove the six lemmas from the original work. Fourth, a mutation study using 13 operators identifies equivalent mutants and detects all 622 non-equivalent mutants within the evaluated fault model. Fifth, a direct Z3 implementation verifies GHZ circuits with up to 262,144 qubits across three topologies on a 16GB laptop. Random H+C-NOT networks show verification cost rises sharply with depth when outputs depend on many inputs. The approach does not target general stabilizer circuits, Y-type stabilizers, fault-tolerant protocols, or physical noise; we identify extensions needed to address these cases.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a bit-vector abstraction for SMT-based quantum circuit verification, covering parametrised codes, arbitrary CSS codes (distances up to 101), a soundness characterisation of the {H,X,C-NOT} fragment, a mutation study, and GHZ verification up to 262,144 qubits.
AI.motivation: Exhaustive Hilbert-space reasoning makes formal verification of quantum circuits computationally expensive as circuit size grows. The authors' prior bit-vector abstraction separated superposition tracking from basis-state behavior to enable SMT-based verification, but was limited to fixed-size error-detection and entanglement circuits with H, X, and C-NOT gates.
AI.method: Five extensions: (1) generalised correctness properties to parametrised repetition and concatenated phase-flip codes with up to 101 logical elements; (2) syndrome extraction verification for CSS codes via arbitrary parity-check matrices (Steane, [[15,7,3]] Hamming, [[15,1,3]] Reed-Muller, rotated surface codes, distances up to 101), considering arbitrary error patterns, detection up to a specified weight, and classical-decoder recovery; (3) characterisation of the {H,X,C-NOT} fragment with proved soundness, necessity shown by counterexamples, validation against state-vector simulation, and proofs of six original lemmas; (4) a mutation study with 13 operators; (5) a direct Z3 implementation for GHZ circuits.
AI.result: Correctness properties were verified for parametrised codes with up to 101 logical elements. Syndrome extraction was verified for CSS codes including Steane, [[15,7,3]] Hamming, [[15,1,3]] Reed-Muller, and rotated surface codes with distances up to 101, yielding counterexamples beyond each code's correction or detection capability. The mutation study identified equivalent mutants and detected all 622 non-equivalent mutants within the fault model. The Z3 implementation verified GHZ circuits with up to 262,144 qubits across three topologies on a 16GB laptop. Random H+C-NOT networks showed sharply rising verification cost with depth when outputs depend on many inputs.
AI.conclusion: The framework is sound and scalable for the targeted {H,X,C-NOT} circuits and CSS-code syndrome extraction. It does not target general stabilizer circuits, Y-type stabilizers, fault-tolerant protocols, or physical noise, and the authors identify the extensions required to address these cases.

title: Exponentially Compressed and Garbage-Free Alias Sampling for Polynomial State Preparation
summary: Coherent alias sampling implement an important subroutine for block encoding and qubitization based quantum simulation using quantum lookup table. Related constructions exploit data lookup and matrix structure to implement block encodings for use in quantum singular value transformation. For a state on $n$ qubits, constructing and storing the alias table requires both classical and quantum resources exponential in $n$. We show that when the amplitudes are samples of a polynomial of degree at most $d$, the table can be represented and evaluated coherently with cost polynomial in $n$, $d$, exponentially reduced from $Θ(2^n)$ classical and quantum cost. We construct a quantum circuit for coherently computing the alias table for polynomial states using reversible integer arithmetic. By employing fast arithmetic, we construct a deterministic circuit for preparing polynomial states over Clifford+$T$ with a complete gate count of $\tilde{O}(ndB+B^2)$, where arithmetic width $B=\tilde{O}(dn+d\log(d+1))$. In the high precision limit for state fidelity $ε$ with fixed $n$ and $d$, it is sufficient have $B=Θ(\log(1/ε))$ and the complete gate count becomes $O(\log^3(1/ε)\log\log(1/ε))$. Additionally, the effective representation of the alias table can also be used for classical sampling algorithms. Furthermore, we develop a novel technique for uncomputing the auxilary register generated by coherent alias sampling. This technique opens a research direction in sampling based initial state preparation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that coherent alias sampling tables can be constructed and evaluated with cost polynomial in n and d when the state amplitudes are samples of a degree-d polynomial, reducing the exponential Θ(2^n) classical and quantum cost to efficient polynomial complexity.
AI.motivation: Coherent alias sampling is a key subroutine for block encoding and qubitization-based quantum simulation, using quantum lookup tables. Existing constructions require classical and quantum resources exponential in n to construct and store the alias table for an n-qubit state, which is a major bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors exploit polynomial structure: when amplitudes are samples of a polynomial of degree at most d, the alias table can be represented and evaluated coherently with polynomial cost. They build a quantum circuit for coherently computing the alias table for polynomial states using reversible integer arithmetic, and employ fast arithmetic to obtain a deterministic Clifford+T circuit. They also develop a novel uncomputation technique for the auxiliary register produced by coherent alias sampling.
AI.result: The construction achieves a complete gate count of Õ(ndB + B²) with arithmetic width B = Õ(dn + d log(d+1)). In the high-precision limit for state fidelity ε with fixed n and d, B = Θ(log(1/ε)) suffices and the complete gate count becomes O(log³(1/ε) log log(1/ε)), exponentially reduced from Θ(2^n). The effective alias-table representation also benefits classical sampling algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial-structured amplitudes enable efficient coherent alias sampling with polynomial rather than exponential resources, yielding exponentially reduced costs and a deterministic Clifford+T circuit. The auxiliary-register uncomputation technique opens a research direction in sampling-based initial state preparation.

title: Ground-state properties of the two-dimensional SWAP spin-glass ensemble
summary: We study the recently introduced SWAP ensemble for Ising spin-glasses, where the spins obtain varying lengths, with length scale $Δ\in [0, 2]$. The lengths can be exchanged in the spirit of the SWAP algorithm for glassy poly-disperse hard-sphere systems. Using an annealing schedule, if the annealing is slow enough, ground states of the corresponding Ising Hamiltonian, where the spin lengths are incorporated into the bonds, can be obtained with high probability. We prove this statement for two-dimensional systems with sizes of up to $L^2=1024^2$ spins by comparison with exact ground states obtained by using graph matching algorithms. In particular, we analyze the nature of the obtained realizations of the disorder by calculating exact zero-temperature domain-wall energies, from exact ground state calculations using periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions. For medium or large values of $Δ$, e.g. $Δ=1$, the realizations turn ferromagnetic if the annealing is slow enough, i.e., they lose their zero-temperature spin-glass property. If $Δ$ is small, the realizations remain glassy, but the SWAP annealing does not easily find a true ground state.

AI.tldr: SWAP annealing, applied to an Ising spin-glass ensemble with variable spin lengths (scale Δ∈[0,2]), finds true ground states with high probability for slow schedules, verified against exact graph-matching results up to 1024² spins; however, for large Δ the annealed realizations become ferromagnetic, losing their zero-temperature spin-glass character, while for small Δ they remain glassy but the algorithm struggles to locate true ground states.
AI.motivation: The SWAP algorithm has proven effective for glassy poly-disperse hard-sphere systems, and a SWAP ensemble was recently introduced for Ising spin-glasses with variable-length spins. Whether slow annealing in this ensemble reliably reaches true ground states, and how the resulting disorder realizations behave, was previously unverified at scale.
AI.method: Define the SWAP ensemble for Ising spin-glasses with spin lengths parameterized by Δ∈[0,2], allowing length exchange in analogy to the hard-sphere SWAP algorithm. Incorporate spin lengths into the bond couplings of the Ising Hamiltonian. Run annealing schedules of varying speed on two-dimensional systems up to L²=1024² spins. Validate against exact ground states computed via graph matching algorithms. Characterize disorder realizations by computing exact zero-temperature domain-wall energies from ground states under periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions.
AI.result: For sufficiently slow annealing, ground states of the corresponding Ising Hamiltonian are obtained with high probability, confirmed by comparison with exact graph-matching ground states on 2D systems up to 1024² spins. Domain-wall energy analysis shows that for medium-to-large Δ (e.g., Δ=1), realizations become ferromagnetic when annealing is slow enough, i.e., they lose their zero-temperature spin-glass property. For small Δ, realizations remain glassy, but SWAP annealing does not easily find a true ground state.
AI.conclusion: SWAP annealing is a valid route to exact ground states for the Δ-dependent Ising spin-glass ensemble provided the schedule is slow enough, but this comes at a cost: at larger Δ the process destroys the spin-glass character of the realizations (they turn ferromagnetic), whereas at small Δ the glassy nature is preserved yet grounding becomes computationally difficult. The favored regime to retain spin-glass behavior while annealing is thus restricted to small Δ.

title: Predicting Noise in a Trapped-ion Quantum Simulation of a Lattice Gauge Theory
summary: A recent trapped-ion experiment realised a lattice gauge theory in which the internal states of the ions carry the gauge field and their vibrations carry bosonic matter. In that experiment, a charge moving around a loop was frozen in place by Aharonov--Bohm interference. The noise of such a device is usually simulated after the measurements have been made. Here we show that it can be predicted before the machine is run. For each quantity that the experiment measures, we derive, from the reported noise rates alone, a formula for how it decays together with a bound it can never exceed. The results reveal a simple pattern. The local conservation law of the theory is a parity of the vibrational mode, so heating violates it at a rate that grows as the mode warms, and the violation accelerates rather than accumulating steadily. At zero electric field, each of the three noise processes of the device leaves its own fingerprint. Heating affects only the conservation law, motional dephasing only the interference, and qubit errors only the stored flux and the frozen state. Once the electric field is switched on, the frozen state begins to leak, and we write an exact formula and a guaranteed bound for that leak.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts, before the experiment runs, how noise decays each measured quantity in a trapped-ion lattice gauge theory, deriving decay formulas and bounds from reported noise rates alone, and revealing that heating violates the parity conservation law at an accelerating rate.
AI.motivation: In prior trapped-ion lattice gauge theory experiments, the noise of the device was only simulated after measurements were taken (post hoc). This work is motivated by the need to predict that noise before the machine is run, so that each measured quantity's decay and its maximum possible value can be known in advance from the reported noise rates.
AI.method: From the reported noise rates alone, the authors derive, for each quantity the experiment measures, a formula describing how it decays together with a bound it can never exceed. They analyze the theory's local conservation law (a parity of the vibrational mode) and treat three distinct noise processes—heating, motional dephasing, and qubit errors—considering both zero and nonzero electric field regimes.
AI.result: A simple pattern emerges: heating violates the parity conservation law at a rate that grows as the mode warms, so the violation accelerates rather than accumulating steadily. At zero electric field, each of the three noise processes leaves its own distinct fingerprint: heating affects only the conservation law, motional dephasing only the interference, and qubit errors only the stored flux and the frozen state. Once the electric field is switched on, the frozen state begins to leak, for which the authors write an exact formula and a guaranteed bound.
AI.conclusion: Noise in the trapped-ion lattice gauge theory device can be predicted before running the machine, with exact decay formulas and guaranteed bounds derived purely from reported noise rates, and each noise process exhibits a distinguishable signature in the measured quantities.

title: Disorder-driven loss of crystalline coherence in two-dimensional electron solids: Quantum Hartree-Fock and classical molecular dynamics
summary: We investigate the effects of quenched disorder on two-dimensional electron solids using Hartree-Fock theory and classical molecular dynamics. Increasing disorder weakens crystalline correlations, broadens the structure factor, and reduces the measured coherence length toward the pristine lattice spacing. This evolution is consistent with the Imry-Ma and Larkin picture: random pinning disrupts translational order on sufficiently long scales, and stronger disorder reduces the distance over which crystalline organization survives. Classical simulations further show that stronger pinning raises the temperature for particle rearrangement even after crystalline order has disappeared. Disorder thus suppresses structural coherence while stabilizing an amorphous solid against thermal rearrangement.

AI.tldr: Quenched disorder suppresses crystalline correlations and translational coherence in 2D electron solids (consistent with Imry-Ma/Larkin physics), yet simultaneously stabilizes the resulting amorphous solid against thermal rearrangement.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how quenched disorder affects the structural order of two-dimensional electron solids, particularly whether random pinning degrades crystalline correlations as predicted by the Imry-Ma and Larkin frameworks.
AI.method: Hartree-Fock theory and classical molecular dynamics are used to model 2D electron solids under increasing quenched disorder, tracking crystalline correlations, structure factor broadening, and coherence length, along with thermal rearrangement temperatures.
AI.result: Increasing disorder weakens crystalline correlations, broadens the structure factor, and shrinks the measured coherence length toward the pristine lattice spacing, consistent with Imry-Ma/Larkin behavior. Classical simulations show stronger pinning raises the rearrangement temperature even after crystalline order vanishes.
AI.conclusion: Quenched disorder suppresses long-range structural coherence while stabilizing the amorphous solid against thermal rearrangement, revealing a dual role of pinning.

title: Driven-Dissipative Ground State Preparation: Mixing Time and Randomness
summary: Dissipative protocols offer a route to ground state preparation that does not require a large initial overlap with the ground state. To move beyond time independent Lindbladians and randomized Lindbladians sampled from a fixed distribution, we study driven-dissipative protocols in which the generator varies over time. Our construction uses a family of randomized Lindbladians whose jump operators are obtained by averaging the unitary evolution of random matrices under a fixed target Hamiltonian. We show that empirical averages of these Lindbladians drive arbitrary initial density matrices to low energy states. The resulting mixing time bounds depend on the Hamiltonian only through its eigenvalue distribution and remain valid even for cold starts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces time-dependent driven-dissipative protocols built from randomized Lindbladians whose jump operators arise from averaging unitary evolution of random matrices under a fixed target Hamiltonian, showing these empirical averages drive arbitrary initial states to low energy.
AI.motivation: Dissipative protocols enable ground state preparation without requiring large initial overlap with the ground state. Existing approaches are limited to time-independent Lindbladians or randomized Lindbladians sampled from a fixed distribution, motivating the study of generators that vary over time.
AI.method: The authors construct a family of randomized Lindbladians whose jump operators are obtained by averaging the unitary evolution of random matrices under a fixed target Hamiltonian, and analyze driven-dissipative protocols in which the generator varies over time using empirical averages of these Lindbladians.
AI.result: Empirical averages of these Lindbladians drive arbitrary initial density matrices to low energy states. The mixing time bounds depend on the Hamiltonian only through its eigenvalue distribution and remain valid even for cold starts.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent driven-dissipative protocols extend beyond time-independent and fixed-distribution randomized Lindbladians, achieving low energy state preparation with mixing time guarantees that depend solely on the Hamiltonian's eigenvalue distribution and hold for cold initial states.

title: Fast mixing of the SYK model at high temperatures
summary: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model is a strongly interacting fermionic system. Its dynamics are difficult to analyze with Lieb-Robinson bounds and cluster expansions due to its all-to-all disordered interactions. We prove that, with high probability over the disorder, the SYK model admits a quantum Gibbs sampler with a system-size-independent spectral gap at sufficiently high constant temperatures. This yields polynomial-time preparation of SYK Gibbs states on a quantum computer. While prior non-rigorous computations that suggested SYK thermalization were limited to studying local correlators, we emphasize that our result holds up to arbitrary inverse polynomial trace distance. Our proof introduces the pseudo-Lindbladian approach to fermions and uses an especially simple SYK analysis based on a comparison to classical dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors prove that the SYK model admits a quantum Gibbs sampler with a system-size-independent spectral gap at sufficiently high constant temperatures, enabling polynomial-time preparation of SYK Gibbs states on a quantum computer.
AI.motivation: The SYK model is a strongly interacting fermionic system whose all-to-all disordered interactions make its dynamics hard to analyze via standard tools like Lieb-Robinson bounds and cluster expansions. Prior non-rigorous computations suggesting SYK thermalization were limited to local correlators, motivating a rigorous, global guarantee.
AI.method: The proof introduces the pseudo-Lindbladian approach to fermions and employs an especially simple SYK analysis based on a comparison to classical dynamics. The result holds with high probability over the disorder.
AI.result: With high probability over the disorder, the SYK model admits a quantum Gibbs sampler with a system-size-independent spectral gap at sufficiently high constant temperatures, yielding polynomial-time preparation of SYK Gibbs states on a quantum computer up to arbitrary inverse polynomial trace distance.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous, efficient thermalization/preparation guarantee for SYK Gibbs states, strengthening earlier correlator-based heuristics to a full trace-distance guarantee.

title: Realizing Braided Fusion 2-Categories as (3+1)D Mixed-State Topological Orders
summary: We construct large families of mixed-state topological orders in (3+1)D, including intrinsically mixed-state topological orders. We realize these theories by relating the data parameterizing braided fusion 2-categories to the strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies that characterize mixed-state topological order. We focus here on bosonic theories, which include theories which admit an emergent fermion in the spectrum of line operators. Our general framework is exemplified on the lattice, where we present concrete models and identify how the data of braided fusion 2-categories are physically encoded. We then formalize this data and show that every braided fusion 2-category arises from a general construction (decoherence followed by strong and weak gauging) as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state, with intrinsically mixed-state topological orders distinguished by the presence of strong higher-form symmetries whose anomalies cannot be realized in any (3+1)D gapped ground state. Notably, we show that (3+1)D admits a new mechanism with no (2+1)D counterpart: intrinsically mixed-state order whose topological operators braid non-degenerately, but which carries a gravitational anomaly.

AI.tldr: The paper builds large families of mixed-state topological orders in (3+1)D, including intrinsically mixed ones, by mapping braided fusion 2-category data to strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies, with lattice realizations and a general decoherence-plus-gauging construction.
AI.motivation: Mixed-state topological order is less understood than its pure-state counterpart, and the (3+1)D setting is especially unexplored. The authors aim to characterize such orders systematically and to identify genuinely mixed-state phases that cannot arise as gapped ground states.
AI.method: The authors relate the data parameterizing braided fusion 2-categories to strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies that characterize mixed-state topological order. They focus on bosonic theories, including those with an emergent fermion in the line-operator spectrum. They present concrete lattice models to show how braided fusion 2-category data are physically encoded, then formalize the data and show that every braided fusion 2-category arises from decoherence followed by strong and weak gauging, realized as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state.
AI.result: Every braided fusion 2-category arises from the general construction as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state. Intrinsically mixed-state topological orders are distinguished by strong higher-form symmetries whose anomalies cannot be realized in any (3+1)D gapped ground state. The authors further show that (3+1)D admits a new mechanism with no (2+1)D counterpart: intrinsically mixed-state order whose topological operators braid non-degenerately but which carries a gravitational anomaly.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general framework tying braided fusion 2-categories, strong higher-form symmetries, and anomalies to (3+1)D mixed-state topological order, exemplified on the lattice. It establishes decoherence-plus-gauging as a universal construction and reveals a distinctly (3+1)D mechanism for intrinsically mixed-state order involving non-degenerate braiding together with a gravitational anomaly.

title: Polynomial-time classical algorithms for mean-field models up to the glass transition
summary: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model is a strongly interacting fermionic system that has been well-studied in condensed matter and high energy physics. It is highly quantum: Gaussian states are far from the thermal state (Hastings and O'Donnell, STOC'22) and representing the thermal state requires large polynomial-size quantum circuits (Anschuetz et al., QIP'25). Very recently, it was nonetheless proven that classical algorithms can estimate local thermal expectations at sufficiently high temperature in quasipolynomial time (Zlokapa, FOCS'26). We show that classical algorithms can in fact estimate local observables at all constant temperatures in polynomial time. Our techniques also extend straightforwardly to classical systems: we resolve an open question about computing thermal expectations of a classical spin glass up to its phase transition (Bencs et al., STOC'26). Our proof develops a fully rigorous quantum cavity method. Due to the success of the classical cavity method in optimization, sampling, inference and learning, we expect the quantum cavity method to find further applications of independent interest. As an example, we give a quantum algorithm that learns SYK Hamiltonians from the Gibbs state at any constant temperature with polynomial time and sample complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper presents polynomial-time classical algorithms for estimating local observables in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model at all constant temperatures, resolving the high-temperature quasipolynomial limitation and extending results to classical spin glasses up to the phase transition, via a rigorous quantum cavity method.
AI.motivation: The SYK model is a strongly interacting fermionic system where Gaussian states are far from thermal and representing the thermal state requires large polynomial-size quantum circuits, making classical estimation of thermal expectations challenging; prior work only achieved quasipolynomial time at sufficiently high temperature, and a classical spin glass open question remained unresolved.
AI.method: The authors develop a fully rigorous quantum cavity method, extending techniques from the classical cavity method to the quantum setting, and apply them to both the SYK model and classical spin glasses.
AI.result: Classical algorithms can estimate local observables at all constant temperatures in polynomial time for SYK, and thermal expectations of a classical spin glass can be computed up to its phase transition. Additionally, a quantum algorithm learns SYK Hamiltonians from the Gibbs state at any constant temperature with polynomial time and sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: The quantum cavity method resolves open problems in quantum and classical thermal estimation and is expected to find further applications in optimization, sampling, inference, and learning.

title: Modular Neural Decoder for Surface Code Memory and Logic on Superconducting Processors
summary: Neural decoders for quantum error correction have achieved high accuracy on surface code memory experiments, but practical fault-tolerant computation requires decoders that transfer across devices, noise conditions, and logical operations. We introduce a modular graph-recurrent decoder designed for this setting. Built from reusable local syndrome encoders, it is pretrained in simulation and fine-tuned to hardware using a common pipeline, with only lightweight spatial aggregation adapted between experiments. The decoder performs competitively on conventional memory benchmarks, outperforming minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) at distances 3 and 5 on an IBM Nighthawk-generation processor and closely approaching AlphaQubit on Google's below-threshold hardware data. We then test the framework in two settings beyond memory decoding on the same IBM device. First, in an $X$-type stability experiment, we continuously tune the effective measurement error rate using a variable pre-readout rotation and train a single decoder jointly across the resulting noise range. It matches or outperforms MWPM across the sweep without requiring a separately calibrated decoder for each setting. Second, we decode a $ZZ$-merge lattice-surgery experiment between two distance-3 surface-code patches, improving the decoded correlation between the merge outcome and the final $ZZ$ parity relative to MWPM on real hardware. Together, these experiments demonstrate neural decoding that is portable not only across hardware, but also across qualitatively different surface code observables and logical operations, using models trainable on single-GPU academic resources.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a modular graph-recurrent neural decoder for quantum error correction that is portable across devices, noise conditions, and logical operations, matching or beating MWPM and approaching AlphaQubit on real hardware while remaining trainable on single-GPU resources.
AI.motivation: Neural decoders achieve high accuracy on surface code memory experiments, but practical fault-tolerant computation demands decoders that transfer across devices, noise conditions, and logical operations, which existing approaches do not adequately address.
AI.method: A modular graph-recurrent decoder built from reusable local syndrome encoders, pretrained in simulation and fine-tuned to hardware via a common pipeline, with only lightweight spatial aggregation adapted between experiments. Evaluated on conventional memory benchmarks, an X-type stability experiment with continuously tuned effective measurement error rate (variable pre-readout rotation) using a single jointly trained decoder, and a ZZ-merge lattice-surgery experiment between two distance-3 surface-code patches.
AI.result: The decoder outperforms MWPM at distances 3 and 5 on an IBM Nighthawk-generation processor and closely approaches AlphaQubit on Google's below-threshold hardware data. It matches or outperforms MWPM across the stability-experiment noise sweep without per-setting calibration, and improves the decoded correlation between merge outcome and final ZZ parity relative to MWPM on real hardware for the lattice-surgery experiment.
AI.conclusion: Neural decoding is demonstrated to be portable not only across hardware but also across qualitatively different surface code observables and logical operations, using models trainable on single-GPU academic resources.

title: On Information Propagation in Krylov Subspaces
summary: Krylov subspace methods provide an efficient tool for modeling any quantum initial value problem as a one dimensional chain. A time ordered path formulation, in which the dynamical generator successively splits probability between paths, yields a speed limit within such dynamical subspaces. For power law growing Lanczos coefficients $b_n \sim n^δ$ we find super ballistic lightcones, with an exponentially spreading lightcone for maximal growth $δ= 1$. Causality in the Krylov chain constrains the Lanczos coefficients to grow at most linearly. We illustrate the validity of the above in the $SL(2, R)$ and Heisenberg Weyl algebras, and in a many body skew field Ising model. Moreover, we extend the above bound to the family of $Q$ complexities. Lastly, mapping to a spin chain gives a Lieb Robinson bound analogue and opens the problem to standard condensed matter methods.

AI.tldr: This work derives a speed limit within Krylov subspace dynamics by using a time-ordered path formulation, showing super-ballistic lightcones for power-law growing Lanczos coefficients, with exponential spreading at maximal linear growth. Causality in the Krylov chain bounds coefficient growth to at most linear. The results are validated in SL(2,R), Heisenberg-Weyl algebras, a many-body skew-field Ising model, and extended to Q complexities, with a spin-chain mapping yielding a Lieb-Robinson-bound analogue.
AI.motivation: Krylov subspace methods efficiently map quantum initial value problems onto a one-dimensional chain, but the propagation speed and causality constraints within this dynamical subspace were not fully characterized. The authors aim to establish a speed limit for such dynamics and to determine how causality restricts the growth of Lanczos coefficients.
AI.method: A time-ordered path formulation is used in which the dynamical generator successively splits probability between paths, yielding a speed limit within the dynamical subspaces. Power-law growing Lanczos coefficients b_n ~ n^δ are analyzed, and causality in the Krylov chain is imposed as a constraint. The framework is illustrated in the SL(2,R) and Heisenberg-Weyl algebras and in a many-body skew-field Ising model, and is extended to the family of Q complexities. A mapping to a spin chain is introduced to connect with condensed matter techniques.
AI.result: For power-law growing Lanczos coefficients, super-ballistic lightcones are found, with an exponentially spreading lightcone for maximal growth δ = 1. Causality in the Krylov chain constrains Lanczos coefficients to grow at most linearly. The findings hold in SL(2,R), Heisenberg-Weyl algebras, and the many-body skew-field Ising model, and the bound extends to Q complexities. The spin-chain mapping produces a Lieb-Robinson-bound analogue.
AI.conclusion: Krylov subspace dynamics obeys a speed limit with super-ballistic lightcones and maximal linear growth of Lanczos coefficients enforced by causality. These results connect quantum dynamics in Krylov space to Lieb-Robinson-type bounds and open the problem to standard condensed matter methods.

title: Robustness of Quantum Signal Processing and Resource-aware Polynomial Design
summary: Quantum signal processing (QSP) realizes operator functions through polynomial transformations of a finite degree. In addition to function approximation errors, realistic implementations incur algorithmic errors also when encoding the input operator and in synthesizing gates into a discrete fault-tolerant gate set. We provide an end-to-end analysis of these errors and show that the input error propagation is governed by the operator-Lipschitz constant $L_\star$ of the implemented function. We then derive an efficient classical algorithm to compute tight lower and upper bounds on $L_\star$, and we show that these bounds induce in turn lower and upper bounds on the total quantum-resource cost (for instance, $T$-gate count) needed for QSP implementations compatible with a target total error. We further devise a procedure to search for a polynomial with minimum cost based solely on its coefficients, yielding a resource-aware polynomial-design procedure for QSP. We illustrate the resulting method for ground state energy estimation via eigenvalue thresholding for the H$_6$ molecular Hamiltonian. In the tested hardware profiles, the resource-aware family improves the total-error budget and reduces the modeled $T$-gate count by $51.9\%$--$56.7\%$ relative to the standard analytical polynomial obtained from an error-function approximation.

AI.tldr: End-to-end error analysis of QSP showing input error propagation is governed by the operator-Lipschitz constant, with an efficient classical algorithm to bound it and a resource-aware polynomial design procedure.
AI.motivation: Realistic QSP implementations incur not only function approximation errors but also algorithmic errors from encoding the input operator and synthesizing gates into a discrete fault-tolerant gate set; these errors are typically not analyzed jointly.
AI.method: Provide an end-to-end error analysis; show input error propagation is governed by the operator-Lipschitz constant L_star of the implemented function; derive an efficient classical algorithm to compute tight lower and upper bounds on L_star; use these bounds to induce lower and upper bounds on total quantum-resource cost (e.g., T-gate count) for a target total error; devise a procedure to search for a minimum-cost polynomial based solely on its coefficients.
AI.result: The resource-aware polynomial family improves the total-error budget and reduces the modeled T-gate count by 51.9%–56.7% relative to the standard analytical polynomial from an error-function approximation, illustrated for ground state energy estimation via eigenvalue thresholding on the H6 molecular Hamiltonian across tested hardware profiles.
AI.conclusion: A resource-aware, coefficient-based polynomial-design procedure for QSP yields significant resource savings while accounting for combined approximation and algorithmic errors.

title: Exact Temporal Criticalities of Entanglement and Negativity in Gaussian and Non-Gaussian Dissipative Kitaev Chains
summary: When the two largest eigenvalues of an entanglement or negativity spectrum meet, the gap of the corresponding entanglement or negativity Hamiltonian closes while entropies stay smooth, an event we call a temporal criticality. We ask when such criticalities occur in open fermionic systems, in which order, and whether they precede the geometric decoherence time, at which the negativity starts to fall. We compare loss and gain, which respect fermion parity only on average (weak symmetry) and keep the state Gaussian, with density dephasing, which respects it in every jump (strong symmetry) and makes the state non-Gaussian. We find that Gaussianity, rather than the symmetry, fixes the criterion for a criticality. In a Gaussian state the entanglement gap of a subsystem closes exactly when its two parity sectors carry equal weight, and the negativity gap closes exactly when this happens for the subsystem or its complement, so the negativity criticality never comes after the entanglement one. Uniform balanced loss and gain only shrink the two parities and leave both criticalities in place at every rate, for any quadratic Hamiltonian. In an open Kitaev chain, weak imbalanced loss and gain shift the criticalities by amounts set by the occupations at the cut, and at strong rates they allow a closing near the relaxation time only when an odd number of neighboring sites pass half filling. For dephasing we solve the non-Gaussian dynamics exactly at the point where the bond terms of the chain commute. Weak dephasing delays both criticalities and, away from the chain ends, moves them ahead of the parity balance, where the parity rules of Gaussian states would place them. As the dephasing rate approaches critical damping, both criticalities recede to infinite time, and at strong dephasing the negativity starts to fall long before either gap begins to shrink.

AI.tldr: This paper studies "temporal criticalities" in open fermionic systems—events where the gap of an entanglement or negativity Hamiltonian closes while entropies remain smooth—asking when they occur, in what order, and whether they precede the geometric decoherence time. The key finding is that Gaussianity, not symmetry, sets the criterion for these criticalities.
AI.motivation: Entanglement and negativity spectra can exhibit gap closings (temporal criticalities) as systems evolve, yet it is unclear when these occur in open fermionic systems, in what order, and how they relate to the geometric decoherence time where negativity begins to decay. The authors aim to identify the underlying criterion governing these criticalities and to contrast physically distinct dissipation channels.
AI.method: The authors compare two classes of open fermionic dynamics: (1) loss and gain, which respect fermion parity only on average (weak symmetry) and preserve Gaussianity, and (2) density dephasing, which respects parity in every jump (strong symmetry) and renders the state non-Gaussian. They analyze entanglement and negativity gaps, parity-sector weights, and solve the non-Gaussian dephasing dynamics exactly at the point where the bond terms of a Kitaev chain commute, examining open Kitaev chains with balanced/imbalanced loss and gain.
AI.result: Gaussianity, rather than symmetry, fixes the criticality criterion. In a Gaussian state, the entanglement gap of a subsystem closes exactly when its two parity sectors have equal weight, and the negativity gap closes when this holds for the subsystem or its complement, so negativity criticality never follows entanglement criticality. Uniform balanced loss and gain merely shrink both parities, preserving both criticalities at every rate for any quadratic Hamiltonian. In an open Kitaev chain, weak imbalanced loss/gain shift the criticalities by amounts set by occupations at the cut, and at strong rates a closing near the relaxation time occurs only when an odd number of neighboring sites pass half filling. For dephasing, weak dephasing delays both criticalities and, away from chain ends, moves them ahead of the parity balance point. As dephasing approaches critical damping, both criticalities recede to infinite time; at strong dephasing the negativity decays long before either gap starts to shrink.
AI.conclusion: The criterion for temporal criticalities in open fermionic systems is governed by Gaussianity rather than the symmetry of the dissipation. Entanglement and negativity gap closings are tied to parity-sector balance, with negativity criticality never occurring after entanglement criticality. Dephasing qualitatively alters this picture: it delays criticalities, can push them ahead of parity balance, and at strong rates causes negativity to decay well before gap shrinkage, revealing a sharp distinction between Gaussian and non-Gaussian dissipation regimes.

title: Quantum-Assisted Optimization Guided by Machine-Learned Risk Maps for Aerial Surveillance Routing
summary: Analog quantum computing with neutral atom computers is rapidly evolving into a promising way to perform combinatorial optimization tasks at scale. As technology matures, exploring real use cases leveraging such unique information processors becomes warranted; one example is logistics management where vehicles are assigned routes to perform a given task. Autonomous aerial vehicles (drones) are increasingly used for surveillance over a given territory. In this paper, we propose an innovative framework integrating classical machine learning forecasts and quantum annealing to find the best combination of tours for a given surveillance criterion. The risk maps produced by machine learning are used to find possible surveillance tours, while a quantum-assisted heuristic chooses the best combination, producing a full surveillance plan. By modelling our decision problem for drone paths as a Team Orienteering Problem (TOP) with additional constraints, we construct a new heuristic using quantum annealing to find good solutions. We apply this framework to wildfire prevention, where finding tours most likely to detect a starting fire has clear benefits. We study the effect of larger quantum resources on heuristic performance and compare those results to the use of classical resources.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid framework combining classical machine learning risk forecasting with quantum annealing to solve a constrained Team Orienteering Problem for drone surveillance routing, applied to wildfire prevention, and evaluates how larger quantum resources affect heuristic performance versus classical approaches.
AI.motivation: Analog neutral-atom quantum computers are maturing as tools for large-scale combinatorial optimization, making it timely to explore real-world use cases. Logistics management—specifically assigning routes to autonomous drones for territorial surveillance—represents such a use case, where selecting the best combination of patrol tours is a hard combinatorial decision problem.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework integrating classical machine learning forecasts with quantum annealing. Machine learning generates risk maps, which are used to derive candidate surveillance tours, while a quantum-assisted heuristic selects the best combination of tours to form a full surveillance plan. The decision problem is modeled as a Team Orienteering Problem (TOP) with additional constraints, and a new heuristic using quantum annealing is constructed to find good solutions.
AI.result: The framework is applied to wildfire prevention, where identifying tours most likely to detect an incipient fire yields clear benefits. The study examines the effect of larger quantum resources on heuristic performance and compares the quantum-assisted results against those obtained using classical resources.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a viable integration of machine learning and quantum annealing for real-world drone logistics, suggesting that scaling quantum resources can influence heuristic performance in practical combinatorial optimization settings.

title: Efficient Quantum Monte Carlo through Cluster Expansions
summary: The sign problem remains a major obstacle to extending the success of Monte Carlo methods to generic quantum many-body systems. A powerful alternative relies on cluster expansions, which provide convergent representations of free energies and related quantities, with applications ranging from tensor network contractions to quantum dynamics and circuits. Within their convergence regime, these expansions often yield deterministic polynomial-time algorithms. However, such methods require exhaustive enumeration of connected clusters, leading to a computational overhead of $(N\varepsilon^{-1})^{\mathcal{O}(\logΔ)}$, where $N$ is the system size, $\varepsilon$ the desired precision, and $Δ$ the interaction-graph degree. This becomes particularly severe in long-range systems, where $Δ\equiv N$, resulting in quasi-polynomial runtimes. Here, we introduce a Markov chain algorithm that samples cluster expansions directly in the space of connected clusters, replacing deterministic enumeration by Monte Carlo sampling. Because sampling occurs in an abstract cluster space rather than a physical configuration space, the conventional exponential sign problem is absent within the convergence regime. For general polymer models, we establish an FPRAS with runtime $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(N^4\varepsilon^{-3})$. For quantum partition functions at temperatures $β\leqβ_{\mathrm{sampling}}\equiv\mathcal{O}(1)$, this improves to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(N^{3+1/D}\varepsilon^{-3})$, where $D$ is the lattice dimension. The framework directly applies to long-range quantum systems with interactions $\propto1/r^α$, including $2$-local models with $α>2D$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that samples cluster expansions directly in the abstract space of connected clusters, avoiding exhaustive enumeration and the exponential sign problem, yielding efficient fully polynomial-time randomized approximation schemes (FPRAS) for polymer models and quantum partition functions, including long-range systems.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo methods face the sign problem for generic quantum many-body systems. Cluster expansions avoid the sign problem within their convergence regime but require exhaustive enumeration of connected clusters, incurring overhead of (N ε^{-1})^{O(log Δ)}. This becomes quasi-polynomial for long-range systems where Δ = N, severely limiting scalability.
AI.method: The authors develop a Markov chain algorithm that samples cluster expansions directly in the space of connected clusters, replacing deterministic enumeration with Monte Carlo sampling. Because sampling occurs in an abstract cluster space rather than a physical configuration space, the exponential sign problem is absent within the convergence regime.
AI.result: For general polymer models, an FPRAS is established with runtime Õ(N^4 ε^{-3}). For quantum partition functions at temperatures β ≤ β_sampling = O(1), the runtime improves to Õ(N^{3+1/D} ε^{-3}), where D is the lattice dimension. The framework applies directly to long-range quantum systems with interactions ∝ 1/r^α, including 2-local models with α > 2D.
AI.conclusion: Sampling cluster expansions in abstract cluster space provides a polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme that sidesteps the sign problem and the enumeration overhead, extending efficient computation to long-range quantum many-body systems within the convergence regime.

title: Quantum Query Complexity and Span Programs from Pre-Geometry
summary:
Span programs provide a general method for designing quantum query algorithms, and for Boolean coordinate queries their optimum cost agrees with the general adversary bound. We develop a matroidal organization of this optimization that separates dependence data determined by the query problem from the dependence structure chosen by a span program. The resulting source matroid records query dependence, target determination, and separation data, while a program matroid records dependencies among the target and response-labeled input elements of a candidate program.
  When a query problem admits a source matroid, we use its structure to organize adversary upper and lower bounds. For separating binary query sets in this setting, the global matroid-span-program optimum equals $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}_{\mathcal Q}(f)$. For a fixed regular program matroid, projective uniqueness reduces optimization over real representations to positive element weights. We express positive and negative costs as weighted basis ratios and derive exact $1$-, $2$-, and $3$-sum reductions, giving a compositional evaluation of the fixed-weight objective along a Seymour decomposition.
  For pointed $R_{10}$ closure, exact certificates give $3.9087553<\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}_{\mathcal Q_R}(f_R)<3.9301$. The natural $R_{10}$ program has optimized cost $5$, while another regular program has cost at most $\sqrt{87/5}$. Recursive self-composition yields a family on $N$ input bits with randomized query complexity $Ω(N^{0.7324867\ldots})$, an explicit quantum algorithm using $O(N^{0.6500178\ldots})$ queries, and $Q(F)=Θ(N^α)$ for $0.6204277\ldots<α<0.6229063\ldots$.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a matroidal organization of span-program optimization for quantum query algorithms. It separates the query problem's dependence data (source matroid) from the program's chosen dependence structure (program matroid), uses this to organize adversary bounds, derives exact reductions along a Seymour decomposition, and applies it to pointed R10 closure to obtain improved quantum query bounds and a recursive family with explicit query-complexity exponents.
AI.motivation: Span programs give a general method for quantum query algorithm design, and for Boolean coordinate queries their optimal cost matches the general adversary bound. However, analyzing and optimizing this quantity is hard because the dependence data intrinsic to the query problem is entangled with the dependence structure chosen by a particular span program. The paper aims to disentangle these two aspects to make optimization more tractable and to obtain tighter adversary upper and lower bounds.
AI.method: The authors introduce a matroidal organization: a source matroid that records query dependence, target determination, and separation data, and a program matroid that records dependencies among target and response-labeled input elements of a candidate program. When a query problem admits a source matroid, its structure organizes adversary upper and lower bounds. For separating binary query sets, the global matroid-span-program optimum is shown to equal Adv^±_Q(f). Fixing a regular program matroid, projective uniqueness reduces real-representation optimization to positive element weights, expressing positive and negative costs as weighted basis ratios and deriving exact 1-, 2-, and 3-sum reductions that give a compositional evaluation of the fixed-weight objective along a Seymour decomposition. This framework is then applied to pointed R10 closure with exact certificates and to recursive self-composition.
AI.result: For separating binary query sets, the global matroid-span-program optimum equals Adv^±_Q(f). For pointed R10 closure, exact certificates yield 3.9087553 < Adv^±_{Q_R}(f_R) < 3.9301. The natural R10 program has optimized cost 5, while another regular program has cost at most sqrt(87/5). Recursive self-composition produces a family on N input bits with randomized query complexity Ω(N^{0.7324867...}), an explicit quantum algorithm using O(N^{0.6500178...}) queries, and Q(F)=Θ(N^α) for 0.6204277... < α < 0.6229063...
AI.conclusion: Organizing span-program optimization matroidally separates problem-intrinsic dependence data from program-chosen structure, enabling adversary bounds to be structured by the source matroid and enabling exact, compositional optimization via reductions along a Seymour decomposition for fixed regular program matroids. Applied to R10 closure, this yields tight certified bounds and, via recursive self-composition, explicit improved upper and lower bounds on quantum query complexity and a Θ(N^α) characterization with a narrow exponent interval.

title: Magic Quantum Code Surgery
summary: Non-Clifford operations required for universal quantum computation can be implemented by measuring logical Clifford operators. We present a generalized framework to fault-tolerantly measure transversal Clifford logical operators in quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes. Our protocol takes any QLDPC code and deforms the code across additional ancillary qubits such that a product of stabilizers measures the desired logical Clifford operator. We prove that the deformed, Clifford-stabilized code remains LDPC and that its distance is preserved up to a constant factor independent of the number of physical qubits. We further prove that the Clifford measurement has a fault distance against data qubit and measurement errors that grows linearly with the distance of the original code. We apply our methods to implement logical non-Clifford gates in algorithmically relevant subroutines and to prepare magic states in quantum stabilizer codes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a generalized framework for fault-tolerantly measuring transversal Clifford logical operators in QLDPC codes by deforming the code with ancillary qubits, preserving LDPC properties and distance, enabling logical non-Clifford gates and magic state preparation.
AI.motivation: Universal quantum computation requires non-Clifford operations, which can be implemented by measuring logical Clifford operators. A general, fault-tolerant method applicable to QLDPC codes is needed.
AI.method: The protocol takes any QLDPC code and deforms it across additional ancillary qubits, so that a product of stabilizers measures the desired logical Clifford operator.
AI.result: The deformed, Clifford-stabilized code remains LDPC; its distance is preserved up to a constant factor independent of physical qubit count; the Clifford measurement has a fault distance against data qubit and measurement errors growing linearly with the original code distance.
AI.conclusion: The methods enable implementation of logical non-Clifford gates in algorithmically relevant subroutines and preparation of magic states in quantum stabilizer codes.

title: Benchmarking Ansatze for Pauli Correlation Encoding in the Maximum Independent Set Problem
summary: The increasing complexity of 5G and emerging 6G wireless networks has intensified the need for scalable optimization techniques capable of addressing computationally challenging combinatorial problems. While quantum optimization offers a promising alternative, current near-term quantum hardware remains limited by qubit availability, noise, and scalability constraints. Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) has emerged as a qubit-efficient optimization framework that addresses these challenges through polynomial variable compression. However, the impact of compression on representability and solution recovery remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the hypothesis that increasing compression ratios introduce representability constraints arising from algebraic closure relationships among encoded Pauli observables. Using Maximum Independent Set benchmark problems, we evaluate multiple PCE ansatz designs and compression ratios. We find that ansatz selection is critical to both solution quality and feasibility, with two ansatz families consistently outperforming alternatives and achieving approximation ratios approaching 0.9. Furthermore, increasing circuit repetitions provides limited benefit and can degrade performance. Most notably, reducing compression by increasing the number of available qubits significantly improves raw solution quality, while post-processed performance remains comparatively stable. These findings suggest that representability effects play an important role in compressed PCE encodings and provide new insight into the relationship among compression, ansatz design, decoding, and solution quality in scalable quantum optimization.

AI.tldr: This work studies how qubit compression in Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) affects representability and solution quality for combinatorial optimization, finding that ansatz choice is critical, more compression constrains representability, and extra qubits improve raw solution quality.
AI.motivation: The growing complexity of 5G/6G networks demands scalable combinatorial optimization, but near-term quantum hardware is limited by qubit count, noise, and scalability. PCE is a qubit-efficient framework relying on polynomial variable compression, yet the effect of compression on representability and solution recovery is poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors hypothesize that higher compression ratios impose representability constraints from algebraic closure relationships among encoded Pauli observables. They evaluate multiple PCE ansatz designs and compression ratios on Maximum Independent Set benchmarks, and examine the effects of circuit repetitions and the number of available qubits.
AI.result: Ansatz selection strongly affects both solution quality and feasibility; two ansatz families consistently outperform alternatives with approximation ratios approaching 0.9. Increasing circuit repetitions yields limited benefit and can degrade performance. Reducing compression by using more qubits significantly improves raw solution quality, while post-processed performance stays comparatively stable.
AI.conclusion: Representability effects play an important role in compressed PCE encodings, offering new insight into the interplay among compression, ansatz design, decoding, and solution quality in scalable quantum optimization.

title: Rydberg-mediated microwave-to-optical transduction with tunable bandwidth
summary: Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction is essential for hybrid quantum networks. Typical transducers, however, have bandwidths set by fixed device parameters and face efficiency-bandwidth tradeoffs. We propose a cavity-based microwave-to-optical transducer mediated by a collective Rydberg excitation, where external driving fields tune the conversion bandwidth in situ from narrowband, spectrally selective operation to broadband operation without modifying cavity parameters. Under impedance-matching conditions, the system operates as a continuous-wave phase-preserving linear transducer, maintaining both near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited added noise throughout the tunable bandwidth range.

AI.tldr: A cavity microwave-to-optical transducer mediated by a collective Rydberg excitation achieves in-situ tunable bandwidth via external driving fields, maintaining near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited noise.
AI.motivation: Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction is essential for hybrid quantum networks, yet typical transducers suffer from bandwidths fixed by device parameters and efficiency-bandwidth tradeoffs.
AI.method: A cavity-based microwave-to-optical transducer mediated by a collective Rydberg excitation, with external driving fields that tune the conversion bandwidth in situ without modifying cavity parameters.
AI.result: The conversion bandwidth is tuned from narrowband, spectrally selective operation to broadband operation; under impedance-matching conditions the system acts as a continuous-wave phase-preserving linear transducer with near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited added noise across the tunable bandwidth range.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Rydberg-mediated cavity transducer overcomes the fixed-bandwidth limitation and efficiency-bandwidth tradeoff of typical transducers, offering in-situ bandwidth tunability with high efficiency and quantum-limited noise.

title: Foundational puzzles on quantum universality: From Wigner's friend to black holes
comment: 332 pages, PhD thesis, University of York, UK (2026)
summary: Despite its remarkable empirical success and predictive power, quantum theory is riddled with mysteries. One such conceptual puzzle is the measurement problem: why do quantum systems in superposition collapse to a single-valued outcome upon being measured? The scenario of Wigner's friend illustrates this tension, with recent extensions deriving strong no-go results for the nature of reality. Another fundamental puzzle arises at the interface of quantum theory and general relativity---the black hole information paradox. This thesis further explores these two foundational paradoxes. Part I of this thesis focuses on extensions of the Wigner's friend scenario. We introduce several novel extended Wigner's friend arguments, and establish connections with notions of nonclassicality, i.e. the study of quantum phenomena that evade classical explanation. Key results are a refined version of the Frauchiger--Renner paradox, new extended Wigner's friend scenarios based on contextuality, and an argument against the absoluteness of free choices based on the Pusey--Barrett--Rudolph theorem. The latter result complements the Local Friendliness no-go theorem, which challenged the absoluteness of experimentally obtained measurement outcomes. In Part II of this thesis, we turn to black hole puzzles and the interplay of quantum theory and gravity. We present a paradox that unifies extended Wigner's friend arguments with black hole puzzles, strengthening the cloning and firewall paradoxes. After discussing subtleties in these paradoxes, we next present an analysis combining elements of quantum theory with gravity, analyzing the detector response near a superposed black hole using elements of quantum reference frames.

AI.tldr: This thesis explores two foundational paradoxes: extensions of the Wigner's friend scenario and the black hole information paradox, connecting them via nonclassicality and quantum-gravity interplay.
AI.motivation: Quantum theory, despite its predictive success, faces conceptual puzzles. The measurement problem—why superpositions collapse to single outcomes—is illustrated by Wigner's friend, and recent extensions yield strong no-go results about the nature of reality. Separately, the black hole information paradox arises at the quantum-gravity interface. The thesis is motivated to deepen understanding of these two foundational paradoxes.
AI.method: Part I develops novel extended Wigner's friend arguments and links them to notions of nonclassicality (quantum phenomena evading classical explanation). Part II formulates a paradox unifying extended Wigner's friend arguments with black hole puzzles, then analyzes detector response near a superposed black hole using quantum reference frames.
AI.result: Key results include a refined version of the Frauchiger–Renner paradox, new extended Wigner's friend scenarios based on contextuality, and an argument against the absoluteness of free choices grounded in the Pusey–Barrett–Rudolph theorem (complementing the Local Friendliness no-go theorem). A unifying paradox strengthens the cloning and firewall paradoxes, and a quantum reference frame analysis of detector response near a superposed black hole is presented.
AI.conclusion: The thesis advances the study of foundational quantum paradoxes, connecting extended Wigner's friend arguments to nonclassicality and to black hole puzzles, and offers quantum-gravity analyses that reinforce and extend existing no-go results and paradoxes.

title: Certification failure in variational-principle observables
summary: Algorithms which prepare states via the variational principle assume that closeness in energy implies closeness in state; we formalise how this assumption can fail by showing that a ground-state energy estimate converged to within $ε$ of the true value is compatible with observable expectation values in error by up to $\sqrt{2εχ_O}$ at leading order, where $χ_O$ is the static susceptibility of the observable. As a result, the observable error can be orders of magnitude larger than the energy error, a mechanism we call non-linear error amplification, and because a variational algorithm cannot guarantee the correctness of these properties from energy alone, energy does not necessarily certify an observable. In light of our findings, we examine three algorithms: the variational quantum eigensolver on the transverse-field Ising chain, the density-matrix renormalisation group on a pair of weakly coupled hydrogen chains, and Krylov quantum diagonalisation on lithium fluoride. In each case we demonstrate that a well-converged energy can leave observables uncertified.

AI.tldr: Energy convergence in variational state-preparation does not guarantee observable accuracy: observable errors scale as √(2εχ_O), a "non-linear error amplification" that can be orders of magnitude larger than the energy error.
AI.motivation: Variational algorithms that prepare quantum states implicitly assume that being close in energy implies being close in state (and hence in observables). The authors formalize how this assumption fails, motivating the need to determine whether energy alone can certify observable expectation values.
AI.method: A theoretical analysis deriving the leading-order bound relating energy error ε to observable error, introducing the static susceptibility χ_O of the observable to characterize amplification. This is complemented by numerical case studies of three algorithms: VQE on the transverse-field Ising chain, DMRG on weakly coupled hydrogen chains, and Krylov quantum diagonalisation on lithium fluoride.
AI.result: A ground-state energy estimate converged to within ε is compatible with observable expectation values in error up to √(2εχ_O) at leading order, and the observable error can be orders of magnitude larger than the energy error across all three studied algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Energy convergence does not certify observable correctness, since a variational algorithm cannot guarantee observable properties from energy alone; well-converged energies can leave observables uncertified.

title: Multi-Indexed Schatten Quasi- and Anti-Norms and Additivity of Conditional Rényi Entropies
summary:
We introduce and study multi-indexed Schatten spaces which lift the commutative $\ell_{q_1}\![\ell_{q_2}\![\ell_{q_3}\![\dots]]]$ -spaces to the quantum toolbox. They extend Pisier's operator-valued Schatten norms and the recently introduced two-indexed Schatten quasi-norms. For every ordered tuple $\mathcal{Q}=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ of non-zero indices we define a quasi-norm (for positive indices) or an anti-norm (for negative indices) on operators on an $n$-fold tensor product of Hilbert spaces. We do this for indices of the same sign satisfying the mutual compatibility condition $|\frac{1}{q_i}-\frac{1}{q_j}|\leq1$. Beyond establishing desirable properties of these quasi- and anti-norms via factorization formulas that combine operator space and matrix-analytic techniques, we lift several central tools and results of the seminal [Devetak, Junge, King, Ruskai, CMP 2006] to the multi-indexed and quasi-normed setting. These include a general non-commutative Minkowski inequality relating swapped systems and two identity-removal equalities. As a consequence, complete hypercontractivity and complete reverse hypercontractivity tensorize for all compatible indices, including negative ones.
  Concerning quantum information theory we prove that the completely bounded minimal and the maximal output conditional entropies are additive under tensor products of quantum channels for all $α\geq\frac12$. This extends the case $α>1$ of [Fawzi, Kochanowski, Rouzé, Van Himbeeck, CMP 2026] and the unconditional results of [Devetak, Junge, King, Ruskai, CMP 2006]. Beyond tensor products, we establish chain rules for $\tilde H^\uparrow_α$, $α\in[\frac12,1)$, for compositions of possibly signaling channels, extending upon the smooth max-entropy chain rule used in device-independent entanglement certification to the whole interval $α\in[1/2,1)$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces multi-indexed Schatten spaces that lift commutative nested ℓ_p-spaces to the quantum setting, extending Pisier's operator-valued Schatten norms and two-indexed Schatten quasi-norms. It establishes factorization formulas, a non-commutative Minkowski inequality, and identity-removal equalities, and derives new results on complete (reverse) hypercontractivity and on additivity and chain rules for conditional entropies of quantum channels.
AI.motivation: Pisier's operator-valued Schatten norms and recently introduced two-indexed Schatten quasi-norms are limited to few indices; a systematic multi-indexed quantum generalization that mirrors the commutative nested ℓ_{q1}[ℓ_{q2}[...]]-spaces was missing, and central tools from Devetak-Junge-King-Ruskai (2006) had not been lifted to a multi-indexed quasi-normed setting. This gap also left unresolved additivity and chain-rule questions for conditional entropies of quantum channels.
AI.method: For an ordered tuple Q=(q1,...,qn) of non-zero indices of the same sign satisfying the mutual compatibility condition |1/qi - 1/qj| ≤ 1, the authors define a quasi-norm (positive indices) or an anti-norm (negative indices) on operators acting on an n-fold tensor product of Hilbert spaces. Properties are established via factorization formulas combining operator space and matrix-analytic techniques.
AI.result: The paper lifts a general non-commutative Minkowski inequality relating swapped systems and two identity-removal equalities to the multi-indexed quasi-normed setting, showing complete hypercontractivity and complete reverse hypercontractivity tensorize for all compatible indices including negative ones. It proves additivity of completely bounded minimal and maximal output conditional entropies under tensor products of quantum channels for all α ≥ 1/2, and establishes chain rules for H̃↑_α, α ∈ [1/2,1), for compositions of possibly signaling channels.
AI.conclusion: Multi-indexed Schatten spaces provide a coherent quantum framework extending operator-valued Schatten norms and two-indexed quasi-norms.
