It accurately simulates 4-photon interference in linear optics with only 32 input/output probe settings and 6-photon interference with 256 probe settings. It also applies to non-unitary channels such as lossy, nonlinear, or arbitrary quantum channels.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables a wide variety of applications implementable with easily attainable coherent light sources and threshold detectors, including characterization of small-scale linear optical quantum computing circuits and quantum sensing/metrology devices.

title: Variational Quantum Attention for Molecular Graph Learning
summary: Molecular property prediction is central to computational drug discovery, where graph neural networks learn to weight neighboring atomic environments during message passing. Yet it remains unclear how variational quantum circuits alter learned attention behavior in molecular graphs. We introduce an edge-aware variational quantum attention mechanism for molecular graph learning, in which the receiving atom, neighboring atom, and connecting bond jointly determine the quantum attention state. Across five molecular property and bioactivity prediction tasks, QGAT achieves competitive performance relative to GATv2, with a consistent improvement on BBBP across all six evaluated circuit ansatzes. We further compare how the quantum and classical attention scores weight molecular structure beyond accuracy. In the Verubecestat BACE1 inhibitor series, QGAT achieves a higher Spearman correlation than GATv2 and assigns positive attributions to several structural changes consistent with reported structure-activity relationships (SARs). This case study shows that the two attention mechanisms can exhibit different prediction and attribution behavior across structurally related BACE1 analogues, while broader validation is required to determine how consistently these differences generalize across chemical series and targets. Circuit ablations further show that performance depends on the circuit design. Together, these results show that variational quantum attention can serve as a viable alternative molecular attention parameterization while inducing circuit- and chemistry-dependent behavior distinct from a matched classical scorer.

AI.tldr: QGAT, an edge-aware variational quantum attention mechanism, achieves competitive molecular property prediction versus GATv2, with consistent BBBP gains and distinct, circuit-dependent attribution behavior.
AI.motivation: Molecular property prediction underpins computational drug discovery, and graph neural networks weight neighboring atomic environments during message passing. However, how variational quantum circuits alter learned attention behavior in molecular graphs remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors introduce an edge-aware variational quantum attention mechanism where the receiving atom, neighboring atom, and connecting bond jointly determine the quantum attention state. QGAT is benchmarked against GATv2 across five molecular property and bioactivity tasks and six circuit ansatzes, with attention-score comparisons and circuit ablations on the Verubecestat BACE1 inhibitor series using Spearman correlation and SAR-aligned attribution analysis.
AI.result: QGAT achieves competitive performance relative to GATv2, with consistent improvement on BBBP across all six evaluated circuit ansatzes. On the Verubecestat BACE1 series, QGAT attains higher Spearman correlation than GATv2 and assigns positive attributions to structural changes consistent with reported SARs. Performance depends on circuit design per ablations.
AI.conclusion: Variational quantum attention is a viable alternative molecular attention parameterization that induces circuit- and chemistry-dependent behavior distinct from a matched classical scorer, though broader validation is needed to establish generality across chemical series and targets.

title: Efficient Quantum State Identity Testing
summary: We study the following quantum state identity problem: given access to copies of $n$ unknown pure quantum states, the goal is to determine whether every pair has fidelity at least $1-\varepsilon$ or some pair has fidelity at most $\varepsilon$. This problem relaxes the identical-or-orthogonal promise considered in previous work. For any fixed overlap parameter $\varepsilon\in(0,1/4)$, we present two quantum algorithms with complementary guarantees on circuit depth and sample complexity. The first runs in constant depth using parallel swap tests and takes $O(\log(n/δ)\log(2/δ))$ copies of each input state to succeed with probability at least $1-δ$. The second uses the Schur transform to reduce the sample complexity to $O(\log(n/δ))$, through an analysis relating Jucys--Murphy elements to Schur sampling. We also prove a matching sample complexity lower bound of $Ω(\log(n/δ))$ for any quantum algorithm with failure probability at most $δ\le 1/2-c$, for any constant $c>0$, establishing that the second algorithm achieves the optimal dependence on both $n$ and $δ$ for fixed $\varepsilon$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the quantum state identity problem for $n$ unknown pure states, relaxing the identical-or-orthogonal promise to a fidelity-threshold promise, and provides two algorithms (constant-depth parallel swap tests and Schur-transform-based) with optimal sample complexity $O(\log(n/\delta))$, matched by a lower bound.
AI.motivation: Previous work handled the stringent identical-or-orthogonal promise. This work relaxes it to a more general fidelity promise (every pair has fidelity $\geq 1-\varepsilon$, or some pair has fidelity $\leq \varepsilon$, for fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1/4)$), enabling more practical and robust state identity certification.
AI.method: First algorithm: constant-depth circuits using parallel swap tests. Second algorithm: uses the Schur transform to reduce sample complexity, with analysis relating Jucys--Murphy elements to Schur sampling. Also proves a sample complexity lower bound via information-theoretic arguments.
AI.result: First algorithm: constant depth, $O(\log(n/\delta)\log(2/\delta))$ copies per state, success probability $\geq 1-\delta$. Second algorithm: $O(\log(n/\delta))$ copies per state. Lower bound: $\Omega(\log(n/\delta))$ for any quantum algorithm with failure probability $\leq \delta\le 1/2-c$, for constant $c>0$.
AI.conclusion: The second algorithm achieves optimal dependence on both $n$ and $\delta$ for fixed $\varepsilon$, establishing the tight sample complexity of the relaxed quantum state identity problem.

title: Multi-Yoked Surface Codes
summary: The surface code is the leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation owing to its planar nearest-neighbor connectivity, high threshold, and efficient decoding, but its low encoding rate demands on the order of a thousand physical qubits per logical qubit in the teraquop regime. Yoked surface codes improve the density by a factor of two or three by concatenating a high-density parity check code on top of the surface code while retaining planar nearest-neighbor connectivity. In this work, we generalize this idea to multiple levels of concatenation and introduce multi-yoked surface codes. Our construction rests on two new ingredients. First, we propose a family of outer codes called chain codes, built by chaining copies of a seed code that detects the block errors of the code one level below; the resulting codes use all logical qubits of the lower level and achieve a high encoding rate within a few concatenation levels. Second, we design a patch allocation in which movable workspaces perform the yoking checks by lattice surgery with a hierarchy of yoking intervals, so that lower-level checks are performed frequently while higher-level checks are performed less often, which avoids the long yoking intervals that a single large-distance outer code would require. As a benchmark, we construct a three-yoked surface code with a $[[256,166,8]]$ outer code and evaluate it numerically under the SI1000 noise model using soft information from the surface code decoder. The logical error rate is suppressed exponentially in the inner code distance, and in the teraquop regime the three-yoked surface code is about 4 to 4.5$\times$ denser than the unyoked surface code.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces multi-yoked surface codes, generalizing yoked surface codes to multiple levels of concatenation via chain codes and a hierarchical yoking-interval patch allocation, achieving roughly 4-4.5x higher density than unyoked surface codes in the teraquop regime.
AI.motivation: The surface code is the leading fault-tolerant quantum computing candidate due to planar nearest-neighbor connectivity, high threshold, and efficient decoding, but its low encoding rate requires on the order of a thousand physical qubits per logical qubit in the teraquop regime. Yoked surface codes improve density by a factor of two or three using a single level of concatenation, motivating further generalization to multiple concatenation levels for greater density.
AI.method: The construction rests on two new ingredients. First, a family of outer codes called chain codes, built by chaining copies of a seed code that detects block errors of the code one level below; these use all logical qubits of the lower level and achieve a high encoding rate within a few concatenation levels. Second, a patch allocation in which movable workspaces perform yoking checks via lattice surgery with a hierarchy of yoking intervals, so lower-level checks run frequently while higher-level checks run less often, avoiding the long yoking intervals a single large-distance outer code would require. A three-yoked surface code with a [[256,166,8]] outer code is constructed and evaluated numerically under the SI1000 noise model using soft information from the surface code decoder.
AI.result: The logical error rate is suppressed exponentially in the inner code distance. In the teraquop regime, the three-yoked surface code is about 4 to 4.5x denser than the unyoked surface code.
AI.conclusion: Multi-yoked surface codes generalize the yoking idea to multiple concatenation levels, combining chain codes with hierarchical yoking intervals to substantially increase logical qubit density while retaining planar nearest-neighbor connectivity, offering a denser route to fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Exact Clifford Optimality for Two-Sided Locally Randomized Classical Shadows
summary: Entangling measurements can reduce the statistical cost of learning many-body correlations. We study Pauli strings with full support on a specified $k$-qubit region using classical shadows with two independent, uniformly random product single-qubit Clifford layers around a controllable unitary acting on that region, followed by computational-basis readout. In this architecture, we prove that a circuit $U_*$ of two collective Pauli rotations attains the exact minimum squared shadow norm over all Clifford choices of the controllable unitary for every $k\geq1$, namely $C_k^{\rm opt}=4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k+3^k-6)$ for odd $k$ and $C_k^{\rm opt}=4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k-3^k+2)$ for even $k$. The asymptotic optimum $(4/3)\cdot(9/5)^k$ establishes Wu et al.'s exponential base as optimal and improves their prefactor from $2$ to $4/3$. For $1\leq k\leq6$, exact rational certificates prove that the same optimum holds over the entire unitary group $\mathrm U(2^k)$, including all non-Clifford unitaries, within the same measurement architecture. These finite-size results motivate the conjecture that $U_*$ is optimal over all unitaries for arbitrary $k$ within this architecture.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the optimal controllable unitary for classical-shadow estimation of full-support Pauli strings on a $k$-qubit region, proving that two collective Pauli rotations minimize the squared shadow norm over all Clifford choices, and (for $k\le6$) over the entire unitary group.
AI.motivation: Entangling measurements can lower the statistical cost of learning many-body correlations. Prior work (Wu et al.) established a favorable exponential scaling base for shadow-norm-optimal estimation of Pauli strings, but the exact optimal measurement and its prefactor were not settled.
AI.method: Classical shadows using two independent uniformly random product single-qubit Clifford layers surrounding a controllable unitary $U$ acting on the target $k$-qubit region, followed by computational-basis readout. The squared shadow norm is minimized over Clifford choices of $U$; exact rational certificates extend the optimum to the full unitary group $\mathrm U(2^k)$ for $1\le k\le6$.
AI.result: A circuit $U_*$ of two collective Pauli rotations attains the exact minimum squared shadow norm $C_k^{\rm opt}=4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k+3^k-6)$ for odd $k$ and $4\cdot 9^k/(3\cdot 5^k-3^k+2)$ for even $k$, for every $k\ge1$. Asymptotically $C_k^{\rm opt}\to(4/3)(9/5)^k$, confirming Wu et al.'s exponential base $9/5$ as optimal while improving the prefactor from $2$ to $4/3$. For $1\le k\le6$, exact rational certificates show the same optimum over all unitaries in $\mathrm U(2^k)$.
AI.conclusion: Two collective Pauli rotations constitute the optimal controllable unitary within this measurement architecture, and the finite-size certificates over $\mathrm U(2^k)$ support the conjecture that $U_*$ is optimal over all unitaries for arbitrary $k$ in this architecture.

title: Bounding Two-Way Average Communication Cost of Simulating Quantum Correlations
comment: 10+10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables; Comments are welcome!
summary: Bell nonlocal correlations cannot be reproduced by local hidden-variable models without communication, making classical communication cost a natural quantitative measure of nonlocality. Although finite communication always suffices to simulate any correlation in a fixed finite Bell scenario, determining the minimum amount needed to (exactly) simulate any given nonlocal correlation remains challenging, especially in the average-cost setting. Here, we derive lower bounds on input-average communication cost from nonlocal games, allowing variable-length, fully interactive two-way protocols. When applied to parallel games, these bounds yield explicit finite quantum correlations for which the exact simulation cost exceeds any prescribed finite input-average communication budget. For $n$ parallel Magic-Square-winning correlations, we prove a lower bound of $n\log_2(3/2)$ bits and give a one-way communication protocol that attains this rate asymptotically. For the quantum correlation maximally winning the $n$-copy of the Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt nonlocal game, we obtain an input-average lower bound of approximately $0.04627n$ bits for exact simulation. Finally, we formulate a hierarchy of lower bounds and complementary upper bounds using deterministic correlations up to chosen communication costs. Both recover the exact input-average cost at their final levels, and if the bounds agree at lower levels, their common value yields the exact input-average cost without needing to consider all communication strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes lower bounds on the input-average communication cost needed to exactly simulate nonlocal correlations, showing that parallel quantum games require communication growing linearly with the number of copies.
AI.motivation: Bell nonlocal correlations cannot be simulated by local hidden-variable models without communication, so classical communication cost is a natural measure of nonlocality. However, determining the minimum communication needed to exactly simulate a given nonlocal correlation is challenging, particularly in the average-cost setting.
AI.method: The authors derive lower bounds on input-average communication cost from nonlocal games, permitting variable-length, fully interactive two-way protocols. They apply these bounds to parallel games and also formulate a hierarchy of lower and complementary upper bounds based on deterministic correlations up to specified communication costs.
AI.result: For n parallel Magic-Square-winning correlations, they prove a lower bound of n log2(3/2) bits and provide a one-way protocol attaining this rate asymptotically. For the quantum correlation maximally winning the n-copy CHSH game, they obtain an input-average lower bound of about 0.04627n bits for exact simulation. The hierarchy recovers the exact input-average cost at its final levels, and agreement at lower levels yields the exact cost without enumerating all strategies.
AI.conclusion: The bounds demonstrate explicit finite quantum correlations whose exact simulation cost exceeds any prescribed finite input-average communication budget, and the hierarchy offers a practical route to pin down exact input-average communication costs.

title: Correlations decide a shallow-circuit advantage
summary: Quantum computers are claimed to produce samples ordinary classical computers cannot reproduce. The sharpest such claim known pits constant-depth quantum circuits, given one entangled state per run, against shallow classical circuits of few-input gates and limited randomness. No efficient test was known that certifies such a claim from classical samples alone. Here we show that what such a test must read is decided by the classical class's pattern of single-bit and pair correlations, not by a distance. The test rests on one inequality: any machine producing the samples sits no further from the target than the fraction it mislabels plus the deviation of its string half, the bits beyond the label, from uniform. A collapse theorem, machine-checked in the Lean~4 proof assistant, confines that second term, one setting of the sampler's random input bits at a time. Four natural checks provably fail; a fifth, reading those same correlations, catches a far-from-target construction they cannot reach, and is exact on the class of few-input gates. The label test is proven and sample-optimal in its own tolerance up to a logarithmic factor; the fifth check is sound, not only effective, on the bounded pinned-residue class, pairwise-uniform samplers whose residue, the string's weight modulo the prime, is pinned by few seeds and whose seed sharing is bounded. What binds an experiment is the $43$-qubit entangled resource state at fidelity near $0.99$, not the readout. What remains are two named open problems; a positive answer to the first would extend the guarantee to the full class.

AI.tldr: No efficient test previously certified the quantum-vs-classical sampling claim from classical samples alone. This work shows the required test depends on the classical class's single-bit and pair correlations rather than a distance measure, gives one inequality, a machine-checked collapse theorem, and a robust fifth check.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers are claimed to generate samples that classical computers cannot reproduce; the sharpest claim pits constant-depth quantum circuits (given one entangled state per run) against shallow classical circuits of few-input gates and limited randomness. However, no efficient test was known that certifies such a separation using classical samples only, so a practical, sound validation procedure was missing.
AI.method: The paper reduces certification to the classical class's pattern of single-bit and pair correlations instead of a distance. It introduces a single inequality bounding the machine's distance from the target by its mislabel fraction plus the deviation of its string half (bits beyond the label) from uniform. A collapse theorem, verified in Lean 4, confines the second term one setting of the sampler's random input bits at a time. Four natural checks are shown to fail; a fifth check reads those same correlations and is exact on the few-input-gate class. The label test is proven and sample-optimal up to a logarithmic factor in its tolerance; the fifth check is sound on the bounded pinned-residue class (pairwise-uniform samplers with residue pinned by few seeds and bounded seed sharing).
AI.result: Four natural checks provably fail, while the fifth correlation-based check detects a far-from-target construction they cannot reach and is exact on the few-input-gate class. The label test is sample-optimal in its tolerance up to a logarithmic factor, and the fifth check is sound on the bounded pinned-residue class. The binding experimental requirement is the 43-qubit entangled resource state at fidelity near 0.99, not the readout.
AI.conclusion: Efficient certification of the quantum-sampling separation from classical samples alone is achievable via a correlation-based test rather than a distance-based one. Two named open problems remain; a positive answer to the first would extend the guarantee to the full classical class.

title: Quantum-State Oblivious Transfer over Quantum Erasure Channels
summary: We study quantum-state oblivious transfer over the quantum erasure channel under information-theoretic security guarantees. Specifically, Alice holds two quantum systems, Bob wishes to recover one of them, and the parties have access to independent channel uses and authenticated public classical communication, with no initial shared entanglement. We consider both honest-but-curious and malicious behavior. We establish finite-blocklength converse and achievability bounds, which match in the honest-but-curious setting. The malicious setting construction combines interactive hashing with tests of whether Bob received selected channel outputs, and distributes each input across several qubits so that erasures conceal an entire input from a dishonest receiver, even when the inputs are entangled with an external reference. We also derive fixed-error asymptotic expansions and show that both malicious and honest-but-curious settings have the same capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum-state oblivious transfer over the quantum erasure channel with information-theoretic security, deriving finite-blocklength converse and achievability bounds for honest-but-curious and malicious settings, and showing both settings share the same capacity.
AI.motivation: Oblivious transfer is a fundamental cryptographic primitive, but its quantum-state variant over realistic noisy channels under information-theoretic security—especially against malicious adversaries—is not well characterized, particularly in the finite-blocklength regime.
AI.method: Alice holds two quantum systems and Bob recovers one; parties use independent channel uses plus authenticated public classical communication with no pre-shared entanglement. The authors derive finite-blocklength converse and achievability bounds, and for the malicious setting combine interactive hashing with tests of whether Bob received selected channel outputs, distributing each input across several qubits so erasures conceal an entire input even when inputs are entangled with an external reference.
AI.result: Finite-blocklength converse and achievability bounds are established and match in the honest-but-curious setting. Fixed-error asymptotic expansions are derived, and both the malicious and honest-but-curious settings are shown to have the same capacity.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-state oblivious transfer over the quantum erasure channel achieves the same information-theoretic capacity against malicious and honest-but-curious adversaries, with matching finite-blocklength bounds in the honest-but-curious case.

title: Stabilizer codes over general phase spaces
summary: We develop a theory of stabilizer codes whose stabilizer groups consist of commuting qudit Paulis, oscillator displacements, and/or planar-rotor displacements. We consider codes whose stabilizer groups form generalized lattices in quantum phase space, a condition that guarantees a finite logical dimension. We construct oscillator-rotor, rotor-qudit, and oscillator-rotor-qubit codes that cannot be decomposed into separate subsystems by generalized Clifford transformations. We also introduce an oscillator-qubit code arising from a partially lifted Golay code, where Construction A is applied to half of the Golay code coordinates. We derive analytical forms of logical operators from the symplectic dual lattice, determine Clifford-Gaussian gates from lattice symmetries, show that the code dimension equals the covolume of the stabilizer lattice, and organize the syndrome subspaces into a vector bundle. Our technique builds on earlier non-commutative geometric results by Rieffel, but it can often be interpreted simply as concatenating a given stabilizer code with a Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code, applying conventional lattice-theoretic results, and unconcatenating. We formulate distances, optimal decoding, and quantum weight enumerators, recovering the Pauli, qudit, and GKP versions together with known MacWilliams identities. We construct finite-energy codewords whose encoding is an isometry up to an error exponentially small in the inverse damping parameter.

AI.tldr: A unified lattice-theoretic theory of stabilizer codes over qudit Paulis, oscillator displacements, and planar-rotor displacements, yielding new hybrid codes, logical operators from symplectic dual lattices, distances, decoders, weight enumerators, and finite-energy encodings.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer codes have been developed separately for qudits (Pauli), oscillators (GKP), and rotors, with disparate formalisms. A unified framework is needed to treat commuting stabilizer groups mixing these degrees of freedom, guarantee finite logical dimension, and recover known Pauli, qudit, and GKP results as special cases.
AI.method: The authors study stabilizer groups forming generalized lattices in quantum phase space, drawing on Rieffel's non-commutative geometric results. They derive analytical logical operators from the symplectic dual lattice, obtain Clifford-Gaussian gates from lattice symmetries, show code dimension equals the lattice covolume, and organize syndrome subspaces as a vector bundle. The construction is often interpretable as concatenating a given stabilizer code with a GKP code, applying lattice-theoretic results, then unconcatenating. They also apply Construction A to half the Golay code coordinates to build an oscillator-qubit code.
AI.result: The framework produces oscillator-rotor, rotor-qudit, and oscillator-rotor-qubit codes that are indecomposable under generalized Clifford transformations, plus an oscillator-qubit code from a partially lifted Golay code. It formulates distances, optimal decoding, and quantum weight enumerators, recovering Pauli, qudit, and GKP versions along with known MacWilliams identities. Finite-energy codewords are constructed whose encoding is an isometry up to an error exponentially small in the inverse damping parameter.
AI.conclusion: A single lattice-based stabilizer formalism unifies discrete and continuous-variable quantum error correction, extends to hybrid rotor systems, explains prior results as concatenation/unconcatenation of GKP codes, and provides practical tools (logical operators, gates, distances, decoders, weight enumerators) with exponentially accurate finite-energy encodings.

title: Sum-of-squares compilation of matrix-model dynamics for NISQ and fault-tolerant hardware
summary: The SU$(N)$ matrix-model potential $V=-\tfrac{g^2}{4}\sum_{I,J}Tr[X_I,X_J]^2$, the interaction of the BFSS/BMN family, whose thermal large-$N$ states are dual to black holes, is diagonal in the coordinate basis and is compiled in the literature as a phase polynomial with $O(d^2N^4Q^4)$ rotations per Trotter step. That cost is close to optimal for its gate class: we show that for a generic Trotter step the Walsh support $m_{\min}$ lower-bounds both the rotation count and the two-qubit count of every circuit over $\{CNOT,CZ,CPhase,R_{ZZ},SWAP,X,R_z\}$, ancillas included, and we build a parity network attaining $1.01$--$1.10\,m_{\min}$. Improvement therefore requires a gate outside that class, and the exact factorisation of $V$ into a sum of squared commutator entries supplies one in each era. For NISQ, Hadamard: each squared entry is added into a Fourier register and squared there, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^3)$ two-qubit gates. For fault tolerance, $T$: reversible arithmetic with one phase-gradient injection per squared entry, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^2)$ T gates and no arbitrary-angle rotation. Both are built and verified. With a native $R_{ZZ}$ the NISQ circuit uses fewer two-qubit gates than every parity network from $Q=6$ at SU(2) and $Q=2$ at SU(5); the oracle beats a precision-matched Hamming-weight-phasing incumbent at every point built except the smallest, by up to $11.9\times$ in T count and, at equal width, $25.5\times$ in surface-code spacetime. An ablation with the same arithmetic but no factorisation costs up to $21\times$ more and loses to that incumbent at $15$ of $17$ points, so the factorisation, not the arithmetic, produces the win. Both constructions survive the supersymmetric deformation to mini-BMN with fermions, and complete Trotter evolutions on a statevector simulator reproduce the exact product formula to $2\times10^{-12}$.

AI.tldr: The SU(N) BFSS/BMN matrix-model potential's phase-polynomial compilation is near-optimal for the Clifford+Rz gate class, provably lower-bounded by the Walsh support m_min. To beat it, the authors exploit the exact factorisation of V into squared commutator entries, yielding a NISQ circuit (Θ(d²N³Q³) two-qubit gates) and a fault-tolerant circuit (Θ(d²N³Q²) T gates, no arbitrary rotations), both verified and superior to incumbents.
AI.motivation: The interaction V of the BFSS/BMN matrix-model family, whose thermal large-N states are dual to black holes, is diagonal in the coordinate basis but compiles to a phase polynomial with O(d²N⁴Q⁴) rotations per Trotter step. This cost is shown to be close to optimal for its gate class, so further improvement demands a gate outside that class, motivating a new construction.
AI.method: The authors (1) prove that for a generic Trotter step the Walsh support m_min lower-bounds both rotation and two-qubit counts of any circuit over {CNOT,CZ,CPhase,R_ZZ,SWAP,X,R_z}, ancillas included, and build a parity network attaining 1.01–1.10 m_min; (2) exploit the exact factorisation of V into a sum of squared commutator entries to introduce new gates: for NISQ, Hadamard-based addition of each squared entry into a Fourier register and squaring there; for fault tolerance, reversible arithmetic with one phase-gradient injection per squared entry.
AI.result: The NISQ circuit uses fewer two-qubit gates than every parity network from Q=6 (SU(2)) and Q=2 (SU(5)) with native R_ZZ. The oracle beats a precision-matched Hamming-weight-phasing incumbent at every built point except the smallest, by up to 11.9× in T count and, at equal width, 25.5× in surface-code spacetime. An ablation without factorisation costs up to 21× more and loses at 15 of 17 points, confirming the factorisation drives the win. Both constructions survive supersymmetric deformation to mini-BMN with fermions, and full Trotter evolutions reproduce the exact product formula to 2×10⁻¹².
AI.conclusion: The exact factorisation of V into squared commutator entries provides gates outside the near-optimal phase-polynomial class, enabling asymptotically better circuit costs: Θ(d²N³Q³) two-qubit gates (NISQ) and Θ(d²N³Q²) T gates with no arbitrary-angle rotations (fault tolerance). These constructions are verified, extensible to mini-BMN with fermions, and empirically outperform existing incumbents, establishing factorisation—not arithmetic—as the source of the advantage.

title: Topology-independent quantum advantage in communication networks
summary: Quantum communication can outperform classical communication in a variety of information-processing tasks, but such advantages are typically established for a fixed communication network. Here we introduce topology-independent quantum advantage, in which a quantum protocol outperforms every classical protocol subject to the same communication constraint, irrespective of how the classical communication resource is distributed among the parties or which communication topology is employed, even when the parties may share unlimited classical randomness. We first demonstrate this phenomenon through a simple three-party equality task: two senders receive ternary classical inputs, while an input-free receiver determines whether the inputs are equal. We then formulate a general framework for topology-independent communication and completely characterize the corresponding classical correlation polytope in the minimal three-party scenario. Its facet inequalities reveal several instances of topology-independent quantum advantage. Remarkably, one of these inequalities enables the semi-device-independent certification of a nonunitary quantum channel, while another certifies a sequential quantum network topology without any prior assumption about the network configuration. Finally, we extend the framework to four-party networks, characterize the relevant classical communication structures, and identify a communication task exhibiting quantum advantages against all admissible classical topologies. Our results establish topology independence as a genuine and robust form of quantum advantage in communication networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "topology-independent quantum advantage," where a quantum protocol beats every classical protocol under the same communication constraint regardless of resource distribution or topology, demonstrated via a three-party equality task and extended to four-party networks.
AI.motivation: Quantum advantages in communication are usually established for a fixed network, leaving open whether quantum protocols can outperform classical ones irrespective of how classical communication resources are distributed or which topology is used.
AI.method: The authors define topology-independent quantum advantage, illustrate it with a three-party equality task (two senders with ternary inputs, an input-free receiver deciding equality), formulate a general framework for topology-independent communication, and characterize the classical correlation polytope in the minimal three-party scenario via facet inequalities. They extend the framework to four-party networks and characterize relevant classical communication structures.
AI.result: They completely characterize the classical correlation polytope in the minimal three-party scenario; its facet inequalities reveal several instances of topology-independent quantum advantage. One inequality enables semi-device-independent certification of a nonunitary quantum channel, and another certifies a sequential quantum network topology without prior assumptions. In four-party networks, they identify a communication task exhibiting quantum advantages against all admissible classical topologies.
AI.conclusion: Topology independence is established as a genuine and robust form of quantum advantage in communication networks.

title: Record consistency under repeated readout and apparatus composition
summary: No-signalling constraints on isolated outcome probabilities do not determine whether an apparatus preserves the joint law of its accessible records under repeated readout, network composition, or reuse. We study these extensions through a conditional-record criterion and four explicit models. For a wrapped-Cauchy retrocausal source, protection under two conditionally independent continuous readouts forces an angle-independent response; three readouts suffice without continuity. A finite angular-bandwidth assumption gives a quantitative leakage bound, whereas continuity alone gives no uniform stability. At a specified two-source Bell junction, the required correction matrix has full nonnegative rank on every even uniform angular grid. A Gaussian controller can cancel branch-mass dependence while leaving a distinguishable joint record, for which we derive exact noise and law-change tradeoffs. Finally, a fixed singlet with shared classical noise reproduces the variable-width isolated outcome family, but retained and refreshed controllers generate different temporal statistics. We prove a finite-resource obstruction and construct positive finite-controller approximations. Numerical studies comprising 8.3 million independent simulated histories support the model-specific predictions. Together, the results identify conditions that must accompany marginal no-signalling when extending an apparatus to richer records and interventions.

AI.tldr: Marginal no-signalling does not fix the joint law of accessible records across readout, network composition, or reuse; a conditional-record criterion and four explicit models identify additional conditions required, supported by 8.3 million simulated histories.
AI.motivation: No-signalling constraints acting only on isolated outcome probabilities are insufficient to determine whether an apparatus preserves the joint law of its accessible records under repeated readout, network composition, or reuse. The paper seeks conditions that must accompany marginal no-signalling when an apparatus is extended to richer records and interventions.
AI.method: A conditional-record criterion plus four explicit models: (1) a wrapped-Cauchy retrocausal source tested under conditionally independent continuous readouts; (2) a finite angular-bandwidth leakage analysis; (3) a two-source Bell junction whose required correction matrix is analyzed via nonnegative rank on even uniform angular grids; (4) a Gaussian controller canceling branch-mass dependence, and a fixed singlet with shared classical noise compared against retained versus refreshed controllers, including a finite-resource obstruction and positive finite-controller approximations.
AI.result: For the wrapped-Cauchy source, protection under two conditionally independent continuous readouts forces an angle-independent response, while three readouts suffice without continuity; finite angular bandwidth yields a quantitative leakage bound, whereas continuity alone gives no uniform stability. The Bell-junction correction matrix has full nonnegative rank on every even uniform angular grid. The Gaussian controller cancels branch-mass dependence yet leaves a distinguishable joint record, with exact noise and law-change tradeoffs. The singlet with shared classical noise reproduces the variable-width isolated outcome family, but retained and refreshed controllers yield different temporal statistics. A finite-resource obstruction is proven and positive finite-controller approximations constructed, with 8.3 million simulated histories supporting the model-specific predictions.
AI.conclusion: Marginal no-signalling alone is insufficient for extending an apparatus to richer records and interventions; the work identifies the supplementary conditions (e.g., continuity, bandwidth, controller retention/refresh structure) that must accompany it, delineated across four explicit models.

title: Competing pathways in polaritonic chemistry and general harmonic environments
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Supplemental: 25 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables
summary: Recent experiments suggest that strong light-matter coupling between molecules and cavity modes can significantly modify chemical reaction rates and yields. Despite multiple proposed mechanisms, a clear microscopic understanding of how vibrational strong coupling alters reaction kinetics remains incomplete. Here, we employ a general quantum-dynamical framework for analyzing competing reaction pathways in polaritonic chemistry by considering reaction coordinates with multiple relevant transition frequencies and general harmonic environments. We extend on a tensor-network formulation of the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) method to compute probability currents between vibrational states, leveraging a concise formulation for effective spectral densities and a controlled compression of Markovian bath modes into system-level jump operators. This allows us to decompose the resulting state-to-state probability currents, revealing how cavity-induced changes in individual transitions propagate through multistep reaction networks. We find that these local modifications can alter kinetic bottlenecks and selectively redistribute reaction flux between competing pathways, changing branching ratios under irreversible conditions without substantially affecting the equilibrium yield in the reversible regime. Finally, for coupled reaction-coordinate, spectator-mode, and cavity environments, we find structured, asymmetric rate profiles arising from interference between hybridized decay channels. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding pathway-specific chemical reactivity under vibrational strong coupling.

AI.tldr: This work develops a tensor-network HEOM framework to compute vibrational-state probability currents in polaritonic chemistry, showing how cavity-induced changes in individual transitions propagate through multistep reaction networks, selectively redistributing flux and altering branching ratios.
AI.motivation: Strong light-matter coupling between molecules and cavity modes has been proposed to modify chemical reaction rates and yields, but a clear microscopic understanding of how vibrational strong coupling alters reaction kinetics remains incomplete.
AI.method: A general quantum-dynamical framework for competing reaction pathways in polaritonic chemistry, considering reaction coordinates with multiple relevant transition frequencies and general harmonic environments. The authors extend a tensor-network formulation of the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) method to compute probability currents between vibrational states, using a concise formulation for effective spectral densities and controlled compression of Markovian bath modes into system-level jump operators, enabling decomposition of state-to-state probability currents.
AI.result: Local cavity-induced modifications of individual transitions can alter kinetic bottlenecks and selectively redistribute reaction flux between competing pathways, changing branching ratios under irreversible conditions without substantially affecting equilibrium yield in the reversible regime. For coupled reaction-coordinate, spectator-mode, and cavity environments, structured asymmetric rate profiles emerge from interference between hybridized decay channels.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding pathway-specific chemical reactivity under vibrational strong coupling.

title: Sidewall spacer passivated epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions for superconducting qubit applications
summary: Epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions are promising alternatives to conventional Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions for superconducting qubits due to their crystalline tunnel barriers and the high transition temperature of NbN. However, their integration into quantum circuits typically requires complex fabrication processes involving amorphous interlayer dielectrics, which can degrade qubit coherence times. To address these issues, we developed sidewall spacer passivated epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN junctions using a fabrication process that reduces both the volume of amorphous dielectric material and fabrication complexity. The fabricated junctions exhibited a large gap voltage of approximately 5.6 mV and low subgap leakage currents. By varying the thickness of the AlN tunnel barrier, high-quality junctions were fabricated over a wide range of critical current densities ${\it J}_c$, from 0.3 to 10$^4$ A/cm$^2$. In addition, the comparison of the current-voltage characteristics before and after buffered hydrofluoric acid treatment indicated that the wet etching process did not degrade the electrical characteristics of the junctions. These results establish a scalable fabrication process for epitaxial Josephson junctions and provide a promising platform for high-coherence nitride-based superconducting qubits.

AI.tldr: Epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions were fabricated with a sidewall spacer passivation process that reduces amorphous dielectric volume and fabrication complexity, yielding high-quality junctions across a wide range of critical current densities.
AI.motivation: Epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN junctions are attractive alternatives to Al/AlOx/Al junctions for superconducting qubits due to crystalline tunnel barriers and NbN's high transition temperature, but their circuit integration typically requires complex fabrication with amorphous interlayer dielectrics that can degrade qubit coherence times.
AI.method: The authors developed sidewall spacer passivated epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN junctions using a fabrication process that minimizes amorphous dielectric volume and reduces process complexity. Junction quality was assessed by measuring gap voltage, subgap leakage, and current-voltage characteristics across varied AlN tunnel barrier thicknesses, including before and after buffered hydrofluoric acid treatment.
AI.result: The junctions exhibited a large gap voltage of ~5.6 mV and low subgap leakage currents. By varying AlN barrier thickness, high-quality junctions were achieved over a wide critical current density range from 0.3 to 10^4 A/cm^2. Comparison of current-voltage characteristics before and after buffered hydrofluoric acid treatment showed no degradation from the wet etching process.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a scalable fabrication process for epitaxial Josephson junctions and provide a promising platform for high-coherence nitride-based superconducting qubits.

title: Epitaxial NbN-junction-based self-shunted superconducting flux qubit with high anharmonicity
summary: We report a demonstration of a self-shunted superconducting flux qubit (SSFQ) as an ultracompact, strongly anharmonic, and long-lifetime qubit by using the full epitaxially grown NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions. The NbN-junction-based SSFQ achieved a high anharmonicity of 797 MHz as well as drastically reduced footprint of the qubit compared to capacitively shunted (C-shunt) flux qubits with a large shunt capacitor. The lifetime of the SSFQ reached 13 - 25 $μ$s, which is comparable to or relatively higher than that of NbN-based C-shunt flux qubits and Al-based flux qubits with more than 10 times smaller junctions. This indicates that the large epitaxial NbN-based junction can be adopted for SSFQ as well as merged-element transmon with the relatively large junctions. The results presented in this work will offer a new choice of the scalable qubits as well as the material platform toward the realization of large-scale superconducting quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a self-shunted superconducting flux qubit (SSFQ) using fully epitaxial NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions, achieving high anharmonicity (797 MHz), an ultracompact footprint, and long lifetimes (13–25 μs), positioning epitaxial NbN junctions as a viable scalable qubit platform.
AI.motivation: Conventional capacitively shunted (C-shunt) flux qubits rely on large shunt capacitors, which increase the device footprint and hinder scalability. There is a need for ultracompact, strongly anharmonic, long-lifetime qubits that can be scaled up for large-scale superconducting quantum computers.
AI.method: The authors fabricated a self-shunted superconducting flux qubit (SSFQ) based entirely on epitaxially grown NbN/AlN/NbN Josephson junctions, eliminating the need for an external shunt capacitor. They characterized its anharmonicity, footprint, and lifetime, and compared these metrics with those of NbN-based C-shunt flux qubits and Al-based flux qubits having much smaller junctions.
AI.result: The NbN-junction-based SSFQ achieved a high anharmonicity of 797 MHz and a drastically reduced footprint compared to C-shunt flux qubits with large shunt capacitors. Its lifetime reached 13–25 μs, comparable to or higher than that of NbN-based C-shunt flux qubits and Al-based flux qubits with more than 10 times smaller junctions.
AI.conclusion: Large epitaxial NbN-based junctions are suitable not only for SSFQs but also for merged-element transmons with relatively large junctions. This work offers a new choice of scalable qubits and material platform for realizing large-scale superconducting quantum computers.

title: Entanglement-of-formation potentials for feedback-assisted classical communication and randomness distillation
summary: We develop entanglement-of-formation potentials for feedback-assisted classical communication and one-way randomness distillation. For a finite-dimensional quantum channel without initial shared entanglement, an exact amortization theorem bounds the increase of message information plus entanglement remaining across the communicating laboratories. This proves a classical-feedback capacity bound using a mixed-convex-roof expression previously studied by Winter and Yang in the context of potential capacities. We determine the capacity of flagged mixtures of noiseless and entanglement-breaking channels, improve a published depolarizing-channel converse, and evaluate the new bound exactly for the amplitude damping channel. A state analogue gives a finite-blocklength upper bound on the net shared randomness obtainable with one-way classical communication. Amplitude-damping Choi states provide exact benchmarks, while a full-rank generalized amplitude-damping Choi state demonstrates a useful improvement where we do not evaluate the operational rate exactly. We also distinguish one-way from two-way randomness distillation: a two-round weak-measurement protocol strictly exceeds the exact one-way rate of every nontrivial qubit isotropic state. The protocol preserves quantum side information during its first decoding and extracts additional randomness in the reverse direction. This shows why the one-way state potential is not a general two-way converse. Together, these results establish a common entanglement-based approach to sharper communication and randomness bounds, while revealing how retained quantum correlations enable two-way distillation to surpass one-way limits.

AI.tldr: The paper develops entanglement-of-formation potentials that unify converses for feedback-assisted classical communication and one-way randomness distillation, yielding exact capacities, improved bounds, and a separation between one-way and two-way randomness distillation.
AI.motivation: Existing converse bounds for feedback-assisted classical communication and one-way randomness distillation are often loose or channel-specific. A common entanglement-based framework is needed to obtain sharper, more widely applicable capacity bounds and to clarify the operational distinction between one-way and two-way randomness distillation.
AI.method: The authors construct entanglement-of-formation potentials. For a finite-dimensional quantum channel without initial shared entanglement, they prove an exact amortization theorem bounding the increase of message information plus residual entanglement across the communicating laboratories. This yields a classical-feedback capacity bound via a mixed-convex-roof expression. A state analogue is derived for one-way randomness distillation. They evaluate these bounds on flagged mixtures of noiseless and entanglement-breaking channels, depolarizing channels, amplitude-damping channels, and their Choi states, and design a two-round weak-measurement protocol for two-way randomness distillation.
AI.result: The amortization theorem proves a classical-feedback capacity bound matching a mixed-convex-roof expression previously studied by Winter and Yang. The authors determine the capacity of flagged noiseless/entanglement-breaking mixtures, improve a published depolarizing-channel converse, and evaluate the new bound exactly for the amplitude-damping channel. The state analogue gives a finite-blocklength upper bound on net shared randomness under one-way classical communication, benchmarked exactly by amplitude-damping Choi states, while a full-rank generalized amplitude-damping Choi state shows improvement where the operational rate is not exactly evaluated. A two-round weak-measurement protocol strictly exceeds the exact one-way rate for every nontrivial qubit isotropic state.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-of-formation potentials provide a common entanglement-based approach to sharper communication and randomness bounds. Retained quantum correlations enable two-way randomness distillation to surpass one-way limits, showing that the one-way state potential is not a valid general two-way converse.

title: Quantum codes in the Lee metric
summary: We introduce a quantum coding framework for discrete small-shift noise, in which errors on qudits are modeled as low-weight $X$- and $Z$-type Pauli shifts, analogous to small phase-space displacements in continuous-variable systems. This structure is approximately respected by nuclear-spin noise and captured by the Lee metric, motivating a quantum extension of classical Lee-metric coding theory. We develop such a formalism for stabilizer codes over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ for arbitrary $q$, using joint and separate Lee metrics for the $X$- and $Z$-components of errors. For qubits, the joint metric counts $Y$ errors twice and can yield codes that detect and correct $X$ and $Z$ errors with fewer physical qubits than codes designed for the conventional Hamming metric. We discuss Lee-weight spreading under Clifford gates and qubitize codes over $\mathbb{Z}_4$ via the Gray map, finding codes with two-fold transversal non-qubit-Clifford gates. For quantum CSS Lee-LDPC codes on $n$ qudits, we prove that the Lee distance cannot exceed $O(n)$, uniformly in $q$, demonstrating an unexpected obstruction to using the large internal Hilbert space of a large-$q$ qudit to make high-Lee-distance codes. Under local Metropolis dynamics, certain classical $q$-ary ``helical repetition codes'' have exponentially long memory times at fixed temperature for sufficiently large $q$ (that grows with system length), which can be understood as spontaneous symmetry breaking at finite temperature, even in local one-dimensional models. Hypergraph products of these helical repetition codes provide local two-dimensional quantum codes that inherit self-correction for $Z$ errors, but self-correction for $X$ errors remains an open question.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum Lee-metric coding framework for qudits under small-shift noise, develops stabilizer codes over Z_q, proves an O(n) Lee-distance bound for CSS Lee-LDPC codes, and connects helical repetition codes to self-correction and finite-temperature symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: Discrete small-shift noise on qudits, such as nuclear-spin noise, is better captured by low-weight X- and Z-type Pauli shifts and the Lee metric than by the conventional Hamming metric, motivating a quantum extension of classical Lee-metric coding theory.
AI.method: The authors develop a stabilizer-code formalism over Z_q for arbitrary q using joint and separate Lee metrics on X and Z error components; analyze Lee-weight spreading under Clifford gates; qubitize Z_4 codes via the Gray map; examine quantum CSS Lee-LDPC codes; and study local Metropolis dynamics of q-ary helical repetition codes and hypergraph products.
AI.result: For qubits, the joint Lee metric counts Y errors twice and can correct X and Z errors using fewer physical qubits than Hamming-metric codes. Gray-map qubitization of Z_4 codes yields two-fold transversal non-qubit-Clifford gates. For CSS Lee-LDPC codes on n qudits, the Lee distance is proven to be at most O(n) uniformly in q, obstructing high-Lee-distance codes from large-q qudits. Classical q-ary helical repetition codes exhibit exponentially long memory times at fixed temperature for sufficiently large q, interpretable as finite-temperature spontaneous symmetry breaking in 1D. Their hypergraph products give local 2D quantum codes self-correcting for Z errors, while X-error self-correction remains open.
AI.conclusion: The Lee-metric quantum coding framework offers qubit-efficient stabilizer codes and transversal non-Clifford gates, but faces a fundamental O(n) Lee-distance limitation for CSS Lee-LDPC codes; helical repetition codes provide a route to 1D finite-temperature self-correction and 2D quantum codes with partial self-correction, leaving X-error self-correction unresolved.

title: Long-lived Coherent Phonons Reveal Competing Thermal and Many-Body Dynamics in $α$-In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$
summary: The fate of quantum coherence following photoexcitation is a central problem in nonequilibrium condensed-matter physics, especially in low-dimensional solids where electronic, structural and many-body energy scales are strongly coupled. Here, we investigate this interplay in ferroelectric $α$-In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ using broadband transient-grating spectroscopy with $\sim$5 fs laser pulses. Photoexcitation launches pronounced oscillations dominated by a $\sim$104 cm$^{-1}$ mode that persists for several picoseconds. Measurements from 10 to 300 K show that its frequency remains nearly unchanged while its coherence is progressively suppressed, distinguishing the lattice coordinate from thermally activated dephasing. Varying excitation energy reveals a distinct crossover in which increasing photoexcitation progressively modifies and damps the coherent response. First-principles calculations assign the dominant oscillation to a 101.47 cm$^{-1}$ $Γ$-point optical phonon involving collective In-Se displacement, while quantum-dynamical simulations reproduce the main transient-grating oscillations. These results establish $α$-In$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ as a model system for independently probing lattice coherence, thermal fluctuations and carrier-density-dependent interactions, revealing how a polar van der Waals semiconductor evolves from coherent lattice motion toward an incoherent many-body state after ultrafast excitation.

AI.tldr: Broadband transient-grating spectroscopy with ~5 fs pulses on ferroelectric α-In₂Se₃ reveals a dominant ~104 cm⁻¹ coherent phonon mode that persists for picoseconds, remains frequency-stable from 10–300 K while dephasing is progressively suppressed, and crosses over to an incoherent many-body state at higher excitation density.
AI.motivation: The fate of quantum coherence after photoexcitation is a central problem in nonequilibrium condensed-matter physics, particularly in low-dimensional solids where electronic, structural, and many-body energy scales are strongly coupled. α-In₂Se₃ is attractive as a model system because its polar van der Waals structure and ferroelectricity allow separate probing of lattice coherence, thermal fluctuations, and carrier-density-dependent interactions.
AI.method: Broadband transient-grating spectroscopy with ~5 fs laser pulses; temperature-dependent measurements from 10 to 300 K; variation of excitation energy/density; first-principles calculations assigning the dominant mode; quantum-dynamical simulations reproducing the transient-grating oscillations.
AI.result: Photoexcitation launches pronounced oscillations dominated by a ~104 cm⁻¹ mode persisting for several picoseconds. From 10 to 300 K its frequency is nearly unchanged while coherence is progressively suppressed, distinguishing a lattice coordinate from thermally activated dephasing. Varying excitation energy produces a distinct crossover in which increasing photoexcitation modifies and damps the coherent response. Calculations assign the dominant oscillation to a 101.47 cm⁻¹ Γ-point optical phonon involving collective In-Se displacement.
AI.conclusion: α-In₂Se₃ serves as a model system for independently probing lattice coherence, thermal fluctuations, and carrier-density-dependent interactions, showing how a polar van der Waals semiconductor evolves from coherent lattice motion toward an incoherent many-body state after ultrafast excitation.

title: Custom Penalty QAOA via Walsh-Hadamard Transform
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Submission to QIP 27. Subject to major changes
summary: Inequality constraints in combinatorial optimization are conventionally handled by introducing slack variables and quadratic penalties, which increase the qubit count and distort the optimization landscape. Slack-free formulations instead apply a nonlinear custom penalty function directly to the constraint, which are difficult to be implemented in quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). We show that the Walsh--Hadamard transform (WHT) removes this obstruction for any penalty function: a penalty applied to a linear constraint is exactly a weighted sum of Pauli-$Z$ strings. We propose this framework as the Walsh custom penalty QAOA (WCP-QAOA). Truncating the expansion at Walsh degree $k$ costs $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$ Pauli terms and leaves the qubit count untouched. The truncation is the optimal degree-$k$ approximation of the penalty in $L^2$, and we give a condition on the discarded Walsh coefficients under which the truncated Hamiltonian still ranks every feasible solution below every infeasible one. Since evaluating a Walsh coefficient from its definition requires all $2^n$ penalty values, we give an algorithm that returns any coefficient in sub-exponential time, so that the degree-$k$ Hamiltonian is obtained in time polynomial in $n$ for fixed $k$. We show that for the exponential penalty, there exists a closed product form of WHT, and hence a closed form expression to calculate the Walsh coefficients. We identify structural shortcuts that shorten the exact spectrum. We also tested WCP-QAOA in solving a 6-qubit knapsack problem.

AI.tldr: WCP-QAOA uses the Walsh–Hadamard transform to express any penalty on a linear constraint as a weighted sum of Pauli-Z strings, yielding slack-free QAOA formulations with a Walsh-degree-k truncation that preserves qubit count and feasible/infeasible ranking.
AI.motivation: Conventional handling of inequality constraints via slack variables and quadratic penalties increases qubit count and distorts the optimization landscape. Slack-free nonlinear custom penalties evade this but are hard to implement in QAOA. The paper aims to remove this implementation obstruction.
AI.method: The Walsh–Hadamard transform (WHT) is applied to express a penalty on a linear constraint exactly as a weighted sum of Pauli-Z strings. This is proposed as Walsh custom penalty QAOA (WCP-QAOA). The Walsh expansion is truncated at degree k, costing O(n^k) Pauli terms, and the truncation is shown to be the optimal degree-k L^2 approximation of the penalty. A sub-exponential-time algorithm computes any single Walsh coefficient, giving the degree-k Hamiltonian in polynomial time for fixed k. For the exponential penalty, a closed product form of the WHT and closed-form Walsh coefficients are derived, and structural shortcuts shorten the exact spectrum.
AI.result: Truncation at Walsh degree k leaves qubit count unchanged and uses O(n^k) Pauli terms. A condition on discarded Walsh coefficients guarantees the truncated Hamiltonian still ranks every feasible solution below every infeasible one. Walsh coefficients are computable in sub-exponential time in general and polynomial time for fixed k; the exponential penalty admits closed-form coefficients. WCP-QAOA is tested on a 6-qubit knapsack problem.
AI.conclusion: WHT provides an exact, slack-free Pauli-Z decomposition of arbitrary linear-constraint penalties, enabling practically implementable QAOA with controlled truncation error, preserved qubit count, and provable feasibility ordering under a stated spectral condition.

title: Pairwise detection, chiral conversion: Resource theory of quantum multistates
summary: Basis-independent coherence of a quantum multistate is fixed by whether its constituent states commute, and for qubits it is detected by pairwise state overlaps alone. What governs its deterministic transformation has been open. We give the exact resource-conversion theory of quantum multistates under common commutativity-preserving operations (CPOs). For qubits, pairwise Bargmann invariants determine the singular values of the unique candidate channel, while a single third-order Bargmann phase determines its orientation. Complete positivity then yields a necessary and sufficient criterion for exact conversion. The criterion identifies a chirality-sensitive shell $\mathcal C_{\rm chir}$, within which targets with identical pairwise geometry can differ in convertibility solely by the sign of their cubic invariant. This yields an order separation, $k_{\rm detect}=2<3=k_{\rm convert}$, for qubit multistates of every size $n\geqslant3$. The chirality-sensitive shell occupies exactly one third of the singular-value simplex, while mirror reflection obstructs two thirds of the admissible orientation-preserving transformations by volume. For $d\geqslant3$, by contrast, the structure is rigid: every resourceful conversion is realized by either an isotropic depolarizing or a transpose-depolarizing channel. Convertibility is then decided by centered Bargmann invariants of degree at most $d^2$.

AI.tldr: This paper develops the exact resource-conversion theory for quantum multistates under commutativity-preserving operations (CPOs), showing that for qubits convertibility is governed by Bargmann invariants (pairwise overlaps for detection, cubic invariant for orientation), yielding a chirality-sensitive convertibility shell and an order separation k_detect=2<3=k_convert, while for d>=3 conversions are rigid and decided by centered Bargmann invariants of degree at most d^2.
AI.motivation: While basis-independent coherence of a quantum multistate is fixed by whether its constituent states commute—and for qubits is detected by pairwise state overlaps alone—what governs its deterministic transformation had remained open. This work aims to fill that gap by providing the exact resource-conversion theory.
AI.method: The authors derive the exact resource-conversion theory of quantum multistates under common commutativity-preserving operations (CPOs). For qubits, they show pairwise Bargmann invariants determine the singular values of the unique candidate channel and a single third-order Bargmann phase determines its orientation; complete positivity then gives a necessary and sufficient conversion criterion. For d>=3, they characterize the structure of realizable channels.
AI.result: For qubits, the conversion criterion identifies a chirality-sensitive shell C_chir in which targets with identical pairwise geometry can differ in convertibility solely by the sign of their cubic invariant, giving an order separation k_detect=2<3=k_convert for all n>=3. The chirality-sensitive shell occupies exactly one third of the singular-value simplex, and mirror reflection obstructs two thirds of admissible orientation-preserving transformations by volume. For d>=3, every resourceful conversion is realized by either an isotropic depolarizing or a transpose-depolarizing channel, and convertibility is decided by centered Bargmann invariants of degree at most d^2.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic transformation of quantum multistates under CPOs is fully characterized: qubit convertibility is chirality-sensitive and governed by Bargmann invariants with a detection-vs-conversion order gap, whereas higher-dimensional (d>=3) conversions are rigid, realized only by depolarizing-type channels and decided by low-degree centered Bargmann invariants.

title: Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness
summary: The quantum PCP conjecture is one of the major open problems in quantum complexity theory. It has resisted attack in part because many primitives used in the proof of the classical PCP theorem, such as locality-preserving gap amplification and alphabet reduction, have no obvious quantum analogues due to quantum no-cloning. Locality-preserving gap amplification is a procedure that takes as input a local Hamiltonian problem instance and produces a new instance with a larger promise gap, without increasing the locality of the Hamiltonian, and instead moderately increasing its local qudit dimension. Obtaining this kind of control over the locality during gap amplification is critical to the success of many known strategies for proving the classical PCP theorem. In this work, we put forth the first known viable template for quantum locality-preserving gap amplification, and we prove that our procedure amplifies the combinatorial gap of local Hamiltonians. Our work introduces a new framework for reasoning about quantum gap amplification in terms of fault-tolerant computation, and illuminates a route toward importing one of the central ingredients in classical PCPs into the quantum setting. In particular, we build upon ideas from the recent classical PCP of Bafna--Minzer--Vyas based on high-dimensional expanders, and the circuit-to-Hamiltonian construction of Anshu--Breuckmann--Nguyen, in addition to several recent advances in quantum coding theory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a viable template for quantum locality-preserving gap amplification and proves it amplifies the combinatorial gap of local Hamiltonians, offering a route to import a central classical PCP ingredient into the quantum setting.
AI.motivation: The quantum PCP conjecture remains a major open problem, partly because key primitives from the classical PCP theorem—such as locality-preserving gap amplification and alphabet reduction—lack obvious quantum analogues due to quantum no-cloning. In particular, achieving gap amplification while controlling locality is critical for known classical PCP strategies, and no quantum analogue was previously available.
AI.method: The authors introduce a framework for reasoning about quantum gap amplification in terms of fault-tolerant computation. Their construction builds on ideas from the classical PCP of Bafna–Minzer–Vyas based on high-dimensional expanders, the circuit-to-Hamiltonian construction of Anshu–Breuckmann–Nguyen, and recent advances in quantum coding theory.
AI.result: They present the first known viable template for quantum locality-preserving gap amplification, which takes a local Hamiltonian instance and produces a new instance with a larger promise gap without increasing locality, instead moderately increasing the local qudit dimension. They prove their procedure amplifies the combinatorial gap of local Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a new framework for quantum gap amplification via fault-tolerant computation and illuminates a route toward importing a central ingredient of classical PCPs into the quantum setting, contributing toward the quantum PCP conjecture.

title: Improved Upper and Lower Bounds for Quantum Convex-Body Volume Estimation
summary: Estimating the volume of a high-dimensional convex body is a fundamental problem in theoretical computer science. Given a quantum membership oracle for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, we show that estimating $\mathrm{vol}(K)$ to relative error $\varepsilon$ takes $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}+d^{3/2}/\varepsilon)$ queries. This improves the previous quantum upper bound $\widetilde O(d^3+d^{9/4}/\varepsilon)$ of Chakrabarti et al. (ACM TQC 2023) and Cornelissen--Hamoudi (SODA 2023), and achieves a larger quantum speedup over the currently best classical upper bound $\widetilde O(d^{7/2}+d^3/\varepsilon^2)$ of Jia et al. (JACM 2026). Our quantum algorithm combines two new ingredients: an input-dependent effective spectral-gap analysis of quantum walks based on uniform classical warm-start mixing bounds, and a single quantum estimator for products of normalizer ratios in simulated annealing based on classical bridge sampling. We also prove an $Ω(d)$ quantum query lower bound for constant relative error, improving the previous $Ω(\sqrt d)$ lower bound.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a quantum membership-oracle algorithm that estimates the volume of a d-dimensional convex body to relative error ε using Õ(d^{5/2} + d^{3/2}/ε) queries, improving prior quantum upper bounds and achieving a larger quantum speedup over the best classical bound.
AI.motivation: Volume estimation for high-dimensional convex bodies is a fundamental problem in theoretical computer science. The work aims to reduce the quantum query complexity of this task, improve the quantum speedup relative to classical algorithms, and strengthen quantum query lower bounds.
AI.method: The quantum algorithm combines two new ingredients: (1) an input-dependent effective spectral-gap analysis of quantum walks based on uniform classical warm-start mixing bounds, and (2) a single quantum estimator for products of normalizer ratios in simulated annealing based on classical bridge sampling.
AI.result: The algorithm estimates vol(K) to relative error ε in Õ(d^{5/2} + d^{3/2}/ε) quantum membership queries, improving the previous quantum upper bound Õ(d^3 + d^{9/4}/ε) of Chakrabarti et al. (ACM TQC 2023) and Cornelissen–Hamoudi (SODA 2023), and yielding a larger quantum speedup over the best classical upper bound Õ(d^{7/2} + d^3/ε^2) of Jia et al. (JACM 2026). It also proves an Ω(d) quantum query lower bound for constant relative error, improving the previous Ω(√d) lower bound.
AI.conclusion: The paper advances quantum convex body volume estimation by lowering the query complexity upper bound and strengthening the matching lower bound, thereby enlarging the demonstrated quantum advantage over classical methods.

title: Blind Remote Implementation of Arbitrary Two-Qubit Unitary Operation via Pre-Shared Entanglement
summary: We propose a protocol for the remote implementation of an arbitrary two-qubit unitary operation using pre-shared entanglement. In our protocol, Bob possesses an unknown two-qubit state, while Alice implements the required operations using calibrated black-box devices. Alice does not need to know the parameters of these operations, and Bob's unknown state never leaves his laboratory. The protocol is based on the Euler decomposition of single-qubit unitary operations and the Cartan decomposition of two-qubit unitary operations. First, we construct protocols for the remote implementation of the single-qubit operation $U = R_z(γ)R_x(β)R_z(α)$ using pre-shared Bell states. We then construct a protocol for the two-qubit operation $R_{zz}(θ)$ using a single pre-shared Bell state and extend it to $R_{xx}(θ)$ and $R_{yy}(θ)$ through local unitary transformations. These elementary protocols are finally combined to implement an arbitrary two-qubit unitary operation. A third party, Charlie, determines the required decomposition and provides Alice with the corresponding black-box devices before the protocol begins. Thus, neither Alice nor Bob requires the classical description of the unitary operation.

AI.tldr: A protocol for remotely implementing an arbitrary two-qubit unitary on Bob's unknown state using pre-shared entanglement, where Alice operates calibrated black-box devices without knowing the operation parameters and Bob's state stays local.
AI.motivation: To enable remote implementation of an arbitrary two-qubit unitary operation while preserving privacy: Alice should not know the operation parameters, and Bob's unknown two-qubit state should never leave his laboratory.
AI.method: The protocol uses pre-shared entanglement and relies on Euler decomposition of single-qubit unitaries and Cartan decomposition of two-qubit unitaries. It first builds a protocol for single-qubit U = R_z(γ)R_x(β)R_z(α) using pre-shared Bell states, then a protocol for R_zz(θ) using a single pre-shared Bell state, extended to R_xx(θ) and R_yy(θ) via local unitary transformations. These elementary protocols are combined to realize an arbitrary two-qubit unitary. A third party, Charlie, determines the decomposition and supplies Alice with the corresponding black-box devices beforehand.
AI.result: Elementary protocols for single-qubit Euler-decomposed operations and for R_zz(θ) (plus R_xx(θ), R_yy(θ)) are constructed and combined into a protocol for an arbitrary two-qubit unitary operation.
AI.conclusion: Arbitrary two-qubit unitary operations can be remotely implemented with pre-shared entanglement, black-box devices, and a third party's decomposition, so neither Alice nor Bob needs the classical description of the unitary operation.

title: The power of time reversal in Hamiltonian property testing
summary: Quantum algorithms enable Heisenberg-limited scaling across many tasks in sensing and learning, achieving precision $\varepsilon$ using $O(1/\varepsilon)$ total evolution time. However, in Hamiltonian property testing, the best known algorithms have $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, unless it is possible to $\textit{reverse}$ the flow of time under the Hamiltonian. In this work, we prove that time reversal is necessary to close this gap. We establish evolution time lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, for a continuous family of error metrics ranging from average- to worst-case. We also prove matching upper bounds for Hamiltonian certification in all cases, both with and without time reversal, showing that the advantage from time reversal persists. Our results follow from a new Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, which is sensitive to time reversal and applicable beyond Hamiltonian property testing. This gives an alternative proof that inverses are required for amplitude amplification and estimation, improving the lower bounds of Tang and Wright and extending to fractional queries. We also show that, for unstructured search, uncertainty in the phase of the oracle destroys the quantum speedup without inverse queries, even when the oracle is fixed and coherent. Our work rigorously establishes time reversal as a resource governing both the precision of quantum measurement and the robustness of quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: This work proves that time reversal (Hamiltonian inverse) is a necessary resource for achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling in Hamiltonian property testing, establishing matching lower and upper bounds via a new Fourier-analytic framework for continuous-time quantum lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Sensing and learning tasks achieve Heisenberg-limited O(1/ε) evolution time, but Hamiltonian property testing appears stuck at O(1/ε²) unless time reversal is available. Whether this gap is fundamental—i.e., whether time reversal is truly necessary—was an open question.
AI.method: A new Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, sensitive to time reversal, yielding evolution-time lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing across a continuous family of error metrics (average- to worst-case). Matching upper bounds for Hamiltonian certification are also established, with and without time reversal.
AI.result: Time reversal is proven necessary to close the O(1/ε²)-to-O(1/ε) gap. Matching upper bounds confirm the time-reversal advantage persists. The framework also yields an alternative proof that inverses are required for amplitude amplification and estimation, improving prior bounds of Tang and Wright and extending to fractional queries. For unstructured search, phase uncertainty of the oracle destroys quantum speedup without inverse queries, even for a fixed coherent oracle.
AI.conclusion: Time reversal is rigorously established as a resource governing both the precision of quantum measurement and the robustness of quantum algorithms.

title: Arbitrary-phase CZ gate and remote readout across spatially separated superconducting nodes
summary: Establishing a complete set of gates across spatially separated quantum nodes is fundamental for distributed quantum computation and communication networks.
