One of the approaches to do so consists of employing a superconducting device as a universal quantum node that is capable of storing and processing quantum information, and traveling microwave photons as means of communication. In this work, we realize an entangling gate across a primitive two-node superconducting circuit QED network consisting of two dilution cryostats, A and B, connected via a 30-m-long cryogenic quantum link. We perform a bidirectional photon transfer protocol, where a microwave photon emitted by the communication qubit at A acquires a conditional phase based on the state of qubit B. We vary the communication photon frequency, hence tuning the conditional phase acquired during the reflection off the remote node, effectively implementing an arbitrary-phase CZ gate. We use this entangling operation to perform single-shot readout of the qubit in node B from node A. An interesting feature of our scheme is that it does not require precise synchronization of the active node with the remote node; in particular, remote readout can be performed without any active participation by the remote node. These protocols add to the quantum communication toolbox with superconducting circuits and provide a way of realizing basic distributed quantum computing operations.

AI.tldr: The authors realize a bidirectional entangling CZ gate across two spatially separated superconducting quantum nodes connected by a 30-m cryogenic link, enabling remote single-shot qubit readout without active participation of the remote node.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computation and communication require a complete gate set across spatially separated quantum nodes. A promising platform uses superconducting devices as universal quantum nodes and traveling microwave photons as communication carriers.
AI.method: A two-node superconducting circuit QED network was built using two dilution cryostats (A and B) linked by a 30-m-long cryogenic quantum link. A bidirectional photon transfer protocol was implemented: a microwave photon emitted by the communication qubit at node A acquires a conditional phase depending on the state of qubit B upon reflection off the remote node. By varying the communication photon frequency, the conditional phase is tuned, realizing an arbitrary-phase CZ gate.
AI.result: An entangling gate across the two-node network was demonstrated, and the entangling operation was used to perform single-shot readout of qubit B from node A. The protocol does not require precise synchronization of the active node with the remote node; remote readout proceeds without any active participation by the remote node.
AI.conclusion: The scheme expands the quantum communication toolbox with superconducting circuits and offers a route toward basic distributed quantum computing operations.

title: Process tensor simulations of non-Markovian open quantum systems with large uncoupled subspaces
summary: Process tensors in matrix product operator representation (PT-MPOs) are a powerful tool to calculate the temporal evolution and multi-time correlations of open quantum systems. While much progress has been made in making the calculation of process tensors for larger system dimensions possible, the numerical cost of the subsequent propagation of the system typically scales as $\mathcal{O}(d^6)$, which renders PT-MPO methods prohibitively expensive for system dimensions above several dozens. Here, we show how PT-MPO methods can be used efficiently when only some of the system states couple to the environment, and how combination with a Taylor expansion method allows for a reduction of the numerical complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$. We show that these methods enable efficient simulations of systems with several hundreds of states. This is particularly relevant for solid-state cavity-QED systems with multiple modes, or when calculating frequency-filtered correlation functions by coupling sensor systems to the system of interest.

AI.tldr: The paper presents methods to reduce the computational cost of propagating process tensors in matrix product operator representation from O(d^6) to O(d^3) by exploiting limited system-environment coupling and a Taylor expansion, enabling simulation of systems with several hundred states.
AI.motivation: Process tensors (PT-MPOs) can now be computed for larger system dimensions, but the subsequent propagation of the system scales as O(d^6), making PT-MPO methods prohibitively expensive for systems with more than several dozen dimensions. This bottleneck limits applications such as solid-state cavity-QED systems with multiple modes and frequency-filtered correlation calculations.
AI.method: The authors exploit the situation where only some of the system states couple to the environment, enabling efficient use of PT-MPO methods. They also combine this with a Taylor expansion method to reduce the numerical complexity of propagation from O(d^6) down to O(d^3).
AI.result: The proposed methods enable efficient simulations of open quantum systems with several hundreds of states, overcoming the previous dimensionality bottleneck of PT-MPO propagation.
AI.conclusion: Combining partial system-environment coupling with a Taylor expansion makes PT-MPO propagation tractable for large system dimensions, which is particularly relevant for multi-mode solid-state cavity-QED systems and for computing frequency-filtered correlation functions via coupled sensor systems.

title: Onset of a quantum Fisher-Selke sequence in the transverse-field ANNNI model and its bilayer
summary: We study the transverse-field axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising (ANNNI) model on the square lattice and on a bilayer. At the classical multiphase point $κ=J_2/J_0=1/2$, every configuration of straight domain walls that separates domains of at least two sites is a ground state. The walls are rigid, so perturbation theory in the transverse field $g=Γ/J_0$ can be carried out for each configuration separately, and we take it to order $g^8$. Quantum fluctuations select $\langle 3\rangle$ ($\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\downarrow\downarrow$) at order $g^2$, because spins next to a wall gain the most energy from virtual flips. The structures $\langle 23\rangle$, $\langle 223\rangle$ and $\langle 2223\rangle$ then open between $\langle 3\rangle$ and the antiphase $\langle 2\rangle$ at orders $g^4$, $g^6$ and $g^8$, in the order of the Fisher-Selke sequence of the classical three-dimensional model. A second layer suppresses each successive phase more strongly, beyond the stiffening of the local fields. We test the two widest phases with stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, comparing the free energies of the competing ordered states by thermodynamic integration, since annealing freezes in the modulation that forms at the ordering transition. The simulations reproduce the $\langle 3\rangle$ wedge to about 1%, and in a pre-registered test $\langle 23\rangle$ is stable at six of seven points, with the seventh resolved by post-hoc runs.

AI.tldr: The transverse-field ANNNI model at the classical multiphase point is studied via order-g^8 perturbation theory and quantum Monte Carlo, showing that quantum fluctuations select the <3> phase first, followed by <23>, <223>, <2223> in Fisher-Selke order; a second layer strongly suppresses successive phases.
AI.motivation: At the classical multiphase point κ=1/2 of the ANNNI model, infinitely many domain-wall configurations are degenerate ground states; the question is how quantum fluctuations (transverse field) lift this massive degeneracy and which modulated phases are selected.
AI.method: Perturbation theory in the transverse field g=Γ/J0 carried to order g^8, exploiting wall rigidity so each configuration can be treated separately, on both the square lattice and a bilayer. Stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo free-energy comparisons via thermodynamic integration (since annealing freezes the modulation) test the two widest phases.
AI.result: Quantum fluctuations select the <3> phase at order g^2; <23>, <223>, and <2223> open at orders g^4, g^6, g^8, following the Fisher-Selke sequence. A second layer suppresses each successive phase more strongly. QMC reproduces the <3> wedge to ~1%, and <23> is stable at six of seven pre-registered points (seventh resolved post-hoc).
AI.conclusion: Quantum fluctuations lift the classical multiphase degeneracy in a structured, layer-dependent way consistent with the Fisher-Selke sequence, and QMC validates the perturbative phase boundaries for the widest phases.

title: Phase-controlled recoverable entanglement in accelerated detector registers
summary: We study recoverable entanglement in a four-qubit cluster-state register whose two detector qubits couple to a scalar field. A local preparation phase leaves the initial reference--register entanglement and detector marginal unchanged, but controls protection under collective noise. At the optimal phase, a fixed decoder recovers a Bell pair after any channel preserving the singlet and triplet sectors. For uniformly accelerated detectors at finite separation, an exact trace-norm formula shows that the same phase is optimal at every time within the secular weak-coupling dynamics. Small separation produces a slow decay, whose rate and phase-dependent amplitude we derive. Matching the local response to an inertial thermal bath gives an analytic optimum time for the entanglement contrast. A detector measurement and conditional phase correction recover a two-qubit teleportation resource. Spatial smearing and an ordered weak-coupling then small-separation limit specify the microscopic scope of the lifetime prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes recoverable entanglement in a four-qubit cluster-state register with two detector qubits coupled to a scalar field, showing that an optimal local preparation phase enables a fixed decoder to recover a Bell pair, and derives exact trace-norm decay formulas, an optimal-time result via inertial-bath matching, and conditions for a teleportation resource under collective noise and acceleration.
AI.motivation: Detector qubits coupled to quantum fields suffer entanglement degradation from collective noise and acceleration, so it is important to identify preparation conditions and decoders that protect and recover useful entanglement in a register, and to characterize how spatial separation and detector response set the recoverable lifetime.
AI.method: A four-qubit cluster-state register with two detector qubits coupled to a scalar field is used. A local preparation phase is applied that leaves the initial reference-register entanglement and detector marginal unchanged but controls protection against collective noise. For uniformly accelerated detectors at finite separation, an exact trace-norm formula is derived within secular weak-coupling dynamics. The local detector response is matched to an inertial thermal bath to obtain an analytic optimum time for the entanglement contrast. A detector measurement followed by conditional phase correction is used to recover a two-qubit teleportation resource. Spatial smearing and an ordered weak-coupling-then-small-separation limit specify the microscopic scope of the lifetime prediction.
AI.result: At the optimal preparation phase, a fixed decoder recovers a Bell pair after any channel preserving the singlet and triplet sectors; the same phase is optimal at every time in the secular weak-coupling regime. Small detector separation yields a slow decay, and its rate and phase-dependent amplitude are derived. Inertial-bath matching gives an analytic optimum time for the entanglement contrast. Measurement plus conditional phase correction yields a recoverable two-qubit teleportation resource. Smearing and the ordered limits constrain the validity range of the lifetime prediction.
AI.conclusion: A suitably chosen local preparation phase provides robust, decoder-fixed entanglement recovery against collective noise, and the optimum persists over time for accelerated detectors at finite separation; the recoverable entanglement enables teleportation, with the lifetime prediction valid under specified spatial-smearing and weak-coupling, small-separation conditions.

title: The quantum-classical bipartite universe and the logical emergence of $\hbar$ from classical temporality
summary: We present a foundational reinterpretation of quantum dynamics based on the standard von Neumann formalism, positing a structural logical bipartition between a classical observational environment and a quantum observed system. Against universalist frameworks, we show that theoretical consistency requires distinct propositional logics: Boolean logic governs the environment, while non-Boolean logic applies to the observed system. Within this framework, an ideal classical clock is represented as an open system whose energy spectrum is uniformly discretized. The dynamics follow from the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation under the constraint that the Hamiltonian remains observable. Although the clock's temporal evolution is driven by dissipative coupling to the measurement apparatus, it admits a stable, deterministic solution corresponding to information-preserving cyclic dynamics. This deterministic regime emerges as a logical attractor, stabilized by the Boolean structure inherent to the measurement interaction. Ultimately, $\hbar$ is derived as a fundamental scaling parameter from the classical clock's action-angle commutation relation, revealing that the quantum of action reflects the discrete logical structure underlying classical temporality. Furthermore, this framework establishes an exact mapping with 't Hooft's cellular automaton formalism, offering an alternative ontological interpretation that not require hidden variables and superdeterministic assumptions. The resulting distinction between quantum dynamics (as potential recontextualization) and classical dynamics (as temporal actualization) provides a novel logical approach to the measurement problem.

AI.tldr: The paper reinterprets quantum dynamics via a logical bipartition between a Boolean classical environment and a non-Boolean quantum system, deriving a stable cyclic clock from the GKSL equation, recovering ħ as a scaling parameter, and mapping onto 't Hooft's cellular automaton without hidden variables.
AI.motivation: The measurement problem and the tension between quantum and classical descriptions motivate a foundational reinterpretation. The authors seek a logically consistent framework that avoids universalist assumptions, hidden variables, and superdeterminism while grounding the quantum-classical distinction in propositional logic.
AI.method: They posit a structural logical bipartition: Boolean logic for the observational environment, non-Boolean logic for the observed system. An ideal classical clock is modeled as an open system with uniformly discretized energy spectrum, evolved under the GKSL master equation with the Hamiltonian constrained to remain observable. They analyze the emergence of a deterministic cyclic solution as a logical attractor and derive ħ from the classical clock's action-angle commutation relation, then establish an exact mapping to 't Hooft's cellular automaton.
AI.result: The dissipatively driven clock admits a stable, deterministic, information-preserving cyclic dynamics stabilized by the Boolean measurement structure. ħ emerges as a fundamental scaling parameter from the action-angle commutation relation, and an exact correspondence with 't Hooft's cellular automaton is established.
AI.conclusion: Quantum dynamics is characterized as potential recontextualization and classical dynamics as temporal actualization, yielding a novel logical approach to the measurement problem. The framework offers an ontological interpretation requiring neither hidden variables nor superdeterministic assumptions, and reinterprets the quantum of action as reflecting the discrete logical structure of classical temporality.

title: JAQSI: Just Another Quantum Simulator
summary: Classical simulation supports the development and validation of quantum algorithms through full-state inspection, controlled noise models and backpropagation, albeit for small quantum systems. Existing frameworks offer gate-level execution, differentiable pulse-level dynamics or optimised hardware execution. Just another quantum simulator (JAQSI) combines gate- and pulse-level simulation in one differentiable circuit model built upon JAX. Circuits are represented as pure functions of numerical inputs which support vectorised batches and JIT compilation. Within a single circuit, matrix-defined operations, gates synthesised from Hamiltonian time evolution and noise channels can be composed freely. For a fast simulation, gate and channel fusion reduces passes over the state, while adjoint differentiation computes expectation-value gradients with a constant number of statevectors. At pulse level, JAQSI reduces evolution under single-term Hamiltonians to a scalar pulse-area integral and reuses cached execution plans and compiled solvers. In a benchmark we compare JAQSI with PennyLane, Qiskit, Qibo, Qulacs, QuTiP and dynamiqs. At gate level, we observe performance either on par or an order of magnitude faster across statevector, density, noise and gradient simulation than the compared simulators up to 12 qubits. Beyond 18 qubits, JAQSI is on par with PennyLane Lightning in both statevector and gradient simulation. In the statevector and noisy density-matrix pulse benchmarks, it is at least 5 times faster than the other simulators, even with its closed-form solve disabled. Disabling the latter increases its runtime by at most a factor of 1.5. We provide JAQSI as open-source software on GitHub and PyPI.

AI.tldr: JAQSI is a differentiable, JAX-based quantum simulator unifying gate- and pulse-level simulation, achieving up to order-of-magnitude speedups over existing simulators via circuit fusion and adjoint differentiation.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation enables quantum algorithm development via full-state inspection, noise models, and backpropagation, but existing frameworks typically separate gate-level, pulse-level, or hardware execution, lacking a unified differentiable model.
AI.method: JAQSI builds a single differentiable circuit model on JAX, representing circuits as pure functions of numerical inputs supporting vectorised batches and JIT compilation. It composes matrix-defined operations, Hamiltonian-synthesised gates, and noise channels; uses gate/channel fusion to reduce state passes; applies adjoint differentiation for constant-statevector gradient computation; and reduces single-term Hamiltonian evolution to a scalar pulse-area integral with cached plans and compiled solvers.
AI.result: Benchmarked against PennyLane, Qiskit, Qibo, Qulacs, QuTiP, and dynamiqs: gate-level performance is on par or up to 10x faster for statevector, density, noise, and gradient simulation up to 12 qubits; beyond 18 qubits, matches PennyLane Lightning; pulse benchmarks (statevector and noisy density-matrix) are at least 5x faster even with closed-form solve disabled, and disabling it increases runtime by at most 1.5x.
AI.conclusion: JAQSI unifies gate- and pulse-level differentiable simulation with strong performance and is released as open-source software on GitHub and PyPI.

title: The magic cost of fermionic randomness
summary: Sampling-based quantum advantage raises a basic resource question: how much non-Gaussianity is needed to reproduce the random-matrix statistics often associated with quantum chaos? Passive fermionic linear optics preserves Gaussian structure, and even Haar-random mode mixing fails to anticoncentrate for Slater inputs. We show that overcoming this obstruction requires an extensive input resource. For any pure half-filled input state, the one-body defect $ν$, defined as the summed occupation variance of the natural orbitals, must scale linearly with system size. For products of bounded-size blocks on $4N$ modes, this condition is also sufficient, with normalized collision moment asymptotic to $2N/ν$, compared with the Porter-Thomas value 2. For four-mode products, the full Porter-Thomas moment hierarchy is recovered precisely when the defect density tends to its maximum. Assuming average-case hardness, approximate classical sampling remains hard near maximal density, with an error tolerance that increases with the density. Two-copy number fluctuations measure $ν$ directly, and the same quantity lower-bounds the combined cost of non-Gaussian resource modes and parity-preserving local gates in deterministic exact preparation. Fermionic randomness therefore carries an extensive magic cost, with a quantitative link between sampling statistics, preparation resources, and an experimentally accessible witness.

AI.tldr: Reproducing random-matrix (Porter-Thomas) statistics via sampling with passive fermionic linear optics requires an extensive non-Gaussianity resource: the one-body defect ν must scale linearly with system size, is sufficient for block-product states, and is directly measurable via two-copy number fluctuations.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based quantum advantage raises the question of how much non-Gaussianity is needed to reproduce random-matrix statistics associated with quantum chaos. Passive fermionic linear optics preserves Gaussian structure, and even Haar-random mode mixing fails to anticoncentrate for Slater inputs, leaving open what resource overcomes this obstruction.
AI.method: Define the one-body defect ν as the summed occupation variance of the natural orbitals of any pure half-filled input state, and analyze its required scaling with system size. For products of bounded-size blocks on 4N modes, derive the normalized collision moment asymptotically, and for four-mode products examine the full Porter-Thomas moment hierarchy. Relate ν to two-copy number fluctuations, to hardness error tolerance, and to a lower bound on the combined cost of non-Gaussian resource modes and parity-preserving local gates in deterministic exact preparation.
AI.result: Overcoming the anticoncentration obstruction requires ν to scale linearly with system size for any pure half-filled input. For products of bounded-size blocks on 4N modes this condition is also sufficient, with normalized collision moment asymptotic to 2N/ν versus the Porter-Thomas value 2. For four-mode products the full Porter-Thomas moment hierarchy is recovered precisely when defect density tends to its maximum. Assuming average-case hardness, approximate classical sampling remains hard near maximal density, with error tolerance increasing with density. Two-copy number fluctuations measure ν directly.
AI.conclusion: Fermionic randomness carries an extensive magic cost, providing a quantitative link between sampling statistics, preparation resources, and an experimentally accessible witness. ν also lower-bounds the combined cost of non-Gaussian resource modes and parity-preserving local gates in deterministic exact preparation.

title: Training Variational Quantum Algorithms Is NP-Hard, Even Locally
summary: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) generally rely on classical optimization to train parameterized quantum circuits. This training seeks to minimize an objective function, and its efficiency is central to the practical success of these algorithms. However, globally minimizing such training objectives over the circuit parameters is known to be $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, limiting the prospect of general guarantees for efficient training. In this Letter, we prove that even the weaker task of finding a local minimum of such VQA training objectives is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, including when the objective admits efficient classical evaluation. Moreover, we show that this hardness persists even for the task of finding a parameter vector within $\ell_p$-distance strictly less than $π/2$ of some local minimizer, for every $p\geq 1$. Our central technical result is that approximating a local minimizer of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. By explicitly constructing quantum circuits whose training objectives reproduce these hard instances, we obtain a polynomial-time reduction to VQA training. Our results establish a fundamental computational barrier to variational quantum training: even reaching the vicinity of a local minimum remains hard in the worst case.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that finding even a local minimum of VQA training objectives—or any parameter vector within ℓ_p-distance less than π/2 of one—is strongly NP-hard, even when the objective is classically efficiently evaluable, via a reduction from approximating local minimizers of Hermitian trigonometric polynomials.
AI.motivation: VQAs rely on classical optimization to train parameterized quantum circuits, and this training efficiency determines their practical success. While global minimization of such objectives is known to be NP-hard, it was unclear whether the weaker task of merely reaching a local minimum might remain tractable. The authors aim to close this gap by characterizing the hardness of local optimization itself.
AI.method: The central technical result is that approximating a local minimizer of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial is strongly NP-hard. The authors then explicitly construct quantum circuits whose VQA training objectives reproduce these hard instances, yielding a polynomial-time reduction to VQA training. This reduction accounts for objectives admitting efficient classical evaluation and extends the hardness to finding parameters within ℓ_p-distance strictly less than π/2 of a local minimizer for every p ≥ 1.
AI.result: Finding a local minimum of VQA training objectives is strongly NP-hard, even for classically efficiently evaluable objectives. Moreover, the hardness persists for the relaxed task of finding a parameter vector within ℓ_p-distance strictly less than π/2 of some local minimizer, for every p ≥ 1.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a fundamental computational barrier to variational quantum training: even reaching the vicinity of a local minimum remains hard in the worst case, tempering prospects for general efficiency guarantees in VQA optimization.

title: The diffusive spectral gap of the qubit eSWAP chain
summary: We prove that the second-moment Hamiltonian of the open qubit eSWAP chain has a diffusive spectral gap, resolving a conjecture of Li, Zheng, Liu, Jiang, and Liu. We also characterise the ground space on every connected interaction graph with at least five vertices and prove a uniform lower bound for the unnormalised complete-graph gap. We apply these results to sequential and brickwork circuits and prove that the periodic chain also has a diffusive spectral gap.

AI.tldr: The authors prove a diffusive spectral gap for the second-moment Hamiltonian of the open qubit eSWAP chain, confirming a conjecture, and characterize its ground space on general connected interaction graphs.
AI.motivation: To resolve a conjecture of Li, Zheng, Liu, Jiang, and Liu regarding the diffusive spectral gap of the second-moment Hamiltonian of the open qubit eSWAP chain.
AI.method: Spectral analysis of the second-moment Hamiltonian; characterization of the ground space on every connected interaction graph with at least five vertices; derivation of a uniform lower bound for the unnormalised complete-graph gap; application to sequential and brickwork circuits.
AI.result: The second-moment Hamiltonian of the open qubit eSWAP chain has a diffusive spectral gap; the ground space is characterized for connected interaction graphs with at least five vertices; a uniform lower bound for the unnormalised complete-graph gap is obtained; the periodic chain also has a diffusive spectral gap.
AI.conclusion: The conjecture is affirmed, and the results extend to sequential, brickwork, and periodic circuit settings, establishing diffusive spectral gaps in these cases.

title: On the Completeness of Quantum Mechanics: Sources, Records and Probabilities
summary: Can quantum mechanics be complete without being fundamental? Under stated source, detector, and statistical conditions, we reconstruct the quantum representation and Born probabilities and prove complete algebraic closure of the admitted quantum predictions without requiring a collapse postulate. We further show that many familiar quantum paradoxes arise from conflating coherent processes with retained records or probabilities with realized outcomes. We also ask whether mathematics as a whole, or the source architecture itself, emerges from a deeper structure.

AI.tldr: Quantum mechanics can be reconstructed as a complete and algebraically closed predictive framework under specified source, detector, and statistical conditions, without needing a collapse postulate; familiar paradoxes stem from conflating coherent processes with retained records and probabilities with realized outcomes.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses whether quantum mechanics can be complete without being fundamental, motivated by questions about the necessity of the collapse postulate and the origin of familiar quantum paradoxes.
AI.method: The authors reconstruct the quantum representation and Born probabilities under stated source, detector, and statistical conditions, then prove the complete algebraic closure of the admitted quantum predictions without invoking a collapse postulate. They analyze paradoxes by distinguishing coherent processes from retained records and probabilities from realized outcomes, and finally probe whether mathematics or the source architecture emerges from a deeper structure.
AI.result: The reconstruction yields complete algebraic closure of quantum predictions without a collapse postulate, and many familiar quantum paradoxes are shown to arise from conflating coherent processes with retained records or probabilities with realized outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics can be complete without being fundamental, requiring no collapse postulate under the stated conditions; apparent paradoxes are artifacts of conceptual conflation, and the paper raises the open question of whether mathematics or the source architecture emerges from a deeper structure.

title: Error-Transparent Code Switching Between Permutation-Invariant Codes with Transversal Clifford and Icosahedral Gates
summary: Code switching moves an encoded qubit between two codes whose transversal gates together are universal, but the switching operation itself is usually not transversal and can spread a single fault into an uncorrectable error. We study switching between two permutation-invariant codes on the same qubits, one with transversal Clifford gates and one with transversal gates from the non-Clifford binary icosahedral group. Both are compatible with transversal $X$, $Z$, and $F = HS^\dagger$, and the encoders with this property form a small linear space. We show that its codes of distance at least three are cut out by at most two quadratic equations, and that all of them have the same error geometry in the sense that their single-qubit error states have the same inner products. It follows that a switching unitary commuting with qubit permutations and with the shared transversal gates at every instant, and tolerating one single-qubit fault at an unknown time, exists if and only if the two codes are joined by a continuous path of distance-three codes. Such a switch can be made error transparent, so that a fault at any moment reaches the target code as the same single-qubit error. For real encoders, the distance-three codes are the solutions of a single quadratic equation, and on thirteen qubits, they form an explicit circle through two Clifford codes and an icosahedral code. We construct the switching unitary along this circle as a collective operator, leaving its synthesis into physical control open, and verify that its recovery infidelity per fault is at machine precision, whereas two natural alternatives leave average infidelities of $0.13$ and $0.85$. A survey over odd qubit numbers up to $29$ lists where such switches exist.

AI.tldr: The paper studies fault-tolerant code switching between two permutation-invariant codes sharing transversal X, Z, F gates, showing that error-transparent switching unitaries tolerating a single fault exist iff the two codes are connected by a continuous path of distance-three codes.
AI.motivation: Code switching between two codes with complementary transversal gates achieves universality, but the switching operation itself is typically non-transversal and can spread a single fault into an uncorrectable error. The paper aims to determine when a single-fault-tolerant, error-transparent switching unitary can exist.
AI.method: Restrict to permutation-invariant codes on the same qubits: one with transversal Clifford gates and one with transversal gates from the non-Clifford binary icosahedral group, both compatible with transversal X, Z, and F = HS^\dagger. Characterize encoders with this property as a small linear space, and analyze its distance-three codes via quadratic equations. Construct the switching unitary along a continuous path of distance-three codes (explicitly a circle on thirteen qubits through two Clifford codes and an icosahedral code), realized as a collective operator commuting with qubit permutations and shared transversal gates at every instant.
AI.result: Codes of distance at least three are cut out by at most two quadratic equations and share the same error geometry (single-qubit error states have identical inner products). An error-transparent switching unitary tolerating one single-qubit fault at an unknown time exists iff the two codes are joined by a continuous path of distance-three codes; such a fault reaches the target code as the same single-qubit error. For real encoders, distance-three codes solve a single quadratic equation; on thirteen qubits they form an explicit circle. The constructed switch achieves recovery infidelity per fault at machine precision, whereas two natural alternatives give average infidelities of 0.13 and 0.85. A survey of odd qubit numbers up to 29 identifies where such switches exist.
AI.conclusion: Single-fault-tolerant, error-transparent code switching between the two permutation-invariant codes is possible exactly when a continuous path of distance-three codes connects them. The explicit thirteen-qubit construction on a circle of real encoders attains machine-precision recovery infidelity, outperforming natural alternatives, though synthesis into physical control remains open. A survey up to 29 qubits maps the existence of such switches.

title: Universal and rigorous asymptotic convergence of standard macroscopic quantum electrodynamics to the modified Langevin noise formalism
summary: The standard Langevin noise formalism (LNF) is a well-established approach for macroscopic quantum electrodynamics in unbounded lossy media, and accordingly, its application to finite objects requires endowing the surrounding vacuum with a fictitious absorption that is taken to asymptotically vanish. Existing justifications for such a singular limiting procedure have been mainly restricted to phenomena governed by vacuum fluctuations and medium-induced interactions (Casimir-Polder forces, thermal radiation, quantum emitter dynamics, etc.), thereby strictly excluding scenarios that involve the scattering of external quantum radiation. Conversely, the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) has recently been established as the complete canonical quantum theory for arbitrary macroscopic systems and electromagnetic processes, entirely bypassing the need for limiting procedures, treating incident quantum radiation fields as independent degrees of freedom, and exactly reducing to the LNF for unbounded media. In this work, we demonstrate that the LNF limiting procedure is universally valid by showing that it recovers any physical prediction of the MLNF across all regimes, including arbitrary quantum scattering processes. Specifically, we introduce a suitable mapping associating any MLNF state and observable with a corresponding entity within the LNF augmented by fictitious vacuum absorption. We then rigorously prove that, as the fictitious absorption tends to zero, every LNF matrix element constructed via this mapping exactly converges to its MLNF original, so that the limiting procedure establishes the asymptotic convergence of the LNF to the MLNF.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the limiting procedure used in the standard Langevin noise formalism (LNF) — endowing surrounding vacuum with a fictitious absorption that asymptotically vanishes — is universally valid, recovering any prediction of the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF), including arbitrary quantum scattering processes, via an exact mapping as the fictitious absorption tends to zero.
AI.motivation: Existing justifications for the LNF limiting procedure were restricted to phenomena governed by vacuum fluctuations and medium-induced interactions (Casimir-Polder forces, thermal radiation, quantum emitter dynamics), strictly excluding scenarios involving scattering of external quantum radiation. Since the MLNF was recently established as the complete canonical quantum theory bypassing limiting procedures, a rigorous validation of the LNF limiting procedure across all regimes was needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce a suitable mapping that associates any MLNF state and observable with a corresponding entity within the LNF augmented by fictitious vacuum absorption. Using this mapping, they rigorously prove that as the fictitious absorption tends to zero, every LNF matrix element constructed via this mapping exactly converges to its MLNF original.
AI.result: The limiting procedure is shown to establish the asymptotic convergence of the LNF to the MLNF, demonstrating that the LNF limiting procedure is universally valid and recovers any physical prediction of the MLNF across all regimes, including arbitrary quantum scattering processes.
AI.conclusion: The LNF limiting procedure is universally valid, as it asymptotically converges exactly to the MLNF for all physical predictions, thereby extending its justification beyond vacuum-fluctuation and medium-induced phenomena to arbitrary quantum scattering processes.

title: Theory of the Edge-of-Chaos Advantage in Quantum Reservoir Computing
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, plus Supplemental Material (17 pages, 2 figures)
summary: Numerical studies suggest that quantum reservoir computing performs optimally near the edge of chaos, a behavior commonly attributed to a balance between memory retention and nonlinear information processing. Here we develop an explicit quantum reservoir model and rigorously analyze its chaotic regime and integrable point. In the chaotic regime, we show that Gaussian-unitary-ensemble statistics lead to rapid memory loss: learning performance decays exponentially with the storage time required by a temporal task. This decay limits the ability of chaotic reservoirs to learn long-range temporal dependencies. At the integrable point, described by a free-fermion model, we prove that amplitude encoding and a linear readout of fermionic two-point correlations cannot learn a representative class of nonlinear tasks coupling present and past inputs. Introducing interactions alleviates this obstruction. By identifying distinct limitations on memory retention in the chaotic regime and nonlinear processing at the integrable point, our analysis provides a theoretical basis for the observed edge-of-chaos advantage and guides the design of quantum reservoirs for temporal learning.

AI.tldr: This work develops an explicit quantum reservoir model and rigorously analyzes its chaotic and integrable limits, showing that chaos causes exponential memory loss while integrability obstructs nonlinear processing—together providing a theoretical basis for the edge-of-chaos advantage.
AI.motivation: Numerical studies suggest quantum reservoir computing performs best near the edge of chaos, but a rigorous theoretical explanation for this advantage has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors construct an explicit quantum reservoir model and analytically study two opposite regimes: a chaotic regime characterized by Gaussian-unitary-ensemble statistics, and an integrable point described by a free-fermion model. They analyze memory retention in the former and nonlinear learning capability (with amplitude encoding and linear readout of fermionic two-point correlations) in the latter.
AI.result: In the chaotic regime, GUE statistics induce rapid memory loss, with learning performance decaying exponentially as a function of the storage time required by a temporal task, limiting long-range temporal learning. At the integrable point, amplitude encoding with a linear readout of fermionic two-point correlations provably cannot learn a representative class of nonlinear tasks coupling present and past inputs; introducing interactions removes this obstruction.
AI.conclusion: By identifying distinct limitations—impaired memory retention under chaos and impaired nonlinear processing at the integrable point—the analysis provides a theoretical foundation for the edge-of-chaos advantage and offers guidance for designing quantum reservoirs for temporal learning.

title: Cups and Gates II: Operads, twists, and addressable intra-code gates
summary: In Part I, we introduced a general framework for constructing logical gates in quantum CSS codes from cohomology invariants, focusing on cup products and their generalizations from topological to qLDPC codes. In particular, we produced a family of $C^{k-1}Z$ logical gates that we called copy-cup on $k$ copies of the same quantum code implemented by finite-depth circuits. Here, we vastly extend this framework by introducing twists incorporating code automorphisms, higher twisted cohomology operations, and folding operations in relative cohomology. The framework includes operations lifting coefficients from $\mathbb{Z}/2$ to $\mathbb{Z}/2^k$, enabling all diagonal logical gates such as single-qubit rotations $\operatorname{R}(2π/2^k)$. Composing these operations with maps that select cohomology classes yields addressable logical gates. Examples include addressable $T$ gates on three- and four-tori and gates in qLDPC codes beyond topological ones. We introduce cohomology operations, such as the higher twisted Pontryagin powers, that to our knowledge have not previously appeared in the mathematics literature. These operations arise from $E_\infty$-structures on cochains, with explicit constructions using cyclic resolutions and the surjection operad. We expect these results to be of independent interest in homotopy theory. Our formalism applies much more broadly to chain complexes carrying suitable operadic structures, and we expect this operadic perspective to uncover further connections between homotopy theory and fault-tolerant quantum gates.

AI.tldr: This sequel extends a cohomology-based framework for logical gates in quantum CSS codes by introducing twists with code automorphisms, higher twisted cohomology operations, and folding in relative cohomology, enabling addressable diagonal logical gates such as R(2π/2^k) and T gates.
AI.motivation: Part I built a framework for logical gates in quantum CSS codes via cohomology invariants (cup products and generalizations) from topological to qLDPC codes, yielding copy-cup C^{k-1}Z gates on k copies. The authors aim to vastly broaden this framework to capture more general and addressable logical gates, including non-topological qLDPC codes.
AI.method: The authors introduce twists incorporating code automorphisms, higher twisted cohomology operations, and folding operations in relative cohomology. They include operations lifting coefficients from Z/2 to Z/2^k. These operations arise from E_infinity-structures on cochains, with explicit constructions using cyclic resolutions and the surjection operad; composing with maps selecting cohomology classes yields addressable logical gates. The formalism applies to chain complexes carrying suitable operadic structures.
AI.result: The framework produces all diagonal logical gates, including single-qubit rotations R(2π/2^k), and addressable logical gates via composition with class-selecting maps. Examples include addressable T gates on three- and four-tori and gates in qLDPC codes beyond topological ones. New cohomology operations, such as higher twisted Pontryagin powers, are introduced, which the authors believe have not previously appeared in the mathematics literature.
AI.conclusion: The extended framework unifies and generalizes the construction of fault-tolerant logical gates, linking homotopy theory and quantum error correction. The introduced operations are expected to be of independent interest in homotopy theory, and the operadic perspective is expected to reveal further connections between homotopy theory and fault-tolerant quantum gates.

title: Efficient Fidelity Estimation of General Quantum Resource States via Clifford Circuits
summary: Fidelity estimation is a fundamental tool for assessing quantum resource states across quantum information science. For small infidelity $ε$, tomography and direct fidelity estimation (DFE) have worst-case sample complexity $O(1/ε^2)$ at fixed relative accuracy and confidence. Direct target projections achieve $O(1/ε)$ but generally require non-Clifford operations whose reliability depends on the resource states that are typically the target of benchmarking. Here, we introduce the Bell--coherence fidelity estimation (BCFE) with optimal sample complexity $Θ(1/ε)$ using only Clifford gates and Pauli measurements. We prove that BCFE is applicable to arbitrary pure targets, possibly multi-qubit, with the statistical error of the single-copy coherence part explicitly controlled. To evaluate BCFE in a practical setting, we apply BCFE to analog rotation resource states in the candidate early-FTQC architecture called the Space-Time Efficient Analog Rotations (STAR) architecture. In the simulations using surface codes, BCFE is estimated to require up to approximately $27$ times fewer resource states than DFE for the same standard error in the infidelity estimate, while its estimates remain close to reference values despite circuit-level noise in the additional Bell measurement operations. These results support efficient resource benchmarking within fault-tolerant quantum computing.

AI.tldr: BCFE achieves optimal Θ(1/ε) sample complexity for fidelity estimation using only Clifford gates and Pauli measurements, applicable to arbitrary pure targets, and requires ~27× fewer resource states than DFE in the STAR architecture.
AI.motivation: Fidelity estimation is fundamental for assessing quantum resource states. Existing methods face trade-offs: tomography and DFE require O(1/ε²) samples, while direct target projections achieve O(1/ε) but rely on non-Clifford operations whose reliability depends on the very resource states being benchmarked.
AI.method: The paper introduces Bell-coherence fidelity estimation (BCFE), which uses only Clifford gates and Pauli measurements to achieve optimal Θ(1/ε) sample complexity. It proves BCFE applies to arbitrary pure targets (possibly multi-qubit) with explicitly controlled statistical error of the single-copy coherence part. BCFE is then evaluated on analog rotation resource states in the STAR architecture using surface code simulations.
AI.result: In surface code simulations, BCFE requires up to ~27× fewer resource states than DFE for the same standard error in the infidelity estimate. Its estimates remain close to reference values despite circuit-level noise in the additional Bell measurement operations.
AI.conclusion: BCFE enables efficient resource benchmarking within fault-tolerant quantum computing, achieving optimal sample complexity with only Clifford operations.

title: Complete Classification of Reversible Entanglement Transformations of Two Qutrits
comment: 22 pages, Comments and collaboration are welcome
summary: Suppose Alice and Bob can transform one shared mixed state into another by local operations and classical communication, and can also recover the first state from the second. What can change in such a conversion? We give a complete classification of reversible conversions between two-qutrit states. We consider exact deterministic LOCC transformations of a single copy, allowing finite protocols and the countable protocols specified here. Local flags are known to allow a separable part to be replaced by local preparation while an entangled block is retained. We prove that such a decomposition is necessary for two mutually convertible entangled states that are not locally unitarily equivalent. The two parts are distinguishable by local measurements. The entangled blocks have the same weight and are locally unitarily equivalent after normalization. Each entangled state has a unique smallest retained block. Two entangled states are reversibly convertible if and only if these unnormalized blocks are locally unitarily equivalent. For a state with negative partial transpose, the smallest block can be found using the negative eigenspace of its partial transpose and at most three matrix zero tests.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a complete classification of reversible LOCC conversions between two-qutrit states: two entangled states are mutually convertible iff their unique smallest retained entangled blocks (obtained by stripping a locally preparable separable part) are locally unitarily equivalent.
AI.motivation: LOCC transformations typically destroy information, but some conversions are reversible. The paper aims to understand exactly what can change—i.e., which structural features are invariant—when two shared mixed states can be interconverted and recovered, addressing the open question of classifying reversible conversions in the two-qutrit setting.
AI.method: Exact deterministic single-copy LOCC transformations are considered, allowing finite protocols and a specified class of countable protocols. Using local flags, a state is decomposed into a separable part replaceable by local preparation plus a retained entangled block. The authors prove necessity of such a decomposition for mutually convertible entangled states not locally unitarily equivalent, show the parts are locally distinguishable, and characterize the entangled blocks via weight and local unitary equivalence after normalization. For negative-partial-transpose states, the smallest retained block is identified using the negative eigenspace of the partial transpose and at most three matrix zero tests.
AI.result: Every entangled state has a unique smallest retained block. Two entangled two-qutrit states are reversibly convertible if and only if these unnormalized blocks are locally unitarily equivalent. The separable and entangled components are distinguishable by local measurements, and the entangled blocks share the same weight and are locally unitarily equivalent after normalization.
AI.conclusion: Reversible LOCC conversion between two-qutrit states is fully governed by the unique smallest retained entangled block, giving a complete classification. The decomposition into a locally preparable separable part and an invariant entangled block is necessary, and the criterion reduces to local unitary equivalence of unnormalized smallest blocks, with a tractable test for NPT states.

title: Origin and classification of fractional dynamical topology in non-Hermitian quantum systems
summary: Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPT) provide a fundamental framework for characterizing nonequilibrium critical phenomena, and have recently been extended to non-Hermitian systems. Half-integer jumps of the dynamical topological order parameter can arise in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, yet their origin in non-Hermitian settings remains unclear. Here, we investigate DQPTs in a two-band non-Hermitian model and show that these fractional jumps originate from the discontinuity in the complex energy spectrum. We demonstrate that this behavior is intrinsically linked to the steady-state phase diagram of the quench Hamiltonian, and also classify the occurrence of DQPT. We further extend our analysis to the multiband Hamiltonian and the two-dimensional model, providing a unified understanding of fractional dynamical topological signatures.

AI.tldr: This work clarifies the origin of half-integer jumps in the dynamical topological order parameter for non-Hermitian dynamical quantum phase transitions, linking them to discontinuities in the complex energy spectrum and the steady-state phase diagram.
AI.motivation: Half-integer jumps of the dynamical topological order parameter appear in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, but their origin in non-Hermitian settings remains unclear.
AI.method: Investigate DQPTs in a two-band non-Hermitian model, analyze the complex energy spectrum and its discontinuity, connect the behavior to the steady-state phase diagram of the quench Hamiltonian, classify DQPT occurrence, and extend the analysis to multiband and two-dimensional models.
AI.result: Fractional (half-integer) jumps originate from discontinuity in the complex energy spectrum, are intrinsically linked to the steady-state phase diagram of the quench Hamiltonian, and admit a classification of DQPT occurrence; the findings generalize to multiband and two-dimensional models.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a unified understanding of fractional dynamical topological signatures in non-Hermitian DQPTs.

title: Quantum n-coloring is undecidable for every n $\ge$ 3
summary: The quantum $n$-coloring problem, given graph $G$, asks whether there exists a perfect quantum strategy for the $n$-coloring game of $G$. Previously it was known that quantum $n$-coloring is undecidable only for $n=3$. We extend this to all $n\geq 3$ with one elementary reduction. Letting $G'=(G\square K_3)\lor K_{n-3}$, we show that $G$ is quantum $3$-colorable if and only if $G'$ is quantum $n$-colorable.

AI.tldr: Quantum n-coloring is undecidable for all n ≥ 3, extending the previously known case of n=3 via an elementary reduction G' = (G □ K_3) ∨ K_{n-3}.
AI.motivation: Prior work established the undecidability of quantum n-coloring only for the special case n=3. The authors aim to generalize this undecidability result to every n ≥ 3, providing a uniform and elementary proof covering all cases.
AI.method: The authors give an elementary reduction: from a graph G they construct G' = (G □ K_3) ∨ K_{n-3}, using the Cartesian product (□) with the triangle K_3 and the join (∨) with the complete graph K_{n-3}. They prove that G is quantum 3-colorable if and only if G' is quantum n-colorable, transferring the known undecidability from n=3 to arbitrary n ≥ 3.
AI.result: The equivalence G quantum 3-colorable ⇔ G' quantum n-colorable holds, establishing that the quantum n-coloring problem is undecidable for all n ≥ 3.
AI.conclusion: The undecidability of the quantum n-coloring problem is extended from n=3 to all n ≥ 3 by a single elementary reduction, yielding a unified treatment of the problem across all values n ≥ 3.

title: Fast Random Compilers for Time-Dependent and Time-Independent Lindbladian Simulation
comment: 43 pages. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Randomized product formulas provide simple and flexible methods for quantum simulation. While qDRIFT-type randomized simulation has been extended to Lindbladian dynamics, higher-order randomized compilers have primarily been developed for Hamiltonian simulation. In this work, we develop first- and second-order randomized sampling algorithms for Lindbladian simulation in both the time-independent and time-dependent settings. Building on first-order qDRIFT-type Lindbladian simulation, we introduce a qSWIFT-type second-order correction for time-independent Lindbladians with a finite local decomposition. For $λt \geq 1$, where $λ$ is the sum of the Hamiltonian coefficients and dissipative rates, the resulting approximation achieves normalized diamond-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ using $r=O(λ^2 t^2/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ time slices, improving the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ precision dependence of the first-order qDRIFT-type approximation. We then develop first- and second-order continuous-time sampling algorithms for general time-dependent Lindbladians, with the second-order construction likewise achieving an $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ dependence on the target precision in the number of time slices. We further extend the time-dependent construction to a linear-combination input model over local Hamiltonian and dissipative generators, allowing the randomized sampler to be formulated in terms of local evolutions rather than the full time-dependent Lindbladian. Because the second-order corrected maps need not be CPTP, we use them to estimate observable expectation values rather than to deterministically prepare output states.

AI.tldr: This work develops first- and second-order randomized sampling algorithms for Lindbladian (open-system) quantum simulation, in both time-independent and time-dependent settings, achieving improved precision scaling over first-order qDRIFT-type methods and providing a local-evolution formulation for time-dependent Lindbladians.
AI.motivation: Randomized product formulas are simple and flexible for quantum simulation, but while qDRIFT-type randomized simulation has been extended to Lindbladian dynamics, higher-order randomized compilers have largely been limited to Hamiltonian simulation. There is a need for higher-order randomized algorithms tailored to Lindbladians to obtain better precision scaling.
AI.method: The authors build on first-order qDRIFT-type Lindbladian simulation and introduce a qSWIFT-type second-order correction for time-independent Lindbladians with finite local decomposition. They then develop first- and second-order continuous-time sampling algorithms for general time-dependent Lindbladians, and extend the time-dependent construction to a linear-combination input model over local Hamiltonian and dissipative generators so the sampler can be expressed via local evolutions. Since second-order corrected maps need not be CPTP, they use them to estimate observable expectation values rather than deterministically preparing output states.
AI.result: For λt ≥ 1, where λ is the sum of Hamiltonian coefficients and dissipative rates, the time-independent second-order approximation achieves normalized diamond-norm error at most ε with r = O(λ²t²/√ε) time slices, improving the ε⁻¹ precision dependence of first-order qDRIFT-type approximation. The time-dependent second-order construction likewise achieves ε⁻¹/² precision dependence in the number of time slices.
AI.conclusion: Second-order randomized sampling algorithms for Lindbladian simulation improve precision scaling to ε⁻¹/² in the number of time slices, in both time-independent and time-dependent settings. The time-dependent construction supports a local linear-combination input model, and because the second-order corrected maps are not necessarily CPTP, the method is suited to estimating observable expectation values rather than deterministically preparing output states.

title: Demonstration of a Structured Agentic Workflow for Applied Quantum Computing Research
summary: Quantum hardware advances now make it practical to explore quantum approaches to scientific problems. Applied quantum computing research sits at the intersection of domain knowledge, algorithms, theoretical physics, device physics, and quantum and classical computational methods. The breadth of expertise required and the inherent project complexity challenge not only any individual researcher, but also generic AI systems. Here, we introduce the Quantum Agentic Operating System (QAOS), a structured agentic research system designed to address this challenge for quantum and computational R&D projects. QAOS is built around a nonlinear workflow graph of heterogeneous multi-agent nodes, with a controlled flow of context and computational resources. It decomposes a complex research project into sandboxed multi-agent tasks executed under constraints from the project graph, task-relevant methodologies, and necessary verification steps. We demonstrate QAOS on a quantum chemistry prototyping task, in which it is asked to set up a minimal model for a proton-transfer problem and to implement its solution using sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), together with classical reference methods such as FCI (exact diagonalization) and density functional theory (DFT). We compare the QAOS solution to those obtained with baseline agents (Claude Sonnet 5 with the Claude Code harness). In contrast to QAOS, the baseline agents silently ignore explicit instructions, and the runs show large variability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QAOS, an agentic operating system built on a nonlinear workflow graph of heterogeneous multi-agent nodes with controlled context and resource flow, and demonstrates it on a quantum chemistry prototyping task, outperforming baseline agents.
AI.motivation: Applied quantum computing R&D requires expertise spanning domain knowledge, algorithms, theoretical and device physics, and quantum/classical methods. This breadth and inherent project complexity challenge individual researchers and generic AI systems alike, motivating a structured agentic research system.
AI.method: QAOS is structured around a nonlinear workflow graph of heterogeneous multi-agent nodes, with controlled flow of context and computational resources. It decomposes complex research projects into sandboxed multi-agent tasks executed under constraints from the project graph, task-relevant methodologies, and necessary verification steps.
AI.result: QAOS was demonstrated on a quantum chemistry prototyping task: setting up a minimal model for a proton-transfer problem and implementing its solution using sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), alongside classical reference methods (FCI and DFT). Compared to baseline agents (Claude Sonnet 5 with the Claude Code harness), QAOS produced a coherent solution, whereas baselines silently ignored explicit instructions and showed large run-to-run variability.
AI.conclusion: QAOS provides a structured agentic approach that addresses the complexity and interdisciplinary demands of quantum R&D, yielding more reliable and instruction-adherent results than generic baseline agents.

title: Lifted surgery for non-Abelian two-block group-algebra codes
summary: Code surgery measures a logical operator of a quantum LDPC code with $O(d)$ rounds of syndrome extraction. Lifted surgery amortises this cost on Abelian group-algebra codes by measuring an orbit of logical operators under a translation symmetry in one merged code. We extend it to two-block group-algebra codes over non-Abelian groups and ask whether non-commutativity lets one merged code measure more operators than any Abelian group of its symmetries. We classify the block-affine automorphisms of these codes and find that, measured against this full group, most apparent non-Abelian gains disappear. We prove that the gain is at most the index of a largest Abelian subgroup. We find codes with exact distance up to $13$ where the gain is two, including codes in which one merged code reads out every logical qubit, and codes over products of $A_4$, $S_4$ and SL(2,3) with gain three for a best logical, up to $[[336,26,12]]$. A merged-distance lemma gives a simple condition for the gadget to preserve the code distance. In circuit-level simulations with Relay-BP decoding, at the error rates we can resolve, the non-Abelian gadget is as reliable as, or more reliable than, the Abelian gadgets it replaces within statistical error, while using two to three times fewer rounds.

AI.tldr: This paper extends lifted code surgery from Abelian to non-Abelian two-block group-algebra codes, classifying block-affine automorphisms to show non-commutativity yields limited gains (at most the index of a largest Abelian subgroup), and demonstrates codes with gain two to three and reliable circuit-level performance with fewer rounds.
AI.motivation: Code surgery measures a logical operator of a quantum LDPC code with O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction, and lifted surgery amortises this on Abelian group-algebra codes by measuring an orbit of logical operators under a translation symmetry in one merged code. The authors ask whether non-commutativity, by extending lifted surgery to two-block group-algebra codes over non-Abelian groups, allows one merged code to measure more operators than any Abelian group of its symmetries.
AI.method: The authors extend lifted surgery to two-block group-algebra codes over non-Abelian groups. They classify the block-affine automorphisms of these codes, measure gains against this full automorphism group, and prove a bound on the gain in terms of the index of a largest Abelian subgroup. They also introduce a merged-distance lemma giving a simple condition for the gadget to preserve code distance, and perform circuit-level simulations using Relay-BP decoding.
AI.result: Measured against the full block-affine automorphism group, most apparent non-Abelian gains disappear. The gain is proven to be at most the index of a largest Abelian subgroup. The authors find codes with exact distance up to 13 where the gain is two, including codes where one merged code reads out every logical qubit, and codes over products of A4, S4 and SL(2,3) with gain three for a best logical, up to [[336,26,12]]. In circuit-level simulations with Relay-BP decoding, at the error rates they can resolve, the non-Abelian gadget is as reliable as or more reliable than the Abelian gadgets it replaces within statistical error, while using two to three times fewer rounds.
AI.conclusion: Non-commutativity provides only limited advantages for lifted surgery: most apparent gains vanish against the full block-affine automorphism group, and the achievable gain is bounded by the index of a largest Abelian subgroup. Nonetheless, concrete non-Abelian codes achieve gain two to three while maintaining or improving reliability at a fraction of the rounds, suggesting practical benefits in syndrome-extraction cost.

title: Shallow Quantum Circuits for Geometrically Local Lindblad Dynamics
summary:
Open-system dynamics govern decoherence, transport, and engineered dissipation in quantum many-body systems. We propose a quantum algorithm for simulating time-independent, finite-range Lindblad dynamics with bounded local strength on a constant-dimensional lattice of $n$ sites, allowing noncommuting jump operators. For time $T\ge1$ and diamond-norm error at most $ε$, it has depth $O(T\operatorname{polylog}(nT/ε))$ and gate count $O(nT\operatorname{polylog}(nT/ε))$. These results extend the HHKL spatial decomposition to open systems. The main obstacle is that the reversible overlap corrections used for unitary dynamics have no direct analogue for dissipative channels. We overcome this by retaining the environment in a shared unitary dilation, keeping information lost from the system coherently available and making the spatial corrections reversible. We prove exponential occupation bounds for the environmental states generated by the decomposition, allowing compact representation and coherent simulation of local factors on the inputs that arise. The construction reduces each short-time evolution to a constant number of parallel layers on regions of logarithmic diameter, using nearest-neighbour gates and polylogarithmic auxiliary density.
  We also prove unconditional worst-case lower bounds using time-independent, purely dissipative processes that transport quantum information. For circuits with local quantum and classical communication, the lower bounds are $Ω(nT)$ for the expected gate count and $Ω(T)$ for depth on time scales up to the lattice diameter. They match the upper bounds' leading time and volume dependence up to polylogarithmic factors. At fixed time and sufficiently small fixed error, we further prove a depth lower bound of $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$, showing that global accuracy can require increasing depth as the lattice grows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum algorithm that simulates finite-range Lindblad (open-system) dynamics on a constant-dimensional lattice with depth O(T polylog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nT polylog(nT/ε)), extends the HHKL spatial decomposition to dissipative channels via a shared unitary dilation, and proves matching worst-case lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Open-system dynamics govern decoherence, transport, and engineered dissipation in quantum many-body systems, yet existing spatial-decomposition simulation techniques were developed for unitary (reversible) dynamics. The key obstacle is that the reversible overlap corrections central to the HHKL decomposition have no direct analogue for dissipative channels, so no efficient simulation with favorable depth/gate scaling was known for Lindblad dynamics with noncommuting jump operators.
AI.method: The authors design a quantum algorithm for time-independent, finite-range Lindblad dynamics with bounded local strength on a constant-dimensional lattice of n sites, permitting noncommuting jump operators. They extend the HHKL spatial decomposition to open systems by retaining the environment in a shared unitary dilation, keeping information lost from the system coherently available so that spatial corrections remain reversible. They prove exponential occupation bounds for the environmental states produced by the decomposition, enabling compact representation and coherent simulation of the arising local factors. Each short-time evolution is reduced to a constant number of parallel layers on regions of logarithmic diameter, using nearest-neighbour gates and polylogarithmic auxiliary density. Unconditional worst-case lower bounds are proved via time-independent, purely dissipative processes that transport quantum information.
AI.result: For time T ≥ 1 and diamond-norm error at most ε, the algorithm achieves depth O(T polylog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nT polylog(nT/ε)). The lower bounds are Ω(nT) for expected gate count and Ω(T) for depth (for local quantum and classical communication circuits) on time scales up to the lattice diameter, matching the upper bounds' leading time and volume dependence up to polylogarithmic factors. At fixed time and sufficiently small fixed error, a depth lower bound of Ω(log n / log log n) is proved, showing global accuracy can require increasing depth as the lattice grows.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first HHKL-style spatial decomposition for open-system (Lindblad) dynamics, achieving nearly linear-in-T depth and near-optimal gate complexity via a shared unitary dilation with exponential occupation bounds. The tight matching upper and lower bounds establish that the algorithm's leading time and volume scaling is essentially optimal for local quantum and classical communication circuits, and the Ω(log n / log log n) depth lower bound reveals a fundamental tradeoff whereby global accuracy demands growing depth with lattice size.

title: Minimax Quantum State Tomography in a Known Trace-Distance Ball
summary:
We study quantum state tomography when the unknown state lies in a trace-distance ball of radius $R$ around a known reference state $ρ$. For arbitrary collective measurements, we determine the minimax expected risk and confidence radius up to universal constants, uniformly over the dimension, center spectrum, radius, and sample size. Write $Γ=d(\mathrm{Tr}\sqrtρ)^2+d^2R$. For $d\ge2$, $0<R\le1$, and $n\ge1$ copies, the expected risk is $Θ(\min\{R,\sqrt{Γ/n}\})$. At failure probability $0<δ\le1/3$, the minimax confidence radius is \[
  Θ\!\left(\min\left\{R,\sqrt{\frac{Γ+\log(1/δ)}{n}}\right\}\right). \] For $\varepsilon\le c_0R$ with a universal $c_0>0$, the copy complexity is $Θ((Γ+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$. For the lower bound we use a weighted trace-norm witness to retain all spectral scales in a square-root perturbation family. For the upper bound, we give a direct spectral and concentration analysis of a modified existing purification-based procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves minimax optimal quantum state tomography for states in a trace-distance ball of radius $R$ around a known reference state, characterizing the expected risk, confidence radius, and copy complexity up to universal constants for arbitrary collective measurements.
AI.motivation: Quantum state tomography near a known reference state is practically important (e.g., verifying or refining a prepared state), but tight dimension-, spectrum-, radius-, and sample-size-uniform guarantees were lacking, especially capturing the mixed dependency on trace and dimension.
AI.method: Lower bound: a weighted trace-norm witness that preserves all spectral scales within a square-root perturbation family. Upper bound: a direct spectral and concentration analysis of a modified purification-based procedure, defining the key quantity $\Gamma = d(\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{\rho})^2 + d^2 R$.
AI.result: For $d\ge2$, $0<R\le1$, $n\ge1$ copies, expected risk is $\Theta(\min\{R,\sqrt{\Gamma/n}\})$; at failure probability $\delta$, minimax confidence radius is $\Theta(\min\{R,\sqrt{(\Gamma+\log(1/\delta))/n}\})$; for $\varepsilon\le c_0 R$, copy complexity is $\Theta((\Gamma+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)$, all uniform over dimension, center spectrum, radius, and sample size.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete minimax characterization of local quantum state tomography with arbitrary collective measurements, showing the optimal rates are governed by $\Gamma = d(\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{\rho})^2 + d^2 R$.

title: On State Distinguishing Without Inverse Queries
summary: In the quantum state distinguishing problem, an algorithm is given copies of a state $|ψ\rangle$ or $|φ\rangle$ separated by trace distance $\varepsilon$, and tasked with deciding which is the case. It is a standard result that $Θ(\varepsilon^{-2})$ copies are required, while having access to a unitary state preparation oracle and its inverse improves this to $Θ(\varepsilon^{-1})$ queries. We study the intermediate case with forward-only access, capturing scenarios where the oracle is a physical process that cannot be reversed. Tang and Wright recently showed that distinguishing a known state from an \emph{unknown} close state requires $Ω(\varepsilon^{-2})$ forward queries in high dimension; we strengthen this result by proving the same bound even when both states are known, as in the state distinguishing setting. Moreover, our lower bound uses a direct hybrid argument, avoiding advanced compressed oracle techniques used in the prior work. In contrast, we give a dimension-independent algorithm solving a continuous-time variant of state distinguishing with only $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ total forward evolution time. The algorithm uses quantum Zeno dynamics to confine evolution to a known two-dimensional subspace. Thus, a quadratic advantage survives without inverse access for a natural continuous-time analogue of state distinguishing.

AI.tldr: Distinguishing two known states separated by trace distance ε with forward-only oracle access requires Ω(ε⁻²) queries (proved via a direct hybrid argument), but a continuous-time analogue is solvable with O(ε⁻¹) forward evolution time using quantum Zeno dynamics.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum state distinguishing needs Θ(ε⁻²) copies, improved to Θ(ε⁻¹) with a reversible unitary state-preparation oracle. The paper addresses the intermediate regime of forward-only oracle access (irreversible physical processes). Prior work (Tang–Wright) proved Ω(ε⁻²) forward queries only for distinguishing a known state from an unknown close state in high dimension; it was open whether the stronger bound holds when both states are known.
AI.method: A direct hybrid argument establishes the Ω(ε⁻²) forward-query lower bound for distinguishing two known states, avoiding the advanced compressed-oracle machinery of prior work. For the continuous-time analogue, a dimension-independent algorithm uses quantum Zeno dynamics to confine evolution to a known two-dimensional subspace, achieving O(ε⁻¹) total forward evolution time.
AI.result: The Ω(ε⁻²) lower bound is strengthened to hold even when both states are known, matching the discrete state-distinguishing setting. Conversely, the continuous-time variant admits an algorithm with only O(ε⁻¹) forward evolution time, independent of dimension, recovering a quadratic advantage without inverse access.
AI.conclusion: Forward-only access generally forfeits the quadratic speedup for discrete state distinguishing, but a quadratic advantage survives for a natural continuous-time analogue, where quantum Zeno dynamics circumvents the need for oracle inversion.

title: Performance Analysis of Multiparty GHZ-State Quantum Conference Key Agreement over Optical Fiber Channel
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Communications [Under Review]
summary: Quantum conference key agreement (QCKA) enables multiple spatially separated users to establish a common key with composable information-theoretic security by exploiting multipartite quantum correlations. Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states are a natural resource for this task, but their distribution over optical fiber is degraded by transmission loss, polarization decoherence, and detector imperfections. We investigate the finite-key performance of an $N$-party GHZ-based QCKA system using the $N$-BB84 protocol, where each optical link is modeled by extending the bipartite erasure--Pauli channel to incorporate detector dark counts. We characterize the impact of this quantum channel on the shared GHZ state and derive closed-form expressions for the error rates. The analytical results reveal that the local bit-error rate depends only on transmissivity and dark counts, while the global phase-error rate compounds over all $N-1$ links and therefore degrades faster with both distance and the number of parties. These error rates are integrated into a finite-key secret-key-rate (SKR) framework, in which we optimize the parameter-estimation probability via Brent's derivative-free method. Numerical results show that increasing fiber distance and network size reduce the achievable SKR. Furthermore, the optimized parameter-estimation probability consistently increases the SKR and extends the maximum secure distance relative to a fixed-allocation baseline, with comparison to the asymptotic limit quantifying the residual finite-key penalty.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes finite-key performance of GHZ-based quantum conference key agreement using the N-BB84 protocol over optical fiber, modeling each link with an erasure–Pauli channel including detector dark counts, deriving closed-form error rates, and optimizing parameter estimation to improve secret-key rate and secure distance.
AI.motivation: GHZ states are natural resources for multipartite QCKA, but fiber distribution suffers from transmission loss, polarization decoherence, and detector imperfections. A rigorous finite-key characterization incorporating these realistic channel and detector effects is needed to assess practical performance.
AI.method: An N-party GHZ-based QCKA system using the N-BB84 protocol is studied. Each optical link is modeled by extending the bipartite erasure–Pauli channel to include detector dark counts. The channel's effect on the shared GHZ state is characterized and closed-form expressions for local bit-error rate and global phase-error rate are derived.
