These are integrated into a finite-key SKR framework, with parameter-estimation probability optimized via Brent's derivative-free method.
AI.result: The local bit-error rate depends only on transmissivity and dark counts, whereas the global phase-error rate compounds over all N−1 links, degrading faster with distance and number of parties. Numerical results show that increasing fiber distance and network size reduce achievable SKR. The optimized parameter-estimation probability consistently increases SKR and extends the maximum secure distance compared with a fixed-allocation baseline; comparison with the asymptotic limit quantifies the residual finite-key penalty.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing the parameter-estimation probability improves finite-key QCKA performance, yielding higher SKR and longer secure distance than fixed allocation. The derived error-rate expressions and finite-key framework provide a basis for evaluating multipartite QCKA under realistic fiber and detector conditions.

title: Game of Nons: Non-Gaussian Nonunitary Environments with Nonlinear Coupling
summary: We develop a perturbative framework for systems coupled quadratically to bosonic environments with quadratic Hamiltonians and linear Lindblad operators. The method applies to both single-mode and multimode environments whose initial states may be non-Gaussian and nonstationary. By combining linear evolution in a doubled operator space with a characteristic-function representation, we express ordered multitime environmental correlation functions in terms of derivatives of the initial characteristic function. These correlation functions enter a recursive construction of the time-convolutionless generator at arbitrary finite order. We illustrate the method with a qubit coupled to a damped mode via a two-photon interaction. Initial Fock and thermal states with identical first and second field moments produce different second-order generators through their fourth moments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a perturbative framework for open quantum systems coupled quadratically to bosonic environments (single- or multimode, possibly non-Gaussian/nonstationary) by combining doubled-operator-space linear evolution with a characteristic-function representation to compute ordered multitime correlation functions and build the time-convolutionless generator to arbitrary finite order.
AI.motivation: Existing perturbative treatments often rely on Gaussian or stationary environment assumptions. The authors aim to handle bosonic environments with quadratic Hamiltonians and linear Lindblad operators whose initial states may be non-Gaussian and nonstationary, which requires a systematic way to evaluate ordered multitime environmental correlation functions.
AI.method: A perturbative approach for quadratic bosonic environments with linear Lindblad operators. It combines linear evolution in a doubled operator space with a characteristic-function representation, expressing ordered multitime environmental correlation functions as derivatives of the initial characteristic function. These correlation functions are then inserted into a recursive construction of the time-convolutionless generator at arbitrary finite order.
AI.result: The method is illustrated with a qubit coupled to a damped mode via a two-photon interaction. Initial Fock and thermal states sharing identical first and second field moments yield different second-order generators due to their differing fourth moments.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables systematic perturbative expansion of the time-convolutionless generator for quadratic bosonic environments beyond Gaussian and stationary initial states, with higher moments (e.g., fourth moments) directly influencing the generator, as demonstrated in the two-photon qubit–mode example.

title: Nonlinear quantum multi-spin dynamics without entanglement
summary: We introduce a distinct route for extending classical atomistic spin dynamics into the quantum regime for arbitrary spin $s$, based on a variational product-state \textit{ansatz} that includes both pure and mixed local states. By construction, intersite entanglement -- expected to remain negligible even on very short time scales in many real materials -- is excluded, while local quantum effects are retained through the nonclassical structure of $s\geq 1$ density operators, and nonlinear dynamics arise from both the mean-field interdependence of the local states and the state-dependent dissipative terms. This framework clarifies the variational and geometric origin of the inequivalence between quantum Landau-Lifshitz and Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics, provides a criterion for their equivalence under a common time rescaling, establishes connections with the classical theory through two qualitatively distinct limits ($s\to\infty$ and a large number of quantum spins $N$), and allows realistic $\mathcal{O}(N)$ simulations of quantum spin dynamics in materials.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a variational product-state ansatz to extend classical atomistic spin dynamics into the quantum regime for arbitrary spin s, retaining local quantum effects while excluding intersite entanglement, and enabling O(N) simulations.
AI.motivation: Classical atomistic spin dynamics needs a route into the quantum regime that avoids the complexity of full quantum many-body treatment while still capturing local quantum effects, since intersite entanglement is expected to remain negligible on relevant time scales in many real materials.
AI.method: A variational product-state ansatz that includes both pure and mixed local states, excluding intersite entanglement but retaining local quantum effects through the nonclassical structure of s>=1 density operators; nonlinear dynamics arise from mean-field interdependence of local states and state-dependent dissipative terms.
AI.result: The framework clarifies the variational and geometric origin of the inequivalence between quantum Landau-Lifshitz and Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics, provides a criterion for their equivalence under a common time rescaling, establishes connections with classical theory through two distinct limits (s->infinity and large number of quantum spins N), and allows realistic O(N) simulations of quantum spin dynamics in materials.
AI.conclusion: The variational product-state approach offers a practical and scalable framework for quantum spin dynamics in materials, bridging quantum and classical descriptions while keeping computational cost at O(N).

title: Optimization Geometry of QAOA and Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Variational quantum algorithms turn choices of Hamiltonian, ansatz, and parameterization into a classical nonconvex optimization problem. We study how this objective function can be visualized and characterized in ways that help explain optimizer behavior. We distinguish two properties of the objective: the number of local minima encountered along sampled directions and the differences in quality among local-search endpoints. We then ask how a local optimizer, represented by BFGS, compares with adaptive differential evolution, represented by jSO. Rather than comparing jSO with a single local run, we allow BFGS multiple starts within the same function-evaluation budget. This gives local search repeated opportunities to explore different basins and provides a stronger baseline for asking when a global evolutionary solver is useful. We study these questions using VQE and QAOA, focusing on how frustra- tion, circuit depth, parameter tying, mixed locality, and nonlinear repa- rameterization change the Hamiltonian expectation-value objective seen by the classical optimizer. Increasing independent circuit depth raises the sampled local-minimum count without making global search more effective. Parameter tying, by contrast, produces both more repeated local structure and much larger differences in quality among local-search endpoints, and in this regime adaptive differential evolution outperforms function-evaluation-matched multistart BFGS. The comparison shows that the number of local minima alone does not determine whether global search is advantageous: the important distinction is whether different basins lead to similarly good solutions or to substantially different objective values. These results provide a practical workflow for connecting model construction, objective- function geometry, empirical diagnostics, and optimizer choice.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the VQA objective function to explain optimizer behavior, showing that simply counting local minima does not predict whether global evolutionary search beats multi-start local search; instead, the key factor is whether different basins yield similar or substantially different solution quality.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms reduce choices of Hamiltonian, ansatz, and parameterization to a classical nonconvex optimization problem whose objective geometry is poorly understood, complicating optimizer selection and explanation of optimizer behavior.
AI.method: Two objective properties are distinguished: the number of local minima encountered along sampled directions and the differences in quality among local-search endpoints. BFGS local optimization is compared against the adaptive differential evolution solver jSO under a function-evaluation-matched budget, where BFGS is given multiple starts rather than a single run, forming a stronger baseline. Experiments use VQE and QAOA and vary frustration, circuit depth, parameter tying, mixed locality, and nonlinear reparameterization.
AI.result: Increasing independent circuit depth raises the sampled local-minimum count without improving global search effectiveness. Parameter tying instead produces both more repeated local structure and much larger differences in quality among local-search endpoints, and in this regime adaptive differential evolution outperforms function-evaluation-matched multistart BFGS.
AI.conclusion: The number of local minima alone does not determine whether global search is advantageous; the decisive distinction is whether different basins lead to similarly good solutions or to substantially different objective values. The work offers a practical workflow linking model construction, objective-function geometry, empirical diagnostics, and optimizer choice.

title: Optimal and Verifiable Quantum Advantages in Communication Complexity
summary:
We establish optimal quantum-classical separations in communication complexity for search problems. We introduce a total search problem called Pelagic Fourier Fishing and show that it admits an $n$-qubit quantum one-way protocol, whereas every randomized two-way protocol requires $Ω(2^n)$ bits of communication. We then introduce a variant of this problem whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time. This variant also admits an $n$-qubit quantum one-way protocol, while every randomized one-way protocol requires $Ω(2^n)$ bits of communication.
  We also construct a family of efficiently verifiable total search problems achieving an $n$ versus $Ω_d(n^d)$ separation between quantum one-way and randomized one-way communication for every fixed $d \ge 2$. In the quantum protocol, Alice prepares her message using a single unitary from the $d$th level of the Clifford hierarchy, and Bob performs a Clifford measurement. This separation is asymptotically optimal under this restriction on Alice's message. For $d = 2$, Alice's message is a stabilizer state and Bob's measurement is Clifford, so the protocol uses no magic, yet achieves an optimal quadratic quantum advantage.
  Finally, we discuss how these separations can be adapted to near-term quantum advantage experiments in which the demonstrated advantage is both unconditional and efficiently verifiable.

AI.tldr: This paper proves optimal quantum-classical communication complexity separations for total search problems, including an exponential (n-qubit vs. Ω(2^n)-bit) separation with efficiently verifiable solutions, and a family of Clifford-hierarchy-based protocols achieving n versus Ω_d(n^d) separations.
AI.motivation: Establish strong, unconditional, and efficiently verifiable quantum advantages in communication complexity, addressing search problems rather than decision problems, and connect these separations to near-term quantum advantage experiments.
AI.method: Introduce Pelagic Fourier Fishing, a total search problem with an n-qubit quantum one-way protocol but Ω(2^n) randomized two-way lower bound; construct an efficiently verifiable variant with n-qubit quantum one-way protocol vs. Ω(2^n) randomized one-way lower bound; build a family of verifiable total search problems using Alice's single unitary from the d-th Clifford hierarchy level and Bob's Clifford measurement.
AI.result: Exponential separation: n-qubit quantum one-way vs. Ω(2^n) randomized two-way (and one-way for the verifiable variant). Polynomial family: n vs. Ω_d(n^d) separation for every d ≥ 2, asymptotically optimal under the restriction. For d=2 (stabilizer state and Clifford measurement), a magic-free protocol achieves an optimal quadratic quantum advantage.
AI.conclusion: The separations yield unconditional, efficiently verifiable quantum advantages and can be adapted to near-term quantum advantage experiments.

title: Autonomous Quantum Memories from Classical Stochastic Processes
summary:
The study of quantum memories out of thermal equilibrium is motivated both by the need for memories that withstand realistic noise in fault-tolerant quantum computers and by the fundamental question of when quantum memory can emerge in autonomous many-body systems. We establish a general equivalence between CSS-based quantum memories subject to Pauli noise and classical memories via two associated probabilistic processes. In the asynchronous setting, where the quantum dynamics is generated by a Lindbladian, we identify a broad class of syndrome-based Lindbladians for which the quantum memory problem is equivalent to memory in continuous-time classical Markov dynamics. In the synchronous setting, we introduce syndrome-based probabilistic cellular automata (SPCAs) and establish a one-to-one correspondence between their classical memories and CSS-based quantum memories under local quantum channels. This framework provides a systematic route for deriving and constructing quantum memories from classical probabilistic processes, and recovers known results, including the fact that the 4D toric code is a quantum memory in the presence of thermal noise.
  As an application, we give the first rigorous proof that the 4D toric code with Toom's rule is a quantum memory in the presence of local Pauli noise, provided the error is below a constant threshold. We prove this both for the corresponding synchronous, PCA-type quantum dynamics and for a Floquet Lindbladian. More generally, we show that classical memory in an SPCA can be lifted to a quantum memory under Floquet Lindbladian dynamics; whether this can be done with a time-independent Lindbladian remains open. Our results provide a general framework for relating classical and quantum memory, shed light on the conditions for fully autonomous quantum memories, and may guide the construction of provable autonomous quantum memories in low dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a general equivalence between CSS-based quantum memories under Pauli noise and classical memories via two probabilistic processes, in both asynchronous (Lindbladian) and synchronous (SPCA) settings, yielding the first rigorous proof that the 4D toric code with Toom's rule is a quantum memory under local Pauli noise below a constant threshold.
AI.motivation: Quantum memories out of thermal equilibrium are needed both for fault-tolerant quantum computers that must withstand realistic noise and for the fundamental question of when quantum memory can emerge autonomously in many-body systems.
AI.method: The authors establish an equivalence between CSS-based quantum memories subject to Pauli noise and classical memories via two associated probabilistic processes: (1) in the asynchronous setting, generated by a Lindbladian, they identify a broad class of syndrome-based Lindbladians whose quantum memory problem is equivalent to memory in continuous-time classical Markov dynamics; (2) in the synchronous setting, they introduce syndrome-based probabilistic cellular automata (SPCAs) and establish a one-to-one correspondence between their classical memories and CSS-based quantum memories under local quantum channels.
AI.result: The framework recovers known results, including that the 4D toric code is a quantum memory under thermal noise. As an application, it gives the first rigorous proof that the 4D toric code with Toom's rule is a quantum memory under local Pauli noise below a constant threshold, proven both for the corresponding synchronous PCA-type quantum dynamics and for a Floquet Lindbladian. More generally, classical memory in an SPCA can be lifted to a quantum memory under Floquet Lindbladian dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a general framework relating classical and quantum memory, shed light on the conditions for fully autonomous quantum memories, and may guide the construction of provable autonomous quantum memories in low dimensions. Whether the lifting can be achieved with a time-independent Lindbladian remains open.

title: Erasure of entanglement-locked energy in multi-cell quantum batteries through decoherence
summary: Charging a quantum battery through a pumped charger can lock a substantial part of its stored energy inside the bipartite correlations that grow between the constituent cells, and this \emph{correlation ergotropy}, being the energy that no local single-cell operation can reach and that only collective operations can recover, is the object of the present study. Following the charging trajectory of two coupled three-level cells, we find that the correlation ergotropy closely tracks the logarithmic negativity, which shows that the locked energy is carried by genuine bipartite entanglement rather than by coherent collective dynamics alone, and that an equal-strength coherent non-entangling drive produces no such locking at all. For a pure two-cell battery we establish an exact, basis-independent closed form in which the locked energy depends only on the sorted eigenvalues of the reduced cell and the cell energy levels, revealing that the locked fraction rises from zero at the separable corners of the Schmidt simplex to unity at the symmetric maximally entangled state and remains invariant under local unitaries. Decoherence and dephasing, which destroy the correlations, do \emph{not} release this energy but erase it, so extraction must be collective and must take place while the correlations persist, while cold damping leaves the effect intact and thermal occupation suppresses it. These results give a resource-theoretic reading of correlations in quantum batteries, sharpen the line between genuine entanglement and coherent collective dynamics, and point to experimentally accessible conditions for correlated-charge and collective-extraction protocols.

AI.tldr: This work studies "correlation ergotropy" — the energy locked in bipartite correlations of a quantum battery that only collective operations can extract. Using two coupled three-level cells, the authors show it tracks logarithmic negativity (entanglement), derive an exact closed form for a pure two-cell battery, and analyze decoherence, cold damping, and thermal effects.
AI.motivation: Charging a quantum battery via a pumped charger can lock a substantial part of stored energy inside bipartite correlations. This "correlation ergotropy" is inaccessible to any local single-cell operation and recoverable only through collective operations, yet its nature and behavior remain to be characterized.
AI.method: The authors follow the charging trajectory of two coupled three-level cells and compare correlation ergotropy against the logarithmic negativity. They contrast this with an equal-strength coherent non-entangling drive, derive an exact basis-independent closed-form expression for a pure two-cell battery, and test robustness under decoherence, dephasing, cold damping, and thermal occupation.
AI.result: Correlation ergotropy closely tracks logarithmic negativity, indicating genuine bipartite entanglement carries the locked energy rather than coherent collective dynamics; an equal-strength non-entangling drive produces no locking. For the pure two-cell battery, the locked energy depends only on the sorted eigenvalues of the reduced cell and cell energy levels; the locked fraction rises from zero at separable corners to unity at the symmetric maximally entangled state and is invariant under local unitaries. Decoherence and dephasing erase rather than release the locked energy, cold damping leaves the effect intact, and thermal occupation suppresses it.
AI.conclusion: These results provide a resource-theoretic reading of correlations in quantum batteries, sharpen the distinction between genuine entanglement and coherent collective dynamics, and identify experimentally accessible conditions for correlated-charge and collective-extraction protocols.

title: A solvable quantum many-body problem
summary: A many-body wavefunction exponential in R, where the square of R is the sum of the squares of the interparticle distances, is shown to be the solution of Schrodingers equation for a potential proportional to the reciprocal of R, for N particles. A set of translationally invariant rotational eigenstates of angular momentum is found.

AI.tldr: A many-body wavefunction of the form exp(-R) (where R² is the sum of squared interparticle distances) exactly solves the Schrödinger equation for an N-particle system under a potential proportional to 1/R, and a family of translationally invariant rotational eigenstates is constructed.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks an exact, closed-form solution to the N-body Schrödinger equation for a specific long-range potential, addressing the general difficulty of solving many-body problems where exact solutions are rare and typically restricted to few particles or special potentials.
AI.method: An ansatz wavefunction exponential in the collective coordinate R, with R² defined as the sum of the squares of all interparticle distances, is substituted into the N-particle Schrödinger equation with a potential V ∝ 1/R. Rotational eigenstates of definite angular momentum are then derived under the requirement of translational invariance.
AI.result: The exponential-in-R wavefunction is confirmed to be an exact solution for the 1/R potential for arbitrary particle number N. A set of translationally invariant rotational eigenstates carrying definite angular momentum is obtained.
AI.conclusion: The 1/R many-body potential admits an exact exponential wavefunction solution for any N, and supports translationally invariant rotational eigenstates, providing a tractable exactly solvable N-body model.

title: Frame-dependent coherence of Gaussian quantum states
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. More details are available on my homepage https://unibuc.ro/user/nicolae.cotfas/
summary: A Hilbert space is usually described using an orthonormal basis, but a more general description can be defined using a tight frame. In the case of continuous-variable Gaussian states, the coherence is usually described using the Hermite-Gauss basis. We present an alternative description using the tight frame of all canonical coherent states. The description of Gaussian states in terms of coherent states is simpler than in terms of Hermite-Gauss basis, and this allows us to obtain an explicit formula describing the frame-dependent coherence of a mixed Gaussian state as a function of the determinant and the trace of covariance matrix. For each mixed Gaussian state, we construct a sequence of discrete-variable quantum states rapidly convergent to it (as concern the purity and coherence) when the dimension of Hilbert space becomes large enough (15 or more). In the discrete case, the coherence is measured with respect to the tight frame of all discrete coherent states.

AI.tldr: The paper describes continuous-variable Gaussian states using the tight frame of canonical coherent states instead of the Hermite-Gauss basis, derives an explicit frame-dependent coherence formula for mixed Gaussian states, and constructs a rapidly convergent sequence of discrete-variable states approximating them.
AI.motivation: Coherence in continuous-variable Gaussian states is conventionally described via the Hermite-Gauss orthonormal basis. However, a tight frame offers a more general and potentially simpler description. The authors seek an alternative, computationally simpler framework for characterizing Gaussian-state coherence.
AI.method: The canonical coherent-state tight frame replaces the Hermite-Gauss basis for describing Gaussian states. Using this frame, the authors derive an explicit expression for the frame-dependent coherence of a mixed Gaussian state as a function of the determinant and trace of its covariance matrix. They also build a sequence of discrete-variable quantum states, measured against the tight frame of discrete coherent states, that converges to each mixed Gaussian state.
AI.result: The coherent-state description of Gaussian states is simpler than the Hermite-Gauss one and yields a closed-form coherence formula depending only on the covariance matrix determinant and trace. The constructed discrete-variable states converge rapidly to the target mixed Gaussian state in both purity and coherence once the Hilbert-space dimension reaches roughly 15 or more.
AI.conclusion: A tight-frame (canonical coherent-state) description provides a simpler and effective alternative to the Hermite-Gauss basis for Gaussian-state coherence, enabling an explicit covariance-matrix-based coherence formula and efficient discrete-variable approximations of mixed Gaussian states.

title: Ground state energy estimation and preparation by the truncated power method
summary: The Guided Local Hamiltonian Problem (GLHP) is the problem of ground state energy estimation and preparation given a guiding state having good overlap with the true ground state. The problem is known to be BQP-complete for small error but is classically tractable for larger error. In this work, we identify an orthogonal regime in which the problem is classically tractable, namely when the true ground state $ψ$ has polynomially bounded $\ell_1$-norm. In particular, we show that the Truncated Power Method (TPM), a classical algorithm introduced by Kirby et al. in the quantum context, has a runtime that is polynomially comparable to quantum algorithms for GLHP in all relevant parameters, except for an extra factor of $\|ψ\|_1^2$. In other words, if $\|ψ\|_1^2$ is polynomially bounded, then TPM dequantizes quantum algorithms for GLHP.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a new classically tractable regime for the Guided Local Hamiltonian Problem (GLHP): when the true ground state has polynomially bounded ℓ1-norm. It shows the classical Truncated Power Method (TPM) matches quantum algorithms for GLHP up to a factor of ‖ψ‖₁², thus dequantizing GLHP when ‖ψ‖₁² is polynomially bounded.
AI.motivation: GLHP—ground state energy estimation and preparation given a guiding state with good overlap—is BQP-complete for small error yet classically tractable for larger error. This leaves the boundary between quantum and classical tractability unclear. The authors seek an orthogonal regime, based on the ℓ1-norm of the ground state, in which GLHP becomes classically tractable.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Truncated Power Method (TPM), a classical algorithm originally introduced by Kirby et al. in the quantum context, and bound its runtime relative to quantum algorithms for GLHP, accounting for the ℓ1-norm of the true ground state ψ.
AI.result: TPM's runtime is polynomially comparable to quantum algorithms for GLHP across all relevant parameters, up to an extra factor of ‖ψ‖₁². Consequently, when ‖ψ‖₁² is polynomially bounded, TPM dequantizes quantum algorithms for GLHP.
AI.conclusion: A new classically tractable regime for GLHP is established: polynomially bounded ℓ1-norm of the ground state. In this regime, the classical TPM dequantizes quantum approaches to GLHP, with only a polynomial overhead of ‖ψ‖₁².

title: Transformer-Based Time-Series Inference of Lindblad Dynamics in Open Quantum Systems
summary: The Lindblad master equation is the standard framework for describing the non-unitary evolution of open quantum systems, where environmental interactions induce dissipation and decoherence. When both the system Hamiltonian and the dissipation rates are partially unknown or explicitly time-dependent, traditional analytical inversion and system-identification techniques become intractable. Recent works have demonstrated that Transformer-based models can infer unknown dissipation rates from observable time series, yet these approaches typically rely on hand-crafted statistical features under idealized and highly restricted conditions. Here we advance the paradigm by introducing a raw time-series Transformer that directly ingests the full trajectories of Pauli expectation values $\langleσ_x(t)\rangle$, $\langleσ_y(t)\rangle$, and $\langleσ_z(t)\rangle$, thereby fully exploiting the self-attention mechanism for temporal modeling. The architecture is further extended to jointly learn unknown Hamiltonian parameters, handle multiple dissipation channels, and operate robustly under realistic measurement noise. Across all tested scenarios the model achieves consistently high reconstruction accuracy while eliminating manual feature engineering. This provides a scalable, robust, and versatile framework for quantum environment sensing in realistic open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A raw time-series Transformer directly ingests full Pauli expectation value trajectories to infer unknown Hamiltonian parameters and dissipation rates in open quantum systems, eliminating hand-crafted features and remaining robust under measurement noise.
AI.motivation: The Lindblad master equation governs non-unitary open quantum system evolution, but when the Hamiltonian and dissipation rates are partially unknown or time-dependent, traditional analytical inversion and system-identification become intractable. Existing Transformer-based approaches rely on hand-crafted statistical features and idealized, restricted conditions, limiting their practicality.
AI.method: The authors introduce a raw time-series Transformer that directly ingests full trajectories of Pauli expectation values (⟨σ_x(t)⟩, ⟨σ_y(t)⟩, ⟨σ_z(t)⟩), fully exploiting self-attention for temporal modeling. The architecture is extended to jointly learn unknown Hamiltonian parameters, handle multiple dissipation channels, and operate robustly under realistic measurement noise.
AI.result: Across all tested scenarios, the model achieves consistently high reconstruction accuracy while eliminating manual feature engineering.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a scalable, robust, and versatile framework for quantum environment sensing in realistic open quantum systems.

title: Universal Improvement of Channel Fidelity via Entanglement Assistance
summary: Communication using quantum channels generally requires encoding and decoding on many identical uses of a quantum channel. In practical settings, decoherence may severely limit our ability to do so, potentially rendering each channel use nonidentical. Given $n$ nonidentical channels, we present an entanglement-assisted encoding and decoding strategy that yields a channel with higher worst-case fidelity than all of the $n$ given channels. The strategy is universal, in the sense that the improvement holds regardless of what channels are given, as long as they satisfy mild assumptions on their initial entanglement fidelities. Our protocol is optimal when the given channels are depolarizing channels, and is essentially the unique one that is universal. This idea can also be extended to classical channels, where shared randomness between the sender and the receiver allows universal enhancement of the probability of correct transmission. We then consider general quantum resource theories, providing a necessary condition and a sufficient condition for the possibility of such universal improvement of quantum resources.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that given n nonidentical noisy quantum channels, an entanglement-assisted encoding/decoding strategy can produce a combined channel with higher worst-case fidelity than any of the individual channels, and this improvement is universal, essentially unique, optimal for depolarizing channels, and extendable to classical channels and general quantum resource theories.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum communication suffers from decoherence, making individual uses of a channel nonidentical and degrading performance. Standard encoding/decoding assumes many identical channel uses, which fails in such realistic settings. The authors seek a universal way to combine nonidentical channels to improve worst-case fidelity.
AI.method: The authors design an entanglement-assisted encoding and decoding strategy over n nonidentical channels. They analyze its universality under mild assumptions on initial entanglement fidelities, prove optimality for depolarizing channels, establish essential uniqueness of the universal protocol, extend the approach to classical channels via shared randomness, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for universal improvement in general quantum resource theories.
AI.result: The strategy yields a channel whose worst-case fidelity exceeds that of all n given channels. It is universal regardless of the specific channels (subject to mild entanglement-fidelity assumptions), optimal for depolarizing channels, and essentially the unique universal protocol. For classical channels, shared randomness enables universal enhancement of correct-transmission probability. General resource theories admit a necessary and a sufficient condition for such universal improvement.
AI.conclusion: Universal enhancement of noisy quantum channels is achievable through entanglement assistance, with optimality and uniqueness guarantees, and the framework generalizes to classical communication and broader quantum resource theories.

title: Momentum-Space Path Integral Approach to Non-Hermitian Symmetry Breaking
summary: A quantum-classical correspondence for non-Hermitian symmetry breaking has recently been established using coordinate-space path integrals, providing a semiclassical understanding of spectral transitions at the level of individual eigenstates. Here we develop its dual formulation in momentum space by constructing the corresponding trace formula and quantization condition. We show that the real or complex nature of individual eigenvalues is determined by the symmetry properties of the associated semiclassical orbits, as in the coordinate-space path-integral approach. Moreover, we demonstrate that the topology of semiclassical orbits determines the natural formulation of the quantization condition: the coordinate- and momentum-space formulations are equivalent for contractible periodic orbits in phase space, whereas for noncontractible orbits, the quantization condition along the winding direction remains valid, but its dual form must be corrected by a boundary term. In particular, real-space-winding and Brillouin-zone-winding orbits naturally select coordinate- and momentum-space quantization, respectively. As a nontrivial application, we investigate the boundary-induced spectral transition of Bloch oscillations in a finite non-Hermitian lattice, where Bloch-oscillation orbits winding across the Brillouin zone preserve the relevant symmetry and yield real energy levels, whereas boundary-reflected orbits form symmetry-related pairs and give rise to complex-conjugate eigenvalues. Our work completes the quantum-classical correspondence framework for non-Hermitian symmetry breaking, extending its applicability to a broader class of non-Hermitian problems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a momentum-space dual of the recently established quantum-classical correspondence for non-Hermitian symmetry breaking, showing that the real or complex nature of individual eigenvalues is governed by semiclassical orbit symmetry and that orbit topology dictates whether coordinate-space or momentum-space quantization applies, with an application to boundary-induced spectral transitions of Bloch oscillations in a finite non-Hermitian lattice.
AI.motivation: A quantum-classical correspondence for non-Hermitian symmetry breaking was previously established only via coordinate-space path integrals, leaving the momentum-space formulation and the role of orbit topology in selecting quantization conditions unexplored.
AI.method: Constructs the momentum-space trace formula and quantization condition as a dual to the coordinate-space path-integral approach, analyzing symmetry properties and the topology (contractible vs. noncontractible) of semiclassical orbits. Applies the framework to Bloch oscillations in a finite non-Hermitian lattice.
AI.result: The real or complex nature of individual eigenvalues is determined by the symmetry of the associated semiclassical orbits in momentum space as well, mirroring the coordinate-space result. Coordinate- and momentum-space quantization are equivalent for contractible periodic orbits, whereas for noncontractible orbits the winding-direction quantization remains valid but its dual form requires a boundary-term correction. Real-space-winding and Brillouin-zone-winding orbits naturally select coordinate- and momentum-space quantization respectively. In the finite non-Hermitian lattice, Bloch-oscillation orbits winding across the Brillouin zone preserve the relevant symmetry and yield real energy levels, while boundary-reflected orbits form symmetry-related pairs giving complex-conjugate eigenvalues.
AI.conclusion: The work completes the quantum-classical correspondence framework for non-Hermitian symmetry breaking and extends its applicability to a broader class of non-Hermitian problems.

title: An efficient Hamiltonian-based quantum algorithm for characters of the symmetric group
summary: Consider a quantum state vector proportional to any given column of the character table of the symmetric group ($S_n$), corresponding to a superposition over the irreps weighted by the character values. It was recently argued that sampling from this state is classically hard under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, while there exists an efficient quantum algorithm for preparing this character state using the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) over $S_n$ [arXiv:2501.12579]. We give an alternative, simpler algorithm to prepare this character state with a sequence of Hamiltonian evolutions, as well as an efficient implementation with reconfigurable qubits that uses only nearest-neighbor gates in 1D. The gate complexity, accounting for Hamiltonian simulation errors, depends on the choice of the column: For fixed target state error, the estimated sufficient total gate count ranges from as few as $O(n)$ gates for the $n$-cycle column, to $\widetilde O(n^{1.75})$ gates near the conjecturally classically hard parameter regime, to provably $\widetilde O(n^{2.5})$ gates in the worst case. In contrast, the QFT subroutine in the prior approach uses $\widetilde O(n^3)$ gates. Our gate count estimates come from leading-order state-dependent Trotter error analysis, and the proven worst-case bound relies on a QSVT-based Hamiltonian simulation method; numerical benchmarks of the Trotter-based protocol suggest that the estimates are conservative. Furthermore, we generalize our protocol to give an explicit algorithm for the quantum character transform (QCT) over $S_n$ using $\widetilde O(n^{2.5})$ gates and $O(n)$ qubits. An application to entanglement entropy of symmetric orbifold conformal field theories is also discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a simpler Hamiltonian-evolution-based algorithm to prepare character states of the symmetric group $S_n$, achieving gate counts from $O(n)$ to $\widetilde O(n^{2.5})$ depending on the column, improving on the prior QFT-based $\widetilde O(n^3)$ approach, with a 1D nearest-neighbor implementation and a generalization to the quantum character transform.
AI.motivation: Preparing the character state of $S_n$ (a superposition over irreps weighted by a character-table column) is classically hard under reasonable complexity assumptions yet quantumly feasible via the QFT over $S_n$. The prior QFT approach, however, uses $\widetilde O(n^3)$ gates, motivating a simpler, more gate-efficient protocol—especially near the conjecturally classically hard parameter regime—and a hardware-friendly nearest-neighbor implementation.
AI.method: The authors prepare the character state via a sequence of Hamiltonian evolutions rather than the QFT, and provide an efficient implementation using reconfigurable qubits with only nearest-neighbor gates in 1D. Gate counts are estimated from leading-order, state-dependent Trotter error analysis; the proven worst-case bound relies on a QSVT-based Hamiltonian simulation method. Numerical benchmarks of the Trotter-based protocol are used to assess the estimates. The protocol is generalized to an explicit quantum character transform (QCT) over $S_n$.
AI.result: For fixed target state error, the estimated sufficient total gate count ranges from $O(n)$ gates for the $n$-cycle column, to $\widetilde O(n^{1.75})$ near the conjecturally classically hard regime, to provably $\widetilde O(n^{2.5})$ gates in the worst case—versus $\widetilde O(n^3)$ for the prior QFT subroutine. Numerical benchmarks suggest the Trotter-based estimates are conservative. The generalized QCT algorithm uses $\widetilde O(n^{2.5})$ gates and $O(n)$ qubits.
AI.conclusion: The Hamiltonian-evolution protocol offers a simpler and substantially more gate-efficient alternative to the QFT-based approach for preparing $S_n$ character states, with concrete 1D nearest-neighbor realizability, and extends to a full quantum character transform. An application to entanglement entropy of symmetric orbifold conformal field theories is also discussed.

title: Certified Randomness Generation against Quantum Adversaries via Energy Constraints
summary:
For quantum random number generators (QRNGs), strong security guarantees can be obtained under various assumptions. The most well-known assumptions are the non-signalling assumption (needed for device-independent (DI) QRNG) and post-quantum computational assumptions (needed for computationally bounded single-prover QRNG protocols). In this work, we study a third model: a simple prepare-and-measure QRNG whose security relies on physically motivated energy constraints. This physically motivated set-up allows for easier implementations of QRNGs and can supply better rates.
  So far, previous works that studied the energy-constrained model either assumed that the adversary is classical in their security proof or supplied relatively weak bounds on the certified randomness, by bounding the conditional min-entropy. In this work, we prove a new, essentially tight, lower bound on the single-round von Neumann entropy against adversaries holding both classical and quantum side-information. Our work reveals that working with the von Neumann entropy, rather than the min-entropy, in the quantum case can lead to a major improvement, nearly matching the classical bound in many cases. We further study the robustness of our entropy bound. Since the single-round von Neumann entropy is the main quantity of interest when characterizing the key rate of QRNGs, our bound establishes the main ingredient for rigorous security proofs against general quantum attacks in this framework.

AI.tldr: The paper studies an energy-constrained prepare-and-measure QRNG model and proves an essentially tight lower bound on the single-round von Neumann entropy against adversaries with classical and quantum side-information, enabling strong security proofs against general quantum attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing QRNG security models rely on either the non-signalling assumption (device-independent QRNG) or post-quantum computational assumptions (single-prover computationally bounded QRNG). A third, simpler model based on physically motivated energy constraints allows easier implementation and better rates, but prior security proofs for it either assumed a classical adversary or provided only weak certified-randomness bounds via conditional min-entropy.
AI.method: The authors analyze a simple prepare-and-measure QRNG under physically motivated energy constraints. They prove a new lower bound on the single-round von Neumann entropy against adversaries holding both classical and quantum side-information, and they study the robustness of this entropy bound.
AI.result: An essentially tight lower bound on the single-round von Neumann entropy is established. Using von Neumann entropy rather than min-entropy in the quantum case yields a major improvement, nearly matching the classical bound in many cases. The bound is also shown to be robust.
AI.conclusion: Since the single-round von Neumann entropy characterizes the key rate of QRNGs, the new bound provides the main ingredient for rigorous security proofs against general quantum attacks in the energy-constrained framework.

title: Quantum Complexity of Solving Linear Equations on Higher-Order Networks
summary: Higher-order networks (HONs) represent interactions among groups of objects, supporting the study of collective behaviour that pairwise models can miss. In simplicial models of these networks, Hodge Laplacian linear systems provide a common mathematical framework for analysis, for example, for solving statistical ranking problems and investigating long-term stability in coupled oscillator systems. The large number of variables associated with edges, triangles, and higher-dimensional simplices can make these systems costly to solve. Recent quantum algorithms address this bottleneck. However, comparisons with particular classical algorithms do not decision output whether solving these linear system problems establishes a quantum complexity foundation for provable quantum advantage. We prove that preparing a quantum state encoding the normalized minimum-norm solution of Hodge Laplacian linear systems is $\mathsf{BQP}$-hard under the specified sparse oracle model and parameter promises. Our sequence of reductions maps an arbitrary polynomial-time bounded-error quantum computation to such linear systems. Each reduction allows efficient recovery of the normalized minimum-norm solution of the preceding linear system. Together with an efficient quantum algorithm for the associated decision problem from the approximate solution state, we show that this problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. These results provide a worst-case complexity foundation for evaluating quantum advantage in HON analysis and show that the $\mathsf{BQP}$-hardness of the quantum linear system problem (QLSP) persists even when the matrices are restricted to Hodge Laplacians.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that preparing a quantum state encoding the normalized minimum-norm solution of Hodge Laplacian linear systems is BQP-hard under a sparse oracle model with parameter promises, and together with an efficient quantum algorithm, establishes BQP-completeness for this problem.
AI.motivation: Higher-order networks (HONs) capture group interactions that pairwise models miss, and Hodge Laplacian linear systems are a common framework for tasks like statistical ranking and coupled-oscillator stability. These systems involve many variables (edges, triangles, higher simplices), making them costly to solve. While recent quantum algorithms target this bottleneck, comparisons with particular classical algorithms cannot determine whether these linear-system problems provide a provable quantum complexity foundation for quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors construct a sequence of reductions mapping an arbitrary polynomial-time bounded-error quantum computation to Hodge Laplacian linear systems. Each reduction permits efficient recovery of the normalized minimum-norm solution of the preceding linear system. They further provide an efficient quantum algorithm for the associated decision problem from the approximate solution state.
AI.result: Preparing a quantum state encoding the normalized minimum-norm solution of Hodge Laplacian linear systems is shown to be BQP-hard under the specified sparse oracle model and parameter promises. Combined with the efficient quantum algorithm for the associated decision problem, the problem is proven to be BQP-complete.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a worst-case complexity foundation for evaluating quantum advantage in HON analysis, and show that the BQP-hardness of the quantum linear system problem (QLSP) persists even when matrices are restricted to Hodge Laplacians.

title: Spectral Analysis Beyond the Spectral Gap: Rapid Mixing of Quantum Gibbs Samplers in One Dimension
summary: We prove rapid mixing of a quantum Gibbs sampler for general one-dimensional non-commuting local spin systems at every fixed positive temperature. In particular, for a system of $n$ sites, we show that the Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) detailed-balanced Gibbs sampler of~\cite{CKG2023} converges from any initial state to trace-norm error $ε$ in time $O(\log^4(n)+\log(1/ε))$. This improves the previous $O(n+\log(1/ε))$ bound and establishes rapid mixing beyond high-temperature and weak-interaction regimes. Our proof explains why the slowest decay rate, captured by the spectral gap, can substantially underestimate the speed of equilibration. The key insight is that a state far from equilibrium must have a substantial component outside the span of low-weight Pauli operators, where stronger dissipation estimates apply. This yields two stages of relaxation: a double-exponential convergence from a bad initial state, followed by exponential convergence near equilibrium. We turn this mechanism into a framework for proving rapid mixing through spectral analysis beyond the gap. Our decay estimate is equivalent to exponential convergence in sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence. Together with the spectral gap, it also implies a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with rate $Ω(\log^{-4}(n))$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves rapid mixing of a quantum Gibbs sampler for general 1D non-commuting local spin systems at every fixed positive temperature, achieving convergence time O(log^4(n) + log(1/ε)), improving prior O(n + log(1/ε)) bounds and extending rapid mixing beyond high-temperature/weak-interaction regimes.
AI.motivation: Previous rapid-mixing results for quantum Gibbs samplers were limited to high-temperature or weak-interaction regimes, and the standard spectral-gap approach can substantially underestimate the true speed of equilibration. The work aims to establish rapid mixing (logarithmic system-size dependence) for general 1D non-commuting local spin systems at any fixed positive temperature.
AI.method: The authors analyze the KMS detailed-balanced Gibbs sampler of CKG2023 and exploit the insight that a state far from equilibrium must have a substantial component outside the span of low-weight Pauli operators, where stronger dissipation estimates hold. This yields a two-stage relaxation mechanism—double-exponential convergence from a bad initial state, then exponential convergence near equilibrium—formalized into a framework for proving rapid mixing via spectral analysis beyond the gap.
AI.result: For n sites, the sampler converges from any initial state to trace-norm error ε in time O(log^4(n) + log(1/ε)), improving the prior O(n + log(1/ε)) bound. The decay estimate is shown to be equivalent to exponential convergence in sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence and, combined with the spectral gap, implies a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with rate Ω(log^{-4}(n)).
AI.conclusion: Rapid mixing holds for general 1D non-commuting local spin systems at every fixed positive temperature. The results show that spectral gap alone can underestimate equilibration speed, and the proposed beyond-gap spectral framework provides a route to rapid-mixing proofs and modified log-Sobolev inequalities.

title: Classical observable coalescence as a discriminating diagnostic for spectral degeneracies in non-Hermitian systems
summary: Exceptional points (EPs) are conventionally identified through eigenvector coalescence, inaccessible in classical platforms lacking a Hamiltonian spectrum. We introduce classical observable coalescence as a diagnostic identifying EPs directly from physical configurations, and demonstrate it in a known non-Hermitian Ising chain with coupling $J$ and staggered imaginary field $γ$, chosen for verifiability against established quantum results. A mean-field reduction of the Heisenberg dynamics yields equilibrium branches organising into two symmetry-related families whose fusion at the boundary of the EP supersurface $|γ|=|J|$ exhibits the characteristic $\sqrt{J^2-γ^2}$ branch-point structure and two-sheeted Riemann topology. Crucially, the degeneracy at $γ=0,η=0 $ is shown to be a diabolic point, producing no observable coalescence, establishing the diagnostic as discriminating rather than merely suggestive. An exact Jordan-Wigner and Bogoliubov-de Gennes treatment confirms eigenvector coalescence at the same threshold, and a coupled gain-loss circuit realisation is proposed, establishing classical observables as experimentally accessible signatures of non-Hermitian criticality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "classical observable coalescence" as a diagnostic for identifying exceptional points (EPs) directly from classical physical observables, circumventing the need for a Hamiltonian spectrum, and validates it on a non-Hermitian Ising chain, distinguishing genuine EP behaviour from a diabolic point.
AI.motivation: Exceptional points are conventionally identified via eigenvector coalescence, which requires access to a Hamiltonian spectrum unavailable in many classical platforms. This limits the experimental detection and characterization of non-Hermitian criticality, motivating a method that can identify EPs from directly measurable classical quantities.
AI.method: A mean-field reduction of the Heisenberg dynamics is performed on a known non-Hermitian Ising chain with coupling J and staggered imaginary field gamma, yielding equilibrium branches that organize into two symmetry-related families. Their fusion at the EP supersurface |gamma|=|J| is analyzed for branch-point structure and Riemann topology. The degeneracy at gamma=0, eta=0 is characterized as a diabolic point. An exact Jordan-Wigner and Bogoliubov-de Gennes treatment is used to confirm eigenvector coalescence at the same threshold, and a coupled gain-loss circuit realization is proposed.
AI.result: The equilibrium branches fuse at the EP supersurface |gamma|=|J| with the characteristic sqrt(J^2 - gamma^2) branch-point structure and two-sheeted Riemann topology. The degeneracy at gamma=0, eta=0 is a diabolic point producing no observable coalescence, showing the diagnostic discriminates genuine EPs. The exact Jordan-Wigner and Bogoliubov-de Gennes analysis confirms eigenvector coalescence at the same threshold.
AI.conclusion: Classical observables serve as experimentally accessible signatures of non-Hermitian criticality, and classical observable coalescence functions as a discriminating diagnostic for exceptional points in platforms lacking a Hamiltonian spectrum.

title: Fusion-assisted decoding of non-Abelian topological order
summary: Maximum likelihood (ML) decoders perform quantum error correction by measuring a set of syndromes, classically computing an optimal recovery based on these syndromes and the noise model, and then performing that recovery. ML decoders are well understood for the toric code and generalize straightforwardly to other surface codes with Abelian anyons, where they can saturate information-theoretic decoding thresholds. On the other hand, codes with non-Abelian anyons have become increasingly relevant because they can support transversal or constant-depth non-Clifford gates and admit efficient preparation protocols in modern quantum devices. However, they present new challenges for decoding: non-Abelian anyons cannot in general be deterministically annihilated, and the logical operators cannot be classified by Abelian homology. In this work, we show that refined syndrome sets, including measurements that resolve non-Abelian anyon fusion outcomes, systematically improve the performance of ML decoders. We demonstrate this concretely by constructing explicit decoders for the $D_4$ quantum double model under charge noise, and obtaining numerical results for thresholds via mappings to classical statistical-mechanics models. We show that there is a nonzero noise threshold below which the entire logical qudit can be recovered with a single round of measurements.

AI.tldr: This work shows that refined syndrome sets, which resolve non-Abelian anyon fusion outcomes, systematically improve maximum likelihood decoding for non-Abelian anyon codes, demonstrated via explicit D4 quantum double decoders under charge noise with nonzero thresholds.
AI.motivation: ML decoders are well understood for toric and Abelian surface codes, where they saturate information-theoretic thresholds, but non-Abelian anyon codes—attractive for transversal/constant-depth non-Clifford gates and efficient preparation—pose new decoding challenges: anyons cannot generally be deterministically annihilated and logical operators are not classifiable by Abelian homology.
AI.method: The authors construct refined syndrome sets that include measurements resolving non-Abelian anyon fusion outcomes, and build explicit ML decoders for the D4 quantum double model under charge noise. Thresholds are obtained numerically via mappings to classical statistical-mechanics models.
AI.result: Refined syndrome sets systematically improve ML decoder performance. For the D4 quantum double model under charge noise, there exists a nonzero noise threshold below which the entire logical qudit can be recovered with a single round of measurements.
AI.conclusion: Resolving fusion outcomes via refined syndromes enables effective ML decoding of non-Abelian anyon codes, establishing nonzero thresholds and single-round recovery of the full logical qudit, extending ML decoding beyond the Abelian setting.

title: Robust Diamond Quantum Sensing in Double-Quantum 4-Ramsey Interferometry by Dual-Feedback Scheme
summary: We developed a highly sensitive and long-term stable diamond quantum magnetometer by integrating a dual-feedback system that compensates for common- and differential-mode frequency shifts in double-quantum (DQ) 4-Ramsey interferometry. Detecting extremely weak magnetic-field signals requires extensive signal accumulation to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. However, deviations from the optimal operating frequencies caused by thermal drift or environmental magnetic noise severely hinder the long-term stability of such a sensing system. To overcome the limitation, we first derived analytical solutions for the signal response to common- and differential-mode detunings based on a detuning-inclusive Hamiltonian to theoretically clarify the robustness limit in DQ 4-Ramsey sensing. Guided by this theoretical model, we introduced synchronized frequency modulation and a dual-feedback scheme to independently track and compensate for these frequency shifts while maintaining an optimal magnetic-field response. The proposed method enabled stable continuous operation against temperature variations of 2.8 K. By maintaining a magnetic field sensitivity of 7.0 pT/Hz^1/2 in the frequency range of 5-100 Hz for a prolonged duration of 4 hours, we achieved an extremely low noise floor of 64 fT/Hz^1/2. During prolonged continuous sensing, the system exhibited the expected 1/T^1/2 scaling with integration time T, and prevented both the underestimation of amplitude and waveform distortion. These results establish a robust approach for long-term DQ 4-Ramsey diamond magnetometry and demonstrate its potential for detecting weak biomagnetic signals.

AI.tldr: A dual-feedback diamond quantum magnetometer compensates common- and differential-mode frequency shifts in double-quantum 4-Ramsey interferometry, achieving 7.0 pT/Hz^1/2 sensitivity over 4 hours and a 64 fT/Hz^1/2 noise floor.
AI.motivation: Detecting extremely weak magnetic fields requires extensive signal accumulation to improve SNR, but thermal drift and environmental magnetic noise shift the system away from optimal operating frequencies, severely degrading long-term stability.
AI.method: Analytical solutions for signal response to common- and differential-mode detunings were derived from a detuning-inclusive Hamiltonian to clarify the robustness limit of DQ 4-Ramsey sensing. Guided by this model, synchronized frequency modulation and a dual-feedback scheme were introduced to independently track and compensate the frequency shifts while preserving optimal magnetic-field response.
AI.result: The system operated stably under 2.8 K temperature variations, maintained 7.0 pT/Hz^1/2 sensitivity over 5-100 Hz for 4 hours, achieved a 64 fT/Hz^1/2 noise floor, exhibited expected 1/T^1/2 scaling with integration time, and avoided amplitude underestimation and waveform distortion.
AI.conclusion: The dual-feedback approach provides a robust solution for long-term DQ 4-Ramsey diamond magnetometry, demonstrating potential for detecting weak biomagnetic signals.

title: Evaluating the performance of QEC primitives on quantum processors at large width and depth
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) relies on repeated parity extraction, mid-circuit measurement (MCM), reset, feed-forward, and scheduling, yet these primitives are usually assessed either in isolation or through resource-demanding experiments. We introduce a few-sample benchmark of QEC-relevant primitives based on an MCM implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) with a fixed set of linear parameters (LR-QAOA). For a chosen code, the QAOA Hamiltonian is constructed from its check structure, such that the resulting circuit mimics the syndrome-extraction connectivity and MCM pattern while producing a direct algorithmic signal, the approximation-ratio r. The LR-QAOA depth, defined by the number of QAOA layers, plays a role analogous to the number of repeated syndrome-extraction rounds in a QEC experiment. From QPU executions, the decay of r with depth defines an effective hardware error, which we map to an equivalent two-qubit depolarizing rate λeff. We compare direct and MCM-mediated implementations across 10 QPUs from IBM, IQM, and Quantinuum, with circuits containing up to 2950 MCM operations. On Quantinuum's Helios-1 and H2-1, we run code-structured LR-QAOA benchmarks for surface-code, triangular color-code, and bivariate-bicycle qLDPC Hamiltonians up to 81, 91, and 48 data qubits, respectively, using up to 480 MCM operations. On IBM ibm_phoenix, we implement the surface-code structure and compare the LR-QAOA response with logical-memory experiments, observing a correlation between the benchmark and the logical performance across different regions of the QPU. Its construction and low resource requirements provide a practical benchmark for comparing hardware generations and QEC implementations before full logical-memory experiments are performed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a few-sample benchmark for QEC-relevant primitives (MCM, reset, feed-forward, scheduling) using depth-parameterized LR-QAOA whose Hamiltonian is built from a code's check structure, yielding an approximation-ratio decay mapped to an effective two-qubit depolarizing rate.
AI.motivation: QEC primitives are typically evaluated in isolation or via resource-demanding experiments, so a low-cost, hardware-comparable benchmark that captures syndrome-extraction connectivity and MCM patterns while producing a direct algorithmic signal is needed.
AI.method: Construct the QAOA Hamiltonian from a chosen code's check structure so the circuit mimics syndrome-extraction connectivity and MCM patterns; use fixed linear parameters (LR-QAOA) where the number of layers parallels repeated syndrome-extraction rounds. Measure decay of the approximation ratio r with depth to extract an effective hardware error mapped to an equivalent two-qubit depolarizing rate λeff. Compare direct and MCM-mediated implementations across 10 QPUs from IBM, IQM, and Quantinuum, including circuits up to 2950 MCM operations; run code-structured benchmarks for surface, triangular color, and bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes up to 81, 91, and 48 data qubits, and compare surface-code LR-QAOA against logical-memory experiments on ibm_phoenix.
AI.result: Benchmarks execute on Quantinuum Helios-1 and H2-1 for surface, triangular color, and bivariate-bicycle qLDPC Hamiltonians up to 81, 91, and 48 data qubits with up to 480 MCM operations. On IBM ibm_phoenix, the surface-code LR-QAOA response correlates with logical-memory performance across different QPU regions.
AI.conclusion: The construction and low resource requirements make this a practical benchmark for comparing hardware generations and QEC implementations before full logical-memory experiments.

title: Joint GKP Encoding for GHZ States Transmission over Bosonic Quantum MIMO Channels
summary: We study transmission of a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state over nonunitary quantum multiple-input multiple-output (QuMIMO) channels using finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding. A coupled-mode model describes coherent mixing, mode-dependent attenuation, and Gaussian noise. The transceiver combines programmable passive meshes, quantum-limited MMSE gain, local GKP recovery, and joint classical syndrome decoding. We optimize complex-Givens lattices using instantaneous channel-state information (CSI), current singular values with channel statistics, or statistics alone. Simulations show that joint lattice shaping outperforms product GKP processing. Under coherent-basis drift, full instantaneous CSI improves GHZ-state preservation, whereas singular-value conditioned and fully statistical designs perform similarly because neither resolves the current singular frames. These findings identify singular-frame geometry as a critical resource beyond attenuation knowledge where joint GKP processing adapts the logical lattice and receiver to anisotropic bosonic noise rather than merely inverting multimode mixing.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates transmitting a GHZ state over nonunitary quantum MIMO channels using finite-energy GKP encoding, showing that joint lattice shaping with instantaneous CSI best preserves the state under coherent-basis drift, and that singular-frame geometry is a critical resource beyond attenuation knowledge.
AI.motivation: Nonunitary quantum MIMO channels with coherent mixing, mode-dependent attenuation, and Gaussian noise degrade multipartite entanglement such as GHZ states, and it is unclear how finite-energy GKP encoding and transceiver lattice design can preserve such states under realistic channel conditions.
AI.method: The authors model the channel as a coupled-mode system capturing coherent mixing, mode-dependent attenuation, and Gaussian noise. The transceiver uses programmable passive meshes, quantum-limited MMSE gain, local GKP recovery, and joint classical syndrome decoding, with complex-Givens lattices optimized under three CSI regimes: instantaneous CSI, current singular values plus channel statistics, and statistics alone.
AI.result: Joint lattice shaping outperforms product GKP processing. Under coherent-basis drift, full instantaneous CSI better preserves the GHZ state, while singular-value-conditioned and purely statistical designs perform similarly because neither resolves current singular frames.
AI.conclusion: Singular-frame geometry is identified as a critical resource beyond attenuation knowledge, enabling joint GKP processing to adapt the logical lattice and receiver to anisotropic bosonic noise rather than merely inverting multimode mixing.

title: Free fermion models with an operator entanglement growing as $O(\sqrt{t})$
summary: We study the time evolution of the Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE) of one-dimensional number-conserving free fermions subject to a random space- and time-dependent evolution. It is known that, in free-fermion systems without randomness, the OSEE of \emph{local} operators grows at most \emph{logarithmically} in time. Here we show that, in the presence of randomness, the OSEE of local spin operators involving a Jordan-Wigner string grows as $\mathcal O(\sqrt t)$, for all values of the Rényi index. We establish this in two models: a Brownian Hamiltonian and a brick-wall matchgate circuit. We also consider the OSEE of the evolution operator, and we show that it also grows as $\mathcal O(\sqrt{t})$, in contrast with the linear growth generically expected without randomness. We analytically compute the average entropies of the two operators by mapping the quantum models to the symmetric simple exclusion process, relying on an assumption of self-averaging which we support numerically. We also consider two other types of randomness: random evolution in time that keeps spatial translation invariance, and quenched disorder. In the former case, we find that the OSEE also grows as $\sqrt{t}$. In the latter case, we find that the entropy grows as $\mathcal O( \log \log t)$ for Hamiltonian evolution both for local operators with a Jordan-Wigner string and for the evolution operator, whereas it remains bounded at all times in the brick-wall matchgate circuit.

AI.tldr: The Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE) of local operators and of the evolution operator in 1D number-conserving free fermions grows as O(√t) under random space- and time-dependent evolution, in contrast to logarithmic or linear growth without randomness. This is shown for a Brownian Hamiltonian and a brick-wall matchgate circuit, with analytical results via mapping to the symmetric simple exclusion process.
AI.motivation: In free-fermion systems without randomness, the OSEE of local operators is known to grow at most logarithmically in time. The effect of randomness on this quantity, and on the OSEE of the evolution operator, was not established, motivating a systematic study of how different types of disorder alter entanglement growth in operator space.
AI.method: The authors study the time evolution of the OSEE of one-dimensional number-conserving free fermions under random space- and time-dependent evolution, using two models: a Brownian Hamiltonian and a brick-wall matchgate circuit. They analytically compute the average entropies by mapping the quantum models to the symmetric simple exclusion process, relying on a self-averaging assumption supported numerically. They also examine two additional randomness types: time-dependent random evolution preserving spatial translation invariance, and quenched disorder.
AI.result: With space- and time-dependent randomness, the OSEE of local spin operators involving a Jordan-Wigner string grows as O(√t) for all Rényi indices, as does the OSEE of the evolution operator, contrasting with the generic linear growth expected without randomness. Under randomness preserving spatial translation invariance in time, the OSEE also grows as √t. Under quenched disorder, the entropy grows as O(log log t) for Hamiltonian evolution for both local operators with a Jordan-Wigner string and the evolution operator, while it remains bounded at all times in the brick-wall matchgate circuit.
AI.conclusion: Randomness qualitatively changes the operator-space entanglement growth of free fermions, producing sublinear O(√t) scaling for space- and time-dependent and translation-invariant random evolution, and O(log log t) or bounded behavior for quenched disorder depending on the model. These findings highlight the sensitivity of OSEE growth to the nature of disorder.

title: Metastability in Quantum Dynamics for Optimization
summary: Metastability separates apparent equilibration from true convergence: a dynamical system can remain near an intermediate state long before reaching its stationary state. In quantum dynamics used for optimization, such a plateau can delay progress toward a target concentrated near the global minimizers of a nonconvex potential. In this paper, we initiate the study of the general mechanisms by which coherent evolution and dissipation shape metastability, using quantum Langevin dynamics (QLD) as a concrete example [CLW+25], where the objective function is encoded in the potential and coherent transfer between wells interacts with tunable dissipation. To quantify this interaction, we solve a two-state model precisely and derive a spectral-separation criterion in terms of tunneling frequency, dissipation strength, and damping imbalance. Extending the analysis to multi-state models, we show that sufficiently weak tunneling between wells can separate slow population transfer from fast relaxation within each well. In addition, we establish conditions under which changing the structure of dissipation shortens the time needed to approach a prescribed target state. Numerical experiments on double-well and multi-well potentials demonstrate these improvements while keeping the target and accuracy fixed and accounting for the time spent on control.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how coherent tunneling and dissipation jointly shape metastability in quantum Langevin dynamics (QLD) for optimization, deriving a spectral-separation criterion and showing that restructuring dissipation can shorten time-to-target.
AI.motivation: Metastability causes dynamical systems to linger near intermediate states long before reaching the true stationary state; in quantum-dynamics-based optimization, such plateaus delay convergence toward a target concentrated near the global minimizers of a nonconvex potential. The mechanisms by which coherent evolution and dissipation together shape this metastability remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Using quantum Langevin dynamics (QLD) as a concrete testbed—where the objective is encoded in the potential and coherent inter-well transfer interacts with tunable dissipation—the authors solve a two-state model exactly and derive a spectral-separation criterion in terms of tunneling frequency, dissipation strength, and damping imbalance. They then extend the analysis to multi-state models.
AI.result: The two-state analysis yields a precise spectral-separation criterion; in multi-state models, sufficiently weak inter-well tunneling separates slow population transfer from fast intra-well relaxation. The authors also establish conditions under which modifying the dissipation structure shortens the time needed to approach a prescribed target state. Numerical experiments on double-well and multi-well potentials confirm these improvements with the target and accuracy held fixed and control overhead included.
AI.conclusion: Coherent evolution and dissipation jointly govern metastability in QLD, and the derived spectral-separation criteria provide a principled basis for accelerating approach to a target state by tuning dissipation structure.

title: Polynomial neural surrogates for designing photonic quantum experiments
summary: Physics simulators can support the discovery of quantum experiments by predicting the states generated by experimental configurations. When these simulators are computationally expensive, repeated simulator calls can limit the search for experiments that generate a desired quantum state. Here, we develop a physics-inspired polynomial neural surrogate for PyTheus, a graph-based quantum-optics simulator, to predict quantum states and use it to design quantum experiments. Its polynomial activations are motivated by the relation between graph perfect matchings and the resulting state amplitudes. We train separate surrogate models for four-, six-, and eight-photon systems and show that they achieve higher prediction accuracy with fewer trainable parameters than standard multilayer perceptrons. We then use the trained surrogates for inverse design of GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states. For the larger systems, the surrogates also enable faster inverse design than direct optimization with PyTheus. These results suggest that incorporating the underlying physics into neural surrogates can provide an efficient approach to quantum experiment design.

AI.tldr: A physics-inspired polynomial neural surrogate for the PyTheus quantum-optics simulator predicts quantum states and enables faster inverse design of GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states, outperforming standard MLPs with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Physics simulators aid quantum experiment discovery by predicting states from experimental configurations, but computationally expensive simulators make repeated calls a bottleneck when searching for configurations that yield a desired quantum state.
AI.method: The authors build a physics-inspired polynomial neural surrogate for PyTheus, a graph-based quantum-optics simulator. Its polynomial activations are motivated by the relationship between graph perfect matchings and resulting state amplitudes. Separate surrogate models are trained for four-, six-, and eight-photon systems.
AI.result: The surrogates achieve higher prediction accuracy with fewer trainable parameters than standard multilayer perceptrons. They are used for inverse design of GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states; for larger systems, they enable faster inverse design than direct optimization with PyTheus.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating underlying physics into neural surrogates offers an efficient approach to quantum experiment design.

title: Materialised symmetries of 2D translationally invariant codes
summary: There has been significant recent interest in near-term qLDPC codes as high-performance alternatives to surface and color codes. One such class of codes is 2-dimensional translationally invariant (TI) codes, such as bivariate bicycle codes, which share similar properties to topological codes. Fundamental objects in the study of such codes are the materialised symmetries, which can be used for the construction of matching-based decoders. These decoders generalise the minimum-weight perfect matching decoder for toric codes and provide similar asymptotic performance guarantees that heuristic decoders such as BP and its variants lack. Despite this, the mathematical structure of symmetries along with their properties under translation and restriction to finite-sized lattices has not been well-studied. We describe a decomposition of symmetry spaces of 2D CSS TI codes on infinite lattices into translation-invariant subspaces which allow us to write an explicit basis of symmetries in a plane-wave-like form. We then describe how to adapt this infinite lattice basis so that any corresponding rectangular periodic lattice basis can be obtained by restriction to basis elements compatible with the periodic boundaries. This allows us to describe how the symmetry space varies with different rectangular dimensions. We illustrate via examples that it is often straightforward in practice to determine a basis of symmetries on twisted boundaries as well, without needing to recompute the decomposition.
