We comment on the applications of this framework to matching-based decoders and provide examples of symmetries of such codes as the gross code.

AI.tldr: This paper studies materialised symmetries of 2D translationally invariant (TI) CSS quantum LDPC codes. It decomposes symmetry spaces on infinite lattices into translation-invariant subspaces, gives plane-wave-like bases, and shows how to restrict these bases to rectangular periodic (and twisted) finite lattices, enabling matching-based decoders.
AI.motivation: Near-term qLDPC codes, especially 2D translationally invariant codes like bivariate bicycle codes, are promising alternatives to surface and color codes. Materialised symmetries enable matching-based decoders with asymptotic performance guarantees that heuristic decoders (e.g., BP and variants) lack. However, the mathematical structure of these symmetries, including their behavior under translation and restriction to finite lattices, has been under-studied.
AI.method: The authors decompose symmetry spaces of 2D CSS TI codes on infinite lattices into translation-invariant subspaces, yielding an explicit plane-wave-like basis of symmetries. They then adapt this infinite-lattice basis to rectangular periodic lattices by restricting to basis elements compatible with the periodic boundary conditions, characterizing how the symmetry space depends on rectangular dimensions. They also show, via examples, that bases on twisted boundaries can often be determined directly without recomputing the decomposition.
AI.result: The framework yields explicit translation-invariant symmetry bases, a systematic restriction procedure to periodic rectangular lattices, and a description of dimension-dependent symmetry spaces. Examples demonstrate easy handling of twisted boundaries and illustrate symmetries for concrete codes such as the gross code.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decomposition provides a structured mathematical understanding of materialised symmetries in 2D TI qLDPC codes and supports the construction and analysis of matching-based decoders. It offers practical tools for determining symmetry bases on finite periodic and twisted lattices, with applications to codes like the gross code.

title: Comparing thresholds of XZZX and rotated surface codes under spatio-temporal correlated noise
comment: 11 pages, 8 plots, simulation codes available on GitHub
summary: While independent and identically distributed noise is typically assumed in quantum computing research, complex error models such as correlated and spatio-temporal errors remain underexplored. In this paper, the performance of $\mathrm{XZZX}$ and rotated surface codes is evaluated under these complex noise models. Standard graph-based decoders struggle with the hyperedges generated by correlated errors on bias-tailored codes. To address this, we employ the Minimum Weight Parity Factor (MWPF) decoder, which natively processes syndrome hypergraphs without artificial edge decomposition. Our simulations show that under strong Z-biased circuit-level correlated noise ($η=100$), the threshold of the rotated code degrades to $\approx 0.36\%$, while the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code drops to $\approx 0.70\%$. Furthermore, a distinct non-monotonic threshold dependence is observed for the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code across different bias ratios. While the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code effectively absorbs high-density Z-type hyperedges at extreme biases, it exhibits a threshold minimum at moderate biases ($η\approx 10$) because transverse X and Y errors actively bridge the diagonal strings, breaking the code's one-dimensional decoupling symmetry. These findings demonstrate that utilizing hypergraph-aware decoders is critical, as the performance of bias-tailored codes is highly sensitive to the geometric structure of spatio-temporal correlated noise.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates XZZX and rotated surface codes under correlated and spatio-temporal noise using a Minimum Weight Parity Factor (MWPF) decoder that natively handles syndrome hypergraphs, revealing that bias-tailored code performance is highly sensitive to noise geometry.
AI.motivation: Most quantum computing research assumes independent and identically distributed noise, leaving complex error models such as correlated and spatio-temporal errors underexplored. Standard graph-based decoders struggle with hyperedges generated by correlated errors on bias-tailored codes, so there is a need to understand and accurately decode codes under realistic complex noise.
AI.method: The performance of XZZX and rotated surface codes is evaluated under complex correlated and spatio-temporal noise models. The Minimum Weight Parity Factor (MWPF) decoder is employed, which natively processes syndrome hypergraphs without artificial edge decomposition, avoiding the limitations of standard graph-based decoders.
AI.result: Under strong Z-biased circuit-level correlated noise (η=100), the threshold of the rotated code degrades to about 0.36%, while the XZZX code drops to about 0.70%. A distinct non-monotonic threshold dependence is observed for the XZZX code across different bias ratios: it effectively absorbs high-density Z-type hyperedges at extreme biases but exhibits a threshold minimum at moderate biases (η≈10) because transverse X and Y errors actively bridge diagonal strings, breaking the code's one-dimensional decoupling symmetry.
AI.conclusion: Utilizing hypergraph-aware decoders is critical, as the performance of bias-tailored codes is highly sensitive to the geometric structure of spatio-temporal correlated noise.

title: Quantum data loading from the learned shared structure of real signals
summary: Preparing quantum states from classical data can cost more than the computation they serve; most loaders tailor a circuit to each input. Here we show that the signals of a real dataset share structure that can be learned once and reused. Our quantum-native loader learns a low-dimensional description of a dataset and prepares every signal with one fixed circuit set by a few numbers. Across seven views of five public datasets it meets the targets of the strongest structured loader at equal gate cost with several times fewer numbers per signal. These numbers can be inferred from a random subset: in a preregistered blind replication the subset needed to come within ten per cent of full-signal accuracy stayed constant within a prespecified margin as signals grew sixteenfold, whereas the structured loader needed ever more. It declines what it cannot represent, covering fewer cases than that baseline and no electrocardiogram.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum-native data loader that learns a reusable low-dimensional description of a dataset once, then prepares each signal with a single fixed circuit parameterized by a few numbers, matching a strong structured loader at equal gate cost with far fewer parameters per signal.
AI.motivation: Loading classical data into quantum states can cost more than the computation it supports, and most existing loaders tailor a distinct circuit to every input, which is inefficient. The authors hypothesize that signals of a real dataset share learnable and reusable structure that can be exploited to avoid per-input circuit design.
AI.method: A quantum-native loader that learns a low-dimensional description of an entire dataset and, using one fixed circuit whose configuration is set by a few numbers, prepares every signal. Evaluation spans seven views of five public datasets, comparing against the strongest structured loader, including a subset-selection study and a preregistered blind replication.
AI.result: The loader meets the targets of the strongest structured loader at equal gate cost while using several times fewer numbers per signal. These numbers can be inferred from a random subset; in the blind replication, the subset size needed to reach within ten per cent of full-signal accuracy stayed constant within a prespecified margin as signals grew sixteenfold, whereas the structured baseline required ever more. It declines what it cannot represent, covering fewer cases than the baseline and no electrocardiogram.
AI.conclusion: Reusable, dataset-level low-dimensional structure enables efficient quantum data loading with few per-signal parameters and favorable scaling of subset requirements, though the approach is more conservative and abstains on cases it cannot represent, limiting coverage relative to the structured baseline.

title: Gaussian Universality and Its Breakdown in Tensor-Network Machine Learning
summary: Gaussian-process limits are powerful in describing overparameterized machine learning models, yet their validity in structured tensor-network architectures remains unclear. Here we analytically present a moment-based approach that identifies precise conditions for the emergence and breakdown of Gaussian universality in tensor-network learning models, with a focus on matrix product states. We prove that in the large bond dimension limit, the learning models with both local and global observables converge to Gaussian processes, with explicit finite-size bounds on higher-order moment deviations. Whereas in the large physical dimension limit, the Gaussian universality no longer persists: while the models with local observables retain Gaussian-process behavior, those global cases exhibit persistent non-Gaussian corrections. Our results reveal that Gaussian-process behavior in tensor-network learning is controlled not only by parameter number, but also by architectural scaling, observable locality, and the spectral properties.

AI.tldr: This work analytically establishes when Gaussian-process (GP) universality holds or breaks down in tensor-network (matrix product state) learning models, showing it depends on architectural scaling, observable locality, and spectral properties—not just parameter count.
AI.motivation: GP limits effectively describe overparameterized ML models, but their validity in structured tensor-network architectures is unclear. The paper aims to determine precise conditions for the emergence and breakdown of Gaussian universality in tensor-network learning, especially matrix product states.
AI.method: A moment-based analytical approach identifying conditions for GP universality. The authors examine two scaling regimes: the large bond dimension limit and the large physical dimension limit, considering models with both local and global observables, and derive finite-size bounds on higher-order moment deviations.
AI.result: In the large bond dimension limit, models with both local and global observables converge to Gaussian processes, with explicit finite-size bounds on higher-order moment deviations. In the large physical dimension limit, GP universality fails: local-observable models retain GP behavior, while global-observable models exhibit persistent non-Gaussian corrections.
AI.conclusion: GP behavior in tensor-network learning is governed not solely by parameter number, but also by architectural scaling, observable locality, and spectral properties.

title: Collective Quantum State Preparation Is Nonadditive
summary: Quantum state preparation is a basic primitive of quantum computation and control, but its resource cost is usually analyzed for one target state or under an independent-copy construction. Here we study the many-copy problem under weighted Pauli control, where a Pauli-product rotation $e^{iφP}$ is charged by its rotation angle $|φ|$, independently of the weight of $P$. We derive the exact single-qubit preparation cost and show that it is strictly nonadditive: a four-pulse collective protocol prepares two $T$ states at lower cost than two optimal one-copy protocols. We further identify finite regions of the Bloch sphere with collective saving, including trajectories that remain product throughout, showing that transient entanglement is not the only mechanism behind the advantage. Complementarily, a dimension-independent Rényi-entropy speed limit gives an extensive lower bound for every coherent target and an exponential fidelity penalty below a finite preparation rate. These results establish a many-copy geometry of state synthesis in which uncorrelated outputs can nevertheless benefit from collective control.

AI.tldr: This paper studies many-copy quantum state preparation under weighted Pauli control, finds the exact single-qubit cost, proves strict nonadditivity (a collective four-pulse protocol beats two optimal one-copy protocols for two T states), identifies Bloch-sphere regions with collective saving even for always-product trajectories, and provides a Rényi-entropy speed limit with extensive lower bound and exponential fidelity penalty below a finite rate.
AI.motivation: Resource costs for quantum state preparation are usually analyzed for a single target state or under an independent-copy construction, leaving the many-copy regime underexplored. The authors aim to understand whether collective control over multiple copies can reduce the preparation cost below that of independent optimal protocols, and to characterize the geometry and limits of such advantages.
AI.method: They adopt weighted Pauli control, charging a Pauli-product rotation e^{iφP} by its angle |φ| irrespective of the weight of P. They derive the exact single-qubit preparation cost and compare collective multi-copy protocols against independent one-copy protocols. They also develop a dimension-independent Rényi-entropy speed limit as a lower-bound tool.
AI.result: The exact single-qubit preparation cost is derived and shown to be strictly nonadditive: a four-pulse collective protocol prepares two T states at lower cost than two optimal one-copy protocols. Finite regions of the Bloch sphere exhibit collective saving, including trajectories that remain product throughout, indicating transient entanglement is not the sole mechanism. The Rényi-entropy speed limit yields an extensive lower bound for every coherent target and an exponential fidelity penalty below a finite preparation rate.
AI.conclusion: These findings establish a many-copy geometry of state synthesis in which uncorrelated outputs can nevertheless benefit from collective control, revealing nonadditivity as a genuine resource phenomenon beyond entanglement-based explanations.

title: Geometric Measure of Entanglement of Rank-2 Mixed Multiqubit States and its Estimation on a Quantum Processor
summary: The geometric measure of entanglement of mixed states is investigated based on its relation to spin correlations. We derive an analytical expression for the entanglement of rank-2 mixed states composed of arbitrary multiqubit pure states within a two-dimensional Hilbert subspace. The dependence of the entanglement of rank-2 mixed multiqubit states on the parameters characterizing arbitrary pure states in the mixture is studied both analytically and using quantum computing. For a particular class of mixed states, namely, equal-probability mixtures of an arbitrary multiqubit state and the Schrödinger cat state, we construct quantum protocols for detecting the geometric measure of entanglement based on its relation to spin correlations. We quantify the entanglement using both the AerSimulator and the ibm_marrakesh quantum computer. The effects of quantum-computing errors are also analyzed. The simulation results reproduce the analytical dependencies, while measurements on the quantum device demonstrate good agreement with theoretical predictions within estimated error bounds.

AI.tldr: The geometric measure of entanglement (GME) for rank-2 mixed multiqubit states is derived analytically via its relation to spin correlations and verified with quantum-computing simulations and real-device measurements.
AI.motivation: Mixed-state entanglement quantification is hard in general; the geometric measure of entanglement of mixed states is investigated exploiting its connection to spin correlations, motivated by the need for analytical expressions and experimentally feasible detection protocols.
AI.method: An analytical expression is derived for the entanglement of rank-2 mixed states composed of arbitrary multiqubit pure states in a two-dimensional Hilbert subspace. The dependence of GME on the parameters of the constituent pure states is studied analytically and via quantum computing. For equal-probability mixtures of an arbitrary multiqubit state with the Schrodinger cat state, quantum protocols for detecting the GME based on spin correlations are constructed. Entanglement is quantified using AerSimulator and the ibm_marrakesh quantum computer, with analysis of quantum-computing errors.
AI.result: Simulation results reproduce the analytical dependencies, and measurements on the quantum device show good agreement with theoretical predictions within estimated error bounds; error effects are characterized.
AI.conclusion: The geometric measure of entanglement of rank-2 mixed multiqubit states admits a tractable analytical form linked to spin correlations, and can be detected and quantified on near-term quantum hardware with acceptable accuracy.

title: When Equivalent Quantum Circuits Lose Synthesis Choices
summary: Quantum compilers synthesize high-level operations, such as the quantum Fourier transform and multi-controlled X gates, into gate-level circuits. Across compilation stages, a circuit may be serialized, exchanged as OpenQASM, converted between compilers, or lowered to gates. These representation changes can preserve computation while removing the high-level operation itself, leaving the receiving compiler unable to apply a requested synthesis method. We call this loss synthesis availability. We study synthesis availability in Qiskit, TKET, and Cirq through controlled experiments, repository analysis, circuits captured from project tests, and a Munich Quantum Toolkit pipeline. Synthesis availability survives serialization when deserialization restores the high-level operation and survives compiler conversion only when the receiving compiler supports that operation. It does not survive the evaluated OpenQASM routes. After a direct OpenQASM 3 round trip, requested synthesis has no effect in all 360 delivered conditions even though compilation succeeds. In the MQT pipeline, OpenQASM 2 interchange increases the two-qubit gate count by 37.2 percent for an eight-qubit Grover circuit. We also introduce Verified, which records high-level operations before a representation change and reconstructs them only when a check confirms that the record still matches the delivered circuit. Verified restores requested synthesis in all 830 recovery runs, with median verification times from 2.0 to 638 ms per operation family. The check rejects every stale record but also some valid records. These results show that preserving functional equivalence alone is insufficient when later synthesis choices depend on retained high-level structure.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and quantifies "synthesis availability"—the loss of high-level operations (and thus the ability to apply requested synthesis methods) across compilation stages, serialization, and inter-compiler exchange—and proposes "Verified," a record-and-check mechanism that restores high-level operations when verified against the delivered circuit.
AI.motivation: Quantum compilers synthesize high-level operations into gate-level circuits, but circuits are frequently serialized (e.g., as OpenQASM), exchanged between compilers, or lowered to gates. These representation changes can preserve functional equivalence while erasing the high-level operation itself, so a downstream compiler can no longer apply a requested synthesis method. The paper argues that preserving functional equivalence alone is insufficient when later synthesis decisions depend on retained high-level structure.
AI.method: The authors study synthesis availability in Qiskit, TKET, and Cirq via controlled experiments, repository analysis, circuits captured from project tests, and a Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) pipeline. They test whether high-level operations survive serialization, compiler conversion, and OpenQASM routes (including OpenQASM 3 round trips and OpenQASM 2 interchange). They then introduce Verified, which records high-level operations before a representation change and reconstructs them only when a verification check confirms the record still matches the delivered circuit.
AI.result: Synthesis availability survives serialization only when deserialization restores the high-level operation, and survives compiler conversion only when the receiving compiler supports that operation; it does not survive the evaluated OpenQASM routes. After a direct OpenQASM 3 round trip, requested synthesis has no effect in all 360 delivered conditions despite successful compilation. In the MQT pipeline, OpenQASM 2 interchange increases the two-qubit gate count by 37.2 percent for an eight-qubit Grover circuit. Verified restores requested synthesis in all 830 recovery runs, with median verification times of 2.0 to 638 ms per operation family; its check rejects every stale record but also some valid records.
AI.conclusion: Representation changes such as serialization and inter-compiler exchange can silently strip high-level operations, making requested synthesis ineffective even when compilation succeeds and functional equivalence is preserved. Preserving functional equivalence alone is therefore insufficient when downstream synthesis choices depend on retained high-level structure. Verified demonstrates that recording and verifying high-level operations before representation changes can recover synthesis availability, at the cost of some false rejections of valid records.

title: What Does It Cost to Simulate a Quantum Sentence Classifier? An Energy and Compute Perspective on Near-Term QNLP
summary: Near-term quantum natural language processing (QNLP) experiments often run on classical simulators, so simulator cost is part of the field's practical compute burden, yet accuracy tables do not show it. We measure that cost for a variational quantum classifier (VQC) on binary SST-2 sentiment classification, using PennyLane's state-vector simulator over a controlled grid of 27 configurations: three balanced training-set sizes (N = 200, 500, 1000), three qubit counts (4, 6, 8), and three circuit depths. Each VQC is compared with logistic regression on the same PCA-reduced input; full TF-IDF logistic regression gives an uncompressed reference. The VQC beats its matched baseline in 6 of 27 single-seed comparisons. After reruns at two further seeds, only 1 of these 6 keeps a positive mean advantage larger than its paired seed-to-seed variability, and paired tests on the fixed validation set do not establish it. VQC training is 886-21,127 times slower in measured wall-clock time than the matched classical fit (median 3,158 times); going from 4 to 8 qubits roughly doubles simulator time, and within the tested range per-step cost is well approximated by a linear function of the parameter count. CodeCarbon energy and CO2 estimates are secondary: they imply an almost constant power of about 41 W, so they add little beyond runtime, and we do not build an energy ratio from them. The study is narrow (one dataset, representation, ansatz, simulator, and CPU environment) and is a reproducible feasibility measurement, not a general verdict on QNLP.

AI.tldr: On binary SST-2 sentiment classification with a PennyLane state-vector simulator, a VQC beats its matched classical baseline in only 6 of 27 single-seed comparisons, but just 1 of those 6 survives multi-seed reruns; VQC training is 886-21,127x slower (median 3,158x) than the matched logistic-regression fit.
AI.motivation: Near-term QNLP experiments typically rely on classical simulators, so simulator cost is a real part of the field's practical compute burden, yet this cost is invisible in standard accuracy tables. The authors aim to measure that hidden cost explicitly and to assess whether a VQC's reported accuracy advantages hold up under seed variation and paired testing.
AI.method: A variational quantum classifier (VQC) is evaluated on binary SST-2 sentiment classification using PennyLane's state-vector simulator across a controlled grid of 27 configurations: three balanced training-set sizes (N = 200, 500, 1000), three qubit counts (4, 6, 8), and three circuit depths. Each VQC is compared against logistic regression on the same PCA-reduced input, with full TF-IDF logistic regression as an uncompressed reference. Comparisons use single seeds, then reruns at two further seeds, with paired tests on a fixed validation set; wall-clock training time and CodeCarbon energy/CO2 estimates are also recorded.
AI.result: The VQC beats its matched baseline in 6 of 27 single-seed comparisons. After reruns at two further seeds, only 1 of these 6 retains a positive mean advantage larger than its paired seed-to-seed variability, and paired tests on the fixed validation set do not establish it. VQC training is 886-21,127 times slower in measured wall-clock time than the matched classical fit (median 3,158 times); moving from 4 to 8 qubits roughly doubles simulator time, and within the tested range per-step cost is well approximated by a linear function of the parameter count. CodeCarbon estimates imply an almost constant power of about 41 W, so they add little beyond runtime, and no energy ratio is derived.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy advantage of the tested VQC is largely fragile: most apparent wins do not survive seed reruns or paired testing, while simulator training cost is orders of magnitude higher than the matched classical fit, making simulator cost a decisive practical factor for near-term QNLP. The study is narrow (one dataset, representation, ansatz, simulator, and CPU environment) and should be read as a reproducible feasibility measurement rather than a general verdict on QNLP.

title: The superb supersinglet
summary: Multipartite systems of high-dimensional particles can host forms of quantum entanglement inaccessible to qubit systems. A particularly fascinating class is formed by the fully antisymmetric states, also known as supersinglets, which possess a remarkable symmetry: they are invariant under arbitrary collective local unitaries. Here, we explore their entanglement properties and establish their quantum information applications. Using convex optimisation, we show that central entanglement features of supersinglets are remarkably robust to noise, substantially surpassing the robustness of several paradigmatic entangled states under certain relaxations. We then develop witness methods, based on collective-spin or randomised measurements, that certify both the depth and dimensionality of their entanglement. Finally, we identify supersinglets as a natural resource for high-dimensional gradient sensing and prove that they enable Heisenberg scaling. Together, these results reveal supersinglets as an exceptionally robust and versatile class of multipartite entangled states, combining striking symmetry and strong entanglement with concrete potential for quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: Supersinglets—fully antisymmetric, collectively invariant states of high-dimensional multipartite systems—are shown to have highly noise-robust entanglement and to serve as resources for certified entanglement detection and Heisenberg-limited gradient sensing.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional multipartite systems can host entanglement forms unavailable to qubits. Supersinglets (fully antisymmetric states invariant under arbitrary collective local unitaries) are especially fascinating, but their entanglement properties and quantum information applications remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors analyze supersinglets using convex optimisation to assess entanglement robustness under noise. They develop entanglement witness methods based on collective-spin measurements and randomised measurements to certify entanglement depth and dimensionality. They also identify supersinglets as a resource for high-dimensional gradient sensing and analyze their metrological performance.
AI.result: Central entanglement features of supersinglets are remarkably robust to noise, substantially surpassing the robustness of several paradigmatic entangled states under certain relaxations. The proposed witnesses certify both entanglement depth and dimensionality. Supersinglets enable Heisenberg scaling for high-dimensional gradient sensing.
AI.conclusion: Supersinglets constitute an exceptionally robust and versatile class of multipartite entangled states, combining striking symmetry, strong entanglement, and concrete potential for quantum sensing.

title: A robust framework for the comprehensive characterisation of parametric down-conversion sources
summary: Reliable verification of squeezed-light sources is essential for photonic quantum technologies. High-dimensional quantum optical networks demand single-mode, pure squeezed states which, in principle, can be generated through careful engineering of parametric down-conversion-based (PDC) sources. However, due to the imperfections of optical components, the generated state is never pure and commonly contains internal mode structure. Existing characterisation techniques, based on either joint spectral intensity or normalized second-order correlation functions, work under the assumption that the probed state is pure, and therefore can result in incomplete or misleading assessment of the source quality. Here, we develop a device-agnostic characterisation framework for PDC-based sources with distinguishable signal and idler fields. Treating the source as a black box producing a mixed multimode Gaussian state, we find a lower bound for the state purity, which can be experimentally determined via mode-unresolved measurements. Our approach enables a holistic assessment of realistic squeezed-light source quality without requiring a detailed model of the nonlinear device and its surrounding optical network, providing practical benchmarks for optimizing sources for state-of-the-art quantum applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a device-agnostic framework to characterize PDC-based squeezed-light sources as black-box mixed multimode Gaussian states, deriving a measurable lower bound on state purity via mode-unresolved measurements.
AI.motivation: Reliable verification of squeezed-light sources is critical for photonic quantum technologies and high-dimensional quantum optical networks, which require single-mode, pure squeezed states. Existing characterization techniques (joint spectral intensity, normalized second-order correlation functions) assume the probed state is pure, so optical component imperfections and internal mode structure cause incomplete or misleading quality assessments.
AI.method: Treating the parametric down-conversion (PDC) source with distinguishable signal and idler fields as a black box producing a mixed multimode Gaussian state, the authors develop a device-agnostic characterization framework. They derive a lower bound for state purity that can be experimentally determined through mode-unresolved measurements, without needing a detailed model of the nonlinear device or its surrounding optical network.
AI.result: A lower bound on the state purity is obtained, which can be experimentally accessed via mode-unresolved measurements, enabling holistic assessment of realistic squeezed-light source quality without detailed device modeling.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides practical benchmarks for optimizing squeezed-light sources for state-of-the-art quantum applications, enabling reliable quality assessment of realistic PDC-based sources.

title: Improved Adaptive Estimation of Quantum Partition Functions with Heisenberg Scaling
summary:
We give quantum algorithms that estimate the log partition function of an $n$-qubit quantum Hamiltonian to additive error $ε$ with Heisenberg scaling, while minimizing calls to thermal-state purification preparation. The input is a block encoding of $H$, unitaries preparing thermofield-double states at chosen inverse temperatures, with their inverses and controlled versions, and an adaptive slowly-varying cooling schedule. The system-size bounds below assume $0\preceq H\preceq hI$ with $h=O(n)$ and block-encoding normalization $α=Θ(h)$. For constant inverse temperature, we show that such a schedule of length $O(\sqrt n)$ always exists and can be generated from overlap estimates with $\widetilde O(\sqrt n)$ further preparations.
  Given such a schedule and classically chosen temperatures, we estimate the log partition function with $\widetilde O(n^{5/4}/ε)$ expected calls to state preparation and to the block encoding, improving by $n^{1/4}$ on non-adaptive strategies. To achieve our result, we use a recursive-doubling identity that expresses each schedule increment as a weighted sum of logarithms of thermofield-double overlaps and of short imaginary-time steps implemented by quantum singular value transformation combined with previously developed variance reduction techniques. If thermofield doubles can be prepared controlled on a temperature register, a quantum inverse-binomial log estimator combined with quantum mean estimation reduces both query counts to $\widetilde O(n/ε)$. We show that the latter scaling is optimal in block-encoding queries up to polylogarithmic factors and discuss end-to-end complexities for one-dimensional partition-function estimation.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithms estimate the log partition function of an n-qubit Hamiltonian to additive error ε with Heisenberg scaling via an adaptive cooling schedule, achieving Õ(n^{5/4}/ε) state-preparation and block-encoding calls, or Õ(n/ε) when thermofield doubles are temperature-controlled, with the latter shown near-optimal in block-encoding queries.
AI.motivation: Estimating the log partition function of a quantum Hamiltonian is a central task in quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics. Prior quantum approaches rely on non-adaptive strategies and fail to attain Heisenberg scaling while minimizing costly thermal-state purification (thermofield-double) preparations. The paper aims to reduce the number of state-preparation and block-encoding queries required for additive-error estimation.
AI.method: The algorithm takes a block encoding of H, unitaries preparing thermofield-double states at chosen inverse temperatures (with inverses and controlled versions), and an adaptive slowly-varying cooling schedule. For constant inverse temperature, a length-O(√n) schedule is shown to exist and is generated from overlap estimates with Õ(√n) additional preparations. Estimation uses a recursive-doubling identity expressing each schedule increment as a weighted sum of logarithms of thermofield-double overlaps and short imaginary-time steps, implemented via quantum singular value transformation combined with variance-reduction techniques. When thermofield doubles can be prepared controlled on a temperature register, a quantum inverse-binomial log estimator combined with quantum mean estimation is applied. Assumptions: 0 ⪯ H ⪯ hI with h=O(n) and block-encoding normalization α=Θ(h).
AI.result: Given the schedule and classically chosen temperatures, the log partition function is estimated to additive error ε using Õ(n^{5/4}/ε) expected calls to state preparation and to the block encoding, improving on non-adaptive strategies by a factor of n^{1/4}. With temperature-controlled thermofield doubles, the quantum inverse-binomial log estimator plus quantum mean estimation reduces both query counts to Õ(n/ε). This latter scaling is proven optimal in block-encoding queries up to polylogarithmic factors. End-to-end complexities for one-dimensional partition-function estimation are also discussed.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive cooling schedules combined with recursive-doubling identities and quantum singular value transformation enable Heisenberg-scaled log-partition-function estimation with substantially reduced query complexity. The Õ(n/ε) block-encoding query count under temperature-controlled thermofield doubles is near-optimal, establishing a benchmark for quantum partition-function estimation.

title: Casimir force screening by a quantum Boltzmann plasma
comment: Submitted to The Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: We develop a finite-temperature field-theoretical description of the Casimir interaction between two perfectly conducting boundaries with the intervening gap filled by a two-component quantum Boltzmann plasma embedded in a homogeneous dielectric background. The quantum motion of the charged particles is represented by imaginary-time worldlines, while the electromagnetic field is treated in the Gaussian approximation. The resulting partition function contains distinct longitudinal and transverse response contributions and an additional quantum-induced source term with no classical counterpart. In the classical limit the theory reduces to the usual Casimir-screening picture: the static longitudinal mode is Debye screened, whereas the transverse electromagnetic sector is unaffected by classical mobile charges. Finite thermal de Broglie wavelengths modify the nonzero Matsubara response and produce the leading quantum correction to the force. In the static long-wavelength limit, the longitudinal dielectric function has, through the leading quantum correction, the same expansion structure as the Lindhard response of a degenerate electron gas under the correspondence $k_{TF}\leftrightarrowκ_D$ and $k_F\leftrightarrowλ_{dB}^{-1}$, while the static transverse response reproduces the leading high-temperature Landau orbital diamagnetic susceptibility.

AI.tldr: A finite-temperature field-theoretical framework describes the Casimir interaction between perfectly conducting plates separated by a two-component quantum Boltzmann plasma in a dielectric background, yielding quantum corrections beyond the classical Debye-screening picture.
AI.motivation: Classical Casimir-screening treatments miss quantum effects of mobile charges; a field-theoretic description is needed to capture finite thermal de Broglie wavelength corrections and connect to known degenerate-electron and diamagnetic response results.
AI.method: Imaginary-time worldline representation of charged-particle quantum motion combined with Gaussian treatment of the electromagnetic field; partition function decomposed into longitudinal and transverse response contributions plus a quantum-induced source term with no classical analogue.
AI.result: Classical limit recovers Debye screening of the static longitudinal mode with transverse sector unaffected; finite de Broglie wavelengths modify nonzero Matsubara response and give the leading quantum force correction. Static long-wavelength longitudinal dielectric function matches the Lindhard expansion structure under k_TF↔κ_D and k_F↔λ_dB^{-1}; static transverse response reproduces leading high-temperature Landau orbital diamagnetic susceptibility.
AI.conclusion: The theory unifies classical Casimir screening with quantum corrections, showing that a quantum Boltzmann plasma interpolates between Debye screening and degenerate Lindhard/diamagnetic behaviour, providing a controlled route to quantum Casimir force corrections.

title: Interferometric braiding of non-Abelian anyons
summary: The manipulation of non-Abelian anyons is a foundational ingredient for topological quantum computing and underlies topologically protected quantum memories. Here we analyze a quantum-impurity-based protocol for braiding non-Abelian anyons. Exploiting mobile impurities with addressable internal spin states, we provide a concrete protocol to experimentally measure the matrix elements of the $R$ and $F$ matrices that characterize the non-Abelian statistics of anyons. In particular, focusing on the case of Ising and Fibonacci anyons, we illustrate how the anyonic nature of the excitations emerges directly in the Ramsey interferometer we propose. Building on this framework, we further introduce a conventional-to-topological qubit encoder to transfer quantum information from conventional flying qubits into a topologically protected quantum memory.

AI.tldr: A quantum-impurity-based braiding protocol is proposed to measure R and F matrix elements governing non-Abelian statistics (Ising and Fibonacci anyons), and extended into a conventional-to-topological qubit encoder for transferring quantum information into a topologically protected memory.
AI.motivation: Manipulating non-Abelian anyons is foundational for topological quantum computing and topologically protected quantum memories, yet experimental protocols to access their defining braiding data remain a key challenge.
AI.method: Mobile impurities with addressable internal spin states are exploited to braid non-Abelian anyons. The resulting anyonic phases are probed via a Ramsey interferometer, allowing direct measurement of the R and F matrix elements. The framework is specialized to Ising and Fibonacci anyons and then used to construct a conventional-to-topological qubit encoder.
AI.result: Anyonic nature of the excitations emerges directly in the proposed Ramsey interferometer, yielding measurable R and F matrix elements for Ising and Fibonacci anyons. The encoder transfers quantum information from conventional flying qubits into a topologically protected quantum memory.
AI.conclusion: The impurity-based scheme provides a concrete experimental route to characterize non-Abelian statistics and to interface conventional flying qubits with topologically protected quantum memories, relevant to topological quantum computing.

title: Unitary RQL Equals RQL
summary: Intermediate measurements let quantum computations discard information and reuse their workspace. Deferring all measurements can require storing their entire history, which need not preserve logarithmic space. Fefferman and Remscrim proved that measurements can nevertheless be eliminated with two-sided bounded error, and asked whether the same holds with one-sided error [FR21]. We prove RQLΓ = RQULΓ for the standard gate set Γ = {H, T, CNOT}, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and exactly zero acceptance on no-instances. Our proof extends the density-matrix doubling method of Girish, Raz and Zhan [ GRZ21 ] to general channels, including resets and classical memory. We also prove measurement elimination for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses, including suitable gates with transcendental entries, and establish gate-set independence for a specified family of algebraic gate sets. A separate history-checking construction proves QMAL1,G = QUMAL1,G under explicit gate assumptions: measurements can also be eliminated from logarithmic-space quantum verification while preserving perfect completeness

AI.tldr: The paper proves RQLΓ = RQULΓ for Γ = {H, T, CNOT}, eliminating intermediate measurements in log-space quantum computation with one-sided bounded error, exactly zero acceptance on no-instances, polynomial time, and logarithmic space. It extends density-matrix doubling to general channels (resets, classical memory), proves measurement elimination for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses (including transcendental entries), establishes gate-set independence for a family of algebraic gate sets, and shows QMAL_{1,G} = QUMAL_{1,G} via a history-checking argument preserving perfect completeness.
AI.motivation: Intermediate measurements let quantum computations discard information and reuse workspace, but deferring all measurements may require storing the entire measurement history, which need not preserve logarithmic space. Fefferman and Remscrim [FR21] showed measurements can be eliminated with two-sided bounded error and asked whether this holds with one-sided error. This paper answers that question affirmatively for the standard gate set and extends the result.
AI.method: The proof extends the density-matrix doubling method of Girish, Raz and Zhan [GRZ21] to general quantum channels, including resets and classical memory. Measurement elimination is also established for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses (including suitable gates with transcendental entries), and gate-set independence is proven for a specified family of algebraic gate sets. A separate history-checking construction handles quantum verification.
AI.result: RQLΓ = RQULΓ holds for Γ = {H, T, CNOT}, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and exactly zero acceptance on no-instances. Measurement elimination holds for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses, including suitable gates with transcendental entries; gate-set independence holds for a specified family of algebraic gate sets. Additionally, QMAL_{1,G} = QUMAL_{1,G} under explicit gate assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate measurements can be eliminated from logarithmic-space quantum computation while preserving one-sided bounded error, zero acceptance on no-instances, polynomial time, and logarithmic space. The density-matrix doubling technique generalizes to general channels, and measurement elimination also applies to logarithmic-space quantum verification while preserving perfect completeness.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall Transport Under Microwave Irradiation Using a Topological Circulator
summary: Edge magnetoplasmons (EMPs) provide a platform for probing chiral charge dynamics and nonreciprocal microwave transport in topological quantum materials. However, detecting small perturbations to EMP propagation remains challenging because their signatures in conventional microwave scattering measurements can be weak. Here, we investigate microwave-photon-induced perturbations of EMP transport using a quantum anomalous Hall topological circulator. Pump--probe measurements reveal a strongly frequency-selective response: while microwave irradiation substantially modifies the EMP transmission at several pump frequencies, the transmission remains nearly unchanged at selected frequencies, including 4 and 7 GHz. We further exploit the non-Hermitian mode hybridization of the coupled EMP-resonator system to probe the response near an exceptional point (EP). The pump-induced change in transmission magnitude near the EP is approximately twice that observed away from the EP, demonstrating an enhanced microwave response to perturbations. These results reveal the interplay among chiral EMP transport, microwave-photon-induced perturbations, and non-Hermitian dynamics, and demonstrate the potential of topological circulators as a promising platform for enhanced microwave spectroscopy and sensing.

AI.tldr: This work uses a quantum anomalous Hall topological circulator to study microwave-photon-induced perturbations of edge magnetoplasmon (EMP) transport, showing a strongly frequency-selective response and an enhanced response near an exceptional point (EP).
AI.motivation: Detecting small perturbations to edge magnetoplasmon (EMP) propagation is challenging because their signatures in conventional microwave scattering measurements are often weak, motivating the search for a more sensitive measurement scheme.
AI.method: Pump-probe microwave measurements on a quantum anomalous Hall topological circulator, combined with a coupled EMP-resonator system operated near an exceptional point (EP) via non-Hermitian mode hybridization.
AI.result: The EMP transmission response is strongly frequency-selective: microwave irradiation substantially modifies transmission at several pump frequencies but leaves it nearly unchanged at selected frequencies (e.g., 4 and 7 GHz). The pump-induced change in transmission magnitude near the EP is about twice that away from the EP, demonstrating enhanced response.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal the interplay among chiral EMP transport, microwave-photon-induced perturbations, and non-Hermitian dynamics, and position topological circulators as a promising platform for enhanced microwave spectroscopy and sensing.

title: High-Fidelity Remote Graph State Preparation for Blind Quantum Computation
summary: Measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) relies on entangled graph states, yet existing remote state preparation (RSP) protocols prepare only separable states, requiring subsequent entangling gates on the remote server. Here, we introduce Remote Graph State Preparation (RGSP), a framework that prepares arbitrary graph states directly from a single high-dimensional photonic qudit. By encoding multiple qubits and their graph connectivity into the photon's structured phase profile, RGSP can reduce or, for small computations, completely eliminate the need for server-side entangling operations among qubits. We show that under a reasonable noise model the resulting state fidelity is independent of the graph topology. Under cumulative fiber phase drift, we demonstrate that this fidelity is significantly enhanced by a ``highest-weight-first'' mode reordering strategy. Finally, we show that RGSP enables reduced-SWAP universal blind quantum computing on arbitrary topologies, reducing qubit overhead e.g., for a six-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform from $420$ RSP qubits with a standard brickwork topology to $48$ RSP qubits. These results establish RGSP as a resource-efficient, topology-invariant primitive for quantum-secured cloud computing.

AI.tldr: RGSP prepares arbitrary photonic graph states directly from a single high-dimensional qudit, eliminating or reducing server-side entangling gates and enabling topology-invariant, resource-efficient blind quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Existing remote state preparation (RSP) protocols for measurement-based quantum computation only prepare separable states, so the remote server must still apply entangling gates. This limits resource efficiency and constrains secure cloud-based quantum computing.
AI.method: RGSP encodes multiple qubits and their graph connectivity into the structured phase profile of one high-dimensional photonic qudit, directly preparing arbitrary graph states. The work analyzes fidelity under a noise model and under cumulative fiber phase drift, and introduces a "highest-weight-first" mode reordering strategy to mitigate drift-induced fidelity loss.
AI.result: State fidelity is shown to be independent of graph topology under a reasonable noise model. The highest-weight-first mode reordering significantly enhances fidelity under cumulative fiber phase drift. RGSP supports reduced-SWAP universal blind quantum computing on arbitrary topologies, cutting qubit overhead for a six-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform from 420 RSP qubits (standard brickwork topology) to 48 RSP qubits.
AI.conclusion: RGSP is a resource-efficient, topology-invariant primitive for quantum-secured cloud computing, reducing or removing server-side entangling operations and lowering qubit overhead.

title: Suppressing Frequency Collisions in a Quantum Processor
summary: Frequency crowding, the close spacing of qubit transitions, limits superconducting quantum processors through crosstalk, leakage, and spectator dependent errors. We introduce a Hamiltonian based framework that maps two- and three-body collision mechanisms onto a Max-k-Cut problem on qubit frequency allocation. In order to make larger lattices tractable, we introduce a cluster-stitching protocol that decomposes larger lattices into overlapping subgraphs and reconciles their local frequency assignments into globally consistent configurations. We tested our proposed framework across multiple qubit architectures to suppress dominant collision penalties by revealing a hardware residual crosstalk. We benchmark digitized counterdiabatic QAOA (DC-QAOA), standard QAOA, and simulated annealing. Counterdiabatic terms improve QAOA optimization near steep collision penalties, while simulated annealing achieves the lowest costs on the tested instances. These results indicate that our hardware-aware optimization connects microscopic interaction physics to processor-level frequency planning. These results enable a systematic solver for benchmarking of scalable software hardware co design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Hamiltonian-based framework that maps two- and three-body collision mechanisms onto a Max-k-Cut problem for qubit frequency allocation, using a cluster-stitching protocol to scale to larger lattices, and benchmarks QAOA variants and simulated annealing.
AI.motivation: Frequency crowding—the close spacing of qubit transitions—degrades superconducting quantum processors via crosstalk, leakage, and spectator-dependent errors. There is a need for hardware-aware frequency planning that connects microscopic interaction physics to processor-level qubit frequency allocation.
AI.method: The authors formulate a Hamiltonian-based framework mapping two- and three-body collision mechanisms onto a Max-k-Cut problem on qubit frequency allocation. To handle larger lattices, they introduce a cluster-stitching protocol that decomposes lattices into overlapping subgraphs and reconciles their local frequency assignments into globally consistent configurations. They benchmark digitized counterdiabatic QAOA (DC-QAOA), standard QAOA, and simulated annealing across multiple qubit architectures.
AI.result: The framework suppresses dominant collision penalties across multiple qubit architectures while revealing a hardware residual crosstalk. Counterdiabatic terms improve QAOA optimization near steep collision penalties, whereas simulated annealing achieves the lowest costs on the tested instances.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware optimization connects microscopic interaction physics to processor-level frequency planning, enabling a systematic solver for benchmarking scalable software-hardware co-design.

title: Adiabatic tracking and optimal schedules for classical and quantum Gibbs-state preparation
summary: We develop a discrete adiabatic framework for Gibbs-state preparation in classical and quantum optimisation algorithms. For finite time-inhomogeneous reversible Markov chains, we derive a tracking theorem that bounds the distance from the evolving distribution to the instantaneous stationary state by combining two effects: contraction of previously accumulated error by the Markov dynamics and the new error generated as the stationary distribution changes from one step to the next. For Gibbs paths, this leads to explicit step-complexity bounds and to gap- and fluctuation-adapted schedules controlled by the Markov-chain spectral gap and the energy-fluctuation scale $V(β)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{π_β}(E)}$. In the weak-damping regime, the resulting schedule takes the form $\dotβ\proptoδ(β)/V(β)$. We then apply the discrete quantum adiabatic theorem to temperature-dependent Szegedy quantum walks. The quantum-walk eigenphase gap satisfies $Δ_w=Θ(\sqrtδ)$, where $δ$ is the spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain. By analysing the finite-difference terms entering the theorem, we show that this square-root spectral amplification translates into a quadratic improvement in the gap dependence only for suitably gap-adapted schedules. Under the corresponding regularity conditions, the quantum adiabatic cost scales as $O(δ_{\min}^{-1/2})$, compared with the classical $O(δ_{\min}^{-1})$ relaxation scale.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a discrete adiabatic framework for Gibbs-state preparation, proving a tracking theorem for finite-time inhomogeneous reversible Markov chains and showing that temperature-dependent Szegedy quantum walks achieve a quadratic speedup in spectral-gap dependence via square-root spectral amplification when gap-adapted schedules are used.
AI.motivation: Preparing Gibbs states is central to classical and quantum optimisation, yet understanding the finite-time cost of adiabatic-style, discrete Markov-chain protocols—and whether quantum walks offer a genuine advantage—lacks a unified rigorous treatment. This work addresses this gap.
AI.method: The authors derive a tracking theorem for finite-time inhomogeneous reversible Markov chains, bounding the distance to the instantaneous stationary state by combining contraction of accumulated error with newly generated error. For Gibbs paths, they obtain explicit step-complexity bounds and gap- and fluctuation-adapted schedules governed by the Markov-chain spectral gap and the energy-fluctuation scale V(β). They then apply the discrete quantum adiabatic theorem to temperature-dependent Szegedy quantum walks, exploiting the eigenphase gap Δ_w = Θ(√δ) and analysing the finite-difference terms.
AI.result: The classical framework yields explicit step-complexity bounds and schedules; in the weak-damping regime the schedule takes the form β̇ ∝ δ(β)/V(β). For quantum walks, the square-root spectral amplification translates into a quadratic improvement in gap dependence only for suitably gap-adapted schedules. Under the corresponding regularity conditions, the quantum adiabatic cost scales as O(δ_min^{-1/2}), versus the classical O(δ_min^{-1}) relaxation scale.
AI.conclusion: Discrete adiabatic Gibbs-state preparation admits rigorous tracking guarantees, and Szegedy quantum walks provide a quadratic speedup in spectral-gap dependence—but only when schedules are properly gap-adapted, underscoring the essential role of schedule design in realising the quantum advantage.

title: Two-Sided Bounds on Ground State Properties in Lattice Gauge Theories
summary: Gauge theories describe fundamental interactions in the standard model of particle physics and build effective theories in condensed matter physics. Being notoriously hard to simulate, these theories are commonly regularized as lattice gauge theories which can be evaluated with high precision through Monte Carlo algorithms or variational methods. However, Monte Carlo algorithms are not applicable in all regimes due to the sign problem; while variational methods, quantum and classical alike, only give upper-bounds on the ground-state energy. Their precision crucially depends on the chosen ansatz. Here, we present a framework based on a hierarchy of semidefinite programs to yield increasingly good lower-bounds on the ground-state energy and propagate these bounds to extended observables like Wilson loops and mesonic strings. We demonstrate the numerical capabilities by applying the algorithm to a (1+1)-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory with dynamic fermionic matter and its pure-gauge version in (2+1)-dimensions. In both cases, we obtain certified intervals for the ground-state energy. For a one-dimensional system with 129 sites, the certified interval has a relative spread of $0.04\%$. For a two-dimensional system with 97 sites (corresponding to a $7 \times 8$ lattice), the relative spread is $2.08\%$. Beyond energy estimates, the proposed method provides rigorous bounds on both short- and long-range observables such as Wilson loops over multiple plaquettes and the magnitude of the mesonic string. The method can be both used as a computational microscope into many-body physics and a way to certify results of quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a hierarchy of semidefinite programs to compute certified lower bounds on ground-state energies of lattice gauge theories, propagating them to observables like Wilson loops and mesonic strings, with numerical demonstrations on Z2 theories.
AI.motivation: Simulating gauge theories is extremely challenging. Monte Carlo methods suffer from the sign problem in certain regimes, and variational methods (quantum and classical) only provide upper bounds on ground-state energy whose precision depends heavily on the ansatz. A method providing rigorous lower bounds would complement these approaches.
AI.method: A framework based on a hierarchy of semidefinite programs (SDPs) that yields increasingly tight lower bounds on ground-state energy and propagates these bounds to extended observables such as Wilson loops and mesonic strings.
AI.result: Applied to a (1+1)-dimensional Z2 theory with dynamic fermionic matter and its pure-gauge version in (2+1)-dimensions, the method yields certified energy intervals. For a 1D system of 129 sites, the relative interval spread is 0.04%; for a 2D 7x8 lattice (97 sites), it is 2.08%. It also gives rigorous bounds on short- and long-range observables including multi-plaquette Wilson loops and mesonic string magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides certified intervals for ground-state energy and rigorous bounds on observables, serving both as a computational microscope for many-body physics and a tool to certify quantum simulator results.

title: Robust subspace designs and the power of a unique small quantum witness
summary:
The concept of subspace designs was introduced by Guruswami and Xing (STOC'13), and explicit constructions were given by Guruswami and Kopparty (FOCS'13). These are families of subspaces that have small intersection with any given subspace of a fixed dimension. We introduce \emph{robust subspace designs}. Informally, these are a quantitative extension in which we demand that not too many subspaces of the family contain directions that lie close to any given subspace of a fixed dimension. We give a probabilistic construction of such a robust subspace design of polynomial size, as well as a non-trivial explicit construction of superpolynomial size.
  Our main application of this new concept is a quantum space-bounded variant of the Valiant-Vazirani theorem (Theor.Comput.Sci.'86), which shows that restricting $\mathsf{NP}$-complete problems to instances with at most one accepting witness preserves hardness under randomized reductions. For quantum witnesses, the analogous quantity is the dimension of an accepting witness subspace. We use our probabilistic construction of robust subspace designs to isolate a unique witness for space-bounded quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols with perfect completeness and an acceptance gap outside their perfectly accepting subspace.
  As further applications, we give a randomized reduction of well-conditioned nullity testing to space-bounded quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols with perfect completeness. Using a similar idea, we find that ordinary subspace designs allow us to recover the classical $\mathsf{C_= L}$ containment of Allender, Beals, and Ogihara (STOC'96) for general nullity testing through a simpler proof.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces robust subspace designs, a quantitative strengthening of subspace designs, provides a probabilistic polynomial-size construction and an explicit superpolynomial-size construction, and applies them to prove a quantum space-bounded Valiant-Vazirani theorem for isolating a unique witness in space-bounded QMA protocols, plus nullity-testing reductions.
AI.motivation: Subspace designs (Guruswami-Xing, Guruswami-Kopparty) guarantee small intersection with any fixed-dimension subspace, but this does not control subspaces that merely lie close to a target direction set. The authors need a stronger notion to isolate a unique accepting witness for quantum witnesses, where the natural measure is the dimension of an accepting witness subspace rather than the number of accepting witnesses. This motivates a robust version of subspace designs.
AI.method: They define robust subspace designs, requiring that not too many family members contain directions close to any fixed-dimension subspace. They give a probabilistic construction of polynomial size and a non-trivial explicit construction of superpolynomial size. They then apply the probabilistic construction to space-bounded quantum Merlin-Arthur protocols with perfect completeness and an acceptance gap outside the perfectly accepting subspace, isolating a unique witness.
AI.result: A probabilistic polynomial-size robust subspace design and an explicit superpolynomial-size construction are obtained. As the main application, a quantum space-bounded Valiant-Vazirani theorem is proved for space-bounded QMA with perfect completeness and an acceptance gap. Further, a randomized reduction of well-conditioned nullity testing to space-bounded QMA with perfect completeness is given; and ordinary subspace designs yield a simpler proof recovering the classical C_=L containment of Allender-Beals-Ogihara for general nullity testing.
AI.conclusion: Robust subspace designs provide a useful quantitative tool that extends classical subspace designs and enables quantum space-bounded witness isolation and nullity-testing reductions, including a simpler recovery of a known classical containment.

title: Quantum Leakage from Shamir Sharing with Correlated Resources
summary: We study leakage from Shamir secret sharing when each device uses its share to produce one qubit from an initial quantum resource independent of the secret and sharing randomness. We prove exponentially small trace distance between the leakage states of any two secrets, when reconstruction requires a sufficiently large fraction of the shares, for fixed stationary chains satisfying an upper operator mixing condition and for resources generated by fixed finite quantum memories with primitive transfer channels. These guarantees permit arbitrary extensions of the device marginal as adversary side information and hold uniformly over prime fields larger than the number of shares. For independent device--reference pairs, which provide the quantitative input to the argument, we determine the optimal exponential base when reconstruction requires all shares: $2\sqrt2/π$ for a qubit and $2/π$ for a classical bit, in both cases allowing arbitrary finite references. A comparison of selected marginals with product states converts the bounds for independent device--reference pairs into security guarantees for the correlated resources.

AI.tldr: The paper proves exponentially small leakage from Shamir secret sharing when each share is used to generate one qubit of a quantum resource, relating device marginal bounds and optimal exponential bases for independent device–reference pairs to security guarantees for correlated resources.
AI.motivation: To understand how much information about the secret leaks from Shamir secret sharing when shares are employed to produce quantum states, and to establish strong security guarantees under reconstruction thresholds and resource constraints.
AI.method: The authors analyze trace distance between leakage states for different secrets under Shamir secret sharing. They impose fixed stationary chains with an upper operator mixing condition, use resources generated by fixed finite quantum memories with primitive transfer channels, allow arbitrary adversary side information, and work uniformly over prime fields larger than the number of shares. For independent device–reference pairs, they optimize the exponential base.
AI.result: They prove exponentially small trace distance between leakage states of any two secrets when reconstruction requires a sufficiently large fraction of shares. For independent device–reference pairs requiring all shares, the optimal exponential base is 2√2/π for a qubit and 2/π for a classical bit, allowing arbitrary finite references. A comparison of selected marginals with product states converts these bounds into security guarantees for correlated resources.
AI.conclusion: Shamir secret sharing remains secure against leakage from quantum resource generation under the stated conditions, and the derived bounds yield quantitative security guarantees that extend to correlated resources, including arbitrary adversarial side information.

title: Adaptive complete quantum search with unknown number of solutions
summary: Unstructured database search is a fundamental problem that requires finding one or more elements satisfying a specific property within a set of candidates. While Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for finding a marked element when the number of solutions is known, finding all solutions when their number is unknown presents additional challenges. In this paper, we thoroughly analyze this problem by considering all the different regimes of combinations of classical, Grover and generalized fixed-point quantum search instances. We unify these into an adaptive Bayesian approach that maximizes the expected success probability per unit execution time at each searching instance. For a problem with a known number of solutions, much lower than the database size, we prove that our proposed approach is asymptotically optimal within the considered search model. Furthermore, we prove that for any probability distribution characterizing the likely number of solutions, in regimes where the classical verification time is at most 25% of the quantum amplitude amplification time, hybrid classical and Grover approaches are preferred to generalized fixed-point. Outside of this regime, we derive an upper bound on the maximal improvement achievable by fixed-point search compared to the best Grover-based score. Additionally, we determine the optimal transition point between classical sampling and quantum searching using an integral approximation of the probability distribution of the number of solutions. The analytical results are also supported by numerical simulations of the proposed algorithm and by comparisons between the generalized fixed-point and Grover-based search policies.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses unstructured database search when the number of solutions is unknown, unifying classical, Grover, and generalized fixed-point quantum search into an adaptive Bayesian framework that maximizes expected success probability per unit execution time.
AI.motivation: Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup for finding a marked element when the number of solutions is known, but finding all solutions when their number is unknown introduces additional challenges not covered by standard Grover search.
AI.method: The authors analyze all regimes combining classical, Grover, and generalized fixed-point quantum search instances and unify them into an adaptive Bayesian approach that maximizes expected success probability per unit execution time at each searching instance.
AI.result: For a known number of solutions much lower than the database size, the proposed approach is proven asymptotically optimal within the considered search model. When classical verification time is at most 25% of quantum amplitude amplification time, hybrid classical and Grover approaches are preferred to generalized fixed-point. Outside this regime, an upper bound is derived on the maximal improvement of fixed-point search over the best Grover-based score. The optimal transition point between classical sampling and quantum searching is determined via an integral approximation of the probability distribution of the number of solutions. Analytical results are supported by numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive Bayesian approach provides an asymptotically optimal and regime-dependent policy for unstructured search with an unknown number of solutions, quantifying when hybrid classical-Grover strategies outperform generalized fixed-point search and identifying the optimal classical-to-quantum transition point.

title: Value of spatially multiplexed SNSPDs with photon-number-resolving capabilities
summary: We develop a combinatorial and Bayesian framework to quantify the information gained by increasing the local photon-number resolution of multiplexed detection systems based on superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs). Motivated by recent studies that attribute photon-number resolving capabilities to a single SNSPD overcoming the typical on/off detection mechanism, we generalize the existing formulation for the binary devices by deriving the probability response tensor of multiplexed systems based on SNSPDs with an arbitrary number of resolvable states. We include finite efficiency through binomial loss convolution and, separately, assess the impact of dark counts. From this response tensor we derive a generalized N-photon detector fidelity, a Bayesian photon-number reconstruction, and the corresponding reconstruction fidelity. We particularize this formulation to study 2-, 3- and 4-state multiplexed systems with different numbers of detectors and show that increasing local photon-number resolution systematically improves both detector fidelity and Bayesian photon-number reconstruction. This substantially relaxes the quadratic scaling between detector number and resolvable photon-number required by purely binary multiplexed arrays. These results provide a quantitative value-of-information assessment for multi-state photon-number-resolving detector arrays.

AI.tldr: A combinatorial and Bayesian framework quantifies the information gained by multi-state (multi-resolution) SNSPD multiplexed detection, showing that local photon-number resolution systematically improves detector and reconstruction fidelity and relaxes the quadratic scaling between detector count and resolvable photon number.
AI.motivation: Recent studies attribute photon-number-resolving (PNR) capability to a single SNSPD beyond the typical on/off mechanism. Existing multiplexed-detector formulations are limited to binary (on/off) devices, leaving a gap in modeling and quantifying the benefit of intrinsic multi-state resolution in multiplexed arrays.
AI.method: The authors generalize the binary multiplexed-detection formulation by deriving a probability response tensor for multiplexed SNSPD systems with an arbitrary number of resolvable states. Finite detection efficiency is incorporated via binomial loss convolution, and dark-count impact is assessed separately. From the response tensor they derive a generalized N-photon detector fidelity, a Bayesian photon-number reconstruction, and its corresponding reconstruction fidelity. The formulation is particularized to 2-, 3-, and 4-state multiplexed systems with varying detector numbers.
AI.result: Increasing local photon-number resolution systematically improves both detector fidelity and Bayesian photon-number reconstruction. It substantially relaxes the quadratic scaling between detector number and resolvable photon number required by purely binary multiplexed arrays. The analysis includes the effects of finite efficiency (binomial loss convolution) and dark counts.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a quantitative value-of-information assessment for multi-state photon-number-resolving detector arrays, demonstrating that local multi-state resolution is an efficient alternative to simply increasing detector count in binary multiplexed schemes.

title: When is the Clifford hierarchy generalized semi-Clifford?
summary: We study semi-Clifford and generalized semi-Clifford structures in the Clifford hierarchy as a function of hierarchy level $k$ and qubit number $n$. We show that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is semi-Clifford if and only if $k\le2$, $n\le2$, or $k=3$ and $n\le6$. We also establish that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is generalized semi-Clifford when $k\le4$ or $n\le3$ and construct counterexamples when $k,n \geq 5$. For $n=4$ and $k\ge5$, we show that every gate defined over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ up to a scalar is generalized semi-Clifford, reduce the general case to a single level, and propose a strategy to prove our conjecture that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is generalized semi-Clifford if and only if $k\le4$ or $n\le4$. Lastly, we go beyond this structure by introducing $n_c$-generalized semi-Clifford gates, which we show are exactly the gates of the form $\sum_x|π(x)\rangle\langle x|\otimes V_x$ up to Clifford gates on both sides, where $π$ permutes the computational basis states of $n_c$ control qubits. We conjecture that for $k\ge3$ every gate in $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ has this form for some $n_c\ge1$ with every $V_x\in\mathcal{C}_{k-3}(n-n_c)$, refining the conjecture of Zeng, Chen, and Chuang.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes when Clifford hierarchy levels $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ are semi-Clifford or generalized semi-Clifford as a function of level $k$ and qubit number $n$, proving sharp thresholds and introducing $n_c$-generalized semi-Clifford gates.
AI.motivation: The Clifford hierarchy is central to fault-tolerant quantum computation and magic state distillation, so understanding its algebraic structure (semi-Clifford and generalized semi-Clifford forms) across all levels and qubit numbers is important. Prior work lacked a complete characterization of when these structures hold.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Clifford hierarchy $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ combinatorially and algebraically, proving exact conditions for semi-Clifford and generalized semi-Clifford structure. They build counterexamples for large $k,n$, prove special cases over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, reduce the general case to a single level, and introduce $n_c$-generalized semi-Clifford gates characterized as $\sum_x|\pi(x)\rangle\langle x|\otimes V_x$ up to Clifford operations.
AI.result: $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is semi-Clifford iff $k\le2$, $n\le2$, or $k=3$ and $n\le6$. It is generalized semi-Clifford when $k\le4$ or $n\le3$, with counterexamples for $k,n\ge5$. For $n=4$, $k\ge5$, every gate over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ up to scalar is generalized semi-Clifford, and the general case reduces to a single level.
AI.conclusion: The paper conjectures that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is generalized semi-Clifford iff $k\le4$ or $n\le4$, and that for $k\ge3$ every gate in $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is $n_c$-generalized semi-Clifford for some $n_c\ge1$ with each $V_x\in\mathcal{C}_{k-3}(n-n_c)$, refining the conjecture of Zeng, Chen, and Chuang.

title: Lindblad equation for the quantum Rabi model in the deep strong coupling regime
summary: We derive a quantum master equation in Lindblad form for the open quantum Rabi model in the perturbative deep strong coupling regime, where the spectrum is close to degenerate and harmonic. The Lindblad form is obtained by combining secular and singular-coupling approximations, working in a Schrieffer-Wolff transformed frame. We benchmark our equation against a Bloch-Redfield one, analyzing the time-evolution and steady state properties of several observables and find excellent agreement. Analytical results are obtained in limiting cases.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a Lindblad-form quantum master equation for the open quantum Rabi model in the perturbative deep strong coupling regime, obtained via secular and singular-coupling approximations in a Schrieffer-Wolff transformed frame, and benchmarks it against a Bloch-Redfield equation with excellent agreement.
AI.motivation: The deep strong coupling regime of the open quantum Rabi model features a near-degenerate, quasi-harmonic spectrum, which complicates the derivation of a valid Markovian master equation. A rigorous Lindblad-form description valid in this regime is needed.
AI.method: Combine secular and singular-coupling approximations, working in a Schrieffer-Wolff transformed frame, to obtain a Lindblad-form master equation. Benchmark against a Bloch-Redfield equation by analyzing time-evolution and steady-state properties of several observables, with analytical results in limiting cases.
AI.result: The derived Lindblad equation shows excellent agreement with the Bloch-Redfield approach for time-evolution and steady-state observables; analytical results are obtained in limiting cases.
AI.conclusion: A valid Lindblad master equation is established for the open quantum Rabi model in the perturbative deep strong coupling regime, providing a reliable and consistent description validated against Bloch-Redfield dynamics.

title: A Practical Introduction to VQE: Methods, Challenges, and Applications in Physics and Chemistry
summary: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) has become a central hybrid quantum-classical method for addressing electronic structure and materials science problems on near-term quantum hardware.
