As researchers across physics, chemistry, and quantum information engage with VQE, they encounter a wide range of algorithmic choices, including problem encoding, ansatz construction, classical optimization, and measurement strategies to choose from. This article provides a structured overview of these components and discusses practical factors that influence VQE performance in real settings, such as noise characteristics, available error-mitigation techniques, and hardware-dependent circuit considerations. Drawing partly on our early experiences, we highlight aspects that may be especially relevant for newcomers and outline common challenges observed in practical workflows. Our aim is to offer an accessible entry point for researchers approaching VQE-based quantum simulation and to support informed decision-making as the method and underlying hardware continue to evolve, which we support by discussion of examples from physics and quantum chemistry.

AI.tldr: This article provides a structured, accessible overview of the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), covering its core algorithmic components and practical performance factors to guide newcomers in VQE-based quantum simulation.
AI.motivation: VQE has become a central hybrid quantum-classical method for electronic structure and materials science on near-term hardware. As researchers from physics, chemistry, and quantum information adopt it, they face many algorithmic choices, so a clear guide is needed to support informed decision-making.
AI.method: The paper offers a structured overview of VQE components, including problem encoding, ansatz construction, classical optimization, and measurement strategies. It discusses practical factors such as noise characteristics, error-mitigation techniques, and hardware-dependent circuit considerations, drawing partly on the authors' early experiences and examples from physics and quantum chemistry.
AI.result: The article identifies aspects especially relevant to newcomers and outlines common challenges observed in practical VQE workflows, supported by illustrative examples from physics and quantum chemistry.
AI.conclusion: The work serves as an accessible entry point for researchers approaching VQE-based quantum simulation and aims to support informed decision-making as the method and underlying hardware continue to evolve.

title: A programmable quantum photonic platform integrating coherent emitters
summary: Photonic quantum technologies require the integration of high-quality quantum light sources with programmable photonic circuitry to enable on-chip quantum information processing. Semiconductor quantum dots have emerged as a leading platform for quantum light generation, yet their monolithic integration with cryogenic-compatible, programmable photonic circuitry remains challenging. Here we demonstrate a programmable quantum photonic platform that enables simultaneous control of highly coherent quantum dot-based single photon emitters and reconfigurable optical elements at cryogenic temperatures. System-level integration enables individual electrical and optical addressing of active components on a single chip, allowing their concurrent operation while preserving coherent non-classical light emission. We demonstrate multiple quantum-photonic functionalities, including pure single-photon generation, two-photon interference, and resonant transmission and reflection measurements of integrated emitters. These results mark a step from isolated quantum-optical devices towards programmable quantum-photonic hardware platforms capable of combining coherent quantum emitters with large-scale photonic functionality.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a programmable cryogenic quantum photonic platform that monolithically integrates coherent quantum dot single-photon emitters with reconfigurable optical elements on a single chip, enabling concurrent control and multiple on-chip quantum-photonic functionalities.
AI.motivation: Photonic quantum technologies need high-quality quantum light sources integrated with programmable photonic circuitry for on-chip quantum information processing. Semiconductor quantum dots are a leading quantum light source, but their monolithic integration with cryogenic-compatible, programmable photonic circuitry remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors fabricate a programmable quantum photonic platform that monolithically integrates quantum dot-based single-photon emitters with reconfigurable optical elements, operating at cryogenic temperatures. System-level integration provides individual electrical and optical addressing of active components on a single chip, allowing concurrent operation while preserving coherent non-classical light emission.
AI.result: The platform achieves multiple quantum-photonic functionalities, including pure single-photon generation, two-photon interference, and resonant transmission and reflection measurements of integrated emitters, while maintaining coherent non-classical emission under concurrent operation.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a step from isolated quantum-optical devices toward programmable quantum-photonic hardware platforms that combine coherent quantum emitters with large-scale photonic functionality.

title: The right entanglement for perfect nonlocality and zero-error communication
summary:
We identify a structural mechanism by which perfect play in a nonlocal game requires and self-tests a specific non-maximally entangled state. To this end, we construct a Flagged Magic-Square game by extending the standard Magic-Square game with an additional ``flag'' outcome and two additional questions for each player. The game admits a perfect strategy using a state with Schmidt coefficients proportional to $(1,\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$. We give a direct algebraic proof that maximally entangled strategies have winning probability bounded away from one, independently of dimension. Moreover, the game self-tests this state, providing an example of a two-party pseudo-telepathy game that certifies a specific non-maximally entangled state. Our construction illustrates how adding suitable constraints to a rigid measurement geometry can enforce specific Schmidt ratios and provides a modular route to further self-tests based on other rigid pseudo-telepathy games.
  We establish a general game-to-channel reduction that transfers separations in the game model to one-shot zero-error communication over classical channels. Applied to the Flagged Magic-Square game, it yields a classical channel for which entanglement permits the zero-error transmission of ten messages in a single use, whereas any finite-dimensional maximally entangled resource permits at most nine. Thus, maximally entangled states are not a universally optimal entanglement resource for zero-error communication over classical noisy channels.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a "Flagged Magic-Square" nonlocal game whose perfect strategy uses a specific non-maximally entangled state with Schmidt coefficients proportional to (1,√2,√2,√2,√2). It proves maximally entangled strategies cannot win perfectly, self-tests the non-maximally entangled state, and via a game-to-channel reduction derives a classical channel where entanglement enables zero-error transmission of ten messages per use while any finite-dimensional maximally entangled resource allows at most nine.
AI.motivation: Nonlocal games typically certify maximally entangled states; there is little understanding of structural mechanisms forcing specific non-maximally entangled states, and whether maximally entangled states are universally optimal for zero-error communication over classical channels remains open.
AI.method: Extend the standard Magic-Square game with a "flag" outcome and two additional questions per player to build the Flagged Magic-Square game. Give a direct algebraic proof that maximally entangled strategies have winning probability bounded away from one in any dimension. Establish a general game-to-channel reduction transferring game-model separations to one-shot zero-error communication over classical channels, then apply it to the game.
AI.result: The game admits a perfect strategy using a state with Schmidt coefficients proportional to (1,√2,√2,√2,√2) and self-tests it, giving a two-party pseudo-telepathy game certifying a specific non-maximally entangled state. The induced classical channel permits zero-error transmission of ten messages per single use with entanglement, whereas any finite-dimensional maximally entangled resource permits at most nine.
AI.conclusion: Adding suitable constraints to a rigid measurement geometry can enforce specific Schmidt ratios, offering a modular route to further self-tests based on other rigid pseudo-telepathy games. Maximally entangled states are not universally optimal entanglement resources for zero-error communication over classical noisy channels.

title: Causal memory and structural complexity of a quantum space series
summary: What makes one quantum process more complex than another? We adopt an operational approach inspired by classical complexity science, which characterises structure through the memory required for causal generation. We develop a fully-quantum extension of computational mechanics for quantum space series: Sequences of quantum outputs that do not return to interact with their generator. For stationary, memoryful quantum space series admitting finite-dimensional, primitive causal models, we show that a memory-minimal model can be chosen to generate the outputs isometrically, without a discarded environment. The resulting canonical matrix product state representation determines both the minimum memory dimension and the minimum memory entropy. The latter is precisely the entanglement entropy across the past-future bipartition, giving entanglement an operational interpretation as irreducible memory for causal generation. Within this class, we further establish a vanishing fundamental entropy rate, the absence of causal asymmetry, and infinite quantum Markov order. These results establish an operational framework for quantifying intrinsic quantum structure, revealing deep connections between causal generation, complexity, memory, entropy, and entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies the complexity of quantum processes by the memory required for causal generation, developing a fully-quantum computational mechanics for quantum space series. For stationary, memoryful series with finite-dimensional primitive causal models, a memory-minimal model generates outputs isometrically, yielding a canonical MPS whose bond dimension and bond entropy give minimum memory dimension and minimum memory entropy (entanglement entropy across past-future).
AI.motivation: To define what makes one quantum process more complex than another, the authors adopt an operational perspective from classical complexity science in which structure is characterized by the memory needed for causal generation, and they aim to extend this to the quantum domain.
AI.method: They develop a fully-quantum extension of computational mechanics for quantum space series (sequences of quantum outputs not returning to interact with their generator). Restricting to stationary, memoryful series admitting finite-dimensional primitive causal models, they construct memory-minimal causal models and a canonical matrix product state (MPS) representation.
AI.result: A memory-minimal model can generate outputs isometrically without a discarded environment. The canonical MPS determines both the minimum memory dimension (bond dimension) and the minimum memory entropy, the latter equal to the entanglement entropy across the past-future bipartition, giving entanglement an operational interpretation as irreducible memory for causal generation. Within this class they also prove vanishing fundamental entropy rate, absence of causal asymmetry, and infinite quantum Markov order.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an operational framework for quantifying intrinsic quantum structure, revealing deep connections among causal generation, complexity, memory, entropy, and entanglement.

title: Classical Simulation of Lossy Gaussian Boson Sampling beyond Square-Root Regime
summary: Photon loss makes Gaussian boson sampling easier to simulate classically. A standard approach replaces the lossy input by classical light, and it stays accurate while the mean number of surviving photons grows no faster than the square root of the number $N$ of squeezed inputs at fixed squeezing and accuracy. We prove that this scale is a limit of replacement by classical light. For explicit interferometers, no state with a nonnegative Glauber--Sudarshan $P$ representation, Gaussian or not and however correlated, keeps the error in the photon count distribution small beyond this scale. We then surpass this limit by approximating the detection instead of the input. The sampler evolves the state exactly between detections and, after each detection, replaces the conditional state by a Gaussian with the same covariance. For every interferometer its total variation error is $O(Nη^3)$ at polynomial expected cost, where $η$ is the photon survival probability. The mean surviving photon number can therefore grow as $N^{2/3}$ at fixed accuracy. A separate pair construction reaches $N^{3/4}$ when every input mode is equally squeezed.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the square-root-of-N scaling is the fundamental limit of input-replacement (classical-light) simulation of lossy Gaussian boson sampling, then surpasses that limit by approximating detection instead of the input, achieving error O(Nη³) at polynomial cost and allowing N^(2/3) (or N^(3/4) for equal squeezing) mean surviving photons at fixed accuracy.
AI.motivation: Photon loss makes Gaussian boson sampling classically simulable, and the standard classical-light replacement approach remains accurate only while the mean surviving photon number grows no faster than the square root of the number N of squeezed inputs. The paper aims to establish whether this √N scale is an intrinsic limit of the replacement-by-classical-light strategy and to find methods that go beyond it.
AI.method: First, a hardness/limit proof: for explicit interferometers, no state with a nonnegative Glauber–Sudarshan P representation (Gaussian or not, and however correlated) keeps the error in the photon count distribution small beyond the √N scale. Second, a new algorithm that approximates the detection rather than the input: the sampler evolves the state exactly between detections and, after each detection, replaces the conditional state by a Gaussian with the same covariance.
AI.result: The √N scale is proven to be a genuine limit of replacement by classical light. The detection-replacement approach achieves total variation error O(Nη³) at polynomial expected cost, where η is the photon survival probability, so the mean surviving photon number can grow as N^(2/3) at fixed accuracy; a separate pair construction reaches N^(3/4) when every input mode is equally squeezed.
AI.conclusion: Replacing the input by classical light cannot beat the √N limit, but approximating the detection sidesteps this barrier, enabling classical simulation to stay accurate for substantially larger mean surviving photon numbers (up to N^(2/3), or N^(3/4) under equal squeezing) at polynomial cost.

title: Closed-Form Arbitrary-Gap Rényi Nonadditivity Above Any Positive Order via Direct Products of Free Groups and High-Girth Graphs
summary: We give a closed-form finite-dimensional construction of quantum channels with real algebraic entries exhibiting arbitrarily large violations of minimum-output Rényi entropy additivity uniformly above any prescribed positive Rényi order, using a different finite realization based on direct products of free groups and fixed-field high-girth graphs. More precisely, for every $p_0>0$ and $g>0$, we construct one channel and one Bell input for which the additivity gap is greater than $g$ simultaneously for all $p\in[p_0,\infty]$. With $r=\lceil2g\rceil$, the construction uses $15r$ output qubits and $O(r2^{30r}+r^2(1+p_0^{-1}))$ input qubits. Compared with the stated parameters of Shou and Gorshkov \cite{ShouGorshkov2026}, our construction uses fewer output qubits for every target gap and has a smaller asymptotic input-qubit bound as the gap grows with the positive cutoff fixed. At the von Neumann order, a separate specialization gives an explicit channel with gap greater than $1/1024$ using $37608898$ input qubits and $8$ output qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a closed-form, finite-dimensional construction of quantum channels with real algebraic entries that violate minimum-output Rényi entropy additivity by arbitrarily large amounts, uniformly over all Rényi orders above any fixed positive cutoff, using fewer resources than prior work.
AI.motivation: Additivity of minimum-output Rényi entropy is a fundamental question in quantum information theory. Prior constructions demonstrating large violations (e.g., Shou and Gorshkov) were resource-intensive. The motivation is to achieve arbitrarily large additivity gaps with improved (reduced) qubit resources, both in output and input qubits, across all Rényi orders simultaneously.
AI.method: The construction is a finite realization based on direct products of free groups and fixed-field high-girth graphs. For every p0 > 0 and gap g > 0, a single channel and Bell input are constructed with additivity gap exceeding g uniformly for all p in [p0, ∞]. With r = ceil(2g), the construction uses 15r output qubits and O(r 2^{30r} + r^2 (1 + p0^{-1})) input qubits. A separate specialization at the von Neumann order yields an explicit channel.
AI.result: The construction achieves additivity gaps greater than any prescribed g for all p in [p0, ∞] using 15r output qubits and the stated asymptotic input-qubit bound. It improves on Shou and Gorshkov's parameters: fewer output qubits for every target gap and a smaller asymptotic input-qubit bound as the gap grows with fixed positive cutoff. At the von Neumann order, an explicit channel gives a gap greater than 1/1024 using 37,608,898 input qubits and 8 output qubits.
AI.conclusion: Large violations of minimum-output Rényi entropy additivity can be realized with explicit finite-dimensional quantum channels using fewer resources than previously known, with improvements in both output qubit count and asymptotic input qubit scaling.

title: The Mermin-Peres Magic Square Game With Three or More Players
summary: We present a generalization of the Mermin-Peres magic square game to $N$ players, in which the square is replaced by an $N$-dimensional hypercube. We show that the winning probability of the optimal classical strategy remains $8/9$ for all $N$, while for $N \ge 3$, a generalization of the quantum strategy for $N = 2$ achieves a winning probability between $1/3$ and $3/4$. This loss of quantum advantage for $N \ge 3$ is a consequence of monogamy.

AI.tldr: The Mermin-Peres magic square game is generalized to N players using an N-dimensional hypercube; the classical optimal winning probability stays 8/9 for all N, but the quantum strategy's winning probability drops to between 1/3 and 3/4 for N ≥ 3, eliminating the quantum advantage due to monogamy.
AI.motivation: The paper extends a well-known quantum game (the Mermin-Peres magic square) to a multi-player setting, seeking to understand how quantum advantage behaves as the number of players grows.
AI.method: Replace the magic square with an N-dimensional hypercube and generalize the N=2 quantum strategy to N players, then compare optimal classical and quantum winning probabilities.
AI.result: The optimal classical winning probability remains 8/9 for all N. For N ≥ 3, the generalized quantum strategy achieves a winning probability between 1/3 and 3/4.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantage is lost for N ≥ 3 in this generalized game, a consequence of monogamy of entanglement.

title: Symmetry and AI-assisted discovery of magic-state factories
summary: Magic-state distillation is a major resource cost in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The cost of a magic-state factory depends strongly on its failure rate, which grows with the number of input magic states. Although symmetry-restricted methods have recently made distance two searches tractable, distance three and above have remained elusive at moderate input counts. We develop symmetry- and AI-assisted methods to search this regime. We present a unified binary-matrix formulation encompassing both triorthogonal-code and direct circuit searches. We show that distance at least three is equivalent to nonzero, pairwise distinct syndromes, separating the choice of syndromes from the search for compatible output gates. We restrict the syndrome search using group symmetry and language-model agents, followed by deterministic solving and independent verification. Our searches yield 699 factory classes, including 564 new ones. These include factories for pure-T states and factories with entangled outputs comprising combinations of T, CS, and CCZ magic states. The pure-T factories [[63, 11, 3]] and [[850, 128, 6]] achieve the lowest overhead exponents we know among protocols with at most 100 and 1000 inputs, respectively, with $γ= 1.589$ and $γ= 1.057$. Our [[1715, 287, 6]] factory, with $γ= 0.998$, is the smallest known pure-T factory with $γ< 1$. We also provide a context directory of search briefs and campaign notes with which readers can train their own agents and tailor the search to their requirements. With these results, we begin constructing an active, open-source repository of magic-state distillation protocols for the quantum community, supplemented by our methods and data, for the practical fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.

AI.tldr: This paper develops symmetry- and AI-assisted search methods that break the distance-three barrier in magic-state distillation, yielding 699 factory classes (564 new) including record-low-overhead pure-T factories and an open-source protocol repository.
AI.motivation: Magic-state distillation is a dominant resource cost in fault-tolerant quantum computing, and factory cost scales strongly with failure rate, which grows with the number of input magic states. Prior symmetry-restricted searches only made distance-two tractable; distance-three and higher regimes remained elusive at moderate input counts, leaving a key gap in discovering low-overhead protocols.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified binary-matrix formulation covering both triorthogonal-code and direct-circuit searches. They prove that distance at least three is equivalent to nonzero, pairwise distinct syndromes, decoupling syndrome selection from the search for compatible output gates. Syndrome search is then constrained via group symmetry and language-model agents, followed by deterministic solving and independent verification. They also release a context directory of search briefs and campaign notes for training custom agents.
AI.result: Searches produced 699 factory classes, 564 of them new, covering pure-T states and entangled-output factories combining T, CS, and CCZ magic states. Notable pure-T factories include [[63, 11, 3]] and [[850, 128, 6]], achieving the lowest known overhead exponents among protocols with at most 100 and 1000 inputs, respectively, with gamma = 1.589 and gamma = 1.057. The [[1715, 287, 6]] factory, with gamma = 0.998, is the smallest known pure-T factory with gamma < 1.
AI.conclusion: The work advances distance-three-plus magic-state distillation searches and establishes an active, open-source repository of distillation protocols for the quantum community, complemented by methods and data, targeting the practical fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.

title: Products of unitaries as continuous evolutions at finite precision
summary: I present a short approach to discretizing continuous unitary evolution. It gives a correspondence in both directions between continuous unitary evolutions and products of unitaries in finite dimensions, and I use it to reduce discrete adiabatic theorems to continuous ones. At fine steps, holding truncated samples of a regulated Hamiltonian on a suitable finite partition gives an approximating product. Conversely, rounding the clock identifies a product of $T$ unit-step samples with a continuous evolution, up to two half-step phases. I bound its operator-norm distance from the original evolution by $O(1/T)$ through cancellation within each time step. This assumes bounded first and second derivatives, bounded spectral width, and eigenvalue differences bounded away from nonzero multiples of $2π$, uniformly in $T$. For a unitary walk with these derivative bounds, a fixed common free spectral arc supplies a Hermitian logarithm path satisfying the comparison hypotheses. Continuous simulation guarantees then transfer to the phase-corrected product, and continuous adiabatic bounds to the product itself, with an explicit additive $O(1/T)$ error and each adiabatic theorem's hypotheses retained. For positive definite quantum linear systems of condition number $κ$, this comparison and continuous adiabatic theory give a rescaled qubitized walk with $O(κ/δ)$ steps for leakage $δ$, matching the scaling previously obtained through a discrete adiabatic theorem. These products need no discrete adiabatic theorem.

AI.tldr: A discretization of continuous unitary evolution is developed that establishes a two-way correspondence between continuous unitary evolutions and products of finite-dimensional unitaries, reducing discrete adiabatic theorems to continuous ones with an explicit O(1/T) operator-norm error. Applied to positive definite quantum linear systems of condition number κ, it yields a rescaled qubitized walk with O(κ/δ) steps for leakage δ, matching prior discrete-adiabatic scalings without needing a discrete adiabatic theorem.
AI.motivation: Discrete adiabatic theorems are needed to analyze products of unit-step unitaries (e.g., quantum walks), but proving them is technically demanding. The paper aims to bypass discrete adiabatic theorems by transferring well-established continuous adiabatic bounds and continuous simulation guarantees directly to discrete products.
AI.method: Approximate a continuous unitary evolution by holding truncated samples of a regulated Hamiltonian on a suitable finite partition (refined steps). Conversely, round the clock to map a product of T unit-step samples to a continuous evolution, up to two half-step phases. Bound the operator-norm distance by O(1/T) via cancellation within each time step, assuming bounded first and second derivatives, bounded spectral width, and eigenvalue differences bounded away from nonzero multiples of 2π uniformly in T. For a unitary walk satisfying these derivative bounds, a fixed common free spectral arc provides a Hermitian logarithm path meeting the comparison hypotheses.
AI.result: A two-way correspondence between continuous unitary evolutions and finite-dimensional unitary products is established, with the O(1/T) operator-norm distance bound. Continuous simulation guarantees transfer to the phase-corrected product, and continuous adiabatic bounds transfer to the product itself with explicit additive O(1/T) error while retaining each adiabatic theorem's hypotheses. For positive definite quantum linear systems of condition number κ, the approach yields a rescaled qubitized walk with O(κ/δ) steps for leakage δ.
AI.conclusion: The correspondence reduces discrete adiabatic theorems to continuous ones, so the discrete products analyzed (including the qubitized walk for quantum linear systems) need no discrete adiabatic theorem. The resulting O(κ/δ) step scaling matches that previously obtained through a discrete adiabatic theorem.

title: Mid-circuit measurements and feedforward implement every unitary exactly in constant depth
summary: Mid-circuit measurements with feedforward reduce the optimal worst-case quantum depth for exact $n$-qubit unitary synthesis from $Θ(n)$ to $O(1)$, using arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and unrestricted ancillary space. Measurements and resets without feedforward remain subject to the circuit causal-cone bound. Our deterministic construction uses single-qubit measurements, $O(1)$ rounds of parity feedforward, and $O(n4^n\log(n+2))$ total qubits, with all ancillas starting and ending in $|0\rangle$. Classical processing is not counted in quantum depth. We teleport only the matrix error of an approximation by Nehoran and Yuen. An exactly prepared ancillary state encodes this error, whose action is added back by coherent interference. At operator-norm error $2^{-n}$, one step of amplitude amplification suffices. Coherent fanout circuits achieve the same constant-depth bound, while circuits using only one- and two-qubit gates attain depth $Θ(n)$ with $O(4^n\log^2(n+2))$ gates. Generic targets require $Ω(4^n/(h+1))$ qubits at depth $h$, even under unrestricted classical control. Our depth-width trade-offs meet this bound within a factor $O(n^2)$ for $1\le h\le2^n$.

AI.tldr: Mid-circuit measurements with feedforward enable exact n-qubit unitary synthesis in constant quantum depth, using parity feedforward and an exactly prepared ancilla that teleports the approximation error of a prior construction, with depth-width trade-offs near optimal.
AI.motivation: Standard exact n-qubit unitary synthesis requires optimal worst-case quantum depth Θ(n) using arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates with unrestricted ancillas. The paper aims to reduce this quantum depth to O(1) by exploiting mid-circuit measurements with feedforward, while clarifying that measurements and resets without feedforward cannot beat the circuit causal-cone bound.
AI.method: A deterministic constant-depth construction using single-qubit measurements, O(1) rounds of parity feedforward, arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates, and unrestricted ancillas; it teleports only the matrix error of a Nehoran-Yuen approximation via an exactly prepared ancillary state whose action is coherently added back, with one step of amplitude amplification at operator-norm error 2^{-n}. Classical processing is excluded from quantum depth. Coherent fanout circuits are also used to achieve constant depth.
AI.result: Exact n-qubit unitary synthesis is achievable in O(1) quantum depth with O(n4^n log(n+2)) total qubits, all ancillas starting and ending in |0>. Coherent fanout circuits match this constant-depth bound, whereas one- and two-qubit-gate-only circuits require depth Θ(n) and O(4^n log^2(n+2)) gates. A generic-target lower bound of Ω(4^n/(h+1)) qubits at depth h holds even under unrestricted classical control, and the constructions meet this bound within a factor O(n^2) for 1 ≤ h ≤ 2^n.
AI.conclusion: Mid-circuit measurements with feedforward reduce optimal worst-case quantum depth for exact n-qubit unitary synthesis from Θ(n) to O(1), with near-optimal depth-width trade-offs. Measurements and resets without feedforward remain limited by the causal-cone bound.

title: CT-bMPS: Approximate Tensor Network Contraction with Boundary MPS on Contraction Trees
summary: We introduce contraction tree boundary matrix product states (CT-bMPS), a scalable approximate contraction method for general closed tensor networks. CT-bMPS represents the boundary tensor and its complementary environment at each edge of a contraction tree as matrix product states. This representation allows local compression based on a reduced transition matrix to incorporate environment information along arbitrary contraction trees, while keeping the time and memory costs polynomial in the network size and bond dimension. We benchmark the method on a variety of models and applications, including Ising partition functions, random tensor networks, kicked Ising dynamics, and quantum error correction decoding. These benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy and computational efficiency over existing general-purpose approximate contraction methods, together with the ability to handle larger and more complex networks. Optimized contraction trees and environment updates substantially improve accuracy without increasing the bond dimension. These results establish CT-bMPS as a general and scalable approximation framework with flexible contraction orders and environment-based compression for a wide range of applications.

AI.tldr: CT-bMPS is a scalable approximate contraction method for general closed tensor networks, representing both boundary tensors and their complementary environments along contraction tree edges as matrix product states, enabling environment-aware local compression with polynomial cost and improved accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: General-purpose approximate contraction of closed tensor networks is challenging because accurate contraction must account for environmental information, and existing methods often face a trade-off between accuracy, scalability, and computational efficiency as networks grow larger and more complex.
AI.method: The authors introduce contraction tree boundary matrix product states (CT-bMPS). At each edge of a contraction tree, the boundary tensor and its complementary environment are each represented as matrix product states. Local compression is performed based on a reduced transition matrix, which incorporates environment information and supports arbitrary contraction orders. Time and memory costs remain polynomial in network size and bond dimension.
AI.result: Benchmarks on Ising partition functions, random tensor networks, kicked Ising dynamics, and quantum error correction decoding show improved accuracy and computational efficiency relative to existing general-purpose approximate contraction methods, along with the ability to handle larger and more complex networks. Optimized contraction trees and environment updates substantially improve accuracy without increasing the bond dimension.
AI.conclusion: CT-bMPS establishes a general and scalable approximate contraction framework that combines flexible contraction orders with environment-based compression, making it suitable for a wide range of tensor-network applications.

title: Shaping double descent in quantum extreme learning through model design
comment: Main: 10 pages, 2 figures; Supplementary: 89 pages, 5 figures
summary: Increasing capacity can induce a machine learning model to generalize worse until it perfectly interpolates the training data, and better once it moves beyond interpolation. This inversion, known as \emph{double descent}, is well understood for independent features. For correlated features, its shape is governed by the spectrum of the feature covariance, but existing analyses typically yield only implicit equations. We first close this gap for classical linear regression, analytically characterizing the entire risk curve through two quantities, namely the condition number of the feature population covariance and a spectral measure of correlation strength. Then, we apply this theory on quantum models, focusing on quantum extreme learning machines (QELMs). We show that three tunable design knobs, \textit{i.e.,} encoding strength, input reuploads, and measurement shots, each regularize the QELM output covariance, and derive conditions under which the interpolation threshold remains stable. Finite measurement shot noise can be leveraged to guarantee this stability. Numerical experiments confirm each prediction, yielding concrete design principles for QELMs that generalize well beyond interpolation.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically characterizes the full double descent risk curve in correlated-feature linear regression via two quantities—the feature population covariance's condition number and a spectral measure of correlation strength—then applies the theory to quantum extreme learning machines (QELMs), showing encoding strength, input reuploads, and measurement shots each regularize the output covariance, with shot noise guaranteeing a stable interpolation threshold.
AI.motivation: Double descent is well understood for independent features, but for correlated features its shape depends on the feature covariance spectrum and existing analyses typically give only implicit equations. The paper aims to close this gap and extend the understanding to quantum models such as QELMs.
AI.method: First, classical linear regression is analyzed to explicitly characterize the entire risk (double descent) curve using two quantities: the condition number of the feature population covariance, and a spectral measure of correlation strength. Second, this theory is applied to QELMs, examining three tunable design knobs—encoding strength, input reuploads, and measurement shots—as regularizers of the QELM output covariance, and deriving conditions for interpolation threshold stability.
AI.result: The full risk curve for correlated-feature linear regression is analytically characterized. For QELMs, each of the three design knobs regularizes the output covariance, and finite measurement shot noise is shown to guarantee stability of the interpolation threshold. Numerical experiments confirm every prediction.
AI.conclusion: The results provide concrete design principles for QELMs that generalize well beyond interpolation, and establish an explicit, closed-form understanding of double descent under correlated features.

title: Information causality does not single out the set of quantum correlations
summary: Information causality (IC) was introduced as a physical principle that imposes constraints on the non-local correlations between two parties (Alice and Bob) in a Bell scenario. Specifically, it states that the information that Bob can gain about an $n$-bit database held by Alice is bounded by the information she communicates to him. To date, the question whether IC for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$ singles out the set of quantum correlations remains open, meaning that it is unknown whether for any number of inputs $m$ and outputs $d$ of the two parties the set of correlations that satisfy IC exactly coincides with the quantum correlations. In this work, we answer this question in the negative. Firstly, we show that for any finite database length $n \geq 2$, there is a bipartite set of correlations that satisfies IC for all compatible protocols and that exhibits post-quantum correlations in the Bell scenario with $n+1$ inputs and $2$ outcomes per party. This result relies on constructing an entropic proof of IC for GPTs that may be of independent interest. We further show that in the Bell scenario with $n+1$ inputs and $2$ outcomes per party, our constructed sets of correlations lead to neither a superset nor a subset of the quantum correlations. Secondly, we construct a set of correlations in the Bell scenario with $3$ inputs and $2$ outputs per party that satisfies IC (for all database sizes $n \in \mathbb{N}$) and that includes post-quantum points. Consequently, all known formulations of information causality fail to fully characterize the bipartite set of quantum correlations, already in the $3$-input, $2$-outcome Bell scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that Information Causality (IC) does not single out quantum correlations: it constructs bipartite correlation sets satisfying IC for all compatible protocols yet exhibiting post-quantum behavior, answering the open question in the negative.
AI.motivation: IC was proposed as a physical principle that might characterize the set of quantum correlations in Bell scenarios. Whether IC for all database sizes n singles out quantum correlations has remained an open question. This work aims to resolve that question.
AI.method: The authors construct, for any finite database length n >= 2, bipartite sets of correlations that satisfy IC for all compatible protocols while displaying post-quantum correlations in the Bell scenario with n+1 inputs and 2 outcomes per party. The construction relies on an entropic proof of IC for generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs). They also build a correlation set in the 3-input, 2-output Bell scenario satisfying IC for all n that contains post-quantum points.
AI.result: For n >= 2, the constructed correlation sets satisfy IC for all compatible protocols yet exhibit post-quantum correlations in the (n+1)-input, 2-outcome Bell scenario. These sets are neither supersets nor subsets of the quantum correlations. Additionally, a set in the 3-input, 2-output scenario satisfies IC for all n and includes post-quantum points.
AI.conclusion: All known formulations of information causality fail to fully characterize the bipartite set of quantum correlations, even in the simplest 3-input, 2-outcome Bell scenario.

title: Staying Sober: A Shot-Free Predictor of Logical Error Rates for Concatenated Quantum Error Correcting Codes
summary: Estimating the logical error rate (LER) of a quantum error-correcting (QEC) code by Monte Carlo sampling takes $O(p^{-\lceil d/2 \rceil}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples at physical error rate $p$, code distance $d$ and relative error $\varepsilon$, which becomes intractable at large distances and low error rates, and especially for concatenated codes, whose distance grows as $d^{\ell}$ with the number of levels $\ell$. The fail fast method reduces this cost by sampling the failures of each weight separately, but it only works for unconcatenated codes, and does not model the soft information that the levels of a concatenated code pass to each other. We propose a predictor that takes the stabilizers, the minimum-weight logical operators and, for odd $d$, the logical operators of weight $d + 1$ of a code, and computes, without sampling, the leading monomial $c\,p^{o}$ of the LER when expressed as a polynomial in $p$, at every level of concatenation, in time polynomial in the code parameters and linear in $\ell$ for fixed budgets. We prove that our prediction is exact for any unconcatenated stabilizer code, for every logical observable and arbitrary per-qubit error rates, whenever no budget is exhausted. Furthermore, for concatenated codes, we construct a recursive approach that computes the leading monomial exactly in exponential time, and our predictor approximates this approach. Our predictions match exact enumeration at level 1 on every code we evaluate, and up to three levels for the iceberg code. Using our predictor, we evaluate and compare $37$ code configurations under four noise biases in $48$ core-hours, where Monte Carlo sampling would need more than $10^{12}$ shots at $p = 10^{-3}$ for $113$ of these $148$ cases.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a sampling-free predictor that computes the leading monomial of the logical error rate (LER) for stabilizer codes, extending the fail-fast idea to concatenated codes by accounting for the soft information passed between levels.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo estimation of LER scales as O(p^{-ceil(d/2)}/eps^2), becoming intractable at large distances, low physical error rates, and especially for concatenated codes whose distance grows as d^ell. The fail-fast method reduces cost by sampling failures per weight but only handles unconcatenated codes and ignores the soft information exchanged between concatenation levels.
AI.method: The predictor takes as input the stabilizers, minimum-weight logical operators, and (for odd d) weight-(d+1) logical operators of a code, and computes the leading monomial c*p^o of the LER polynomial without sampling, at every concatenation level, in time polynomial in code parameters and linear in the number of levels ell for fixed budgets. For concatenated codes, a recursive construction computes the leading monomial exactly in exponential time, which the predictor approximates.
AI.result: The prediction is proven exact for any unconcatenated stabilizer code, for every logical observable and arbitrary per-qubit error rates, whenever no budget is exhausted. Predictions match exact enumeration at level 1 for every evaluated code and up to three levels for the iceberg code. Using the predictor, 37 code configurations under four noise biases are evaluated in 48 core-hours, whereas Monte Carlo would need over 10^12 shots at p=10^-3 for 113 of the 148 cases.
AI.conclusion: The predictor provides a scalable, sampling-free method for estimating the leading LER monomial of stabilizer and concatenated codes, bridging the gap left by fail-fast sampling and enabling efficient comparison of many code configurations at low error rates and large distances.

title: Quantum codes are quantized codes: Stabilizer codes from quantization over finite fields
summary: We present a discrete analogue of geometric quantization over finite fields which, when applied to certain classical error-correcting codes, yields quantum error-correcting codes. This provides a physical interpretation for a previously known quantum-classical correspondence in coding theory.

AI.tldr: A discrete analogue of geometric quantization over finite fields links classical error-correcting codes to quantum error-correcting codes, giving a physical interpretation of a known quantum-classical correspondence in coding theory.
AI.motivation: There exists a previously known quantum-classical correspondence in coding theory, but it lacked a physical interpretation. This work aims to supply one.
AI.method: The authors construct a discrete analogue of geometric quantization over finite fields and apply it to certain classical error-correcting codes.
AI.result: Applying the discrete quantization to certain classical error-correcting codes yields quantum error-correcting codes.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a physical interpretation for the known quantum-classical correspondence in coding theory.

title: Quantum Krylov Linear Solving Beyond Global Conditioning via Spectral Compression and Directional Stability
summary: Global condition-number dependence can substantially overestimate the difficulty of preparing normalized quantum linear-system solutions. Many existing beyond-conditioning approaches are favorable when globally ill-conditioned directions have limited relevance to the target solution. Here we study a harder regime for time-evolution quantum Krylov linear solving (QKS), where a vanishing eigenvalue remains solution-relevant and must be retained. We identify a QKS regime in which the solution-relevant spectrum is compressed into a compact reduced space where the ill-conditioning is concentrated along a soft direction aligned with the solution, so that normalization removes the divergent amplification along that direction and leaves only a bounded transverse response. Consequently, the normalized-state complexity need not inherit the divergence of the global condition number. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We show that the solution-relevant information admits a compact and stable QKS representation, with bounded subspace dimension, evolution time, and reconstruction overhead as the relevant eigenvalue vanishes. (2) We show that normalized-state difficulty is governed by whether inverse amplification changes the solution direction, rather than by the small eigenvalue alone; even an arbitrarily ill-conditioned reduced system can remain directionally stable when the amplification is solution-aligned. (3) We prove that this stability persists under finite projected-system errors and transfers to the actual QKS output, yielding an end-to-end complexity bound without inverse dependence on the retained small eigenvalue. An explicit separation family further shows that a full inverse-amplification criterion can diverge while the corresponding QKS quantities remain bounded.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a regime of time-evolution quantum Krylov linear solving (QKS) where a vanishing eigenvalue is solution-relevant, and shows that normalized-state complexity need not inherit the divergence of the global condition number because the ill-conditioning is solution-aligned and removed by normalization.
AI.motivation: Global condition-number dependence can substantially overestimate the difficulty of preparing normalized quantum linear-system solutions. Existing beyond-conditioning approaches work when globally ill-conditioned directions are irrelevant to the target solution, but this paper targets the harder case where a vanishing eigenvalue remains solution-relevant and must be retained.
AI.method: The authors analyze time-evolution QKS in a regime where the solution-relevant spectrum is compressed into a compact reduced space, with ill-conditioning concentrated along a soft direction aligned with the solution. They characterize normalized-state difficulty through whether inverse amplification changes the solution direction rather than through the small eigenvalue alone, and prove stability under finite projected-system errors that transfers to the actual QKS output.
AI.result: The solution-relevant information admits a compact, stable QKS representation with bounded subspace dimension, evolution time, and reconstruction overhead as the relevant eigenvalue vanishes. Normalized-state difficulty is governed by directional stability of inverse amplification, so even an arbitrarily ill-conditioned reduced system can remain directionally stable when amplification is solution-aligned. An end-to-end complexity bound without inverse dependence on the retained small eigenvalue is obtained, and an explicit separation family shows a full inverse-amplification criterion can diverge while corresponding QKS quantities remain bounded.
AI.conclusion: Normalized-state QKS complexity need not inherit the divergence of the global condition number when ill-conditioning is concentrated along a solution-aligned soft direction and removed by normalization. The paper establishes an end-to-end complexity bound free of inverse dependence on the retained small eigenvalue, supported by an explicit separation family.

title: Large Language Model-Guided Discovery of Weight-Five Bivariate Bicycle Codes
summary: Building on our earlier program-evolution workflow guided by large language models (LLMs), we study weight-five bivariate bicycle (BB) and perturbed bivariate bicycle (PBB) codes. The resulting catalogue contains 1,142 distinct code proposals, including 1,081 nonbaseline proposals attributable to LLM-generated programs. Across the catalogue, we certify connected Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) realizations [[96,4,10]], [[140,6,10]], and [[180,4,14]]. A post-search comparison certifies seven imported Lin--Pryadko archive constructions. For leading parameter triples also represented in that archive, we provide exact distance evidence, explicit bivariate presentations, and verified component reductions. A basis-independent connectivity analysis identifies 409 of the 1,142 catalogue entries as disconnected and shows that 73.1\% of the classes with exact distance certificates contain repeated connected components. Algebraic analysis organizes the connected CSS classes into order-3, order-7, and order-15 cyclotomic-kernel strata. The strongest exact connected PBB parameter point is [[216,4,10]], attained by two distinct component classes. Among the 936 distinct CSS proposals from the LLM-guided campaign with a recorded positive distance, 816 (87.18\%) are certified at $d\geq5$. For comparison, three random-search controls each sample 6,444 CSS code proposals uniformly without replacement, using the same per-lattice and encoded-dimension sample counts as the LLM-guided campaign. In these controls, 4,672--4,785 proposals (72.50--74.26\%) meet the same criterion. The LLM-guided campaign has the higher certified yield, while the random controls cover more connected classes. Together, these results extend LLM-guided discovery to a more constrained code family and provide a reproducible structural and exact-distance account of its strongest candidates.

AI.tldr: An LLM-guided program-evolution search over weight-five BB/PBB codes yields 1,142 proposals (1,081 LLM-generated), certifying connected CSS codes [[96,4,10]], [[140,6,10]], [[180,4,14]], and the strongest PBB point [[216,4,10]]; 87.18% of 936 proposals with positive distance reach d>=5, beating random controls (72.50-74.26%) in certified yield though controls cover more connected classes.
AI.motivation: To extend prior LLM-guided program-evolution workflows to a more constrained quantum code family — weight-five bivariate bicycle (BB) and perturbed bivariate bicycle (PBB) codes — and to provide a reproducible structural and exact-distance account of its strongest candidates, including comparison against Lin-Pryadko archive constructions and random-search baselines.
AI.method: An LLM-guided program-evolution workflow searches weight-five BB and PBB codes, producing 1,142 distinct proposals. Candidates are analyzed via basis-independent connectivity analysis, exact-distance certification, explicit bivariate presentations, verified component reductions, and algebraic stratification of connected CSS classes into order-3, order-7, and order-15 cyclotomic-kernel strata. Three random-search controls each sample 6,444 CSS proposals uniformly without replacement, matched on per-lattice and encoded-dimension sample counts.
AI.result: The catalogue contains 1,142 distinct proposals, 1,081 of them nonbaseline LLM-generated programs; connected CSS realizations [[96,4,10]], [[140,6,10]], [[180,4,14]] are certified, plus seven imported Lin-Pryadko archive constructions. Connectivity analysis labels 409/1,142 entries disconnected, and 73.1% of exact-distance-certified classes contain repeated connected components. The strongest exact connected PBB point is [[216,4,10]], from two component classes. Of 936 distinct CSS proposals with recorded positive distance, 816 (87.18%) are certified at d>=5, versus 4,672-4,785 (72.50-74.26%) in random controls.
AI.conclusion: LLM-guided discovery extends effectively to the more constrained weight-five BB/PBB family, yielding higher certified d>=5 yield than random search, while random controls cover more connected classes. The work supplies a reproducible structural and exact-distance account of the strongest BB/PBB candidates, including cyclotomic-kernel stratification and certified leading parameters.

title: Destroying and Preserving Measurement Incompatibility over a Quantum Channel
summary: A quantum channel is called incompatibility-breaking if it always destroys the incompatibility of quantum measurements. On the other extreme are incompatibility-preserving channels, which never destroy incompatibility. This work studies both types of channels through the mathematical framework of zonotopes and zonoids, an approach that provides a complete characterization of compatibility for dichotomic measurements and is particularly powerful in the qubit setting. Using the language of zonoids, we present necessary and sufficient conditions for when a qubit unital channel is incompatibility-breaking, which are also sufficient for nonunital channels. As one of our main results, we demonstrate the superactivation phenomenon of two incompatibility-breaking qubit channels that are no longer incompatibility-breaking when used in parallel. Translating this result into the task of quantum steering, it says that two copies of a two-qubit Werner state can be steered at noise threshold $1/2$, even though this is impossible using just one copy. For the problem of incompatibility preservation, we prove that a quantum channel with matching input and output dimensions will preserve general incompatibility if and only if it is a unitary transformation. When the output dimension is larger, this result no longer holds, and we offer a conjectured form of a general incompatibility-preserving channel.

AI.tldr: Using zonotopes and zonoids, the paper characterizes incompatibility-breaking and incompatibility-preserving quantum channels, proves a superactivation phenomenon for two qubit channels, and applies it to quantum steering, showing two copies of a two-qubit Werner state become steerable at noise threshold 1/2.
AI.motivation: Quantum channels can either destroy or preserve the incompatibility of quantum measurements, but a complete characterization of these two extremes—incompatibility-breaking and incompatibility-preserving channels—is lacking. The paper aims to fill this gap, especially in the qubit setting, and to explore how such channels behave when combined.
AI.method: The authors employ the mathematical framework of zonotopes and zonoids, which provides a complete characterization of compatibility for dichotomic measurements and is particularly effective in the qubit setting. Within this framework, they derive necessary and sufficient conditions for qubit unital channels to be incompatibility-breaking (sufficient for nonunital channels), and they analyze incompatibility-preserving channels of varying input/output dimensions.
AI.result: Necessary and sufficient conditions are given for a qubit unital channel to be incompatibility-breaking, which are also sufficient for nonunital channels. A superactivation phenomenon is demonstrated: two incompatibility-breaking qubit channels, when used in parallel, are no longer incompatibility-breaking. Translated to quantum steering, two copies of a two-qubit Werner state can be steered at noise threshold 1/2, although one copy cannot. For incompatibility preservation, a channel with matching input and output dimensions preserves general incompatibility if and only if it is a unitary transformation; when the output dimension is larger, this result fails, and a conjectured general form is offered.
AI.conclusion: Zonotope/zonoid methods yield a sharp characterization of incompatibility-breaking qubit channels and reveal non-additive superactivation effects where combining two such channels restores incompatibility. Incompatibility-preserving channels with equal input/output dimensions are exactly unitaries, while larger output dimensions admit a broader, conjectured class. The results connect channel incompatibility to quantum steering tasks.

title: Kramers' Theorem Leaves a Topological Footprint in Classical Records
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, including 2 pages of End Matter
summary: Time reversal $Θ$ squares to $-1$ on a half-integer spin, so every state is orthogonal to its time reverse. This sign has been read only from quantum objects. The equilibrium state loses it, but the classical record keeps it. For a detector that resolves handedness, the probabilities that one stretch of record is followed by the time reverse of another measure the cohomology class of time reversal, $Θ^2=\pm1$. Their matrix carries this sign in its signature, a topological integer that survives equal emission and absorption losses. A programmed emitter on quantum processors reads it in about $10^3$ shots.

AI.tldr: Time reversal squaring to −1 (the fermionic/Kramers sign) is usually read only from quantum systems; a classical record can retain it. A handedness-resolving detector measures probabilities between a record segment and the time reverse of another; the resulting matrix's signature encodes Θ²=±1 as a topological integer robust to equal emission/absorption losses, read in ~10³ shots on quantum processors.
AI.motivation: The sign of time reversal (Θ²=−1 for half-integer spin) has been observable only in quantum objects, since equilibrium states lose it. The paper seeks a way to detect and preserve this sign in a classical record.
AI.method: Use a detector that resolves handedness to measure the probabilities that one stretch of record is followed by the time reverse of another. These probabilities define a matrix whose measured cohomology class of time reversal is Θ²=±1; analyze its matrix signature as a topological invariant. A programmed emitter on quantum processors performs the readout.
AI.result: The matrix carries the Θ²=±1 sign in its signature—a topological integer that survives equal emission and absorption losses. The programmed emitter reads this invariant in about 10³ shots.
AI.conclusion: The fermionic sign of time reversal can be encoded and detected in a classical record via a handedness-resolving detector, yielding a loss-robust topological integer read out in ~10³ shots on quantum processors.

title: Quantum Gibbs State Preparation via Relative Decoding: From Fast-Mixing Sources to Broader Target Classes
summary: Provable guarantees for preparing quantum Gibbs states, such as rapid mixing or gapped coherent preparation paths, are known only for restricted Hamiltonian families and usually must be re-derived for each new family. Building on homomorphic polynomial transduction, a generalization of decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) and Hamiltonian DQI (HDQI), we show how relative decoding transfers such a guarantee from a source Hamiltonian $H_A$ to a target $H_B$. Writing each Hamiltonian as a sum of $m$ Pauli terms, the subsets of terms whose product is proportional to the identity, its relations, form a binary linear code, $K_A$ for the source and $K_B$ for the target, with the Pauli-label matrix as parity-check matrix as in DQI. Starting from the canonical thermofield double (TFD) of $H_A$, a Bell transform, a reversible label map, and a coherent decoder for the quotient code $K_B/K_A$ prepare an approximate TFD of $H_B$, and hence its Gibbs state. Because this decoder only resolves target relations absent from the source, the reachable inverse temperature is set by the relative distance $d_{\rm rel}$, the fewest terms in any such relation. It can far exceed the ordinary distance $d_{\rm ord}$, the fewest terms in any target relation, which bounds the uniform exact decoding radius of DQI and HDQI. We show that linear $d_{\rm rel}$ with efficient decoding at linear radius certifies a constant inverse temperature. As an example, starting from a nearest-neighbor spin chain whose TFD is known to be preparable at every finite temperature, a sparse classical parity-check matrix yields bounded-degree, geometrically nonlocal, noncommuting targets with $d_{\rm ord}=3$ and $d_{\rm rel}=Θ(m)$. To our knowledge, this gives a new class of efficiently preparable TFDs.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) and Hamiltonian DQI via homomorphic polynomial transduction, showing that relative decoding transfers preparation guarantees from a source Hamiltonian H_A to a target H_B. The key parameter is the relative distance d_rel, which can far exceed the ordinary distance d_ord and enables preparing Gibbs states/TFDs at constant inverse temperature for a new class of nonlocal, noncommuting Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: Provable guarantees for preparing quantum Gibbs states (e.g., rapid mixing, gapped coherent preparation paths) are known only for restricted Hamiltonian families and typically must be re-derived for each new family. A general, transferable framework is needed.
AI.method: Building on homomorphic polynomial transduction (a generalization of DQI/HDQI), the authors encode each Hamiltonian's identity-product Pauli term subsets as a binary linear code (K_A, K_B) with the Pauli-label matrix as parity-check matrix. Starting from the canonical thermofield double (TFD) of H_A, they apply a Bell transform, a reversible label map, and a coherent decoder for the quotient code K_B/K_A to prepare an approximate TFD of H_B. The reachable inverse temperature is governed by the relative distance d_rel (fewest terms in any target relation absent from the source).
AI.result: The decoder only resolves target relations absent from the source, so the inverse temperature is set by d_rel, which can far exceed d_ord (bounding the uniform exact decoding radius of DQI/HDQI). Linear d_rel with efficient decoding at linear radius certifies constant inverse temperature. As an example, a sparse classical parity-check matrix yields bounded-degree, geometrically nonlocal, noncommuting targets with d_ord = 3 and d_rel = Θ(m), starting from a nearest-neighbor spin chain whose TFD is preparable at every finite temperature.
AI.conclusion: Relative decoding enables transferring Gibbs-state/TFD preparation guarantees from a source to a target Hamiltonian, yielding a new class of efficiently preparable TFDs with bounded-degree, nonlocal, noncommuting targets at constant inverse temperature.

title: Climbing the Fusion Tree: Center Ordering and Decoding Hierarchy in Non-Abelian Mixed States
summary: We develop an operational approach to strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (sw-SSB) of a non-Abelian symmetry group G. We formulate it as the decoding task of distinguishing two strongly symmetric states that differ by a pair of inserted irreps, after both are corrupted by strongly symmetric decoherence. For finite G, this task is dual to distinguishing logical states of the quantum double D(G) under pure-charge noise. We derive a hierarchy of statistical mechanics models describing optimal decoding from the fusion outcomes measured on successively larger nested regions. As for maximum-likelihood decoders of Abelian codes the measured irreps act as quenched disorder obeying a Nishimori-like condition. Strikingly, because local irreps do not determine how they fuse globally, the strong $G\times G$ symmetry is realized only nonlocally, and irreps trivially charged under Z(G) (the center of G) can hide inside noise-generated ones. As a result, the strong symmetry spontaneously breaks down to Z(G), times the weak symmetry. The only transition at nonzero error rate is then an ordering of the center, whose threshold cannot decrease as the hierarchy is ascended. This conclusion holds at any finite level of the hierarchy for non-nilpotent groups. We confirm these predictions with tensor-network calculations for $S_3$ and SU(2). At the first level, the $S_3$ model, whose center is trivial, shows no transition, and the fidelity correlations of all irreps provably decay to non-zero values. The SU(2) model exhibits a $Z_2$ transition consistent with the Nishimori-Ising universality class, where the fidelity correlations of spin-$1/2$ irreps become long-range. The threshold rises from the first to the second level of the hierarchy by $16\%$. Our results provide a systematic framework for studying non-Abelian sw-SSB and for constructing decoders for non Abelian topological codes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an operational decoding framework for strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (sw-SSB) of non-Abelian groups, showing that the strong G×G symmetry breaks only nonlocally and transitions are governed by ordering of the group center Z(G), with tensor-network results for S₃ and SU(2).
AI.motivation: Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (sw-SSB) requires an operational characterization that extends beyond Abelian symmetries. Non-Abelian groups pose a distinct challenge: local irrep measurements do not fix global fusion outcomes, so it is unclear whether and how strong symmetry breaks, what order parameter controls the transition, and how decoding relates to non-Abelian topological codes.
AI.method: sw-SSB is formulated as a decoding task: distinguish two strongly symmetric states differing by a pair of inserted irreps after strongly symmetric decoherence. For finite G this is dual to distinguishing logical states of the quantum double D(G) under pure-charge noise. A hierarchy of statistical mechanics models is derived from fusion outcomes on nested regions, with measured irreps acting as quenched disorder satisfying a Nishimori-like condition. Tensor-network calculations are performed for S₃ and SU(2).
AI.result: Because local irreps do not determine global fusion, the strong G×G symmetry is realized only nonlocally, and irreps trivially charged under the center Z(G) can hide inside noise-generated irreps. Consequently the strong symmetry breaks down to Z(G) times the weak symmetry, and the sole nonzero-error-rate transition is an ordering of the center, with a threshold that cannot decrease as the hierarchy is ascended. For S₃ (trivial center) the first-level model shows no transition and all irrep fidelity correlations provably decay to nonzero values. For SU(2), a Z₂ transition in the Nishimori-Ising universality class appears, spin-1/2 irrep fidelity correlations become long-range, and the threshold rises by 16% from the first to the second hierarchy level.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for studying non-Abelian sw-SSB and for constructing decoders for non-Abelian topological codes. The central finding is that the strong symmetry breaks to Z(G) times the weak symmetry, with the center's ordering dictating the only finite-error-rate transition; conclusions hold at any finite hierarchy level for non-nilpotent groups, and are verified numerically for S₃ and SU(2).

title: Measurement-free Preparation of Surface-Code States with Digital-Analog Counterdiabatic Drivings
summary: Preparing stabilizer-code states with shallow circuits is an important primitive for near-term quantum error correction in superconducting circuits, where logical-state initialization requires four-body stabilizer correlations from native one- and two-body controls. We introduce a digital-analog method for the preparation of surface-code ground-state manifolds. The method exploits a structural property of the adiabatic gauge potential, mapping stabilizer-local counterdiabatic terms to digital-analog blocks on the superconducting layout using fixed-angle two-qubit \(XY\) gates, single-qubit rotations, and analog exchange-interaction evolutions. The dressed blocks generate higher-order operators used as the variational ansatz to determine the counterdiabatic terms within the Sels-Polkovnikov adiabatic-gauge-potential framework. We benchmark checkerboard plaquette-stabilizer grids up to \(4\times4\), the square-grid instances correspond to rotated surface codes, while the rectangular cases probe the scaling of the method. For all grids, the proposed method generates the dominant four-body counterdiabatic basis and, at short evolution times substantially improves the ground-state preparation as compared with bare adiabatic evolution. We further generalize the construction to \(n\times m\) stabilizer lattices and show that digital-analog synthesis can reduce the entangling depth by an order of magnitude. Together, these results establish a direct connection between stabilizer geometry, the structure of the counterdiabatic gauge potential, and digital-analog control for measurement-free preparation of stabilizer-code states on near-term superconducting architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a digital-analog method that exploits the structure of the adiabatic gauge potential to prepare surface-code ground-state manifolds, mapping stabilizer-local counterdiabatic terms to fixed-angle two-qubit XY gates, single-qubit rotations, and analog exchange evolutions, achieving improved ground-state preparation and an order-of-magnitude reduction in entangling depth.
AI.motivation: Preparing stabilizer-code states with shallow circuits is a key primitive for near-term quantum error correction in superconducting circuits, where logical-state initialization requires four-body stabilizer correlations from native one- and two-body controls. Existing approaches struggle to generate these higher-order correlations efficiently, motivating a method that bridges stabilizer geometry, counterdiabatic control, and hardware-native operations.
AI.method: The method exploits a structural property of the adiabatic gauge potential, mapping stabilizer-local counterdiabatic terms to digital-analog blocks on the superconducting layout using fixed-angle two-qubit XY gates, single-qubit rotations, and analog exchange-interaction evolutions. The dressed blocks generate higher-order operators employed as a variational ansatz to determine the counterdiabatic terms within the Sels-Polkovnikov adiabatic-gauge-potential framework. The construction is generalized to n×m stabilizer lattices.

Digital-analog synthesis reduces the entangling depth by an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a direct connection between stabilizer geometry, the structure of the counterdiabatic gauge potential, and digital-analog control for measurement-free preparation of stabilizer-code states on near-term superconducting architecture.

title: Random-Oracle Unitary Synthesis is Impossible
summary:
A major open problem in quantum complexity is the question of unitary synthesis---namely, is it possible to efficiently implement any unitary, given the ability to evaluate any classical function in superposition? Inspired by a recent work by Brakerski and Yuen (CRYPTO 2026), we propose an ``average-case'' unitary synthesis problem, which asks whether it is possible to efficiently implement a Haar random unitary given access to a random Boolean function. We then demonstrate a superpolynomial query lower bound, establishing that unitary synthesis in this model is impossible.
  Along with our main result, we settle in the negative a question Brakerski and Yuen pose, of whether scalable pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) can be implemented in the ROM-PRU model. In particular, we show that in the ROM-PRU model, no $Ω(N^{1+γ})$ unitary design on $n$ qubits, where $N=2^n$, can be efficiently achieved for any $γ> 0$. On the other hand, we construct an $O(N)$-design in $\text{poly}(n)$ queries in the same model, surpassing the previously best known results which constructed $O(\sqrt{N})$-designs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies an average-case unitary synthesis problem, proving a superpolynomial query lower bound showing Haar random unitaries cannot be efficiently implemented from a random Boolean function. It negatively resolves whether scalable PRUs exist in the ROM-PRU model, showing no Ω(N^{1+γ}) unitary design is efficiently achievable for any γ>0, while constructing an O(N)-design in poly(n) queries.
AI.motivation: Unitary synthesis—efficiently implementing any unitary given the ability to evaluate any classical function in superposition—is a major open problem in quantum complexity. Motivated by recent work of Brakerski and Yuen (CRYPTO 2026), the authors investigate whether this is possible in an average-case setting and whether scalable pseudorandom unitaries can be realized in the ROM-PRU model.
AI.method: The authors formulate an average-case unitary synthesis problem asking whether a Haar random unitary can be efficiently implemented given access to a random Boolean function, and prove a superpolynomial query lower bound. They also analyze the ROM-PRU model, deriving a negative answer to the question posed by Brakerski and Yuen regarding scalable PRUs, and construct an improved unitary design within that model.
AI.result: A superpolynomial query lower bound establishes that average-case unitary synthesis in this model is impossible. In the ROM-PRU model, no Ω(N^{1+γ}) unitary design on n qubits (N=2^n) can be efficiently achieved for any γ>0, disproving the possibility posed by Brakerski and Yuen. Conversely, an O(N)-design is constructed in poly(n) queries, surpassing prior best results that achieved only O(√N)-designs.
AI.conclusion: Unitary synthesis is impossible in the proposed average-case model, and scalable PRUs cannot be realized in the ROM-PRU model, negatively settling the Brakerski–Yuen question. Nevertheless, the ROM-PRU model still permits an O(N)-design via poly(n) queries, improving over previous O(√N)-design constructions.

title: Optimal compression with quantum retrieval
summary: We consider the following data compression problem. Given a string $x \in \{0,1\}^m$ of Hamming weight at most $n$, compress it into a shorter string $y \in \{0,1\}^s$ so that any bit $x_i$ of $x$ can be retrieved without any error using at most $t$ quantum queries to the standard oracle encoding of $y$. If queries are allowed to be adaptive we show how optimal compression up to a logarithmic factor can be achieved. If the queries are required to be made non-adaptively, we show schemes whose space is optimal in its dependence on $m$ except for a logarithmic factor, and is at most quadratically worse when compared to the optimum in its dependence on $n$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies compressing sparse binary strings into short codewords that support local quantum bit retrieval with few queries, giving optimal-up-to-log schemes for adaptive queries and near-optimal schemes for non-adaptive queries.
AI.motivation: The work addresses a data compression problem where a sparse string x of length m and Hamming weight at most n must be stored as a shorter string y, while still allowing each original bit x_i to be recovered exactly via limited quantum oracle queries to y. The motivation is to characterize the trade-off between compressed space and local quantum query access.
AI.method: The string x is encoded into y, and each bit x_i is retrieved by making quantum queries to the standard oracle encoding of y. The paper analyzes two query models: adaptive queries and non-adaptive queries, and constructs compression schemes for each.
AI.result: For adaptive queries, optimal compression up to a logarithmic factor is achieved. For non-adaptive queries, the schemes use space that is optimal in its dependence on m up to a logarithmic factor, and at most quadratically worse than optimal in its dependence on n.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes achievable compression bounds for sparse strings under local quantum query access, distinguishing adaptive and non-adaptive settings and showing logarithmic and quadratic gaps from optimality in the respective parameters.

title: Out-of-control Hamiltonian Learning
summary:
Learning the Hamiltonian of a many-body system from its dynamics is a central task in quantum science, yet the algorithms with the strongest provable guarantees assume some level of quantum control--fast, arbitrary single-qubit gates interleaved with time evolution, and measurements in arbitrary bases--that is beyond the capabilities of near-term analog quantum simulators. Motivated by analog atom- and ion-based platforms, we study Hamiltonian learning under minimal access models.
  Uniform state preparation and measurements: We first consider the setting where in every experiment, one can rotate each qubit to the same state, perform short-time evolution, and measure every qubit in the same basis. Surprisingly, we show that for generic 2-local Hamiltonians on any interaction graph, all of the parameters can be reconstructed from such experiments.
  Computational basis state preparation and measurements: We then consider a similarly constrained setting, but where state preparation and measurement are restricted to the computational basis. For nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians with only Pauli $X/Z$ interactions, a class which captures contemporary Rydberg atom platforms, we show that over 1D and 2D rectangular lattices, all of the parameters can be reconstructed from such experiments up to unavoidable gauges.
  Our protocols introduce new techniques for solving structured polynomial systems over an extensive number of parameters. Taken together, our results suggest that one can learn a great deal from the dynamics of quantum many-body systems even under the most stringent experimental constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Hamiltonian learning on analog quantum simulators with minimal control, showing that generic 2-local Hamiltonians can be reconstructed using only uniform state preparation/measurement, and that X/Z nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians on 1D/2D lattices can be learned from computational-basis-only experiments up to gauges.
