AI.motivation: Most Hamiltonian learning algorithms with strong provable guarantees rely on fast, arbitrary single-qubit gates and arbitrary-basis measurements, which near-term analog atom- and ion-based platforms cannot provide. The authors are motivated to determine what can still be learned under realistic, minimally controlled analog access models.
AI.method: The authors define constrained access models. In the first, each experiment allows rotating every qubit to the same state, short-time evolution, and measuring all qubits in the same basis. In the second, state preparation and measurement are restricted to the computational basis. They develop protocols based on solving structured polynomial systems with many parameters to reconstruct Hamiltonian coefficients.
AI.result: For generic 2-local Hamiltonians on any interaction graph, all parameters can be reconstructed from uniform-preparation/measurement experiments. For nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians with only Pauli X/Z interactions on 1D and 2D rectangular lattices, a class covering contemporary Rydberg atom platforms, all parameters can be reconstructed from computational-basis experiments up to unavoidable gauges.
AI.conclusion: The protocols introduce new techniques for solving structured polynomial systems over many parameters. The results indicate that substantial Hamiltonian information can be learned from many-body dynamics even under the most stringent experimental constraints of analog quantum simulators.

title: Tight Query Lower Bounds for Quantum Sampling, with an Application to Certified Randomness
summary: Random circuit sampling experiments, the leading demonstrations of quantum computational advantage, are tested with the linear cross-entropy benchmark (XEB), which scores outcomes by their ideal probabilities. We study what a high XEB score certifies about an untrusted quantum device. In the quantum query model, we show that the honest sampler's ideal score acts as a Tsirelson bound for efficient devices and certified randomness. First, exceeding the ideal score by a constant requires $Ω(N^{1/3})$ queries for the Haar and Fourier oracle ensembles with $N$ outcomes, and this bound is tight; this proves an earlier conjecture for Haar-random states and extends it to Fourier sampling. Second, for Fourier sampling and for Haar-random states accessed through the canonical state-preparation oracle, the $n$-bit output of a device that makes polynomially many queries and scores within $o(1)$ of the ideal score has $n-O(\log n)$ bits of smooth min-entropy, even against an adversary who is entangled with the device and later learns the oracle; this is nearly optimal. As a corollary, sampling the collision distribution, which is proportional to the square of the ideal distribution, has query complexity $Θ(N^{1/3})$, and a coherent version of the same algorithm approximately prepares quantum Hadamard products of states with uniform amplitude magnitudes. Both lower bounds rest on progress measures that bound the excess over the ideal score and increase only slightly with each query. For Fourier sampling the measure is the norm of the coherent amplitudes for removing pairs in a purification of the random function, combining the polynomial method with the compressed oracle technique; for Haar-random states it is the square root of the average level in an expansion in Dirichlet orthogonal polynomials, controlled by an exact identity for the effect of one observation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies what a high linear cross-entropy benchmark (XEB) score certifies about an untrusted quantum device in the quantum query model. It shows the honest sampler's ideal score acts as a Tsirelson-type bound: exceeding it by a constant requires Ω(N^{1/3}) queries (tight for Haar and Fourier oracle ensembles), and devices scoring within o(1) of ideal produce n-O(log n) bits of smooth min-entropy even against entangled adversaries. Both lower bounds use progress measures that grow slowly with each query.
AI.motivation: Random circuit sampling, tested with XEB, is the leading demonstration of quantum computational advantage, but it is unclear what a high XEB score actually certifies about an untrusted device. The work aims to establish rigorous limits and certified randomness guarantees for XEB-based verification.
AI.method: Query-complexity lower bounds via progress measures bounding the excess over the ideal score, increasing only slightly per query. For Fourier sampling, the measure is the norm of coherent amplitudes for removing pairs in a purification of the random function, combining the polynomial method with the compressed oracle technique. For Haar-random states, it is the square root of the average level in a Dirichlet orthogonal polynomial expansion, controlled by an exact identity for one observation.
AI.result: Exceeding the ideal score by a constant requires Ω(N^{1/3}) queries for Haar and Fourier ensembles with N outcomes, and this is tight, proving an earlier Haar-random conjecture and extending it to Fourier sampling. For Fourier sampling and canonical-oracle Haar states, polynomially many queries scoring within o(1) of ideal yield n-O(log n) bits of smooth min-entropy even against adversaries entangled with the device who later learn the oracle—nearly optimal. As a corollary, the collision distribution sampling has query complexity Θ(N^{1/3}), and a coherent algorithm approximately prepares quantum Hadamard products of uniform-magnitude states.
AI.conclusion: The ideal XEB score functions as a Tsirelson bound for efficient devices and certified randomness. High XEB performance cannot be substantially exceeded efficiently, and near-ideal scores certify near-optimal entropy, giving a rigorous basis for XEB as a verification and randomness-certification benchmark.

title: Certifying Measurement Incompatibility under Bounded Classical Communication
summary: Measurement incompatibility enables quantum advantages in communication and state discrimination. It is also necessary for Bell nonlocality, which is used in device-independent protocols for quantum key distribution and private randomness generation. Classical communication can influence the receiver's outcome and must therefore be accounted for when certifying measurement incompatibility. We introduce union maximal leakage, which quantifies the information needed for a common classical explanation of all observed probabilities and is computed from them by a linear program. If a message of at most $k$ bits precedes the receiver's independent measurement choice, compatible measurements for each message give union maximal leakage at most $k$. This bound holds with any input-independent nonsignalling shared resource. In quantum theory, a violation also implies that the initially shared state is entangled. Conversely, union maximal leakage determines the minimum classical communication needed to reproduce the observations with compatible measurements and arbitrary nonsignalling assistance. For a fixed shared quantum state and receiver measurements, a violation is possible exactly when, for some message value, the receiver's measurements are Bell-nonlocal against two-outcome sender measurements on that state. For binary receiver outcomes, we show that a violation also certifies randomness private from the sender, even when the receiver's measurement depends on the sender's message and the sender retains quantum side information. We quantify this privacy through an explicit conditional entropy bound and establish composably secure randomness extraction in sequential protocols with device memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "union maximal leakage," a linear-program-computable measure quantifying the classical information needed for a common classical explanation of observed probability distributions. It proves that if ≤k bits of classical communication precede the receiver's measurement, compatible measurements yield union maximal leakage ≤k, holding under any input-independent nonsignalling shared resource. Violations imply entanglement, certify Bell nonlocality, and (for binary outcomes) private randomness, with explicit conditional entropy bounds and composably secure randomness extraction in sequential protocols with device memory.
AI.motivation: Measurement incompatibility underpins quantum advantages in communication, state discrimination, and Bell nonlocality used in device-independent protocols. Since classical communication can influence the receiver's outcome, certifying measurement incompatibility requires accounting for it. The paper aims to develop a tool that distinguishes genuine quantum incompatibility from classical communication effects and characterizes its resources, entanglement, nonlocality, and privacy implications.
AI.method: The authors define union maximal leakage, computed via a linear program from observed probabilities, quantifying information for a common classical explanation of all observed distributions. They analyze scenarios where a message of at most k bits precedes the receiver's independent measurement choice, proving upper bounds when measurements are compatible for each message. They extend results to input-independent nonsignalling shared resources, derive entanglement implications in quantum theory, and connect violations to Bell nonlocality against two-outcome sender measurements. For binary receiver outcomes, they establish privacy via an explicit conditional entropy bound and show composably secure randomness extraction in sequential protocols with device memory.
AI.result: Union maximal leakage is at most k when ≤k bits of classical communication precede the receiver's independent measurement choice with compatible measurements, holding under any input-independent nonsignalling resource. In quantum theory, a violation implies the shared state is entangled. The measure determines the minimum classical communication needed to reproduce observations with compatible measurements and arbitrary nonsignalling assistance. For a fixed state and receiver measurements, violation is possible exactly when, for some message value, the receiver's measurements are Bell-nonlocal against two-outcome sender measurements on that state. For binary receiver outcomes, violation certifies randomness private from the sender, even when the receiver's measurement depends on the sender's message and the sender retains quantum side information.
AI.conclusion: Union maximal leakage provides a linear-program-computable operational measure that certifies measurement incompatibility accounting for classical communication, bounding information via k bits, implying entanglement, and characterizing Bell nonlocality and private randomness. It yields explicit conditional entropy bounds and enables composably secure randomness extraction in sequential protocols with device memory, offering a unified framework linking incompatibility, nonlocality, and device-independent privacy.

title: Approximate cloning of structured pure states
summary: The no-cloning theorem is a cornerstone result in quantum mechanics that forbids copying of general quantum information. More quantitatively, even given $N$ copies of an unknown state, any channel producing an $(N+1)$-copy state incurs a nonzero trace-distance error on some inputs. Turning this around, one can ask about the sample complexity of approximate $N\rightarrow N+1$ cloning: for a desired small error $ε$, what $N$ suffices? For arbitrary pure states on a Hilbert space $H$, the answer is $N\simeq \dim H/ε$ - astronomically large for most $H$ of interest. What if the input is promised to lie in a structured family? We examine a range of families fundamental to many-body physics and quantum information: $n$-mode fermionic Gaussian and Slater states, $n$-mode bosonic Gaussian states, and qudit phase states. For fermions, we construct optimal cloning channels, reducing the complexity from exponential to polynomial in $n$. For bosonic Gaussian states, we construct an explicit cloner that certifies polynomial complexity, without any constraint on the energy of the state; this channel, however, is not optimal in general. The fermionic and bosonic results follow from a single representation-theoretic framework, which generalizes previous work by Werner and by Chiribella and Yang; it also yields the cloners' unitary implementation. Furthermore, we explain why for many families the cloning complexity is linear in the dimension of the family manifold, via a controlled saddle-point evaluation of the frame potential at high $N$. The same calculation accounts for the analogous scaling of tomography complexity. The above framework does not cover phase states; for these we give an independent construction of a channel with optimal cloning fidelity. Our work complements recent results on cloning stabilizer states.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the sample complexity of approximate N→N+1 cloning for structured quantum state families (fermionic Gaussian/Slater states, bosonic Gaussian states, and qudit phase states), showing that restricting to these families reduces complexity from exponential to polynomial in the mode number n, and derives these results from a unified representation-theoretic framework.
AI.motivation: The no-cloning theorem implies that for arbitrary pure states approximate N→N+1 cloning requires N ≃ dim H/ε copies, which is astronomically large for most Hilbert spaces of interest. The authors ask whether a promise that the input lies in a structured family can dramatically reduce this sample complexity, examining families fundamental to many-body physics and quantum information.
AI.method: The authors construct optimal cloning channels for fermionic Gaussian and Slater states, and an explicit (generally non-optimal) cloner for bosonic Gaussian states with no energy constraint. Both results follow from a single representation-theoretic framework that generalizes prior work by Werner and by Chiribella and Yang and also provides unitary implementations of the cloners. They analyze cloning complexity via a controlled saddle-point evaluation of the frame potential at high N, and for qudit phase states give an independent construction of a channel with optimal cloning fidelity.
AI.result: For fermions, optimal cloning channels reduce the complexity from exponential to polynomial in n. For bosonic Gaussian states, an explicit cloner certifies polynomial complexity without any energy constraint on the state, though it is not optimal in general. The framework explains why for many families the cloning complexity is linear in the dimension of the family manifold, and the same calculation accounts for the analogous scaling of tomography complexity. For phase states, an optimal-fidelity channel is independently constructed.
AI.conclusion: Structured input promises can dramatically lower the sample complexity of approximate quantum cloning, with fermionic and bosonic Gaussian families admitting polynomial-in-n cloners derived from a unified representation-theoretic framework, and phase states handled by a separate optimal construction. The work complements recent results on cloning stabilizer states and links cloning complexity to the manifold dimension and to tomography complexity.

title: Random Order in Quantum Streaming: Replenishment and Robust Lower Bounds
summary:
How can random order change the role of quantum memory in streaming? Later classical input can restore the usefulness of a quantum state consumed by earlier queries. We call this replenishment.
  We construct an artificial problem based on Hidden Matching, with repeated coordinate data and online matching requests. It admits a one-pass quantum algorithm using polylogarithmic space in uniformly random order, but unconditionally requires polynomial space both classically in random order and quantumly when all updates precede the requests.
  To prove the quantum lower bound, we strengthen the consumability bounds of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean for Multiple Hidden Matching. Without prior entanglement, any quantum encoding supporting $r$ independent matching requests requires $Ω(r)$ qubits for $r\le N^{1/2-δ}$ and every fixed $δ\in(0,1/2)$, even with simultaneous revelation and arbitrary joint decoding. For sequential requests, the linear bound extends through $r=Θ(\sqrt N)$.
  We also adapt Kallaugher's triangle-counting algorithm to uniformly random streams in which every edge is repeated equally often. Rebuilding the quantum sketch and resampling the classical estimator improve its expected-space bound in suitable parameter regimes.
  Finally, we extend the robust Noisy Gap Cycle framework of Assadi and Sundaresan to quantum streaming. A quantum communication lower bound for Block Hidden XOR yields an $Ω(n)$ space lower bound in random edge order for large enough cycles, with consequences for several graph problems.
  Thus random order can enable replenishment of small quantum representations, while substantial space requirements persist for other tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how uniformly random input order changes the power of quantum memory in streaming. It introduces "replenishment": later classical data can revive a quantum state consumed by earlier queries. The authors construct a Hidden-Matching-based problem solvable with polylogarithmic quantum space in random order, yet unconditionally requiring polynomial space classically in random order and quantumly when updates precede requests; they prove the space separation via strengthened consumability bounds and extend related algorithms and lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Quantum sketches are typically consumed by measurement, so once queries are answered the quantum state is used up. The paper asks whether a random arrival order can alter this limitation, specifically whether later classical input can restore the usefulness of an already-consumed quantum state. The motivation is to understand when random order enables small quantum streaming space and when substantial space remains unavoidable.
AI.method: The authors construct an artificial problem based on Hidden Matching with repeated coordinate data and online matching requests. They prove quantum lower bounds by strengthening the consumability bounds of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean for Multiple Hidden Matching, analyzing independent and sequential matching requests with simultaneous revelation and arbitrary joint decoding. They also adapt Kallaugher's triangle-counting algorithm to uniformly random streams with equally repeated edges by rebuilding the quantum sketch and resampling the classical estimator. Finally, they extend the robust Noisy Gap Cycle framework of Assadi and Sundaresan to quantum streaming, using a quantum communication lower bound for Block Hidden XOR.
AI.result: The constructed problem admits a one-pass quantum algorithm using polylogarithmic space in uniformly random order, but unconditionally requires polynomial space classically in random order and quantumly when all updates precede requests. For Multiple Hidden Matching without prior entanglement, any quantum encoding supporting r independent matching requests requires Ω(r) qubits for r ≤ N^{1/2−δ} and every fixed δ ∈ (0,1/2), even with simultaneous revelation and arbitrary joint decoding; for sequential requests the linear bound extends through r = Θ(√N). Adapting Kallaugher's triangle-counting algorithm improves its expected-space bound in suitable parameter regimes. The quantum extension of robust Noisy Gap Cycle yields an Ω(n) space lower bound in random edge order for large enough cycles, with consequences for several graph problems.
AI.conclusion: Random order can enable replenishment of small quantum representations, allowing polylogarithmic-space quantum streaming in some settings. However, substantial space requirements persist for other tasks, as shown by the polynomial and Ω(n) lower bounds. The results delineate when random order helps quantum memory and when strong lower bounds remain.

title: Qubit CSS codes with Universal Transversal Gates
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. The ancillary file depth_one_universal_codes.json lists all 110 codes with their stabilizers, logical operators, depth-one generators, seed and kernel codes, and coupling circuits
summary: The Eastin-Knill theorem rules out a universal set of transversal logical gates on any code that detects single-qubit errors. The theorem constrains one partition of the qubits at a time. We show that depth-one layers of few-qubit gates, each respecting its own partition, can together generate a universal logical gate set on an error-correcting code. Each logical gate generator is then a single depth-one layer followed by error correction of the same stabilizer code, with no magic-state distillation, code switching, gauge fixing, lattice surgery, or other gadgets. We show that such codes can be found by applying an entangling circuit to a lower-distance "seed" code admitting a depth-one non-Clifford gate and an appropriate "kernel" code. We construct 47 codes with depth-one generating sets that tolerate at least one faulty gate per layer, including a [[37,1,7]] and a [[59,1,9]] code, both of check weight at most eight.

AI.tldr: By using multiple qubit partitions, depth-one layers of few-qubit gates can jointly generate a universal logical gate set on an error-correcting code, circumventing the Eastin-Knill theorem without magic-state distillation or other gadgets, yielding 47 explicit codes including [[37,1,7]] and [[59,1,9]] constructions.
AI.motivation: The Eastin-Knill theorem forbids a universal transversal logical gate set on any code detecting single-qubit errors, since transversality is defined with respect to a single qubit partition. This poses a fundamental obstacle to fault-tolerant universal quantum computation, typically forcing costly remedies such as magic-state distillation, code switching, gauge fixing, or lattice surgery. The paper seeks a construction that evades the theorem's constraint while preserving fault tolerance.
AI.method: The key observation is that the Eastin-Knill theorem constrains only one qubit partition at a time. The authors consider depth-one layers of few-qubit gates, each layer respecting its own partition, and show that a collection of such layers can together generate a universal logical gate set. Each logical gate generator consists of a single depth-one layer followed by error correction of the same stabilizer code, avoiding magic-state distillation, code switching, gauge fixing, lattice surgery, or other gadgets. Such codes are constructed by applying an entangling circuit to a lower-distance "seed" code that admits a depth-one non-Clifford gate together with an appropriate "kernel" code.
AI.result: The construction yields 47 codes with depth-one generating sets that tolerate at least one faulty gate per layer. Notable instances include a [[37,1,7]] code and a [[59,1,9]] code, both with check weight at most eight.
AI.conclusion: The Eastin-Knill theorem can be circumvented by exploiting multiple qubit partitions, enabling universal logical gate sets via depth-one layers plus standard error correction. This provides a conceptually simple, gadget-free route to fault-tolerant universal quantum computation, with explicit small-distance code constructions demonstrating feasibility.

title: Streaming Regev's Quantum Factoring Algorithm
summary:
A major practical obstacle to Regev's factoring algorithm is its large space usage. In particular, the algorithm was believed to be incompatible with "qubit recycling," which streams the control qubits in phase estimation rather than storing them all simultaneously. We show how to fix this streaming problem. We build on the construction of Ragavan and Vaikuntanathan, which used Fibonacci accumulators to reduce the qubit count from $O(n^{1.5})$ to $11.32n$. We make two key improvements. First, we use superposition masking to prevent unwanted information from entering the accumulators, removing the need for uncomputation. Second, we show how to perform phase estimation using Fibonacci powers of a unitary operation rather than powers of two. This avoids various encoding conversions required by the construction of Ragavan and Vaikuntanathan. After these improvements, the phase-estimation qubits are used only once in the circuit, allowing them to be streamed.
  Our improvements reduce the space usage of Regev's factoring algorithm to $n+M(n)+O(\sqrt{n})$, where $M(n)$ is the space required for an in-place multiplication. For example, using the in-place multiplier of Luo et al. (2026), Regev's algorithm can factor an $n$-bit integer using $4n+O(\sqrt{n})$ qubits. Although our construction still falls short of the $n/2+εn$ qubits sufficient for leading implementations of Shor's algorithm, it is the lowest-space instantiation of Regev's algorithm to date and suggests that Regev's algorithm is still far from fully optimized.

AI.tldr: This paper reduces the space usage of Regev's factoring algorithm by enabling qubit recycling via superposition masking and Fibonacci-power phase estimation, achieving $n+M(n)+O(\sqrt{n})$ qubits (e.g., $4n+O(\sqrt{n})$), the lowest for Regev's algorithm to date.
AI.motivation: Regev's factoring algorithm suffers from large space usage, and it was previously believed incompatible with "qubit recycling" — streaming control qubits in phase estimation instead of storing them simultaneously. This space barrier limits practical implementation.
AI.method: Building on Ragavan and Vaikuntanathan's Fibonacci-accumulator construction (which cut qubits from $O(n^{1.5})$ to $11.32n$), the authors make two improvements: (1) superposition masking to keep unwanted information out of the accumulators, eliminating the need for uncomputation; and (2) phase estimation using Fibonacci powers of a unitary rather than powers of two, avoiding various encoding conversions. Consequently, phase-estimation qubits are each used only once and can be streamed.
AI.result: Space usage is reduced to $n+M(n)+O(\sqrt{n})$, where $M(n)$ is the space for an in-place multiplication. With the in-place multiplier of Luo et al. (2026), Regev's algorithm factors an $n$-bit integer using $4n+O(\sqrt{n})$ qubits.
AI.conclusion: While still short of the $n/2+\varepsilon n$ qubits sufficient for leading Shor's algorithm implementations, this is the lowest-space instantiation of Regev's algorithm to date, implying Regev's algorithm remains far from fully optimized.

title: Characterizing Photonic Partial Distinguishability Through Gram Matrix Tomography
summary: Partial distinguishability affects multiphoton interference, which is central to large-scale photonic experiments such as Boson Sampling and to applications of multiphoton states across quantum technologies. Characterizing the internal degrees of freedom responsible for this behavior is challenging: in many scenarios they cannot be accessed directly and even their dimension or physical nature may be unknown \emph{a priori}. Here we introduce Gram-matrix tomography for independently prepared photons with pure or nearly pure internal states. For pure states, the Gram matrix contains all information required to predict the statistics of experiments that are insensitive to the internal degrees of freedom. We reconstruct this matrix, up to physically irrelevant phase choices, from a quadratic number of measurable Bargmann invariants (quantities encoding overlap magnitudes and collective phases). We access these quantities using two complementary approaches: targeted Fourier interferometers and two- and three-body photon-number correlations measured in a single random interferometer. We derive explicit error bounds that control the total-variation distance between predicted and actual outcome distributions for any subsequent experiment that is insensitive to the internal states. These guarantees account for finite sampling and deviations from purity. Crucially, the total sample complexity of the protocol is independent of the internal Hilbert-space dimension and polynomial under mild assumptions on overlaps of internal states. Our protocol uses standard interferometric measurements and turns them into a robust and operationally grounded characterization of partially distinguishable photons.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Gram-matrix tomography," a protocol to characterize partially distinguishable photons with pure or nearly pure internal states by reconstructing their Gram matrix from a quadratic number of measurable Bargmann invariants, using standard interferometric measurements.
AI.motivation: Partial distinguishability governs multiphoton interference, central to Boson Sampling and other photonic quantum technologies. Characterizing the internal degrees of freedom behind this is hard because they often cannot be accessed directly, and even their dimension or physical nature may be unknown a priori.
AI.method: For independently prepared photons with pure or nearly pure internal states, the authors reconstruct the Gram matrix up to physically irrelevant phase choices. They do so from a quadratic number of measurable Bargmann invariants (encoding overlap magnitudes and collective phases), accessed via two complementary approaches: targeted Fourier interferometers, and two- and three-body photon-number correlations in a single random interferometer. Explicit error bounds are derived, accounting for finite sampling and purity deviations.
AI.result: The protocol reconstructs the Gram matrix with explicit error bounds controlling the total-variation distance between predicted and actual outcome distributions for any subsequent internal-state-insensitive experiment. Crucially, total sample complexity is independent of the internal Hilbert-space dimension and polynomial under mild assumptions on internal-state overlaps.
AI.conclusion: The protocol leverages standard interferometric measurements to provide a robust, operationally grounded characterization of partially distinguishable photons, enabling reliable prediction of multiphoton interference statistics.

title: Anti-symmetrization is cheap and useful
summary: We consider the computational task of anti-symmetrization of an unknown mixed quantum state: Given iid copies of a rank-$r$ qudit state $ρ=\sum_{i=1}^r λ_i |\varphi_i\rangle\!\langle\varphi_i|$, prepare a copy of the state proportional to $Π_{\mathrm{anti}}^r (|\varphi_1\rangle\otimes \ldots\otimes|\varphi_r\rangle)$, with $Π_{\mathrm{anti}}^r$ the anti-symmetric subspace projector. We first give a simple algorithm for anti-symmetrization that uses $\widetilde{O}(r / λ_{\min})$ copies of $ρ$, where $λ_{\min}$ is the minimum non-zero eigenvalue of $ρ$. This algorithm works even in the streaming setting with small working memory, and it uses only simple quantum operations like controlled-SWAPs and constantly many layers of single-qubit gates. As an application of this streaming anti-symmetrization procedure, we give a reduction from gapped mixed-state one-way state generators to pure-state one-way state generators. Then, using tools from Schur-Weyl duality, we give and analyze a second (non-streaming) anti-symmetrization procedure that uses $O(r / λ_{\min})$ copies of $ρ$, which then serves as a building block in new algorithms for weak Schur sampling and unitary Schur sampling, outperforming existing approaches in some regimes of number of copies $n$ and local dimension $d$, as well as in an algorithm for optimal purity amplification for qudit states.

AI.tldr: The paper studies anti-symmetrization of unknown mixed quantum states, providing a simple streaming algorithm using O~(r/λ_min) copies and a Schur-Weyl-based non-streaming algorithm using O(r/λ_min) copies, with applications to one-way state generators, Schur sampling, and purity amplification.
AI.motivation: Anti-symmetrization maps copies of a rank-r mixed qudit state to the anti-symmetric subspace of its eigenstates. This primitive is useful because it concentrates a state's support onto a canonical anti-symmetric subspace, enabling reductions and algorithms. Prior approaches lacked simple, memory-efficient procedures and did not exploit anti-symmetrization for tasks like one-way state generators, Schur sampling, and purity amplification.
AI.method: Two algorithms are proposed. (1) A simple streaming algorithm using O~(r/λ_min) copies of ρ, requiring only small working memory and simple operations (controlled-SWAPs and constantly many layers of single-qubit gates), yielding a state proportional to Π_anti^r(|φ_1⟩⊗...⊗|φ_r⟩). (2) A non-streaming algorithm based on Schur-Weyl duality using O(r/λ_min) copies. These are applied to gapped mixed-state one-way state generators, weak/unitary Schur sampling, and optimal purity amplification.
AI.result: The streaming anti-symmetrization gives a reduction from gapped mixed-state one-way state generators to pure-state one-way state generators. The Schur-Weyl anti-symmetrization serves as a building block for new algorithms for weak Schur sampling and unitary Schur sampling that outperform existing approaches in certain regimes of the number of copies n and local dimension d, and for an algorithm achieving optimal purity amplification for qudit states.
AI.conclusion: Anti-symmetrization of unknown mixed quantum states can be achieved efficiently with O~(r/λ_min) copies (streaming) or O(r/λ_min) copies (Schur-Weyl), providing a versatile primitive with applications to one-way state generators, Schur sampling, and purity amplification.

title: Free entropy and quantum minimum description length
comment: 8pp; see also a concurrent long article
summary: In free probability, Voiculescu's free entropy counts matrix microstates that approximate an operator. It is a non-commutative analog of the Shannon entropy, distinct from any quantum entropy of a density operator, but it has had no physical meaning in quantum theory. We define a finite-dimensional physical free entropy at finite resolution and show that it directly characterizes, up to an explicit constant, the minimal quantum memory needed to program many copies of a state with known eigenvalues and unknown eigenbasis. This task is a variant of Schumacher compression, and we call its optimal cost the quantum minimum description length. We briefly discuss how free entropy differs from quantum entropies and its potential applications in quantum physics.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a finite-dimensional physical free entropy at finite resolution and shows it equals, up to an explicit constant, the minimal quantum memory (quantum minimum description length) needed to program many copies of a state with known eigenvalues but unknown eigenbasis, giving Voiculescu's free entropy a physical operational meaning via a Schumacher-type task.
AI.motivation: Voiculescu's free entropy is a non-commutative analog of Shannon entropy but has lacked physical meaning in quantum theory, and its relation to quantum entropies is unclear. The authors aim to give it an operational, physical interpretation.
AI.method: They introduce a finite-dimensional physical free entropy at finite resolution and analyze a Schumacher-compression variant: programming many copies of a quantum state whose eigenvalues are known but whose eigenbasis is unknown. They define the optimal cost as the quantum minimum description length and relate it to the free entropy.
AI.result: The physical free entropy directly characterizes, up to an explicit constant, the minimal quantum memory required for this state-programming task, i.e., it matches the quantum minimum description length.
AI.conclusion: Free entropy gains a concrete physical/operational meaning, is shown to differ from standard quantum entropies, and may find applications in quantum physics.

title: Quantum minimum description of density matrices
comment: 32pp; see also a concurrent letter; Lean certificate: https://github.com/JWang226/Quantum-Minimum-Description-Length
summary: We study a variant of Schumacher compression. The task asks for the minimal memory cost for compressing many copies of a density matrix with known spectrum and unknown eigenbasis, without preserving its purification. For fixed dimension and distinct positive eigenvalues, we obtain the cost through its additive constant. Achievability uses a generalization of Werner's cloning map to $\mathrm{GL}(d,\mathbb C)$ irreducible representations, with finite trace-distance bounds controlled by highest-weight differences and row gaps. The matching converse follows from a quantitative form of Koashi--Imoto incompressibility for irreducible group orbits under a spectral-gap assumption. We also identify the relation between this quantum minimum description length and universal lossless coding overhead, and its connection to free entropy is explained in a companion letter. We provide a Lean certificate for our proofs.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the minimal memory cost (to its additive constant) for a variant of Schumacher compression of many copies of a density matrix with known spectrum but unknown eigenbasis, without preserving purification, and links this quantum minimum description length to universal lossless coding overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard Schumacher compression assumes the eigenbasis is known. The paper addresses the harder setting where the spectrum is known but the eigenbasis is unknown and purification need not be preserved, raising the question of the exact minimal memory cost in this variant.
AI.method: For fixed dimension and distinct positive eigenvalues, the authors pin down the cost via its additive constant. Achievability generalizes Werner's cloning map to GL(d,C) irreducible representations, with finite trace-distance bounds governed by highest-weight differences and row gaps. The matching converse uses a quantitative Koashi--Imoto incompressibility for irreducible group orbits under a spectral-gap assumption. A Lean certificate is provided for the proofs.
AI.result: The minimal memory cost is characterized up to its additive constant for fixed dimension and distinct positive eigenvalues, with matching achievability and converse bounds. The relation between this quantum minimum description length and universal lossless coding overhead is identified, and a connection to free entropy is described in a companion letter.
AI.conclusion: The compression cost of this purification-free, unknown-eigenbasis variant of Schumacher compression is exactly determined to its additive constant, tying quantum minimum description length to universal lossless coding overhead and to free entropy, with formally verified proofs.

title: Efficient Logic with Ultra-High-Rate Quantum Codes
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes offer a promising route to reducing the qubit overhead of fault tolerance, with recent ultra-high-rate constructions achieving encoding rates above one half. In this work, we develop fast and parallel logical computation methods for ultra-high-rate codes. We first utilize the group symmetries of the codes to partition the logical qubits into orbits, and then apply parallel surgery methods to implement group-invariant collections of logical Pauli-product measurements. These measurements are highly programmable, as we may arbitrarily couple logical orbits as long as each measurement is repeated across the whole orbit(s). To reduce the space and time overheads, we develop a technique called chain-map convolution, which uses the group structure to boost both the spatial and temporal distances of our protocol in a highly efficient manner. As case studies, we construct distance-preserving parallel measurement gadgets for the [[256, 68, 12]], [[576, 148, 18]] pair-partition codes, and a [[1152, 580, 12]] rate-$1/2$ code, with only around $2.5\times$ space overhead and 3-4 rounds of syndrome extraction each. The same methods also enable parallel injection of cultivated magic states into high-rate codes. Finally, we extend programmability through subgroup restrictions, revealing a tradeoff between logical control and the spacetime resources required for fault tolerance and highlighting the crucial role structured parallelism plays in reducing overhead. These results provide new methods for designing qLDPC logical operations with low spacetime overhead, opening a route toward more efficient fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

AI.tldr: This work develops fast, parallel logical computation methods for ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes by exploiting group symmetries to partition logical qubits into orbits, applying parallel surgery for group-invariant Pauli-product measurements, and introducing chain-map convolution to boost spatial and temporal distances efficiently.
AI.motivation: Ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes promise reduced qubit overhead for fault tolerance, but fast and parallel logical computation methods for such codes remain underdeveloped. Efficient logical operations with low spacetime overhead are needed to translate high encoding rates into practical fault-tolerant architectures.
AI.method: The authors exploit group symmetries of qLDPC codes to partition logical qubits into orbits, then apply parallel surgery methods to implement group-invariant collections of logical Pauli-product measurements. They introduce chain-map convolution, a technique leveraging group structure to boost both spatial and temporal distances efficiently. The measurements are highly programmable, permitting arbitrary coupling of logical orbits provided each measurement repeats across the whole orbit(s). Subgroup restrictions extend programmability.
AI.result: Distance-preserving parallel measurement gadgets are constructed for the [[256, 68, 12]], [[576, 148, 18]] pair-partition codes and a [[1152, 580, 12]] rate-1/2 code, achieving only ~2.5× space overhead and 3-4 rounds of syndrome extraction each. The methods also enable parallel injection of cultivated magic states into high-rate codes. Subgroup restrictions reveal a tradeoff between logical control and the spacetime resources required for fault tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Structured parallelism is crucial for reducing overhead in qLDPC logical operations. The proposed methods enable low-spacetime-overhead logical computation, opening a route toward more efficient fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

title: Discovering New Problems for Decoded Quantum Interferometry
summary: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) uses classical error correction to solve optimization problems, but it is hard to tell which problems could give it a quantum advantage. We develop soundness rules that screen candidate problems by their code parameters, decoding guarantees and classical baselines. For the standard objective of counting satisfied constraints, we prove that under worst-case Hamming decoding DQI's guarantee can exceed Prange completion by at most $(\sqrt{2}-1)/2$. Optimal polynomial intersection (OPI) attains this margin cap asymptotically, so no candidate in this setting can exceed OPI's margin. We also derive a performance law for real-valued objectives: the objective fixes both the solution quality and which errors the decoder must correct. An AI-agent search guided by these rules found two candidate applications. Alternant max-agreement on McEliece-type public keys tests what a secret decoder is worth to DQI against classical solvers that see only the public instance. Multiplicative polynomial intersection, a knapsack-type problem built from discrete logarithms, pairs a cosine objective with a public decoder for signed errors. For both we prove decoding guarantees and finite-length comparisons with Prange restarts, and on the larger instances we tested, DQI's expected quality exceeds what our classical solvers reach within fixed budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper develops "soundness rules" for Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) that screen optimization problems by code parameters, decoding guarantees, and classical baselines, proving a margin cap of (√2−1)/2 over Prange completion for the constraint-counting objective, and using an AI-agent search to identify two candidate applications where DQI's expected quality exceeds classical solvers within fixed budgets.
AI.motivation: DQI uses classical error correction to solve optimization problems, but it is difficult to determine which problems could yield a quantum advantage. The authors seek principled criteria to screen candidate problems and to understand where DQI can outperform classical baselines.
AI.method: The authors derive soundness rules based on code parameters, decoding guarantees, and classical baselines. For the standard objective of counting satisfied constraints, they analyze worst-case Hamming decoding and prove a bound. They derive a performance law for real-valued objectives. An AI-agent search guided by these rules is used to find candidate applications: alternant max-agreement on McEliece-type public keys and multiplicative polynomial intersection (a knapsack-type problem from discrete logarithms).
AI.result: For worst-case Hamming decoding, DQI's guarantee can exceed Prange completion by at most (√2−1)/2, and Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) attains this margin cap asymptotically, so no candidate in this setting can exceed OPI's margin. The performance law for real-valued objectives shows the objective fixes both solution quality and which errors the decoder must correct. The AI-agent search found two candidates, and for both the authors prove decoding guarantees and finite-length comparisons with Prange restarts; on the larger tested instances, DQI's expected quality exceeds what the classical solvers reach within fixed budgets.
AI.conclusion: The soundness rules provide a principled way to screen optimization problems for DQI's potential quantum advantage, revealing a hard margin cap over Prange completion under worst-case Hamming decoding, with OPI as the asymptotically optimal candidate in that regime. Two new candidate applications—alternant max-agreement on McEliece-type keys and multiplicative polynomial intersection—show promise, as DQI's expected quality surpasses the classical solvers within fixed budgets on the larger instances tested.

title: Finite-bath projected ensembles in dual-unitary circuits
summary: We study the emergent randomness in projected ensembles generated by dual-unitary circuits. Specifically, we consider evolution by solvable dual-unitary brickwork circuits followed by measurements on part of the system, which induce an ensemble of states on the unmeasured subsystem. Previous work has established that this projected ensemble of states forms a quantum state design in the limit where the bath size is large, but the rate of convergence at finite bath size has not been rigorously established. Under three inverse-polynomial assumptions, local permutation mixing, a bound on recurrent backward motion, and contraction at the measured boundary, we fill this gap and prove that a bath of polynomial size suffices to form approximate $k$-designs. In establishing our results, we develop a microscopic transport interpretation of emergent randomness in the projected ensemble, in which deviations from local permutation operators appear as defects, and make connections with the theory of quantum walks.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a polynomially-sized bath suffices for projected ensembles from dual-unitary brickwork circuits to form approximate k-designs, under three inverse-polynomial assumptions, and develops a microscopic transport interpretation of emergent randomness.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed projected ensembles form quantum state designs only in the limit of large bath size, leaving the finite-bath convergence rate unestablished. This paper aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors analyze solvable dual-unitary brickwork circuits followed by measurements on part of the system, proving approximate k-design formation under three inverse-polynomial assumptions: local permutation mixing, a bound on recurrent backward motion, and contraction at the measured boundary. They interpret deviations from local permutation operators as defects, connecting to quantum walk theory.
AI.result: Under the stated assumptions, a bath of polynomial size is proven sufficient to form approximate k-designs.
AI.conclusion: The paper closes the gap on finite-bath convergence for projected ensembles and offers a microscopic transport framework linking emergent randomness to quantum walks.

title: The Grothendieck Game and Self-Testing Continuous Groups
summary: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without requiring a description of the devices that produce them. In this work we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first robust self-test of the full continuous family of measurements generated by Majorana operators. We achieve this by showing that the Grothendieck game, a two-player nonlocal game in which the players receive directions on a sphere and return binary answers, is a self-test of Majorana observables. That is, any near-optimal performance certifies an entire continuously parameterized family of quantum measurements. We further extend this certification to products of Majorana observables, obtaining a robust self-test of the spin representation of the continuous pin group.

AI.tldr: This work presents the first robust self-test for the full continuous family of Majorana measurement observables, achieved via the Grothendieck game, and extends it to certify products of Majorana observables constituting the continuous pin group spin representation.
AI.motivation: Self-testing allows certification of quantum states and measurements purely from observed correlations, without device descriptions. Prior self-tests largely address discrete or restricted measurement sets; a robust self-test covering an entire continuously parameterized family of measurements was lacking.
AI.method: The authors show that the Grothendieck game — a two-player nonlocal game where players receive directions on a sphere and return binary answers — serves as a self-test of Majorana observables. They then extend this certification to products of Majorana observables.
AI.result: Near-optimal performance in the Grothendieck game certifies the entire continuously parameterized family of quantum measurements generated by Majorana operators, and the certification extends to products of Majorana observables, yielding a robust self-test of the continuous pin group's spin representation.
AI.conclusion: The Grothendieck game provides the first robust self-test of a full continuous family of Majorana measurements and their products, enabling device-independent certification of the continuous pin group spin representation.

title: Nonadditivity in fermionic quantum Shannon theory
summary: We study collective state preparation and channel encoding in fermionic systems under parity superselection and composition governed by the canonical anticommutation relations. For a two-mode Gaussian state $τ$, we obtain the exact entanglement of formation, $E_{\mathrm F}^{\mathrm{phys}}(τ^{\otimes m})=\lceil m/2\rceil\log2$ for every $m\geq1$. Two copies have the same formation value as one, violating additivity and strong superadditivity, while regularization halves the single-copy value. For an associated Gaussian channel, we determine the minimum output entropy and Holevo information at every blocklength and prove nonadditivity of both. Together, these results give exact answers to the fermionic counterparts of the four additivity questions associated with Shor and Hastings. One physical use carries no classical information, whereas two uses transmit one bit perfectly. The unassisted classical and zero-error classical capacities both equal one half bit per mode. A sharp finite-block bound gives a strong converse: the decoding success probability vanishes at every rate above capacity. These optimizations cover all physical pure-state decompositions and channel inputs, with Gaussian ensembles and classical codes attaining the optima. The formation and minimum output entropy formulas hold for every Rényi order $α\in(0,\infty]$. We also determine the unassisted quantum and zero-error quantum capacities, both equal to one half logical qubit per mode, and prove a strong converse: entanglement fidelity vanishes at every rate above capacity. For a noisy Gaussian family, we determine the one- and two-copy formation values and prove strict nonadditivity at full rank. For $τ$, Bell violation under local parity-preserving measurements first appears at three copies.

AI.tldr: Exact entanglement of formation of m copies of a two-mode Gaussian fermionic state equals ⌈m/2⌉log2, breaking additivity and strong superadditivity, with matching nonadditive channel capacities and strong converses.
AI.motivation: To answer the fermionic counterparts of the four additivity questions of Shor and Hastings, characterizing collective state preparation and channel encoding in fermionic systems subject to parity superselection and canonical anticommutation relations.
AI.method: Compute exact entanglement of formation of τ^{⊗m} for a two-mode Gaussian state τ under physical (parity-superselected) pure-state decompositions; determine minimum output entropy and Holevo information of an associated Gaussian channel at every blocklength; analyze capacities, finite-block bounds, generalized Rényi-order formulas, and Bell violation under local parity-preserving measurements.
AI.result: E_F^phys(τ^{⊗m}) = ⌈m/2⌉log2 for all m ≥ 1; two copies equal one copy, violating additivity and strong superadditivity, while regularization halves the single-copy value. Minimum output entropy and Holevo information are nonadditive. One channel use carries no classical information but two uses transmit one bit perfectly; unassisted classical and zero-error classical capacities equal 1/2 bit per mode with a strong converse. Formation and minimum output entropy formulas hold for every Rényi order α∈(0,∞]. Unassisted quantum and zero-error quantum capacities equal 1/2 logical qubit per mode with a strong converse on entanglement fidelity. For a noisy Gaussian family, one- and two-copy formation values are determined with strict nonadditivity at full rank; Bell violation for τ first appears at three copies.
AI.conclusion: Fermionic superselection and anticommutation structure produce strong nonadditivity and superadditivity violations across state preparation and channel coding, yielding exact fermionic answers to the Shor–Hastings additivity questions; Gaussian ensembles and classical codes attain all optima.

title: A classical oracle separation between QMA and QMA(2)
summary: We exhibit a classical oracle relative to which QMA \neq QMA(2). The separation is based on a separable Hamiltonian problem defined by signed edge constraints on a graph. The YES instances have zero-energy product states, while the NO instances, constructed using the antisymmetric subspace, have entangled zero-energy states but no low-energy product states. For the QMA lower bound, we use compressed-oracle techniques to track the information learned by a quantum computation making few queries to a YES instance. The key step is to map the resulting superpositions of partial oracle records to the NO family without significantly changing the verifier's behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a classical oracle under which QMA ≠ QMA(2), separating the two classes via a separable Hamiltonian problem on signed-edge graphs.
AI.motivation: QMA versus QMA(2) is a fundamental open question in quantum complexity theory, where QMA(2) allows two unentangled but possibly entangled-with-each-other witnesses. A classical oracle separation provides evidence about the classes' distinctness and probes the power of separable witnesses.
AI.method: The authors define a separable Hamiltonian problem using signed edge constraints on a graph. YES instances admit zero-energy product (separable) states; NO instances, built from the antisymmetric subspace, have entangled zero-energy states but no low-energy product states. For the QMA lower bound, they employ compressed-oracle techniques to track information learned by a quantum computation making few queries to a YES instance, and map superpositions of partial oracle records to the NO family while preserving the verifier's behavior.
AI.result: A classical oracle exists relative to which QMA ≠ QMA(2), establishing a separation of the two classes in the oracle model.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that separable versus entangled witnesses can be distinguished relative to a classical oracle, yielding a QMA ≠ QMA(2) separation and highlighting the role of the antisymmetric subspace and compressed-oracle methods.

title: Hypercontractivity and entropy decay for infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers
summary: We derive rates of exponential relative-entropy decay for a broad class of infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers. A key technical ingredient is a perturbative stability theory for hypercontractive estimates and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. For suitably chosen dissipative couplings, we obtain exponential entropy decay for full multimode Bose-Hubbard samplers with arbitrary hopping and repulsive density interactions. For harmonically confined quantum Coulomb gases and molecular systems, we prove exponential entropy decay for every fixed finite-rank low-energy truncation of the interaction. Finally, we exhibit a periodic charging model with a positive spectral gap but no finite-time $L^2$-to-$L^p$ bound for any $p>2$.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes exponential relative-entropy decay rates for a broad class of infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers, using a perturbative stability theory for hypercontractive estimates and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities.
AI.motivation: Quantum Gibbs samplers in infinite dimensions are central to preparing thermal states, but proving exponential entropy decay is difficult because hypercontractivity and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities are hard to establish and do not generally survive perturbation. The paper aims to develop tools that make such decay guarantees accessible for physically relevant infinite-dimensional models.
AI.method: Results are derived via a perturbative stability theory for hypercontractive estimates and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. By choosing suitable dissipative couplings, the authors analyze full multimode Bose-Hubbard samplers with arbitrary hopping and repulsive density interactions, harmonically confined quantum Coulomb gases, and molecular systems, proving exponential entropy decay for fixed finite-rank low-energy truncations of the interaction.
AI.result: For suitably chosen dissipative couplings, exponential entropy decay is obtained for full multimode Bose-Hubbard samplers. For harmonically confined quantum Coulomb gases and molecular systems, exponential entropy decay holds for every fixed finite-rank low-energy truncation of the interaction. A periodic charging model is exhibited with a positive spectral gap but no finite-time L2-to-Lp bound for any p>2.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that exponential relative-entropy decay is achievable for a broad class of infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers, extending hypercontractivity and logarithmic Sobolev techniques via perturbative stability. It also shows that a positive spectral gap alone is insufficient to guarantee finite-time hypercontractive bounds, highlighting the need for stronger conditions than spectral gap in infinite dimensions.

title: Fermions and the Tsirelson Problem in Real Quantum Theory
summary:
In a previous work, we showed that real quantum theory (RQT) cannot be experimentally distinguished from ordinary quantum theory (QT). In this paper, we investigate whether this indistinguishability survives two natural extensions of the setting: allowing separated measurements to be represented by commuting rather than tensor-product observables, and imposing superselection rules, as in fermionic information theory. We show that it does in both cases.
  Our first result is a positive answer to the Tsirelson problem in RQT: commuting and tensor-product measurements generate the same finite-dimensional correlations. This is surprisingly not a trivial consequence of the standard complex proof, as it does not carry over to the reals. The proof obstruction becomes particularly relevant in the presence of superselection rules, which is why we first establish the equivalence in RQT before extending the framework to superselected RQT.
  Our second result is a local, real quantum formulation of superselected theories. We extend the RQT framework to accommodate a representation of superselection over the reals and show, in particular, that it admits a fermionic version whose predictions are experimentally indistinguishable from those of fermionic information theory. More generally, the construction extends to all superselected QTs.

AI.tldr: Real quantum theory (RQT) is experimentally indistinguishable from standard quantum theory (QT); this paper shows the indistinguishability persists when measurements are commuting (not tensor-product) observables and when superselection rules (e.g., fermionic) are imposed.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed RQT cannot be experimentally distinguished from QT, but it was unclear whether this indistinguishability survives natural extensions: allowing separated measurements represented by commuting rather than tensor-product observables, and imposing superselection rules as in fermionic information theory. The standard complex proof of the relevant equivalence does not carry over to the reals, so a direct extension is nontrivial.
AI.method: First, the authors prove a positive answer to the Tsirelson problem in RQT, establishing that commuting and tensor-product measurements generate the same finite-dimensional correlations; the standard complex proof's obstruction is identified and handled over the reals. Second, they develop a local, real quantum formulation of superselected theories by extending the RQT framework to represent superselection over the reals. They then apply the earlier equivalence to this superselected RQT, constructing in particular a fermionic version.
AI.result: The indistinguishability of RQT from QT survives both extensions. Commuting and tensor-product measurements generate identical finite-dimensional correlations in RQT (Tsirelson problem solved positively). The real formulation of superselected theories admits a fermionic version whose predictions are experimentally indistinguishable from fermionic information theory, and the construction extends to all superselected QTs.
AI.conclusion: Real quantum theory remains experimentally indistinguishable from ordinary quantum theory even under commuting measurements and superselection rules. The results establish the Tsirelson equivalence in RQT and provide a local real quantum formulation applicable to all superselected theories, including a fermionic version matching fermionic information theory.

title: Complexity separations for optimal matchgate-Clifford synthesis
summary: Clifford and matchgate circuits are canonical families of classically simulable quantum circuits. Their intersection, the matchgate-Clifford group, plays an important role in randomized fermionic protocols and in matchgate synthesis. Its adjoint action is isomorphic to the group of unit-determinant signed permutations of $2n$ Majorana modes, and we study optimal exact synthesis in this group. That is, given a target unitary and a gate set, output an $n$-qubit circuit implementing the target using the fewest operations. We show that the complexity of this problem strongly depends on the gate set. In particular, we study gate sets consisting of Majorana braids with different connectivity graphs. For path and complete graphs, we prove that the problem is classically solvable in $\mathcal{O}\left(n^2\right)$ time, and we provide explicit gate-optimal compilers. In addition, we prove that when the connectivity graph is a tree, the decision version of the optimal synthesis problem becomes NP-complete. Finally, we benchmark our optimal compiler on chains of up to $n=80$ qubits against those of \texttt{Qiskit} and \texttt{Tket}, obtaining circuits with constant factor improvements $\times2.57$ and $\times2.28$ in the total number of gates, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper studies optimal exact synthesis for the matchgate-Clifford group, whose adjoint action is isomorphic to unit-determinant signed permutations of 2n Majorana modes. It shows the complexity depends on the gate set: for Majorana-braid gate sets with path or complete connectivity graphs, optimal synthesis is solvable in O(n^2) time with explicit gate-optimal compilers, while for tree graphs the decision version becomes NP-complete. The compiler is benchmarked on chains up to n=80 qubits, achieving constant-factor gate-count improvements over Qiskit and Tket.
AI.motivation: Clifford and matchgate circuits are canonical classically simulable circuit families, and their intersection (the matchgate-Clifford group) is important for randomized fermionic protocols and matchgate synthesis. However, optimal exact synthesis within this group had not been characterized: it was unclear how the complexity of finding minimal-gate implementations depends on the available gate set.
AI.method: The authors exploit the isomorphism between the adjoint action of the matchgate-Clifford group and the group of unit-determinant signed permutations of 2n Majorana modes, reducing synthesis to a problem in this permutation group. They analyze gate sets consisting of Majorana braids with different connectivity graphs (path, complete, and general tree), deriving complexity results and constructing explicit gate-optimal compilers. They then benchmark the optimal compiler on chains up to n=80 qubits against Qiskit and Tket.
AI.result: For path and complete connectivity graphs, the optimal exact synthesis problem is classically solvable in O(n^2) time, with explicit gate-optimal compilers provided. For tree connectivity graphs, the decision version of optimal synthesis is proven NP-complete. On chains up to n=80 qubits, the compiler produces circuits with constant-factor improvements of ×2.57 and ×2.28 in total gate count compared to Qiskit and Tket, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The complexity of optimal exact synthesis in the matchgate-Clifford group is strongly gate-set dependent: it is efficiently solvable for path and complete Majorana-braid connectivity but NP-complete for trees. The proposed O(n^2) compilers are practical, yielding consistent gate-count reductions over standard tools.

title: Fast convergence of propagation algorithms for open quantum systems
summary: We establish general conditions for the rapid convergence of propagation algorithms for computing expectation values of local observables in quantum many-body systems, covering both spin and fermionic systems. Our results apply to evolutions that are sufficiently contractive, providing a general mechanism by which contractivity controls the growth generated by local interactions and enables efficient classical simulation. As a first application, we consider noisy time evolution generated by local Hamiltonians on arbitrary interaction graphs. We show that the dynamics can be efficiently simulated when the noise strength $λ$ is sufficiently large compared to the degree of the interaction graph. More generally, for systems with an interaction strength $u$, our bounds determine a time horizon $t_{\text{max}}$ as a function of the interaction strength $u$, the noise strength $λ$, and the interaction structure below which the algorithm is efficient. In the noiseless limit, $λ=0$, our analysis extends the efficiently simulable time scale from $\log(1/u)$ proved in Facelli, Fawzi, and Fawzi (2026) to $t_{\text{max}} \sim 1/u$ matching the recent improvement by Zhao, Marvian and Tong (2026). As a second application, we apply the same framework to the computation of local observables in Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians. We consider a pseudo-Lindbladian whose steady state is the Gibbs state and show that, at sufficiently high temperature, its propagation algorithm converges rapidly. In particular, for weakly-interacting systems with interaction strength $u$, our result applies up to inverse temperatures $β\sim\log(1/u)$.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes general conditions for rapid convergence of propagation algorithms computing local observables in quantum many-body systems (spin and fermionic), showing contractivity yields efficient classical simulation. Applications include noisy time evolution (efficient when noise λ is large vs. graph degree) and Gibbs state observables (efficient at high temperature, up to β ~ log(1/u) for weak interactions).
AI.motivation: Efficient classical simulation of quantum many-body dynamics and Gibbs state observables is a central challenge. A general mechanism linking contractivity of the evolution to controlled growth from local interactions is needed to unify and extend existing efficient-simulability time scales.
AI.method: The authors derive general convergence conditions for propagation algorithms computing expectation values of local observables, applying to sufficiently contractive evolutions in spin and fermionic systems. They analyze (i) noisy dynamics from local Hamiltonians on arbitrary interaction graphs, and (ii) a pseudo-Lindbladian whose steady state is the Gibbs state.
AI.result: For noisy evolution, dynamics are efficiently simulable when λ is sufficiently large relative to the interaction graph degree; bounds give a time horizon t_max(u, λ, interaction structure). In the noiseless limit λ=0, the simulable time scale improves from log(1/u) to t_max ~ 1/u, matching Zhao, Marvian and Tong (2026). For Gibbs states, the propagation algorithm converges rapidly at high temperature, applying up to β ~ log(1/u) for weakly-interacting systems.
AI.conclusion: Contractivity provides a general mechanism controlling interaction-generated growth, enabling efficient classical simulation of both noisy time evolution and Gibbs state observables, unifying and extending prior simulability results.

title: Engineering logical gates with irrep surface codes
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically relies on a fixed set of logical primitives, while realizing other desired operations can require substantial resources. We introduce irrep surface codes (ISCs), two-dimensional topological quantum error-correcting codes engineered to transversally implement a prescribed set of logical gates. The engineered gates only need to satisfy two conditions: (i) they generate a finite group, which, up to global phases, is forced by the Eastin-Knill theorem, and (ii) they are irreducible, meaning that any operator commuting with the set of gates must be proportional to the identity. This accommodates arbitrary finite groups of diagonal gates and arbitrary reversible classical gates, since each can be embedded into a larger irreducible finite group of gates. It also enables logical gates outside every finite level of the Clifford hierarchy. To incorporate these operations into surface-code computations, we further develop lattice-surgery protocols to transfer the encoded information between surface codes and ISCs obeying either of two sufficient conditions. Together, these results establish a systematic method for tailoring topological codes to desired logical operations and integrating them into conventional computations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces irrep surface codes (ISCs), 2D topological quantum error-correcting codes that transversally implement a prescribed finite, irreducible group of logical gates, enabling gates beyond any finite Clifford-hierarchy level, and provides lattice-surgery protocols to interface them with standard surface codes.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation conventionally relies on a fixed set of logical primitives, and realizing other desired logical operations demands substantial resources. A systematic way to design topological codes tailored to a desired set of logical gates is lacking.
AI.method: The authors engineer ISCs to transversally implement prescribed logical gates satisfying two conditions: (i) the gates generate a finite group (forced up to global phases by the Eastin-Knill theorem), and (ii) they are irreducible, i.e., any operator commuting with the gate set is proportional to the identity. This accommodates arbitrary finite groups of diagonal gates and arbitrary reversible classical gates via embedding into a larger irreducible finite group, and also enables logical gates outside every finite level of the Clifford hierarchy. They further develop lattice-surgery protocols to transfer encoded information between surface codes and ISCs satisfying either of two sufficient conditions.
AI.result: ISCs provide a systematic framework for tailoring 2D topological codes to desired logical operations. Lattice-surgery protocols enable transfer of encoded information between standard surface codes and ISCs under two sufficient conditions, allowing integration of these engineered transversal gates into conventional surface-code computations.
AI.conclusion: Together, these results establish a systematic method for tailoring topological codes to desired logical operations and integrating them into conventional computations.

title: Informed Trading model with quantum walks
summary: The seminal Kyle model offers a framework to understand the price impact of an informed trader in a market model for a single asset. We study variants in which the asset's future value is modeled by a classical random walk and by a continuous-time quantum walk, respectively. With these assumptions, we analytically approximate and numerically identify the market equilibrium between risk-neutral market maker and informed trader. In the classical equilibrium, the informed trader possesses a linear strategy, whereas the market maker's pricing rule resembles a logistic curve. The informed trader's profit is also identified to grow sub-linearly with time t. In the quantum equilibrium, the informed trader's strategy forms multiple clusters and the pricing rule exhibits multiple jumps correspondingly. Despite the increasing non-linearity of the equilibrium, the informed trader's profit grows linearly with time t.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the seminal Kyle model to settings where the asset's future value follows a classical random walk versus a continuous-time quantum walk, deriving and comparing the resulting market equilibria between a risk-neutral market maker and an informed trader.
AI.motivation: The original Kyle model provides a framework for understanding the price impact of an informed trader for a single asset. This work is motivated by exploring how alternative stochastic specifications of the asset's future value—specifically a classical random walk and a continuous-time quantum walk—alter market equilibrium behavior.
AI.method: The authors formulate variants of the Kyle model in which the asset's future value is modeled by (i) a classical random walk and (ii) a continuous-time quantum walk. They analytically approximate and numerically identify the market equilibrium between a risk-neutral market maker and an informed trader in each case.
AI.result: In the classical equilibrium, the informed trader adopts a linear strategy, while the market maker's pricing rule resembles a logistic curve; the informed trader's profit grows sub-linearly with time t. In the quantum equilibrium, the informed trader's strategy forms multiple clusters and the pricing rule exhibits multiple corresponding jumps; despite increased non-linearity of the equilibrium, the informed trader's profit grows linearly with time t.
AI.conclusion: Specifying the asset's future value via a quantum walk rather than a classical random walk qualitatively changes equilibrium strategies and pricing rules, yet can yield a more favorable, linear profit growth for the informed trader over time.

title: Pretty good shadow tomography
summary:
We give a shadow tomography algorithm that uses $O(\log(m) \log(m/δ) / \varepsilon^2)$ copies of the input state. Specifically, given a quantum state $ρ$ and observables $O_1,\ldots,O_m$, the algorithm outputs estimates of $\mathrm{tr}(O_iρ)$ for all $i\in[m]$ that are all accurate to within $\pm\varepsilon$, except with probability at most $δ$. The key idea is to work in the average-case setting: for a random state drawn from a known prior, a pretty good measurement on $O(\log(m)/\varepsilon^2)$ copies gives a constant-error guarantee on all but a small fraction of the prior. Boosting this guarantee gives an average-case shadow tomography algorithm, and the minimax principle then (non-constructively) implies the existence of a measurement with the same worst-case guarantee.
  We also identify an obstruction to further improvement with this approach. While pretty good measurements amplify success over the randomness of the prior, they do not amplify success over the randomness of measurement. This issue appears to be inherent, and gives rise to the remaining $\log(m)$ factor separating the complexity of the quantum problem from its classical counterpart.

AI.tldr: A shadow tomography algorithm estimates all m observable expectation values to within ε using O(log(m)log(m/δ)/ε²) copies of the state. The approach works in the average case via pretty good measurements, then uses the minimax principle for a non-constructive worst-case guarantee.
AI.motivation: Shadow tomography aims to predict many observable expectation values tr(O_i ρ) from few copies of ρ. Prior work left a log(m) gap between the quantum complexity and the classical counterpart for estimating such quantities; the paper targets this and identifies why the gap persists.
AI.method: The algorithm operates in an average-case setting with a known prior over states. On O(log(m)/ε²) copies, a pretty good measurement yields a constant-error guarantee for all but a small fraction of the prior. Boosting this success gives an average-case algorithm, and the minimax principle non-constructively implies a measurement achieving the same worst-case guarantee.
AI.result: The algorithm uses O(log(m) log(m/δ)/ε²) copies and outputs estimates of tr(O_i ρ) for all i accurate within ±ε, with failure probability at most δ. It also identifies an obstruction: pretty good measurements amplify success over prior randomness but not over measurement randomness.
AI.conclusion: The paper achieves a shadow tomography sample complexity of O(log(m)log(m/δ)/ε²). The remaining log(m) factor separating the quantum from the classical problem is inherent to this approach, since pretty good measurements fail to amplify success over measurement randomness.

title: Quantum-optimized phase closure for robust interferometric imaging
summary: Closure phase enables imaging with ground-based interferometric arrays by canceling telescope-dependent phase errors due to atmospheric fluctuations. It can be obtained by measuring fringe phases on individual baselines forming a triangle and summing them. We show that closure phases can be measured more accurately with fewer photons by performing joint measurements on multiple photons.
