We first establish that at least three photons from the same atmospheric temporal phase-stability window are required for closure-phase information to survive the unknown telescope-dependent phase noise, and show that joint three-photon measurements already provide an advantage over single-photon measurements in the minimal three-telescope setting. We then turn to large arrays and consider estimating all bispectra---complex quantities whose phases are the closure phases---under a global mean-square error criterion. Although an $m$-telescope array contains $Θ(m^2)$ independent triangle bispectra, we show that physical constraints on the visibilities make the total information content grow only nearly linearly with $m$ at fixed accuracy. Exploiting this structure, we construct an efficient protocol using at most three-photon joint measurements with photon cost $\tilde{O}(m)$, whereas any sequential single-photon protocol requires $Ω(m^2)$ photons. When the number of detected photons per temporal stability window scales linearly with the array size, this allows the required exposure time to remain independent of $m$ up to logarithmic factors. We further analyze the complementary high-precision regime using multiparameter quantum metrology and find a similar advantage for collective measurements. Overall, our results show that quantum information processing techniques can substantially improve the sensitivity and robustness of optical interferometry.

AI.tldr: Closure phases, used in ground-based optical interferometry to cancel atmospheric phase noise, can be measured more accurately and with fewer photons using joint multi-photon measurements rather than sequential single-photon detection. Three-photon joint measurements establish a fundamental quantum advantage, and for large arrays an efficient ~O(m)-photon protocol estimates all bispectra, versus Ω(m^2) photons for any single-photon approach.
AI.motivation: Ground-based interferometric imaging relies on closure phase to cancel telescope-dependent atmospheric phase errors, but measuring fringe phases on each baseline demands substantial photon counts. Improving the photon efficiency and accuracy of closure-phase (and bispectrum) estimation directly benefits the sensitivity and feasibility of optical interferometry, motivating a quantum-enhanced measurement strategy.
AI.method: The authors analyze closure-phase estimation under unknown telescope-dependent phase noise. They first prove that at least three photons from the same atmospheric temporal phase-stability window are required for closure-phase information to survive the noise, and show that joint three-photon measurements outperform single-photon measurements in the minimal three-telescope case. For large arrays, they estimate all bispectra (complex quantities whose phases are closure phases) under a global mean-square error criterion, exploiting physical constraints on the visibilities that limit the growth of total information content. They construct an efficient protocol using at most three-photon joint measurements, and complement this with a multiparameter quantum metrology analysis of the high-precision regime for collective measurements.
AI.result: Three-photon joint measurements give an advantage over single-photon measurements in the minimal three-telescope setting. Although an m-telescope array contains Θ(m^2) independent triangle bispectra, physical constraints on the visibilities make the total information content grow only nearly linearly with m at fixed accuracy. An efficient protocol using at most three-photon joint measurements achieves photon cost Õ(m), whereas any sequential single-photon protocol requires Ω(m^2) photons. When the number of detected photons per temporal stability window scales linearly with array size, the required exposure time remains independent of m up to logarithmic factors, and a similar collective-measurement advantage appears in the high-precision regime.
AI.conclusion: Quantum information processing techniques can substantially improve the sensitivity and robustness of optical interferometry, enabling accurate closure-phase and bispectrum estimation with far fewer photons, and yielding exposure times that are essentially independent of array size (up to logarithmic factors) under favorable photon-scaling conditions.

title: Computational entanglement distillation beyond pure states: efficient protocols and fundamental limitations
summary: The information-theoretic approach to entanglement typically relies on arbitrarily many input copies and unboundedly complex operations; however, the available resources are constrained in reality. This motivates the study of entanglement theory with limited resources. One of its central questions is which quantities characterize entanglement manipulations, and so far, only the idealized case of pure states has been well explored. In this work, we address entanglement distillation from mixed states and identify the Rényi coherent information as the quantity determining the optimal rate in the worst case under two distinct resource constraints. We first characterize the sample-efficient regime, in which unbounded computational power is allowed. Our universal protocol achieves this rate without knowledge of the input state under certain polynomial rank constraints. This rate is optimal among universal protocols: we construct states whose distillable entanglement is nearly extensive, yet from which no universal sample-efficient protocol attains a rate above their Rényi coherent information. We then push this characterization to the computationally efficient frontier: the same bound holds for any efficient protocol even when the input state is known, and another universal protocol achieves this rate efficiently under additional polynomial constraints on the marginal ranks. Overall, our results give the Rényi coherent information a novel operational meaning in two computational settings: universal distillation with limited copies and efficient distillation even with knowledge of the input state.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entanglement distillation from mixed states under limited resources and identifies the Rényi coherent information as the quantity determining the optimal distillation rate in two regimes: sample-efficient (unbounded computation) and computationally efficient settings.
AI.motivation: Standard information-theoretic entanglement theory assumes arbitrarily many input copies and unboundedly complex operations, which is unrealistic given real-world resource constraints. Prior work on resource-limited entanglement theory focused almost exclusively on idealized pure states, leaving mixed-state entanglement manipulation poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze entanglement distillation from mixed states under two distinct resource constraints. They first characterize a sample-efficient regime allowing unbounded computational power, designing a universal protocol that achieves the optimal rate without knowledge of the input state under polynomial rank constraints. They then extend the analysis to the computationally efficient frontier, proving bounds for efficient protocols even when the input state is known, and giving a universal efficient protocol under additional polynomial marginal-rank constraints.
AI.result: The Rényi coherent information is shown to determine the optimal worst-case distillation rate. A universal sample-efficient protocol attains this rate under polynomial rank constraints; this rate is optimal among universal protocols, as states with nearly extensive distillable entanglement still admit no universal sample-efficient protocol exceeding their Rényi coherent information. The same bound holds for any efficient protocol even with known input states, and another universal protocol achieves this rate efficiently under extra polynomial marginal-rank constraints.
AI.conclusion: The Rényi coherent information acquires a novel operational meaning in two computational settings: universal distillation with limited copies and efficient distillation even with knowledge of the input state. This advances resource-limited entanglement theory beyond pure states to mixed-state manipulation.

title: Characterizing Quantum Advantage for Generalizations of the Boolean Hidden Matching Problem
summary:
We study the one-way communication complexity of the $f$-Boolean Hidden Partition problem. Here, Alice is given an $n$-bit string and Bob is given $Ω(n)$ disjoint blocks of its indices together with a string of labels. Under the promise that the evaluations of $f$ on these blocks either agree with all of the labels or disagree with all of them, Bob must determine which is the case using a single message from Alice. This problem generalizes the Boolean Hidden Matching and Hidden Hypermatching problems, which capture the special case where $f$ is the parity function.
  We establish classical and quantum communication bounds for $f$-Boolean Hidden Partition in terms of the sign degree $d$ of $f$, proving a conjecture of Doriguello and Montanaro (TQC 2020). Their prior work gave logarithmic communication upper bounds for classical protocols when $d \le 1$ and quantum protocols when $d \le 2$, as well as polynomial lower bounds for certain structured functions with larger sign degree. We show that for every $f$ of sign degree $d \ge 2$, the randomized classical communication complexity of this problem is $Θ(n^{1-1/d})$ while its quantum communication complexity lies between $Ω(n^{1-2/d})$ and $\bO{n^{1-1/\lceil d/2 \rceil} \log n}$. This completely characterizes the functions $f$ admitting polynomial quantum advantage as those for which $d \ge 2$, with a new infinite family of exponential separations given by the case $d = 2$.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the one-way communication complexity of the f-Boolean Hidden Partition problem in terms of the sign degree d of f, proving a conjecture of Doriguello and Montanaro and showing that polynomial quantum advantage occurs exactly when d ≥ 2.
AI.motivation: The problem generalizes Boolean Hidden Matching and Hidden Hypermatching (the parity case), and prior work by Doriguello and Montanaro (TQC 2020) gave partial bounds and conjectured a sign-degree-based characterization. A complete characterization of when quantum protocols outperform classical ones was missing.
AI.method: The authors analyze the one-way communication complexity of f-Boolean Hidden Partition using the sign degree d of the Boolean function f, establishing matching upper and lower bounds for randomized classical protocols and quantum protocols.
AI.result: For every f of sign degree d ≥ 2, the randomized classical communication complexity is Θ(n^{1−1/d}), while the quantum communication complexity is between Ω(n^{1−2/d}) and O(n^{1−1/⌈d/2⌉} log n).
AI.conclusion: The results confirm the conjecture and fully characterize functions f admitting polynomial quantum advantage as exactly those with sign degree d ≥ 2, yielding a new infinite family of exponential separations in the case d = 2.

title: Local universality of non-local quantum resources in rotationally invariant scattering
summary: Elastic scattering can generate entanglement and non-local magic between the spins of the two outgoing particles. The amount of entanglement and magic produced is encoded in the S-matrix; a unitary quantum gate that acts on the joint Hilbert space of the two spin-J particles. Previous work derived the entanglement power in terms of the scattering phase shifts for rotationally invariant S-matrices with J=1/2,1,3/2. In this paper, a closed form solution is derived for all J. We further prove that a broad class of non-local quantum resources depend to leading order only on the squared projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the nearest non-entangling gate. This holds for the entanglement power and non-local magic power, and the choice of resource simply changes the overall normalization. This universality establishes a common geometric origin for the leading resource-generating capacity of scattering, independent of the details of the interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a closed-form expression for the entanglement power of rotationally invariant S-matrices for arbitrary spin J, and proves that a broad class of non-local quantum resources (including entanglement and non-local magic) depends to leading order only on the squared projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the nearest non-entangling gate, up to overall normalization.
AI.motivation: Elastic scattering can generate entanglement and non-local magic between the spins of two outgoing spin-J particles, with the amount encoded in the S-matrix. Prior work only handled rotational-invariant S-matrices for J=1/2, 1, 3/2, leaving a general understanding for all J and a unifying principle across different resource measures unexplored.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form solution for the entanglement power in terms of scattering phase shifts valid for all J. They further analyze a broad class of non-local quantum resources and show that, to leading order, these depend only on the squared projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the nearest non-entangling gate.
AI.result: A closed-form expression for the entanglement power is obtained for arbitrary spin J. The entanglement power and non-local magic power are both found to depend to leading order solely on the squared projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the nearest non-entangling gate, with the specific resource choice affecting only the overall normalization.
AI.conclusion: The leading resource-generating capacity of scattering exhibits a universal geometric origin independent of interaction details, governed by the projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the nearest non-entangling gate, and this universality holds across a broad class of non-local quantum resources for all spin J.

title: Error Mitigation From a Single Unmodified Error-Corrected Circuit
summary: Recent work has shown that syndrome information obtained during error-corrected quantum computation can be utilized for logical error mitigation (LEM), yielding exponential reductions in runtime overhead compared to external'' LEM methods, which do not make use of syndrome data. However, these syndrome-aware LEM methods (SALEM) generally require adaptive circuit operations based on real-time processing of syndromes. Here, we introduce syndrome-based offline logical error mitigation (SOLEM), a framework that utilizes syndrome data entirely in post-processing, without any modification to the given error-corrected circuit. In this sense, SOLEM is built into'' error-corrected circuits, and is in fact simpler to implement than external LEM protocols. The basic idea of SOLEM is to use naturally occurring syndrome-conditioned logical error channels in place of deliberate circuit modifications. We develop unbiased and heuristic estimators within this framework, including offline logical versions of probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) and zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), as well as a global-regression estimator. SOLEM's fully offline nature leads to three significant advantages. First, SOLEM can post-process syndromes with a more powerful decoder than the one used in real time. Second, multiple estimators can be constructed from the same measured data and optimized using empirical statistical errors and related performance metrics. Third, logical error characterization is needed only in post-processing, allowing characterization data to be collected during circuit execution and reducing sensitivity to hardware drift. Remarkably, SOLEM estimators can achieve these advantages while attaining a runtime overhead which is exponentially lower than that of external LEM and is comparable to that of corresponding SALEM estimators.

AI.tldr: SOLEM is a framework that performs syndrome-based logical error mitigation entirely in post-processing, replacing deliberate circuit modifications with naturally occurring syndrome-conditioned logical error channels, achieving exponentially lower runtime overhead than external LEM and comparable to SALEM.
AI.motivation: External logical error mitigation (LEM) methods ignore syndrome data and incur exponential runtime overhead. Syndrome-aware LEM (SALEM) methods exploit syndrome information for exponential overhead reduction but require adaptive circuit operations based on real-time syndrome processing, complicating implementation.
AI.method: SOLEM uses syndrome data entirely in post-processing without modifying the error-corrected circuit, exploiting naturally occurring syndrome-conditioned logical error channels instead of deliberate circuit modifications. It develops unbiased and heuristic estimators, including offline logical probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), offline logical zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), and a global-regression estimator.
AI.result: SOLEM achieves three advantages: (1) syndromes can be post-processed with a more powerful decoder than the real-time one; (2) multiple estimators can be constructed from the same measured data and optimized via empirical statistical errors and performance metrics; (3) logical error characterization is needed only in post-processing, allowing data collection during execution and reducing sensitivity to hardware drift. Its runtime overhead is exponentially lower than external LEM and comparable to SALEM.
AI.conclusion: SOLEM offers a simpler-to-implement, built-into-the-circuit alternative to external LEM that retains the exponential overhead benefits of syndrome-aware mitigation while being fully offline, with advantages in decoding power, estimator flexibility, and robustness to hardware drift.

title: Testing bosonic and fermionic Gaussian states with a constant number of copies
summary: Bosonic and fermionic Gaussian quantum states are families of quantum states that play a central role in quantum physics and quantum information processing. We study the problem of testing whether a given state is either Gaussian, or has bounded overlap with any Gaussian state. Previous analyses of this testing problem led to tests that require a number of copies of the state that scales with the number of modes (the system size). In this work we show that a constant number of copies of the state suffices. We derive these results based on the symmetries of identical copies of Gaussian states, and by bounding the distance to the set of Gaussian states through a gradient flow and a spectral bound studied previously for the Kac random walk on a sphere.

AI.tldr: Testing whether a quantum state is Gaussian (or far from any Gaussian state) requires only a constant number of copies, independent of system size.
AI.motivation: Bosonic and fermionic Gaussian quantum states are central to quantum physics and quantum information processing. The prior problem of testing Gaussianity required a number of state copies scaling with the number of modes (system size), which is impractical.
AI.method: The authors exploit the symmetries of identical copies of Gaussian states and bound the distance to the set of Gaussian states using a gradient flow together with a spectral bound previously studied for the Kac random walk on a sphere.
AI.result: A constant number of copies of the state suffices to test whether it is Gaussian or has bounded overlap with any Gaussian state, improving over the prior mode-dependent scaling.
AI.conclusion: Gaussianity testing is possible with constant sample complexity, independent of the number of modes, enabled by symmetry arguments and gradient-flow/spectral techniques.

title: From Quantum Tunneling to Classical Optimization through Instantons
summary: We use an instanton-based analysis to show that Path Integral Stochastic Gradient Descent (PISGD), a classical optimization algorithm instantiated from path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC), can inherit the quantum tunneling mechanism. Quantum tunneling is the phenomenon in which a quantum particle passes through a potential barrier that a classical trajectory cannot cross in the same way. This mechanism can contribute to the performance of quantum optimization algorithms, since a common bottleneck in optimization is that the solution becomes trapped in a local minimum, separated from better solutions by a potential barrier. Classical noise-driven optimizers, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD), have escape times that scale exponentially with the potential barrier height. For quantum tunneling, the escape time is instead exponential in the bounce action, which equals twice the Agmon distance between the two basins. When the barrier is tall but thin, quantum tunneling can allow escaping local minima faster than such classical methods. Remarkably, this scaling is not exclusive to algorithms with genuine quantum dynamics. For PISGD applied to classical nonconvex global optimization, we adapt Kramers' escape-rate theory to path space and obtain the same exponential scaling as quantum tunneling, in terms of the bounce action rather than the barrier height. We confirm this scaling numerically by implementing PISGD for both separable and nonseparable potentials. That said, PISGD retains only incoherent tunneling, since coherence among multiple tunneling paths is absent. Our analysis therefore does not rule out a potential quantum advantage for quantum-tunneling-based algorithms over classical ones in general.

AI.tldr: Using instanton-based analysis, the authors show that Path Integral Stochastic Gradient Descent (PISGD) inherits an incoherent quantum-tunneling escape mechanism, with escape times scaling exponentially in the bounce action (twice the Agmon distance) rather than barrier height, confirmed numerically on separable and nonseparable potentials.
AI.motivation: A central bottleneck in nonconvex optimization is trapping in local minima separated by potential barriers from better solutions. Classical noise-driven optimizers like SGD have escape times scaling exponentially with barrier height. Quantum tunneling can escape faster (exponentially in the bounce action) when barriers are tall but thin, motivating the question of whether quantum-derived optimization algorithms convey this advantage.
AI.method: The paper applies an instanton-based analysis to PISGD, a classical optimization algorithm instantiated from path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC). Kramers' escape-rate theory is adapted to path space to derive escape-time scaling. Numerical experiments implement PISGD on both separable and nonseparable potentials to confirm the predicted scaling.
AI.result: PISGD achieves the same exponential escape-time scaling as quantum tunneling, expressed in terms of the bounce action (equal to twice the Agmon distance between basins) rather than barrier height. This scaling is confirmed numerically for both separable and nonseparable potentials.
AI.conclusion: PISGD retains only incoherent tunneling, as coherence among multiple tunneling paths is absent. Consequently, the analysis does not rule out a potential quantum advantage for genuine quantum-tunneling-based algorithms over classical ones in general.

title: Bell nonlocality does not imply violation of nonlocal games
summary: Nonlocal games offer a conceptually clear way to reason about Bell nonlocality. However, we show that as originally defined, and most commonly used, i.e. with a deterministic predicate, they cannot be complete witnesses of nonlocality. Concretely, we prove the existence of nonlocal behaviours which do not violate any such nonlocal game. Furthermore, we also show that quantum mechanics can produce these game-classical nonlocal behaviours. We prove that this phenomenon exists in every bipartite scenario $(X,Y,A,B)$ with $X,Y\geq2$ and $A,B\geq4$.

AI.tldr: Nonlocal games with deterministic predicates are not complete witnesses of Bell nonlocality: there exist nonlocal behaviours (even quantum-realisable ones) that violate no such game, a phenomenon present in every bipartite scenario with at least 2 inputs and 4 outputs per party.
AI.motivation: Nonlocal games are widely regarded as a conceptually clear framework for reasoning about Bell nonlocality, and the deterministic-predicate version is the most commonly used. The paper questions whether this standard formulation can fully characterise nonlocality, i.e. whether violating such a game is necessary for a behaviour to be nonlocal.
AI.method: The authors give a proof-based (constructive/existential) argument rather than an experimental or numerical study. They analyse the standard definition of nonlocal games with deterministic predicates and construct behaviours that are nonlocal yet fail to violate any game of this class, then show these behaviours admit a quantum realisation, establishing the result for all bipartite scenarios with input sizes ≥2 and output sizes ≥4 per party.
AI.result: Deterministic-predicate nonlocal games are shown to be incomplete witnesses of nonlocality. The authors prove the existence of nonlocal behaviours that do not violate any such nonlocal game, and further demonstrate that quantum mechanics can produce these game-classical nonlocal behaviours, in every bipartite scenario (X,Y,A,B) with X,Y≥2 and A,B≥4.
AI.conclusion: The common deterministic-predicate definition of nonlocal games cannot serve as a complete witness of Bell nonlocality. This incompleteness is not a rare edge case but a generic phenomenon across a broad family of bipartite scenarios, and it persists even for quantum-achievable correlations, indicating that the framework must be extended (e.g. to non-deterministic or weighted predicates) to fully capture nonlocality.

title: Tight bounds for hybrid quantum-classical query algorithms

AI.tldr: The paper establishes tight query-complexity bounds for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms where at most q oracle queries occur per quantum subroutine before full measurement, covering phase/amplitude estimation, search, and AND-OR trees, plus a general lower-bound framework.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms are increasingly relevant, but lower bounds for them have been ad-hoc. The paper aims to provide a systematic framework and matching upper/lower bounds across the full range of subroutine query sizes q, from classical (q=1) to unrestricted quantum query complexity Q(f).
AI.method: The computation model allows quantum subroutines with at most q oracle queries, with all qubits measured and discarded between subroutines. Lower bounds are proved via analysis of probability distributions over measurement transcripts and progress measures capturing distinguishability. The AND-OR tree bound combines two progress measures tracking classical and quantum information separately.
AI.result: Matching upper and lower bounds are proven: phase estimation requires Θ(1/(qε²)); amplitude estimation requires Θ(p(1-p)/(qε²)); search requires Θ(N/q); two-level AND-OR tree requires Θ(nm/q). These hold optimally up to constants for all q from 1 to Q(f). A hybrid lower bound for distinguishing two distributions from a state-preparation unitary is also derived, tight up to a logarithmic factor.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides optimal hybrid quantum-classical query bounds for several fundamental problems and, importantly, develops general methods for proving such hybrid lower bounds, replacing prior ad-hoc approaches.

title: Quantum 1-PCA with Pauli Measurements in Nearly Linear Time
summary: We consider the problem of quantum 1-PCA: given copies of an unknown $n$-qubit mixed state, recover a classical description of its leading eigenvector. Our goal is to do so using non-adaptive and single-qubit measurements. For an $n$-qubit state with top eigenvalue $λ$ and spectral gap at least $Δ> 0$, we give an algorithm that recovers the leading eigenvector to fidelity at least $1 - \varepsilon$ with high probability using $\tilde{O}\left( {2^n \cdot η^2} / {Δ^3 \varepsilon^3}\right)$ copies and $\tilde{O}((2^n/Δ\varepsilon) \cdot \operatorname{poly}(η/Δ\varepsilon))$ time, where $η= \max (1 - λ, \varepsilon)$. All of our measurements are non-adaptively chosen, and performed in single-qubit Pauli bases. When the spectral gap is constant and the desired accuracy is comparable to the noise level, i.e. $\varepsilon = Ω(η)$, our runtime and copy complexity become $\tilde{O} (2^n / \varepsilon)$. This generalizes the guarantees of Grewal et al. [arXiv:2601.04444], who achieved similar rates, but under the assumption $η= 0$, i.e., that the state was pure. Our results show that the same rates hold in the presence of state misspecification, up to polylogarithmic factors. From a technical perspective, our algorithm works by recursively constructing low-dimensional subspaces that approximately preserve the target eigenvector. To achieve nearly linear runtime dependence on the dimension of the Hilbert space, we develop a novel structured Pauli sampling scheme that enables fast batched computation of exponentially many projected Pauli matrices.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a non-adaptive, single-qubit-Pauli-measurement algorithm for quantum 1-PCA of mixed states, recovering the leading eigenvector to fidelity 1−ε with tilde-O(2^n η²/(Δ³ε³)) copies and near-linear-in-2^n time, generalizing prior pure-state guarantees to noisy states.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Grewal et al.) achieved similar copy/time rates for quantum 1-PCA only under the assumption η = 0, i.e., that the state is pure (no misspecification). This paper aims to show the same rates hold when the state is mixed and there is state misspecification, i.e., between accuracy and noise level, using non-adaptive single-qubit measurements.
AI.method: The algorithm recursively constructs low-dimensional subspaces that approximately preserve the target leading eigenvector. To obtain nearly linear runtime dependence on the Hilbert space dimension 2^n, the authors develop a novel structured Pauli sampling scheme that enables fast batched computation of exponentially many projected Pauli matrices. Measurements are chosen non-adaptively and performed in single-qubit Pauli bases.
AI.result: For an n-qubit state with top eigenvalue λ and spectral gap at least Δ>0, the algorithm recovers the leading eigenvector to fidelity ≥ 1−ε with high probability using tilde-O(2^n η²/(Δ³ε³)) copies and tilde-O((2^n/Δε)·poly(η/Δε)) time, where η = max(1−λ, ε). When the gap is constant and ε = Ω(η), these become tilde-O(2^n/ε).
AI.conclusion: The same copy and runtime rates previously established for pure states extend to mixed states under state misspecification, up to polylogarithmic factors, using non-adaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements and a structured Pauli sampling scheme.

title: Finding Gaussian Structure in Bosonic States
summary:
We study agnostic tomography of pure bosonic Gaussian states: given copies of an arbitrary $n$-mode bosonic state $ρ$, the goal is to output a pure Gaussian state whose infidelity with $ρ$ is at most $\mathrm{opt} + ε$, where $\mathrm{opt}$ is the minimum infidelity achievable by any pure Gaussian state.
  We give efficient protocols achieving this in both the high and low fidelity regimes. When $\mathrm{opt}$ is below some universal constant, our protocol has runtime and copy complexity which is strongly polynomial in $n, 1/ε$ and $\log \log E$, where $E$ is the energy of the closest pure Gaussian state. For arbitrary $\mathrm{opt}$, our protocol uses $(n+1)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/ε)} \mathrm{poly}\left(1+\log\log(E)\right)$ copies and runtime. As a corollary, we obtain the first truly tolerant Gaussianity testing protocol for distinguishing whether $\mathrm{opt} > c + ε$ or $\mathrm{opt} < c - ε$, for any threshold $c\in(0,1)$. We also prove $\mathrm{poly}(n,1/ε)$ runtime is impossible, unless $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}$.
  Our protocols follow a shared paradigm: first, we iteratively use general Gaussian measurements combined with techniques from classical robust statistics to obtain a good warm start estimate, then we leverage non-Gaussian measurements to refine this warm start using convex and non-convex optimization methods. Interestingly, we prove that non-Gaussian measurements are necessary to match the strong agnostic guarantees we obtain, and in fact these guarantees are provably superior to what is possible for robustly estimating classical Gaussians.

AI.tldr: This paper studies agnostic tomography of pure bosonic Gaussian states, providing efficient protocols in high and low fidelity regimes, a tolerant Gaussianity test, and a hardness result (poly(n,1/ε) is impossible unless NP ⊆ BQP).
AI.motivation: Agnostic tomography seeks to approximate the best-fitting pure Gaussian state to an arbitrary n-mode bosonic state, capturing the minimum infidelity opt. Prior work lacked efficient protocols achieving opt + ε guarantees, tolerant Gaussianity testing, and an understanding of the measurement resources needed.
AI.method: The protocols share a paradigm: (1) iterative use of general Gaussian measurements combined with classical robust statistics to obtain a warm-start estimate; (2) non-Gaussian measurements to refine the warm start via convex and non-convex optimization. Both high-fidelity (small opt) and general-opt regimes are handled, with the latter using (n+1)^{poly(1/ε)} poly(1+log log E) copies and runtime.
AI.result: For opt below a universal constant, runtime and copy complexity are strongly polynomial in n, 1/ε, and log log E. For arbitrary opt, copies and runtime scale as (n+1)^{poly(1/ε)} poly(1+log log E). This yields the first truly tolerant Gaussianity testing protocol for any threshold c ∈ (0,1). A lower bound shows poly(n,1/ε) runtime is impossible unless NP ⊆ BQP. Non-Gaussian measurements are proven necessary and the guarantees are superior to robust estimation of classical Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: Efficient agnostic tomography of pure bosonic Gaussian states is achievable with strong polynomial guarantees, enabled by a warm-start plus refinement paradigm using non-Gaussian measurements. The results establish tolerant Gaussianity testing and separate quantum Gaussian agnostic learning from classical robust Gaussian estimation.

title: Polynomial-time simulation of non-Clifford quantum error correction
summary: We show that every intermediate state of a broad class of non-Clifford quantum error-correction circuits is a third-order phase-polynomial state, even under stochastic Pauli noise. The class includes magic state distillation and cultivation, code switching and gauge fixing, transversal non-Clifford gates with syndrome extraction, and injection of diagonal magic states. Third-order phase-polynomial states strictly generalize stabilizer states, and we prove that they are exactly the stabilizer states of the diagonal-Clifford-and-Pauli (DCP) stabilizer formalism that we introduce. We characterize these states and show that their representations can be updated in polynomial time. This yields an exact polynomial-time simulation algorithm for these circuits and, more broadly, a framework for reasoning about their internal states and about magic states in general. We provide an open-source implementation, \texttt{merlin}, and benchmark it against existing non-Clifford simulators on distillation, cultivation, and code switching circuits. The benchmarks demonstrate improved runtime and memory scaling as the number of logical outputs grows in Bravyi-Haah distillation, and simulation of a code switching circuit beyond the reach of all other tested simulators.

AI.tldr: Every intermediate state of a broad class of non-Clifford quantum error-correction circuits is a third-order phase-polynomial state, even under stochastic Pauli noise; this enables exact polynomial-time simulation.
AI.motivation: Non-Clifford quantum error-correction circuits (magic state distillation/cultivation, code switching, gauge fixing, etc.) are hard to simulate, and little is known about their internal states. The authors aim to characterize these intermediate states and provide a tractable simulation framework.
AI.method: They prove that intermediate states of this circuit class are third-order phase-polynomial states, which strictly generalize stabilizer states. They introduce the diagonal-Clifford-and-Paul (DCP) stabilizer formalism and show these states are exactly the stabilizer states of that formalism. They characterize the states and show their representations can be updated in polynomial time, yielding an exact polynomial-time simulation algorithm. They provide an open-source implementation, merlin.
AI.result: The framework gives an exact polynomial-time simulation algorithm and a way to reason about internal states and magic states. Benchmarks against existing non-Clifford simulators show improved runtime and memory scaling as the number of logical outputs grows in Bravyi-Haah distillation, and simulation of a code switching circuit beyond the reach of all other tested simulators.
AI.conclusion: Third-order phase-polynomial states, characterized via the DCP stabilizer formalism, capture a broad class of non-Clifford error-correction circuits and enable exact, efficient simulation, offering a general framework for analyzing magic states.

title: Protecting Quantum Computers against Untrusted Users
comment: 10 pages, 5 pages of Appendix, 2 Figures, and 1 Table. Comments welcome!
summary: Publicly accessible fault-tolerant quantum computers must preserve scientific utility while limiting cryptanalytic power. We propose the restricted model of computation, 1/2BQP_1: a quantum server provides random computational-basis inputs, revealed only after execution, and one designated output bit. This interface permits arbitrary circuits and system sizes. We conjecture that a classical client making polynomially many adaptive requests cannot efficiently factor RSA moduli. The model subsumes the well-known one-clean-qubit model DQC1, retaining its applications to infinite-temperature multi-time correlations, out-of-time-order correlators, and suitably normalized partition functions. We propose a candidate for separating 1/2BQP_1 from DQC1 based on testing classical predictions of quantum spin dynamics. We argue security in two steps. First, we show that one-bit readout makes the quantum stages of standard factoring algorithms classically simulable, even when their preparation and postprocessing are redesigned within a broad family around a single arithmetic-oracle call. This covers the quantum stages of Shor, Ekera-Hastad, Kitaev, and Regev factoring constructions. Second, we examine the workaround of coherently implementing rational reconstruction to release a factor bit. Random inputs obstruct this straightforward attack: known techniques accommodate logarithmic-depth classical circuits, but rational reconstruction has resisted such parallelization for decades. Therefore, we show that security of our protocol is built on not only classical hardness for factoring, but also conjectured circuit lowerbounds for rational reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 1/2BQP_1, a restricted quantum computation model with a one-bit output interface where random computational-basis inputs are revealed only after execution, conjectured to preserve scientific utility while preventing efficient RSA factoring by classical clients.
AI.motivation: Publicly accessible fault-tolerant quantum computers must retain scientific utility while limiting cryptanalytic power. A restricted computation model is needed that blocks cryptanalytic capabilities (e.g., factoring RSA moduli) yet still supports valuable scientific applications such as simulating quantum dynamics and computing correlators.
AI.method: Introduces 1/2BQP_1: a quantum server supplies random computational-basis inputs revealed post-execution and one designated output bit, allowing arbitrary circuits and system sizes. Security is argued in two steps: (1) showing one-bit readout renders quantum stages of standard factoring algorithms (Shor, Ekera-Hastad, Kitaev, Regev) classically simulable under redesigned preparation/postprocessing around a single arithmetic-oracle call; (2) analyzing a coherent rational-reconstruction workaround, which random inputs obstruct since rational reconstruction has resisted logarithmic-depth parallelization.
AI.result: 1/2BQP_1 subsumes the one-clean-qubit model DQC1, retaining applications to infinite-temperature multi-time correlations, out-of-time-order correlators, and normalized partition functions. Factoring's quantum stages become classically simulable under the restricted interface. A candidate separation of 1/2BQP_1 from DQC1 is proposed based on testing classical predictions of quantum spin dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Security of the protocol rests not only on classical hardness of factoring but also on conjectured circuit lower bounds for rational reconstruction. A classical client making polynomially many adaptive requests cannot efficiently factor RSA moduli under these assumptions.

title: CV-QAOA: Efficient Low-Depth Quantum Optimization of Continuous Variables
summary: We study a Continuous-Variable Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CV-QAOA) for high-dimensional continuous optimization. Our formulation extends an earlier CV-QAOA proposal with a variationally optimized initial state and recovers the convergence guarantees of Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) in the high-depth limit. We prove rigorous performance guarantees of CV-QAOA on several families of cost functions. First, we show $d$-step CV-QAOA minimizes any $d$-dimensional strictly convex quadratic function with $2d$ quantum queries to the cost function. We then analyze a family of nonconvex "Rotated Double Well" (RDW) functions with $2^d$ local minima introduced by arXiv:2311.00811. While prior work showed QHD reaches its global minimum with $\tilde O(d^3)$ queries, we prove that 1-step CV-QAOA solves RDW with just two quantum queries. Although general-purpose classical solvers need superpolynomial time for RDW and structure-awareness can reduce the cost to polynomial time, we show that the 1-step CV-QAOA protocol can be efficiently dequantized, and that a gradient-aligned line search succeeds with $O(d)$ queries, nearly matching the information-theoretic $Ω(d/\log d)$ query lower bound. To move beyond the dequantizable regime, we introduce a ``Rotated Square Well'' (RSW) problem, whose globally flat landscape suppresses useful local gradient information. For this family, we show that an adiabatic evolution simulated by CV-QAOA can reach the global minimum using $d^{o(1)}$ queries. On the other hand, any classical algorithm that learn the hidden rotation in RSW provably requires $Ω(d^2/\log d)$ queries, a bound we nearly match with an explicit $Θ(d^2\log d)$-query classical algorithm.Numerical simulations on deflected corrugated spring and Easom functions illustrate the promising performance of CV-QAOA on more general problems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a Continuous-Variable Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CV-QAOA) with a variationally optimized initial state for high-dimensional continuous optimization, proving rigorous query-complexity guarantees on convex quadratics, Rotated Double Well, and a new Rotated Square Well problem, and showing a provable quantum advantage that is not dequantizable.
AI.motivation: Extending an earlier CV-QAOA proposal to recover the convergence guarantees of Quantum Hamiltonian Descent in the high-depth limit, and to probe whether continuous-variable quantum algorithms can deliver genuine, non-dequantizable speedups over classical optimizers on structured nonconvex landscapes.
AI.method: A CV-QAOA formulation with variationally optimized initial state; rigorous query-complexity analysis on strictly convex quadratic functions, Rotated Double Well functions, and a newly introduced Rotated Square Well (RSW) problem; a dequantization study of the 1-step CV-QAOA protocol and a gradient-aligned line search; an adiabatic evolution simulated by CV-QAOA; a query lower bound for classically learning the hidden rotation; and numerical simulations on deflected corrugated spring and Easom functions.
AI.result: d-step CV-QAOA minimizes any d-dimensional strictly convex quadratic with 2d quantum queries; 1-step CV-QAOA solves RDW with two quantum queries (versus tilde-O(d^3) for QHD); the 1-step protocol is efficiently dequantized, with gradient-aligned line search achieving O(d) queries, nearly matching the Omega(d/log d) lower bound; for RSW, adiabatic CV-QAOA reaches the global minimum with d^{o(1)} queries, while any classical algorithm learning the hidden rotation requires Omega(d^2/log d) queries, nearly matched by an explicit Theta(d^2 log d)-query classical algorithm. Simulations on deflected corrugated spring and Easom functions show promising performance.
AI.conclusion: CV-QAOA attains strong provable query guarantees and, on the flat-landscape RSW family, exhibits a genuine non-dequantizable quantum advantage over classical rotation-learning algorithms; the dequantizable RDW case delineates where the advantage vanishes, and numerical results suggest the approach extends to more general cost functions.

title: The complete phase diagram of detailed-balanced Gibbs samplers for the mean-field Heisenberg model
summary: We study the spectral gap of recently discovered families of KMS-detailed-balanced Gibbs-sampler Lindbladians for the mean-field Heisenberg model on $n$ spins. We show that the spectral gaps of these natural families of Lindbladians admit the same phase diagram: the gap is constant above the critical temperature (i.e., in the disordered phase), scales as $1/\sqrt{n}$ at the critical temperature, and as $1/n$ below the critical temperature (i.e., in the ordered phase). Our result builds on and extends the recent work of Basso et al.~(2026) which characterized this phase diagram for the GNS-detailed-balanced Davies generator, but only partially resolved the gap scaling at the critical temperature.

AI.tldr: The spectral gaps of KMS-detailed-balanced Gibbs-sampler Lindbladians for the mean-field Heisenberg model follow the same phase diagram as the Davies generator: constant in the disordered phase, ~1/√n at criticality, and ~1/n in the ordered phase.
AI.motivation: Recently discovered families of KMS-detailed-balanced Gibbs-sampler Lindbladians are natural candidates for dissipative quantum Gibbs sampling, but their convergence properties—specifically how their spectral gap depends on system size across the phase diagram—were not established for the mean-field Heisenberg model. The prior work (Basso et al., 2026) resolved the gap phase diagram only for the GNS-detailed-balanced Davies generator and left the critical-temperature scaling only partially resolved.
AI.method: The authors analyze the spectral gap of KMS-detailed-balanced Gibbs-sampler Lindbladians for the mean-field Heisenberg model on n spins, determining its scaling with n in the disordered, critical, and ordered phases, building on and extending the Davies-generator analysis of Basso et al. (2026).
AI.result: The spectral gaps of these natural families of Lindbladians exhibit a common phase diagram: the gap is constant above the critical temperature (disordered phase), scales as 1/√n at the critical temperature, and scales as 1/n below the critical temperature (ordered phase).
AI.conclusion: KMS-detailed-balanced Gibbs-sampler Lindbladians share the same gap phase diagram as the GNS-detailed-balanced Davies generator for the mean-field Heisenberg model, thereby extending Basso et al. (2026) and resolving the critical-temperature gap scaling.

title: Improved bounds on stabilizer extent and Clifford rank
summary:
We prove that every pure state of stabilizer rank at most $k$ has stabilizer extent at most $2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$, and establish the analogous bound for the squared Clifford coefficient norm of Clifford-rank-$k$ operators. This implies stabilizer fidelity at least $2^{-O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$, resolving the quantitative conjecture of (Mehraban-Tamasbi, STOC, 2025), and proves an $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ lower bound for the approximate stabilizer rank of tensor powers of any non-stabilizer qubit state. The latter result generalizes the best-known lower bound for tensor powers of $T$-states (Mehraban-Tamasbi, STOC, 2024) to arbitrary non-stabilizer qubit states, including magic states.
  As a consequence of the Clifford rank--norm inequality, we obtain an $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ lower bound for exact representations of $n$-bit AND function by quadratic phases, improving the previous best-known linear bound. Further consequences rule out pseudorandom state and unitary ensembles with approximate stabilizer and Clifford rank $O((\log n)^2/\log\log n)$, respectively, a $\log n$ improvement over prior work (Kalra-Sinha, Quantum, 2026). We also obtain tomography algorithms for states of stabilizer rank at most $k$, with $poly(n)2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$ time and copy complexity, a nearly square-root improvement in the exponent over the best-known algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that stabilizer rank $k$ implies stabilizer extent at most $2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$ (with an analogous Clifford-rank/norm bound), resolving a quantitative conjecture and yielding improved lower bounds for approximate stabilizer rank of tensor powers, quadratic-phase representations of AND, pseudorandomness, and faster tomography.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer rank and Clifford rank quantify the cost of representing states/operators via stabilizer states/Clifford operations, but the tight quantitative relation between rank and its "extent"/norm measures was unknown. The authors aim to resolve the quantitative conjecture of Mehraban-Tamasbi (STOC 2025) and to extend optimal lower bounds for tensor powers from T-states to arbitrary non-stabilizer qubit states.
AI.method: The core technical result is a rank--extent inequality: pure states of stabilizer rank at most $k$ have stabilizer extent at most $2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$; the analogous inequality is established for the squared Clifford coefficient norm of Clifford-rank-$k$ operators. These bounds are then combined with reduction arguments to derive applications (tensor-power lower bounds, quadratic-phase representation lower bounds, pseudorandomness exclusions, and tomography algorithms).
AI.result: Stabilizer extent of rank-$k$ states is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$; consequently stabilizer fidelity is at least $2^{-O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$, resolving the Mehraban-Tamasbi conjecture. This gives an $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ lower bound on approximate stabilizer rank of tensor powers of any non-stabilizer qubit state (including magic states), matching/ generalizing the best T-state bound. From the Clifford rank--norm inequality they get an $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ lower bound for exact quadratic-phase representations of $n$-bit AND, improving the prior linear bound. They rule out pseudorandom state/unitary ensembles with approximate stabilizer and Clifford rank $O((\log n)^2/\log\log n)$, a $\log n$ improvement over Kalra-Sinha (Quantum 2026). They also obtain tomography for rank-$k$ states in $poly(n)2^{O(\sqrt{k\log(k+1)})}$ time and copies.
AI.conclusion: The rank--extent (and Clifford rank--norm) inequalities are a central tool tying combinatorial rank measures to analytic norm measures, with broad consequences: resolving a conjecture, strengthening tensor-power and quadratic-phase lower bounds, improving pseudorandomness exclusions, and giving faster, lower-copy tomography algorithms.

title: Designing Group-Valued Codes with Full Regular Low-Weight Bases
summary:
Efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures benefit from low-weight logical operators. However, reported canonical bases for high-rate, high-distance codes can be several times heavier than the code distance, and fundamental obstructions can prevent minimum-weight logical operators from forming a complete canonical basis. To address this issue, we develop design principles for group-valued quantum error-correcting codes with low-weight full regular canonical logical bases, generated by translating a set of seed operators. We introduce frame width $f$, the smallest weight cutoff that permits a complete canonical logical basis, as an additional code parameter alongside distance $d$ and check weight $w$. Cataloguing these parameters together with explicit logical bases can inform resource estimates and the compilation of fault-tolerant logical operations.
  First, we identify a structural obstruction: for fully populated binary monomial CSS checks over a group of odd order, full regularity forces distance two, while for groups of power-of-two order, full row rank of both check matrices after replacing every group element by $1$ guarantees full regularity. Second, we demonstrate our principles through explicit high-rate lifted-product (LP) and pair-partition (PP) codes: an $[[1088,128,22]]$ LP code with $f=22$ and an $[[1024,256,24]]$ PP code with $f \leq 27$, both at $w=10$. At $w=11$, our PP constructions attain either $d=25$ with $f \leq 27$ or $d=24$ with the proved optimum $f=25$, demonstrating both a tradeoff among these parameters and a strict separation between distance and frame width. Finally, we propose a method combining symmetry reduction and stabilizer-based pruning for exhaustive distance certification, and use it to efficiently establish exact distances for LP examples with more than a thousand qubits.

AI.tldr: This work introduces "frame width" as a code parameter for quantum LDPC codes, deriving design principles for group-valued codes with low-weight regular canonical logical bases, and constructs high-rate LP and PP codes with favorable distance and frame-width parameters.
AI.motivation: Low-weight logical operators are crucial for efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing, but canonical bases for high-rate, high-distance codes can be several times heavier than the code distance, and fundamental obstructions can prevent minimum-weight logical operators from forming a complete canonical basis.
AI.method: The authors develop design principles for group-valued quantum error-correcting codes with low-weight full regular canonical logical bases generated by translating seed operators. They introduce frame width f as a parameter (smallest weight cutoff allowing a complete canonical logical basis) alongside distance d and check weight w. They identify structural obstructions for binary monomial CSS checks over odd-order and power-of-two-order groups, construct explicit high-rate lifted-product (LP) and pair-partition (PP) codes, and propose a method combining symmetry reduction and stabilizer-based pruning for exhaustive distance certification.
AI.result: For fully populated binary monomial CSS checks over odd-order groups, full regularity forces distance two; for power-of-two-order groups, full row rank of both check matrices (after replacing every group element by 1) guarantees full regularity. Explicit constructions include an [[1088,128,22]] LP code with f=22 and an [[1024,256,24]] PP code with f ≤ 27, both at w=10. At w=11, PP constructions attain either d=25 with f ≤ 27 or d=24 with proven optimum f=25, showing a tradeoff and strict separation between distance and frame width. Exact distances were efficiently established for LP examples with over a thousand qubits.
AI.conclusion: Frame width f serves as a valuable additional code parameter for resource estimation and compilation of fault-tolerant logical operations, and the proposed design principles enable high-rate codes with low-weight regular canonical logical bases, with efficient distance certification via symmetry reduction and stabilizer-based pruning.

title: Natural proofs for quantum state preparation lower bounds
summary: We identify a barrier that helps explain why proving stronger quantum state-preparation lower bounds has been so difficult. In particular, we establish a quantum analogue of the Razborov-Rudich natural proofs barrier for state-preparation lower bounds. We call a property of quantum states \emph{natural} if it holds for a sufficiently large fraction of Haar-random states and can be efficiently tested when given all of the state's amplitudes. Under a standard cryptographic assumption, we show that no natural property can prove superpolynomial state-preparation lower bounds even against a fixed level of the Magic Hierarchy. We show that several existing state-preparation lower-bound techniques are natural in our sense, including arguments based on approximate degree, not being a unique ground state of a local Hamiltonian, and mutual information.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a quantum analogue of the Razborov-Rudich natural proofs barrier for quantum state-preparation lower bounds, showing that no "natural" property can prove superpolynomial lower bounds even against a fixed level of the Magic Hierarchy, under a standard cryptographic assumption.
AI.motivation: Proving stronger quantum state-preparation lower bounds has been notoriously difficult. The authors seek to explain this difficulty by identifying a fundamental barrier, analogous to the natural proofs barrier in classical circuit complexity.
AI.method: The authors define a property of quantum states as "natural" if it holds for a sufficiently large fraction of Haar-random states and can be efficiently tested given all of the state's amplitudes. They then prove, under a standard cryptographic assumption, that no natural property can establish superpolynomial state-preparation lower bounds even against a fixed level of the Magic Hierarchy.
AI.result: The paper shows that several existing state-preparation lower-bound techniques are natural in their sense, including arguments based on approximate degree, not being a unique ground state of a local Hamiltonian, and mutual information. This demonstrates that these techniques are subject to the identified barrier.
AI.conclusion: The results identify a natural proofs barrier for quantum state-preparation lower bounds, explaining the difficulty of proving stronger bounds and showing that common existing techniques fall within its scope.

title: The practical cost of magic state cultivation
summary: Magic state cultivation is a promising method for preparing high-fidelity non-Clifford resource states - a central component of fault-tolerant quantum computing - with low spacetime overhead. In benchmarking cultivation, existing resource estimates assume access to noiseless transversal measurement of the output magic state to allow for postselection during the final escape stage of the cultivation process. However, such measurements would destroy the magic state and are therefore unavailable during computation. We develop an open-boundary postselection method, Caliper, that uses only nondestructive mid-circuit syndrome information and substantially outperforms existing methods operating under these constraints. In some regimes, our postselection method uniquely recovers the resource efficiency of prior estimates. However, in other cases, we observe a tradeoff. At spacetime costs reported in previous works, the achievable logical error rates can be orders of magnitude higher, and recovering the reported logical error rate requires substantially larger codes and longer escape stages. Our results highlight how practical considerations involving mid-circuit postselection can impact the design and performance of magic state cultivation protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Caliper, an open-boundary postselection method for magic state cultivation that relies only on nondestructive mid-circuit syndrome information, revealing a tradeoff between spacetime cost and achievable logical error rate.
AI.motivation: Existing resource estimates for magic state cultivation unrealistically assume access to noiseless transversal measurement of the output magic state for postselection during the final escape stage. Such measurements would destroy the magic state and are therefore unavailable during actual computation, motivating a practical postselection method that respects this constraint.
AI.method: The authors develop Caliper, an open-boundary postselection method that uses only nondestructive mid-circuit syndrome information to benchmark cultivation without destroying the magic state.
AI.result: Caliper substantially outperforms existing methods operating under the same constraints. In some regimes, it uniquely recovers the resource efficiency of prior estimates. In other cases, a tradeoff emerges: at previously reported spacetime costs, achievable logical error rates can be orders of magnitude higher, and recovering the reported logical error rates requires substantially larger codes and longer escape stages.
AI.conclusion: Practical considerations involving mid-circuit postselection can significantly impact the design and performance of magic state cultivation protocols, highlighting the gap between idealized benchmarking assumptions and realistic fault-tolerant quantum computing constraints.

title: Energy-constrained two-way capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel
summary: We determine the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint. For transmissivity $η$ and mean photon number $N$, all four capacities coincide and are given by $g(N)-g((1-η)N)$, where $g$ is the entropy of a thermal mode. This resolves the longstanding finite-energy capacity problem by establishing the optimality of the reverse-coherent-information rate introduced in 2009. Our central tool is sector teleportation simulation, which we develop specifically to transfer the input-energy constraint to the shared entanglement resource, thereby preserving the constraint throughout converse arguments for general adaptive protocols. For every $N>0$, we further show that the corresponding strong-converse thresholds coincide with the unconstrained value $-\log_2(1-η)$. For parallel protocols with a hard total-photon-number cutoff, the same finite-energy capacity formula instead satisfies an exponential strong converse. Together, these results establish a unified finite-energy framework for adaptive bosonic communication and reveal how energy constraints fundamentally reshape both attainable rates and converse bounds.

AI.tldr: This work determines several quantum capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint, showing the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities all coincide and equal g(N) − g((1−η)N), thereby proving optimality of the 2009 reverse-coherent-information rate.
AI.motivation: The finite-energy capacity problem for the pure-loss bosonic channel had remained unresolved: while a reverse-coherent-information rate was proposed in 2009 as a candidate, its optimality under an input-energy constraint was not established. Existing converse arguments could not directly handle the energy constraint throughout general adaptive protocols.
AI.method: The central tool is sector teleportation simulation, developed to transfer the input-energy constraint to the shared entanglement resource, thereby preserving the constraint throughout converse arguments for general adaptive protocols. The paper also analyzes strong-converse thresholds and hard-photon-number-cutoff parallel protocols.
AI.result: For transmissivity η and mean photon number N, all four capacities coincide and equal g(N) − g((1−η)N), where g is the entropy of a thermal mode. For every N > 0, the strong-converse thresholds coincide with the unconstrained value −log₂(1−η). For parallel protocols with a hard total-photon-number cutoff, the same finite-energy capacity formula satisfies an exponential strong converse.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a unified finite-energy framework for adaptive bosonic communication and reveal how energy constraints fundamentally reshape both attainable rates and converse bounds.

title: Distributional Quantum Query Complexity
summary:
Quantum query complexity enjoys a variety of pleasing joint computation properties: for example, a composition theorem asserting $Q(f\circ g)=Θ(Q(f)Q(g))$ for all Boolean functions $f$ and $g$; a direct sum theorem asserting that computing $k$ copies of a function (or search problem) costs $Ω(k)$ times as much as the cost of computing one copy; and a direct product theorem asserting that for Boolean functions, even succeeding at the direct sum problem with exponentially small probability still requires $Ω(k)$ times the cost of computing one copy to bounded error.
  However, all of these results are strictly for worst-case quantum query complexity. For example, if we have a fixed distribution $μ$ over inputs, the direct sum theorem says nothing about the quantum query complexity of computing $k$ copies of $f$ when the input comes from the product distribution $μ^k$ instead of being worst-case. (Note that while a standard Yao-type minimax theorem guarantees a hard distribution for the direct sum problem, there's no guarantee that this hard distribution is a product distribution.) A similar problem occurs for the direct product theorem and the composition theorem: none of these results respect distributions.
  In this work, we give distributional joint computation lower bounds for the composition, direct sum, and direct product problems. Along the way, we introduce some new tools for handling quantum query lower bounds, including (a) a new ``multiplicative'' variant of the $γ_2$ norm (which we use in place of the multiplicative adversary method for proving the direct product theorem), and (b) a new ``Shaltiel-free'' measure of quantum query complexity, which we show characterizes the composition behavior of distributional quantum query complexity and satisfies pleasing properties.

AI.tldr: This work establishes distributional (not just worst-case) joint computation lower bounds for composition, direct sum, and direct product in quantum query complexity, introducing a multiplicative variant of the γ₂ norm and a new "Shaltiel-free" measure of quantum query complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum query complexity results—the composition theorem (Q(f∘g)=Θ(Q(f)Q(g))), the direct sum theorem (Ω(k) times one-copy cost), and the direct product theorem (Ω(k) times one-copy cost even for exponentially small success)—all hold only for worst-case complexity. Under a fixed distribution μ, these say nothing about computing k copies under the product distribution μ^k: a Yao-type minimax theorem guarantees a hard distribution for the direct sum problem, but not that it is a product distribution. Thus no existing results respect distributions, motivating distributional joint computation lower bounds.
AI.method: The authors prove distributional lower bounds for the composition, direct sum, and direct product problems. To do so they develop new tools: (a) a new "multiplicative" variant of the γ₂ norm, used in place of the multiplicative adversary method for proving the direct product theorem; and (b) a new "Shaltiel-free" measure of quantum query complexity, shown to characterize the composition behavior of distributional quantum query complexity and to satisfy pleasing properties.
AI.result: Distributional joint computation lower bounds are obtained for all three problems—composition, direct sum, and direct product—extending the corresponding worst-case results to the distributional setting. The new multiplicative γ₂-norm variant supports the direct product theorem, and the Shaltiel-free measure characterizes distributional quantum query complexity under composition.
AI.conclusion: Quantum query complexity's joint computation properties can be extended beyond worst-case to the distributional setting, yielding distributional lower bounds for composition, direct sum, and direct product, enabled by a multiplicative γ₂-norm variant and a new Shaltiel-free complexity measure.

title: Semi-Cliffordness of the Clifford hierarchy for a single qudit in composite dimensions
summary: An important question in quantum information theory asks whether every gate in the Clifford hierarchy is semi-Clifford or not, as such gates admit resource-efficient implementations via gate teleportation. Extending recent results for prime dimensions~\cite{silva_clifford_2025}, we prove that every hierarchy gate on a single qudit of dimension \(d\) is semi-Clifford, if and only if \(d\) is square-free. In composite dimensions, \(\mathbb{Z}_d^2\) is a symplectic module rather than a vector space, motivating a distinction between four types of gates. Semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{SC}$) are the ones that become diagonal under left and right multiplication by Clifford gates, while a broader class $\mathcal{N}$ admits a permutation diagonal form, under left and right multiplication by Cliffords. Lagrangian semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{LSC}$) conjugate some maximal abelian Pauli subgroup to another, whereas generalized semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{GSC}$) map some maximal abelian Pauli subalgebra to another under conjugation. In square-free dimensions, we have \(\mathcal{SC}=\mathcal{LSC}\) and \(\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{GSC}\), but when \(d\) is not square-free, these equivalences can fail, as Lagrangian submodules can become non-free. We also show that every third-level gate of the one-qudit Clifford hierarchy is a generalized semi-Clifford in arbitrary dimensions.

AI.tldr: Every single-qudit Clifford hierarchy gate is semi-Clifford if and only if the qudit dimension d is square-free; in non-square-free composite dimensions four distinct gate classes arise, and every third-level gate is generalized semi-Clifford in all dimensions.
AI.motivation: Semi-Clifford gates admit resource-efficient implementations via gate teleportation, so determining whether all Clifford hierarchy gates are semi-Clifford is an important open question in quantum information theory. Prior work resolved the prime-dimension case; this paper extends the classification to arbitrary single-qudit dimensions d.
AI.method: The authors work in composite dimension where Z_d^2 is a symplectic module rather than a vector space, and use this module structure to distinguish four gate classes: semi-Clifford (SC, diagonalizable by left/right Clifford multiplication), the broader permutation-diagonal class N, Lagrangian semi-Clifford (LSC, conjugating one maximal abelian Pauli subgroup to another), and generalized semi-Clifford (GSC, mapping one maximal abelian Pauli subalgebra to another). They characterize these classes via the freeness of Lagrangian submodules.
AI.result: For square-free d, every hierarchy gate is semi-Clifford, and moreover SC = LSC and N = GSC. For non-square-free d, these equalities can fail because Lagrangian submodules may be non-free. Additionally, every third-level gate of the one-qudit Clifford hierarchy is shown to be generalized semi-Clifford in arbitrary dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The semi-Clifford property of single-qudit Clifford hierarchy gates is exactly characterized by square-freeness of the dimension d; composite non-square-free dimensions require the finer LSC/GSC and N distinctions due to non-free Lagrangian submodules, while the third level remains generalized semi-Clifford universally.

title: A Spectrum-Based Converse for Quantum State Discrimination and Its Applications to Classical-Quantum Channel Coding
summary: We investigate converse bounds on the average decoding error probability in finite-blocklength classical-quantum channel coding. We first present a lower bound for multiple quantum hypothesis testing in terms of pairwise trace distances and derive a corresponding fidelity bound. We then obtain a spectrum-based converse that depends only on the a priori probabilities and spectra of the states. We show that the converse bound remains tight for the quantum depolarizing channel under suitable conditions. For codes with product-state outputs, this converse takes an explicit form involving products of output-state eigenvalues. We apply it to binary codes over the quantum amplitude damping channel using the input states $\vert+\rangle$ and $\vert-\rangle$. For this setting, we also discuss a normal approximation to the spectrum-based converse in the large blocklength regime. In all numerical examples considered, the spectrum-based converse is tighter than the other converse bounds at low noise levels.

AI.tldr: The paper derives spectrum-based converse bounds on average decoding error probability for finite-blocklength classical-quantum channel coding, showing tightness for the depolarizing channel and improved tightness at low noise.
AI.motivation: Finite-blocklength classical-quantum channel coding lacks sharp converse bounds, particularly ones capturing finite-blocklength behavior. Existing converses often require detailed state information and may be loose. The authors seek bounds depending only on a priori probabilities and spectra of the output states, aiming for tighter characterizations at low noise.
AI.method: First, a lower bound for multiple quantum hypothesis testing via pairwise trace distances and a corresponding fidelity bound. Then a spectrum-based converse depending only on a priori probabilities and state spectra. Specialization to product-state output codes yields an explicit form in terms of products of output-state eigenvalues. Application to binary codes over the quantum amplitude damping channel with input states |+> and |->, plus a normal approximation in the large blocklength regime.
AI.result: The spectrum-based converse remains tight for the quantum depolarizing channel under suitable conditions. For product-state outputs, an explicit eigenvalue-product form is obtained. Numerical examples show the spectrum-based converse is tighter than other converse bounds at low noise levels.
AI.conclusion: A spectrum-based converse is established that depends only on a priori probabilities and spectra, is tight for depolarizing channels, and outperforms other converses at low noise, supported by a normal approximation for large blocklengths.

title: Quantum information processing under maximal distance measures
summary: The measures of distance frequently used in quantum information, such as trace distance or fidelity-based purified distance, are the smallest extensions of the corresponding distance measures in classical information theory. However, this way of extending classical distances is not unique, and a whole spectrum of other extensions can be defined. Here we study the question of how quantum information processing tasks are affected by a change of the error metrics to the maximal extensions of the classical distance measures, imposing more demanding error requirements on operational tasks. We find that the performance of some tasks, such as channel coding or quantum resource distillation, is not affected whatsoever by this change. However, for other tasks such as channel simulation and quantum resource dilution, we show that the rates are now given not by functions of the standard (Umegaki) quantum relative entropy, but ones based on the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy. Our results connect the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy with operational tasks and reveal that known reversibility results in quantum information, including the reverse Shannon theorem and the asymptotic reversibility of quantum resource transformations, no longer hold under maximal distance measures.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how quantum information processing tasks change when error metrics are switched to the maximal extensions of classical distance measures, and shows that some tasks' rates become governed by the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy rather than the Umegaki relative entropy.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum distances like trace distance and purified distance are the smallest extensions of classical distances, but this extension is not unique. A whole spectrum of extensions exists, and it is unclear how operational quantum tasks behave under more demanding, maximal extensions of classical error metrics.
AI.method: The authors analyze a range of quantum information processing tasks under maximal extensions of classical distance measures, comparing the resulting achievable rates against those obtained with standard metrics, and identify which relative entropies characterize the new rates.
AI.result: Channel coding and quantum resource distillation are unaffected by the change to maximal distance measures. In contrast, channel simulation and quantum resource dilution have rates governed not by the standard Umegaki quantum relative entropy but by the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy.
AI.conclusion: The findings link the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy to operational tasks and show that known reversibility results—including the reverse Shannon theorem and the asymptotic reversibility of quantum resource transformations—fail under maximal distance measures.

title: Rewire and reset are all you need: Minimal resources for manipulating non-Abelions
summary: Braiding and fusing anyons are fundamental to topological quantum computation, yet existing circuit protocols often employ ancillas and measurements. We determine the minimal circuit resources for performing such anyon operations in quantum double models of generic finite groups. Our approach braids anyons through a sequential unitary circuit without ancillas. Intuitively, this is obtained by deforming the underlying graph on which the anyons live. More generally, we introduce graph rewiring, a diagrammatic calculus that assigns a geometric interpretation to individual two-qudit gates and tracks their action on stabilizers. For fusion, we prove a general no-go theorem excluding purely unitary protocols for fusing unknown anyon types without introducing ancillas. Remarkably, we show such "input-agnostic" fusion is enabled by simply using a qudit reset. Hence, contrary to folklore, ancilla resources are not needed to braid or fuse non-Abelian anyons (non-Abelions). This work has implications in experimental efforts in error correction: our fusion protocol highlights reset as an underutilized primitive for error correction without the spacetime-overhead of ancillas and measurements.

AI.tldr: This work determines the minimal circuit resources to braid and fuse anyons in quantum double models of finite groups, showing that graph rewiring enables ancilla-free braiding and that a qudit reset (rather than ancillas) suffices for input-agnostic fusion, disproving the belief that ancilla resources are necessary.
AI.motivation: Braiding and fusing anyons underpin topological quantum computation, but existing circuit protocols typically rely on ancillas and measurements, which are resource-intensive. The paper aims to identify the minimal circuit resources needed for these anyon operations.
AI.method: The authors braid anyons through a sequential unitary circuit without ancillas by deforming the underlying graph. They introduce graph rewiring, a diagrammatic calculus that assigns a geometric interpretation to individual two-qudit gates and tracks their action on stabilizers. For fusion, they prove a no-go theorem excluding purely unitary protocols for fusing unknown anyon types without ancillas, then enable input-agnostic fusion via a qudit reset.
